Legal Compliance 1.1

1.1.1 – The UoC shall hold all applicable legal licences and permits.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should be responsible for:
    • Having a good understanding of local licensing and permit systems that apply
    • Obtaining all necessary documentation for siting, constructing and operating their facilities. Examples of these can include:

      • business/operational licences,

      • land deeds,

      • leases or concession agreements,

      • construction permits,

      • water use permits,

      • effluent permits,

      • landfill operation permits,

      • fire safety certificate,

      • building fitness certificate,

      • permit or licence to store fuel (such as oil and/or gas),

      • licences or permits to house workers in provided accommodation,

      • changes to labour legislation, regulations and laws are reflected in workers’ contracts.

  • Paying attention to:

    • pending licence renewal for applications of, e.g. relocation of sites, biomass increase;

    • conditions set as part of the licence/permits.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Up-to-date documentation for siting, constructing and operating, including any applications in progress.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documentation confirming required legal licences and permits are in place.

  • Conditions required as part of business licence applications are adhered to. For example:

    • In some parts of the world, a business licence is not issued unless mandatory certificates of building fitness and emergency preparedness
      for natural disasters are obtained.

Useful Resources

  • Assistance in determining necessary licences and permits can be sought from governmental agencies dealing with business and the environment and communities.

1.1.2 – The UoC shall comply with all applicable legal requirements, including those relevant to the Criteria within the ASC Farm Standard.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ‘Applicable legal requirements’ refers to any type of law or regulation that is relevant to the scope of the ASC Farm Standard.

  • The UoC should be responsible for:

    • having a good understanding of laws and regulations including their applicability to the local context; and

    • facilitating any inspections by authorities.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A register for legal compliance, for example, listing:

    • relevant applicable laws and regulations, including, for labour-related laws and regulations, those within the home country of any migrant employees; and

    • compliance status, and any future actions needed to remain complaint; and

    • any measures needed to correct potential non-compliance with a law or regulation.

  • Certificates or other records to confirm compliance with legal requirements.

  • Documented outcomes and records of any inspections by authorities.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Existence of any legal documentation, outcomes of inspections, or records kept by UoC to demonstrate legal compliance.

  • Management understands the legal context in which they are operating.

Useful Resources

  • The International Labour Organization (ILO) maintains NATLEX (www.ilo.org/dyn/natlex), a database of national labour, social security and related human rights legislation across 196 countries and more than 160 territories and subdivisions. NATLEX is a free source of information for all users.

Management Systems for ASC-Certified Farms

1.2.1 – The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a management system to support the implementation of the ASC Requirements that is appropriate to the size and complexity of the UoC.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The scope of the management system should suit the operation that it is designed for. For example:

    • A site situated at a remote distance at sea might not need additional elements in the management system to work with communities, or

    • A site operating a RAS system might not need additional elements in the management system to manage the risks of escapes.

  • A management system should include:

    • Policies: explain why a site is operating in such a way.

      • they can be beneficial for employees to understand their rights and duties.

      • it is not necessary to have a policy for every topic in the ASC Farm Standard and sometimes topics are grouped together in one policy.

        • for example, forced labour, child labour, discrimination, collective bargaining and freedom of association and others can all be addressed together through the human rights policy.

      • policies are most valuable for topics which are not straightforward in the local context.

        • for example, where employees have an inconsistent or incomplete understanding of an issue, a policy might be needed.

    • Procedures: explain how a site operates in a certain way and specify how to put policies into operation to ensure the outcome intended.

    • Records: provide an essential source of information for both internal self-assessments and external audits, documenting that policies and procedures have been followed in specific instances.

      • sites can use recording templates to guide the user through all of the steps of a record and provide accurate information in a set format.

      • records should be adequately maintained and controlled, including ensuring only up-to-date versions of documents are used.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents of the management system, including policies, procedures and records.

  • Evidence that demonstrates management’s ownership of the management system (see Indicator 1.2.2).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Existence of up-to-date policies, procedures and records.

  • Management’s ownership of the management system:

    • attendance at management reviews (see Indicator 1.2.4).

    • active role in the development, implementation and maintenance of the management system.

      • demonstrable during interviews with the management.

Useful Resources

  • The ISO 9001:2015 management system standards: https://www.iso.org/management-system-standards.html

  • Plan Do Check Act Cycle: https://asq.org/quality-resources/pdca-cycle

1.2.2 – The UoC shall appoint at least one member of management responsible for the implementation of the ASC Requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The responsible person may be one person or several persons, covering the wide range of issues addressed by the ASC Requirements.

    • For example, a human resources manager may be responsible for the requirements on labour rights and working conditions, and a fish health and welfare manager may be responsible for the requirements on fish health;

      • senior management should be responsible for seeking more specialised knowledge when needed.

  • The responsibility should be embedded in the organisational structure documentation to ensure clear accountability.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • that evidence the responsible person(s) were designated by the management.

    • role description of the responsible person(s) for the implementation of ASC Requirements.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The management designated responsible person(s) for the implementation of the ASC Requirements.
    • through records and interviews with employees and the management.
  • Role description of the responsible person(s) for the implementation of the ASC requirements.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.2.3 – The UoC shall ensure that relevant employees have the necessary skills and training to implement the ASC Requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • At the site, it should be clear who is responsible for what tasks and management should ensure all employees are competent for the role that they will be carrying out. Employees should have:

    • Knowledge,

    • Experience,

    • Training (theory and on the job),

    • Capacity, and

    • Decision-making permissions.

  • ‘Relevant employees’ and ’necessary competencies’ refer to an employee’s function and area of responsibility:
    • For example, a Health and Safety Manager is able to carry out and regularly update the Health and Safety risk assessment and define mitigating measures, but might not have the experience to treat injuries. Or the person responsible for first aid can take immediate action in the case of an injury and has access to and an overview of all first aid supplies, but might not have the experience to carry out a Health and Safety risk assessment.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Job descriptions of all employees.

  • Organisational chart with clarity on who is responsible for what.

  • Records and documents of training.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Employees and management are clear on their roles and responsibilities in the implementation of ASC Requirements.

  • Employees have the necessary competencies, knowledge and experience to implement the ASC Requirements.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.2.4 – The UoC shall annually review the management system and revise it where necessary to ensure its continued suitability, adequacy and effectiveness in implementing the ASC Requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC’s management system review should provide the opportunity to assess its suitability, adequacy and effectiveness in continuously ensuring conformance with the ASC requirements.

  • The review should consider:

    • Progress and effectiveness of changes implemented following the previous management review.

    • Financial and personnel resources necessary to maintain the management system.

    • Changes in the internal and external context of the site which may give rise to previously unanticipated issues.

    • Performance review since the previous management review.

    • Internal and external audit outcomes.

    • Grievances raised.

    • Progress towards longer-term ASC targets, e.g. an increase in wage payments.

    • Progress towards site commitments.

    • A mechanism for employees’ feedback on the effectiveness of the management system

  • The outcome of the review should include addressing any need for changes and opportunities for improvement in the management system, which is documented and communicated to relevant employees for implementation.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • of the review and its outcomes.

    • meeting minutes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Review is conducted at least annually.

  • Records.

Useful Resources

N/A

Business Ethics 1.3

1.3.1 – The UoC shall discourage all forms of corruption and shall encourage ethical behaviour and integrity in their business operations.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Corruption can:

    • Happen anywhere;

    • Involve anyone;

    • Take many forms11https://www.transparency.org/en/what-is-corruption. For example:

      • extortion

      • embezzlement

      • bribery

  • Examples of corruption are:

    • A manager buys supplies from a friend and in return, the friend gives 20% of the profits to the manager. This may go as far as the manager excluding other appropriate suppliers from the system of approved suppliers.

    • A piece of infrastructure has an unsafe mechanism and the owner pays the manager cash to not disclose this at the next audit.

  • Examples of extortion are:

    • Employee A threatens to provide information to the manager which could get Employee B into trouble or fired, unless Employee A is paid a requested amount of money.

    • A site owner threatens to hurt the owner of the neighbouring plot of land unless the land-owner agrees to give up some of his land so that the site can build an additional building.

  • Examples of embezzlement are:

    • A site manager getting cash from the first point of sale in exchange for under-declaring harvest volumes (i.e. the purchaser receiving more product that they are paying for).

    • A sourcing manager purchases cheaper non-eligible feed but registers them as eligible and provides documentation falsely declaring it as more costly eligible feed, as financial sourcing performance increases the sourcing manager’s bonus.

  • Examples of bribery are:

    • A supplier buys a new car for a site manager, in exchange for the site manager giving the sourcing contract to that supplier.

    • A site pays cash to customs officials to speed up the passage of their feed through the import and export system.

    • A sustainability manager offers auditors excessive accommodation and lunches to reduce the audit effort or to turn a blind eye to non-conformities.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Policies preventing corruption, including extortion, embezzlement and bribery.

  • Terms of dismissal should employees engage in these practices.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Management and employees are aware of:

    • what these practices involve and how to recognise them.

    • the policies in place for preventing corruption, including extortion, embezzlement and bribery.

Useful Resources

  • Transparency International: https://www.transparency.org/en

1.3.2 – The UoC shall ensure that information provided as evidence of conformance to the ASC Requirements is not falsified or misrepresented.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Records are documented information that provides permanent evidence about past events. They should:

    • Be completed and maintained in a way that ensures information is accurate and preserved;

    • Be genuine;

      • they should be completed at the time of the checks or shortly after.

    • Capture and illustrate information when processes do not perform as expected.

      • for example, if the cooling system ceases to work, it is important that temperatures above the acceptable range according to internal requirements are recorded so that management can learn from these events.

        • recording temperatures only within the acceptable range will lead to management not understanding that a backup temperature regulator might be needed.

    • Be legible;

    • Be complete;

      • which may include a form of authorisation through the initials of the supervisor verifying records are complete;

  • Be stored appropriately:

    • paper records should be stored in a way that prevents damage.

    • where records are stored electronically, this storage should be backed up.

  • If incidences of falsification of records or misrepresentation of information are identified, corrective action and actions to prevent recurrence should be taken.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • that demonstrate genuineness.

    • corrective action and actions to prevent recurrence when incidences of falsification of records or misrepresentation of information are identified.

Auditors should confirm:

  • records and their genuineness

  • effectiveness of corrective action and actions to prevent

Useful Resources

N/A

Traceability and Disclosure 1.4

1.4.1 – The UoC shall identify, evaluate and mitigate risks of mixing and substituting ASC certified products with non-certified products at all sites.

1.4.2 – The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a traceability system, covering all sites, to ensure that the following conditions are met:

  1. only larvae/juveniles that conform with the requirements in Criterion 1.5 are used to produce certified product; and

  2. all stocked animals are traceable back to the supplier; and

  3. all batches of ASC certified and non-certified product are identifiable and segregated at all sites and at all times; and

  4. all batches of ASC certified product are traceable at all times to:

    • the site(s) used ; and

    • the production unit(s) used; and

  5. corrective actions are taken if non-conforming product is identified, sold or dispatched; and

  6. accompanying documentation shall identify product sold or dispatched as ASC certified or non-certified.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC is responsible for ensuring it mitigates risks of substitution and mixing of certified and non-certified products.

  • The UoC may use the Risk Assessment Method outlined in Appendix 3 of the ASC Farm Standard, Section 3.2, to identify, evaluate and mitigate risks of mixing and substituting ASC certified products with non-certified products at all sites (Indicator 1.4.1).

  • Certified and non-certified products shall be identifiable and segregated at all sites and at all times within the UoC (Indicator 1.4.2(c)).

    • This includes during production while fish are alive.

  • Certified products shall be traceable at all sites and at all times within the UoC (Indicator 1.4.2(d)).

  • The UoC may decide to sell products from the UoC as non-certified (Indicator 1.4.2(f)).

    • In this case, the products shall be identified as non-certified when sold or dispatched.
  • The requirements of these indicators establish a consistent, streamlined approach for traceability, identification and segregation at all ASC certified sites.
    • They relieve the need for separate Chain of Custody certification to cover farming activities.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • risk assessment and any resulting actions.

    • use or verification of the effectiveness of the traceability system, for example:

      • outcome of input-output exercises and traceability tests.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Risks have been adequately assessed and mitigated.

  • Effective traceability and segregation systems are in place.

  • Outcome of any input-output exercises and traceability tests.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.4.3 – The UoC shall demonstrate that feed products, subject to conformance with Indicator 2.12.1, are accompanied by the following information:

Indicator applicability: every UoC using compound feed

  1. the originating feed mill holds valid certification against the ASC Feed Standard with the appropriate scope of certification in relation to the ASC Production Model (i.e. Mass Balance Production Model or Segregation Production Model product); and

  2. feed is traceable as ASC-conforming throughout all steps between the feed mill and site; and

  3. documentation accompanying the feed identifies the feed as ASC-conforming; and

  4. documentation accompanying the feed identifies the production model applied (i.e. Mass Balance Production Model or Segregation Production Model); and

  5. for ASC-conforming Segregation Production Model feed, the product is identifiable by a distinct feed name in formal documentation accompanying the product and is listed on the schedule to the feed mill certificate.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Indicator 2.12.1 requires the UoC to only use ASC-conforming compound feed.
    • Use of non-conforming feed will be treated as a non-conformity against Indicator 2.12.1.
  • For product which is sold under the segregation model, identifying the feed production model and distinct feed name is required by the ASC Feed Standard, Indicator 3.3.2.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Process to confirm the originating feed mill holds valid certification against the ASC Feed Standard

  • Records:

    • traceability system and its verification, for example:
      • use of a digital traceability system
      • outcome of any input-output exercises and traceability tests.
  • accompanying documents incorporating information required by 1.4.3(c), (d) and (e).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Process to confirm the originating feed mill holds valid certification against the ASC Feed Standard.

  • Effective traceability and segregation systems are in place.

  • Outcome of any input-output exercises and traceability tests.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.4.4 The UoC shall disclose to all buyers of their ASC certified product when a product’s feed contains >0.9%22European Council. (2003). Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 concerning the traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms and the traceability of food and feed products produced from genetically modified organisms and amending Directive 2001/18/EC. European Parliament, Council of the European Union. Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO) or macro ingredients produced from GMO.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using compound feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The required disclosure is to the UoC’s buyers of ASC certified
    products.

  • A public disclosure is possible but not required.

  • The UoC shall ensure buyers are informed when a product’s feed contains or is produced from GMO.

    • Disclosure may be provided to buyers individually or collectively.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • disclosure to buyers.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Evidence of disclosure to buyers.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.4.5 – The UoC shall not sell or dispatch the following as ASC certified:

  1. crustaceans treated with antibiotics at the UoC, or

  2. any product treated with antimicrobials listed as Critically Important Antimicrobials for Human Medicine by the World Health Organisation (WHO), at any stage in the lifecycle of the product.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This requirement addresses situations where a product may conform to the Standard, however it cannot be sold or dispatched as ASC certified.

  • The UoC should:

    • Maintain detailed records of any antibiotic treatments applied prior to the UoC (see Indicator 1.5.2).

    • Implement a process to ensure that the product under 1.4.5(a) or (b) is not sold or dispatched as ASC certified.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:
    • antibiotic treatments, including those applied prior to the UoC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • UoC’s process to ensure that the product under 1.4.5(a) or (b) is not sold or dispatched as ASC certified.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.4.6 The UoC shall disclose to buyers of their ASC certified product, upon request, a list of all veterinary therapeutants applied to the product.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

1.4.7 The UoC shall report to ASC the production volumes and sales/dispatch volumes of ASC certified and non-certified products originating from each site, and submit specified traceability data (when requested), according to ASC data submission procedures.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

Supply Chain 1.5

1.5.1 – The UoC shall map their supply chain using the ASC Supply Chain Mapping Template, provided on the ASC website.

1.5.2 – The UoC shall only stock ASC certifiable product if accompanied by a completed ASC Stock Status Record33The ASC Stock Status Record holds batch-specific information on products moving through the supply chain. This includes information on origin of broodstock, treatments, feed, and ASC certification status., provided on the ASC website.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Traceability in the supply chain is essential for ensuringtransparency, improving product quality and safety, and promptly identifying and addressing issues.

  • The indicators allow for information related to the status of ASC certified products to be passed along the supply chain.

  • The scope of the supply chain that needs to be mapped includes all sites supplying certifiable products, from broodstock onwards.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Completed ASC Supply Chain Mapping Template listing the supply chain from broodstock sites onwards.

  • Completed ASC Stock Status Record.

Auditors should confirm:

  • ASC Supply Chain Mapping Template is completed listing the supply chain from broodstock sites onwards.
    • Crosscheck mapping with purchase records.
  • ASC Stock Status Record completed.

Useful Resources

N/A

1.5.3 – The UoC shall44An exemption applies to sites in the supply chain that hold valid ASC certification. These sites do not need to comply with Indicator 1.5.3. only stock ASC certifiable product if it can be demonstrated that all sites55An exemption applies to broodstock sites. in the supply chain conform with the requirements in Appendix 14. An exception applies for salmon sites that are supplied with product from other cage site(s), in which case all cage site(s) in the supply chain shall be ASC certified.

Indicator applicability: freshwater trout, flatfish, seabass, seabream, meagre and salmon

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Appendix 14 (14.1) establishes that documentation is required to be maintained from the sites in the supply chain to demonstrate that these sites conform with the requirements of this appendix.

    • The documentation should provide information to the extent necessary to ensure that the supplier sites conform with the requirements of Appendix 14 (14.1).

  • Different applicability examples are provided below:

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentation that demonstrates suppliers of the site conform with the requirements of Appendix 14 (14.1).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documentation that demonstrates the suppliers of the site conform with the requirements of Appendix 14 (14.1)

Environmental Risk Assessment 2.1

2.1.1 The UoC shall conduct an Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) per site, following the method outlined in Appendix 3 (3.3).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) determines the risk level of environmental risks resulting from operational activities in the vicinity of the site. A default set of environmental risks are listed in Appendix 3.1.

  • The outcome of the ERA will be used to determine compliance and impacts on Ecologically Important Habitats (Criterion 2.2) and Wildlife Interactions (Criterion 2.3).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An ERA has been conducted, following the method outlined in Appendix 3.1, and records are available to demonstrate that actions are taken to reduce risks with risk level ‘medium’ or ‘high’.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The UoC has presented the ERA, which was conducted in accordance with the method in Appendix 3.1.

Useful Resources

  • European Food Safety Authority: Environmental Risk Assessment: Environmental risk assessment | EFSA.

2.1.2 The UoC shall ensure that the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1) is conducted by a person with the necessary competencies, experience and training that is appropriate to the size and complexity of the site.

For larger, more complex sites, an independent person shall conduct the ERA. This person shall:

  1. have an academic background in Biology, Ecology, Environmental Science, or an equivalent field of study; and

  2. have a minimum of 5 years of experience in conducting ERA, including survey design, data collection, data analysis and interpretation.

In cases where legal requirements are defined, the UoC shall ensure that the person conducting the ERA complies with these requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • An independent person is required to conduct the ERA for larger, more complex sites. However, small-scale or extensive aquaculture sites are not expected to contract an independent person to conduct the
    ERA.

  • To demonstrate competence, personnel conducting the ERA for small-scale or extensive aquaculture sites should be able to:

    • Analyse environmental risks.

    • Conduct data analysis.

    • Record, review and authorise the release of results.

    • Contribute to or produce reports that can clearly and concisely follow the method outlined in Appendix 3.1.

    • Have undergone training, or have experience, relating to ERAs.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents outlining the person conducting the ERA has experience and competences that are relevant to the size and complexity of the site.

  • For larger, more complex sites, documents outlining the qualifications and experience of the independent person conducting the
    ERA.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Evidence and documents have been presented to demonstrate the person conducting the ERA has the necessary experience, competencies and qualifications.

  • Auditor discretion is permitted to determine whether the experience, competences and qualifications are suitable for the size of the site.

Useful Resources

N/A

Ecologically Important Habitats 2.2

2.2.1 The UoC shall66An exemption applies for the following species groups: tilapia, pangasius, bivalve and abalone ensure that the site is not located in Protected Areas (PA). An exception applies where conditional siting is allowed according to Appendix 4.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Conditional allowances to the siting in Protected Areas (PA) have been taken from the ASC species standards while work is ongoing to develop updated conditional allowances.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Whether the site is in a PA and if so, provide evidence that the PA meets the conditional allowances specified in Appendix 4. This includes the demonstration of the Protected Areas Management Plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Whether the site is in a PA. If so, evidence has been provided to demonstrate that the site meets the conditional allowances in Appendix 4 (4.2).

Useful Resources

  • Protected Planet: World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA): Explore the World’s Protected Are as.

2.2.2 The UoC shall ensure that the site has a low risk of negative impact on critical habitats, as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) will determine whether there are critical habitats within the vicinity of the site and the risk drivers that increase the likelihood of negative impacts on any critical habitats.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An ERA report has been completed, which assesses the risk of negative impacts on any relevant critical habitats.

  • The ERA report demonstrates whether the risk of negative impacts on critical habitats is ‘low’.

    • In cases where the risk level is not ‘low’, the ERA report identifies the risk drivers.

    • In cases where the risk level is ‘medium’ or ‘high’, the site demonstrates the actions taken to reduce the risk level to ‘low’.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Whether there are critical habitats in the vicinity of the site. If so, evidence has been provided in the ERA that the risk of negative impacts on the critical habitats is minimal.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.2.3 The UoC shall preserve any critical habitat identified within the site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • In accordance with Indicator 2.2.2, the ERA report will identify whether critical habitats are located within the boundaries of the site.
    • The size and biodiversity characteristics of critical habitats should either remain the same since the ERA was conducted or have increased/improved.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ERA report has identified the presence of critical habitats within the boundaries of the site.

  • Documented measures and outcomes, which demonstrate critical habitats have been preserved, and that their size and biodiversity has not decreased.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Whether critical habitats have been identified in the ERA report.

  • If critical habitats are present, evidence has been provided to demonstrate measures to preserve the documented critical habitats.

    • Outputs of preservation measures should also be available where appropriate.

Useful Resources

  • GIS portal: GIS portal – ASC International (asc-aqua.org)

2.2.4 The UoC shall ensure that the site has a low risk of negative impact on sensitive habitats, as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) will determine whether there are sensitive habitats within the vicinity of the site and the risk drivers that increase the likelihood of negative impacts on any sensitive habitats.

    • The ERA will determine whether the risk of negative impacts on the identified sensitive habitats is minimal.

  • Appendix 3.3 outlines the risk factors that shall be considered as a minimum when conducting the ERA.

    • Appendix 3.3 also outlines the types of sensitive habitats that shall be considered as a minimum.

    • Other types of sensitive habitats may be identified in the ERA.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An ERA report has been completed, which assesses the risk of negative impacts on any relevant sensitive habitats.

  • The ERA report demonstrates whether the risk of negative impacts on sensitive habitats is ‘low’.

Auditors should confirm:

  • An ERA has been completed, which includes at a minimum the risk factors outlined in Appendix 3.3.

  • The ERA determined whether sensitive habitats are located within the vicinity of the site.

    • If sensitive habitats were identified, the ERA determined whether the risk of negative impacts on the sensitive habitats is minimal.

Useful Resources

  • GIS portal: GIS portal – ASC International (asc-aqua.org)

2.2.5 The UoC shall maintain any natural wildlife corridors within the site, as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1).

Indicator applicability: land-based systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Maintaining wildlife corridors mitigates impacts on biodiversity and allows for wildlife movement across larger landscapes within their habitats or natural ranges.

    • Examples include ensuring corridors are maintained to allow the movement of wildlife to and from feeding or breeding sites either side of the site.

  • The ERA shall determine whether any wildlife corridors are present within the site and whether the site has taken adequate measures to maintain them.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ERA demonstrates whether wildlife corridors are present within the site and whether the corridors are adequately maintained.

  • Spatial data and maps over a relevant timescale can determine if wildlife corridors are maintained.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Whether the ERA report has identified the presence of wildlife corridors within the site.

  • If present, the ERA determines the site is maintaining the wildlife corridors.

  • The UoC has presented maps or spatial data to demonstrate wildlife corridors have been maintained.

Useful Resources

  • GIS portal: GIS portal – ASC International (asc-aqua.org)

2.2.6 The UoC shall maintain a riparian zone between the site and any freshwater body, with a minimum width of either 15m or as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1), whichever is stricter.

Indicator applicability: land-based systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Riparian zones provide a buffer between natural waterbodies and adjacent terrestrial ecosystems.

    • A 15m buffer zone is the minimum width to provide habitats for wildlife, minimise erosion and run-off, improve water quality and stabilise the ecosystem around the water source.

  • The ERA will determine the minimum width of the riparian zone which needs to be maintained to ensure the functioning of the zone.

    • The ERA should also assess the functioning of the riparian zone, for example species diversity.
  • The UoC shall ensure the width of the riparian zone is at least 15m, or greater if the ERA determines the buffer zone needs to be wider.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ERA report demonstrates the required width of the riparian zone.

  • The site ensures the riparian zone is maintained and is at least 15m wide. The buffer zone shall be wider if determined by the ERA.

    • Spatial data and maps over a relevant timescale can demonstrate the width of the riparian zone is maintained.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The ERA report has assessed the suitable width and functioning of the riparian zone.

  • The width of the riparian zone is at least 15m, or wider as determined by the ERA.

  • Evidence has been presented, e.g. spatial data and maps, demonstrating the riparian zone is maintained at 15m or greater (as determined by the ERA).

Useful Resources

  • GIS portal: GIS portal – ASC International (asc-aqua.org)

  • United States Environmental Protection Agency (2005): Riparian Buffer Width, Vegetative Cover, and Nitrogen Removal Effectiveness: A Review of Current Science and Regulations: Riparian buffer width, vegetative cover, and nitrogen removal effectiveness: A review of current science and regulations

  • Climate ADAPT (2023): Establishment and restoration of riparian buffers: Establishment and restoration of riparian buffers.

  • National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (2005): Review of Riparian Buffer Zone Effectiveness: Review of Riparian Buffer Zone Effectiveness.

2.2.7 The UoC shall maintain a coastal barrier between the site and any marine or brackish waterbody, with a minimum width of either 100m or as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1), whichever is stricter.

Indicator applicability: land-based systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Coastal barriers can be either artificial or natural and mitigate concerns relating to storm or flood risks. The ERA will assess the
    required width of the coastal barrier to mitigate these risks.

    • An additional benefit of coastal barriers is that they control environmental events directly linked to escapes and disease transfer.
    • Communities can also access marine resources through the maintenance of a coastal barrier.
  • The UoC shall ensure the width of the coastal barrier is at least 100m, or greater if the ERA determines the coastal barrier needs to be wider.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ERA has determined the suitable width of the coastal barrier.

  • The maintained coastal barrier has a minimum width of 100m or greater, as determined by the ERA.

  • Spatial data and maps can provide evidence of the width of the coastal barrier and its maintenance.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The ERA has assessed the width of the coastal barrier.

  • The coastal barrier is 100m or greater, as determined by the ERA.

  • Spatial data or maps are presented to demonstrate the width of the coastal barrier and that it is maintained.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.2.8 The UoC shall have successfully restored a minimum of 50% of natural wetland converted before May 1999.

Indicator applicability: land-based systems

2.2.9 The UoC shall not convert natural wetland after May 1999. An exception applies where conversion is needed for establishing and maintaining pumping stations, water pipes or canals, in which case the UoC shall successfully restore 100% of the converted area.

Indicator applicability: land-based and suspended systems

2.2.10 The UoC shall report to ASC the area of the restored wetland, according to ASC data submission procedures.

Indicator applicability: land-based and suspended systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Rehabilitation projects should be located within or adjacent to farming activities, to restore ecosystem function close to where it has originally been lost.

    • If this is not feasible, the UoC may contribute to regional rehabilitation activities.
    • Restoration activities should ensure habitats and biodiversity are equivalent to habitat and biodiversity lost through conversion.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Spatial mapping of the converted and restored areas:

    • Time series maps showing changes in the cover of natural wetlands.

    • Polygons or measurements of the converted and restored areas showing the surface areas of conversion and rehabilitation.

    • This evidence shall be submitted to ASC in accordance with Indicator 2.2.10.
  • The location of rehabilitation projects. If local rehabilitation efforts were not possible, evidence should be presented demonstrating why they were not possible.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The appropriate area of natural wetland has been successfully rehabilitated.

  • Polygons or measurement of the areas showing conversion and rehabilitation have been presented by the UoC.

Useful Resources

  • Best Practice Guidelines for Mangrove Restoration developed by the Global Mangrove Alliance and the Blue Carbon Initiative: Best-Practice-Guidelines-for-Mangrove-Restoration_v4.pdf.
    • The guidelines lay out the steps for rehabilitation project design, setting goals and assessing feasibility, project implementation, monitoring, evaluation and adaptive management.
  • Spatial mapping tools:

    • GIS portal: GIS portal – ASC International (asc-aqua.org)

    • Clark Labs Coastal Habitat Mapping: Mangrove and Pond Aquaculture Conversion Coastal Habitat Mapping: Mangrove and Pond Aquaculture Conversion – Clark Labs.

    • Global Mangrove Watch country-level information on mangrove habitat extent and change: Global Mangrove Watch.

  • Additional rehabilitation tools:
    • The Climate-Smart Mangrove Tool (CSMT) is designed to aid conservation practitioners in selecting appropriate “climate-smart” actions to reduce the current and future impacts of climate change on mangrove ecosystems: https://www.worldwildlife.or
      g/publications/the-climate-smart-mangrove-tool-excel-based-workbook      .
  • Where to restore mangrove habitats:

    • The Mangrove Restoration Potential Mapping Tool provides information on the ecosystem services provided in restoration of regions within a country https://maps.coastalresilience.org/mangrove-restoration/.

    • SFP Technical Paper: How coastal shrimp farming can support effective mangrove regeneration: FINAL – Shrimp Farming and Mangroves Technical Paper Dec2022.pdf – Google Drive.

    • To help the farmed shrimp industry more effectively identify and protect mangrove habitat, SFP and Longline Environment developed the Aquascape mangrove-shrimp pond mapping tool to show where shrimp farming regions and mangrove habitat overlap in India, Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam. Register to use the tool at: Mangrove mapping tool – Sustainable Fisheries Partnership.

2.2.11 The UoC shall77An exemption to Indicator 2.2.11 applies for situations where the total surface area of aquaculture within a waterbody is less than 10% of the total surface area of the waterbody. ensure that total bivalve culture in a waterbody does not result in phytoplankton depletion either by:

Indicator applicability: bivalve culture

  1. demonstrating that the waterbody has a ratio of Clearance Time (CT) over Retention Time (RT) > 1, following the method outlined in Appendix 5. Where CT over RT is <1, demonstrate that the waterbody has a ratio of CT over Primary Production Time (PPT) > 3, following the method outlined in Appendix 5; or

  2. conducting a modelling study that demonstrates that the carrying capacity of the waterbody is not exceeded.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The ratio of Clearance Time (CT) and Retention Time (RT) demonstrate whether the carrying capacity of a waterbody for bivalve production has been exceeded.

  • Primary Production Time (PPT) is calculated when cultured bivalves may negatively impact the carrying capacity of a waterbody.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The method used to calculate CT, RT and PPT, in accordance with Appendix 5.

    • Maps demonstrating whether the site is in an easily definable waterbody. This will support the selection of the correct method in Appendix 5 (5.2) regarding estimating the zone of influence.

  • Results demonstrating the ratio of CT over RT, or CT over PPT.

  • A modelling study has been conducted to demonstrate the carrying capacity of the waterbody, if the method outlined in Appendix 5 has not been followed.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Methods and results have been presented demonstrating the ratio of CT over RT, or CT and PPT depending on whether CT over RT > 1, in accordance with Indicator 2.11.

  • A modelling study has been conducted to demonstrate the carrying capacity of the waterbody, if the method outlined in Appendix 5 has not been followed.

    • The modelling study shall demonstrate carrying capacity has not been exceeded.

Wildlife Interactions 2.3

2.3.1 The UoC shall ensure the site has a low risk of Human-Wildlife Conflict within the site and in the area surrounding the site, as determined through the ERA (see Indicator 2.1.1).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Indicator 2.1.1 and Appendix 3.1 outline the site-specific Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) following the Standardised Risk Methodology.

  • Mitigation measures may need to be implemented to manage Human-Wildlife Conflict within the site and in the area surrounding the site.

  • The risk level and identified mitigation measures (if applicable) should be identified in the ERA.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ERA assesses the risk of Human-Wildlife Conflict. Evidence should be presented to demonstrate whether the risk is low.

  • Mitigation measures implemented to manage Human-Wildlife Conflict to maintain the low risk level.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The ERA has assessed the risk of Human-Wildlife Conflict and determined the risk level is low.

  • Mitigation measures are implemented (if required and recommended by the ERA) to maintain the low risk level.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.3.2 The UoC shall not cause the mortality of any Threatened Species.

An exception applies for occasional incidents that do not affect the population status, and where a written statement from a registered veterinarian or the responsible authorities is available to confirm that:

  1. injured animals are unlikely to recover; or

  2. immediate human safety is threatened; or

  3. legal requirements mandate emergency euthanasia.


2.3.3 The UoC shall not injure or cause mortality of mammals, elasmobranchs or reptiles (excluding vermin).

An exception applies for occasional incidents where:

  1. injured animals are unlikely to recover; or

  2. immediate human safety is threatened; or

  3. legal requirements mandate emergency euthanasia.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Mortalities include animals intentionally killed through lethal action, as well as accidental deaths through entanglement or other means.

  • Occasional incidents of injury or mortality will be rare and only occur in exceptional circumstances which are necessary for the reasons outlined in Indicators 2.3.2 and 2.3.3. All other feasible measures should be pursued prior to causing injuries or mortality.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A list of Threatened Species, mammals, elasmobranchs and reptiles which are present in the vicinity of the site should be presented.

  • Records of any interactions, injuries and mortalities to/of these species should be maintained.

  • Where there are occasional incidents of interactions with or mortalities of Threatened Species, evidence has been maintained to demonstrate that the incidents will not affect the population status.

    • A written statement has also been obtained from a registered veterinarian or the responsible authorities to confirm at least one of the three points (a-c) in Indicator 2.3.2 has been met.
  • Records demonstrating that if there are occasional injuries or mortalities of mammals, elasmobranchs or reptiles, the incidents meet the exception in Indicator 2.3.3.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records of interactions with Threatened Species, mammals, elasmobranchs and reptiles have been maintained. Specifically, records of any injuries or mortality.

  • Written statements are present from a registered veterinarian or the responsible authorities, in accordance with Indicators 2.3.2, if mortalities of Threatened Species have occurred.

    • The statement confirms that at least one of the three points (a-c) in Indicator 2.3.2 have been met.
  • Records have been presented to demonstrate that if there are occasional injuries or mortalities of mammals, elasmobranchs or reptiles, the incidents meet the exception in Indicator 2.3.3.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.3.4 The UoC shall investigate all wildlife mortality incidents to determine the root cause and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records showing that the UoC has investigated each mortality incident and how the investigation has led to the implementation of appropriate actions to prevent recurrence.

  • Documents demonstrating the actions have been implemented and prevented recurrence.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Investigations have taken place following each mortality event.

  • Actions have been implemented to prevent recurrence of wildlife mortalities.

2.3.5 The UoC shall only use aquatic
acoustic deterrence where scientific evidence suggests that it does not result in significant stress or injury to, or mortality of, the affected species or its population(s).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Acoustic deterrence includes any device or method used in which acoustic (‘sound’/’noise’) is used to deter wildlife. This includes, but is not limited to, the use of acoustic deterrent devices (ADDs) and acoustic harassment devices (AHDs).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records of the use of any aquatic acoustic deterrence, which includes the frequency and duration and duration of the deterrence.

  • If aquatic acoustic deterrence is used, scientific reports/publications are obtained which demonstrate that the deterrence does not result in significant stress, injuries to, or mortality of, the species impacted/targeted by the deterrence.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records are provided to demonstrate whether any aquatic acoustic deterrence has been used.

  • If aquatic acoustic deterrence has been used, scientific reports/publications have been presented by the UoC to demonstrate that the deterrence does not result in significant stress, injuries to, or mortality of, the species impacted/targeted by the deterrence.

2.3.6 The UoC shall only stock fish that is hatchery-raised.

Indicator applicability: all fish species

An exception applies where the UoC can demonstrate the following for Seriola/Cobia, in which case wild caught fish are permitted to be stocked:

  1. the species is not listed as a Threatened Species; and

  2. the originating fishery is certified to an ASC-recognised fisheries certification scheme88Refer to the ASC website for details of ASC-recognised fisheries certification schemes.; and

  3. traceability back to the originating fishery is provided.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Batch records or other documentations are maintained to demonstrate stocked fish are hatchery-raised.

  • For Seriola/Cobia, where wild caught fingerlings are stocked, documentation demonstrating the species is not listed as a Threatened Species and records demonstrating the traceability of the fish.

    • The IUCN Red List can be used to check whether the species is listed as Threatened.

    • Documentation demonstrating the fish was sourced from an ASC-recognised fisheries certification scheme can facilitate traceability back to the fishery if chain of custody documentation has been maintained.
    • Traceability documentation should include the species, catch method and area in which the fish was caught.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Batch records or other documentation are presented to demonstrate stocked fish are hatchery-raised.

  • For Seriola/Cobia stocked from a wild fishery, adequate documentation is presented to demonstrate traceability back to the fishery and the certification of the originating fishery (to an ASC-recognised fisheries certification scheme).

2.3.7 The UoC shall not use Threatened Species for wild broodstock.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

    • The IUCN Red List can be used to check whether the wild broodstock species is listed as Threatened.

    • Traceability documentation can be used to demonstrate the origin of the wild broodstock species. Traceability should be back to the source fishery.

2.3.8 The UoC shall only stock larvae that is hatchery-raised

Indicator applicability: all crustacean species

An exception applies where the UoC can demonstrate the following for extensive crustacean production, in which case wild larvae are permitted to be stocked:

  1. the larvae are collected passively; and

  2. the production system is a non-fed, low-intensive pond production system; and

  3. inflow of larvae occurs through natural tidal flow into the ponds.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Hatchery permits and import licences which demonstrate the source of the larvae.

  • If applicable, documentation that confirms crustacean production is extensive.

    • Documentation demonstrating points a-c under the exception in Indicator 2.3.8 are met if wild larvae are sourced and stocked for extensive crustacean production.

    • If the UoC is not vertically integrated, larvae suppliers should provide documentation to the UoC to verify how wild larvae are collected.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Hatchery permits and import licences are presented which demonstrate wild larvae is hatchery-raised.

  • If crustacean production is extensive and wild larvae are stocked, documents are presented demonstrating the exception in
    Indicator 2.3.8 is met.

Useful Resources

2.3.9 The UoC shall only source from hatcheries that have procedures to address genetic concerns specific to the species and geographical region where the seed will be stocked.

Indicator applicability: hatchery-raised bivalve seed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The translocation of wild bivalve seed can pose risks to the genetic diversity of wild populations.
    • Genetic risks to wild populations therefore need to be assessed and procedures need to be implemented to address any genetic risks. These will be based on the species and geographic region where the seed will be stocked.
  • Efforts should be made to address genetic concerns specific to the species and the geographic region where the seed will be stocked.
    • This may include preserving diversity of broodstock and seed by:

      • Using local broodstock,

      • Rotation of broodstock within spawning seasons and between years, and

      • Avoiding the use of hatchery-propagated stock in the hatchery as broodstock.

    • The scale of farming and the reproductive potential of crops (e.g. whether diploid or triploid, or considering age at harvest and age at first maturation) are well below the size and reproductive potential of the natural population within a reasonable ‘dispersal kernel’ from the site.
    • Sterile seed may be produced for stocking.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An assessment of genetic risks presented from the translocation of wild bivalve seed, based on the species and geographic region where the seed will be stocked.

  • The hatchery has procedures and measures in place to address any genetic concerns. For example:

    • Documentation of the use of local, wild broodstock to address genetic concerns specific to the species and the geographic region where the seed will be out-planted.

    • Documentation of the scale of farming activities and the reproductive potential of crops (e.g. whether diploid or triploid, or considering age at harvest and age at first maturation) are well below the size and reproductive potential of the natural population within a reasonable ‘dispersal kernel’ from the site.

    • Documentation on the production of sterile seed for out-planting from breeding programmes that intentionally alter wild stocks for improved culture traits, such as growth, yield, survival and morphology.

    • Provide documentation of cooperation with restoration efforts in the geographic region using out-planting that involves the intentional divergence from wild stocks to produce disease resistant wild populations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Evidence has been presented that genetic risks to wild populations have been assessed and the hatchery has implemented procedures and measures to address these risks. For example:

    • Verify that efforts have been made to address genetic concerns specific to the species and the geographic region where the seed will be out-planted.

    • Document the site’s use of the local, wild population for the broodstock with appropriate rotation of spawned individuals. If there is uncertainty about whether a broodstock is of local origin, record source locality.

    • Verify that the reproductive potential (e.g. whether diploid or triploid, or considering age at harvest and age at first maturation) of the hatchery produced seed is well below the size and reproductive potential of the natural population within a reasonable ‘dispersal kernel’ from the site.

    • Verify the existence of a breeding programme that produces altered sterile seed for out-planting.

    • Verify that the site’s breeding programme is in coordination with existing restoration efforts in the geographic region.

N/A

Indicator applicability: all bivalve species

  1. the species is not listed as a Threatened Species; and

How do I interpret this requirement?

    • Traceability documentation can be used to demonstrate the origin of the species used for wild caught seed.

    • Traceability should be back to the source and demonstrate it is regulated and not from an open-access, unregulated source.

Auditors should confirm:

    • This may include verifying traceability documentation, demonstrating traceability back to the source.

    • The evidence demonstrates the source is well regulated and not from an open-access unregulated source.

2.3.11 The UoC shall only use seed originating from native wild broodstock (not selectively bred animals).

Indicator applicability: all abalone farming in regions where the farmed species is Threatened

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Wild abalone populations can be impacted through selectively bred animals recruiting into, and breeding with, wild abalone populations.

  • Potential genetic impacts to at-risk populations can be mitigated by means of minimising escapes from abalone sites and by farming with stock originating from the same genetic stock as the local wild populations surrounding the site.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentation demonstrating the origin of seed and that it originates from native wild broodstock.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documentation has been presented demonstrating the origin of seed and that it originates from native wild broodstock.

Escapes and Native Biodiversity 2.4

2.4.1 The UoC shall not stock transgenic animals.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The stocking and culture of transgenic animals is not permitted on ASC certified sites.
    • Transgenic animals are not common in aquaculture, but transgenic stocks of Atlantic salmon, rainbow trout, channel catfish and Nile tilapia are known to exist.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Evidence that non-transgenic animals are stocked should be presented to the auditor. This could consist of a declaration from the hatcheries that non-transgenic animals are used.

    • In case of doubt regarding origin, submitting animals for DNA-testing could be considered.

Auditors should confirm:

  • All stock is from non-transgenic origin.

2.4.2 The UoC shall implement escape prevention measures that include the installation, inspection and maintenance of containment structures suitable for the species, life stages and environmental conditions under which the site is operating.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to prevent the escape of cultured animals. It focuses on three key aspects:

    • Installation of containment structure; these structures must be appropriate for:

      • The species; consider size and behaviour

      • Different life stages; consider that smaller animals require different mesh sizes compared to bigger animals

      • Environmental conditions; consider currents, tides, floodings, floating debris, natural predators that can damage the containment structure.

    • Inspection of containment structures to check for structure integrity, including:

      • Signs of damage or weaknesses; consider especially moving elements of the construction for ‘wear and tear’ signs

      • Environmental conditions that impact the structure (e.g. erosion)

      • Species-specific behaviours (e.g. net-biting, burrowing)

    • Maintenance of containment structure:

      • Regular maintenance needs to be conducted so that containment structures are kept in, or restored to, a good state, or to prepare for known severe weather events (e.g. forecasted storms, flooding, etc.).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Escape prevention measures are installed according to construction specifications that incorporate environmental conditions and species-specific characteristics.

  • Documents demonstrating inspection and maintenance is occurring regularly and when needed (e.g. after a storm).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Escape prevention measures have been installed according to construction specifications and are appropriate to environmental conditions and species-specific characteristics.

  • Documents have been presented which demonstrate inspection and maintenance has occurred regularly and as required.

  • https://www.g
    ov.scot/publications/aquaculture-code-practice-containment-prevention
    -escape-fish-fish-farms-relation-marine-mammal-interactions/pages/1/

2.4.3 The UoC shall carry out a site-specific handling and containment risk assessment, approved by a member of management, following the method outlined in Appendix
3.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to conduct a site-specific risk assessment to proactively identify and mitigate risks associated with handling and containment of cultured animals. The Indicator emphasises the need for tailored evaluation rather than a generic approach as site-specific circumstances might require different responses. Management approval ensures that the assessment is formally reviewed, acknowledged and integrated into wider management structures.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentational evidence of a risk assessment, the identification of appropriate risk levels and any mitigation actions taken (including the implementation thereof). The evidence should also include proof of management approval and periodic review of the risk assessment to ensure that it remains relevant.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Presence of a documented risk assessment, which:

    • Is specific to the conditions of the site.

    • Covers all handling and containment risks.

  • That the risk assessment identifies:

    • Risk factors and the associated risk levels.

    • Mitigation actions and records the implementation, including the desired outcome (i.e. reduction of risk level).

  • That the risk assessment is approved (e.g. signed off) by management and shows evidence of periodic review to keep it relevant.

2.4.4 The UoC shall ensure that any person involved in handling activities is trained on handling procedures to minimise escapes.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Training and handling procedures includes:

    • An understanding of which staff are involved in animal handling (including external services providers that conduct activities at the site).

    • Coverage of relevant training content, e.g. correct handling process, correct use of equipment and emergency protocols.

    • Appropriate means of training delivery relevant to the site-specific conditions (e.g. considering whether a workshop is sufficient or whether ‘live training’ on-site is more appropriate).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Training documents and records of staff attendance.

  • Presence of relevant procedures/protocols.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Training documents and records of staff attendance.

  • Presence of relevant procedures/protocols.

  • Interviews with staff.

2.4.5 The UoC shall log all handling and containment incidents and near misses.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This indicator requires the UoC to log (i.e. register) all handling and containment incidents, including near misses, in order to inform the risk assessment (see Indicator 2.4.3) and the training (2.4.4) on situations that could result, or have resulted, in registered escapes.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A documented register of all handling and containment incidents and near misses.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Presence of the register.

  • Interviews with employees to confirm that employees are aware of the register and that it is being used.

2.4.6 The UoC shall make efforts to address genetic concerns specific to the species and geographic region where hatchery-raised seed will be out-planted.

Indicator applicability: bivalve culture

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to take efforts to mitigate genetic risks associated with releasing hatchery-raised bivalve seed into the environment.

    • The emphasis is on species-specific and region-specific genetic concerns, meaning the UoC must consider the local ecosystem and population genetics before out planting.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Any of the following:

    • Documentation of the use of local, wild broodstock to address genetic concerns specific to species and the geographic region where the seed will be out-planted;

    • Documentation of the scale of farming activities and the reproductive potential of crops (e.g. whether diploid or triploid, or considering age at harvest and age at first maturation) are well below the size and reproductive potential of the natural population within a reasonable ‘dispersal kernel’ from the site;

    • Documentation of the production of sterile seed for out-planting from breeding programmes that intentionally alter wild stocks for improved culture traits, such as growth, yield, survival and morphology;

    • Documentation of cooperation with restoration efforts in the geographic region using out-planting that involves the intentional divergence from wild stocks to produce disease-resistant wild populations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • In relationship to the items listed under ‘Evidence of implementation’:

    • Verify that the site uses local, wild population for the broodstock with appropriate rotation of spawned individuals;

    • Verify that the reproductive potential (e.g. whether diploid or triploid, or considering age at harvest and age at first maturation) of the hatchery produced seed is well below the size and reproductive potential of the natural population within a reasonable ‘dispersal kernel’ from the site;

    • Verify the existence of a breeding programme that produces altered sterile seed for out-planting;

    • Verify that the site’s breeding programme is in coordination with existing restoration efforts in the geographic region.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to report the relevant data to ASC, as per data submission procedure.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Verify that UoC holds evidence that data has been submitted to ASC.

Indicators 2.4.8 – 2.4.13: Additional impact prevention measures

2.4.8 The UoC shall not exceed a maximum number of known escapes per production cycle or year, whichever is stricter, of the following:

Indicator applicability: species with an EICAT Category MO

  1. marine salmonids: 300 individuals

  2. other fish species: 6%

If the maximum number of known escapes is exceeded more than once in a six-year period, the UoC shall, by the next working day:

  1. submit a formal notification to the CAB for cancellation of certification; and

  2. notify ASC of the exceedance of known escapes, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Note: Indicator 2.4.8 only applies for species/regions that are classified as ‘Category Moderate (MO)’ in the EICAT Species Factsheet.
  • This Indicator requires a strict limit on the number of known escapes allowed per production cycle or per year, whichever threshold is stricter.
    • ‘Known escapes’ refers to escape incidents that are either observed directly or detected through monitoring. It does not include unverified or speculative losses.
  • Escape limits:

    • Marine salmonids (e.g. Atlantic salmon, trout): A hard limit of 300 individuals per production cycle. The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6.1.

    • Other fish species: A percentage-based limit of 6% of the total stocked population per production cycle or year (whichever is stricter). The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6.1.

  • If the UoC exceeds the set limit, a formal notification to the CAB shall be submitted by the next working day.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The UoC has a register of known escapes in which exceedance of the set limit is monitored.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records of known escapes are maintained.

  • Escape limits remain below the set threshold and that calculations are made correctly.

2.4.9 The UoC shall not exceed one Mass Escape Event in a six-year period, defined as:

Indicator applicability: species with an EICAT Category MO

  1. marine salmonids: >5000 individuals

  2. other fish species: >6% Total Escape Count

If a mass escape event occurs more than once in a six-year period, the UoC shall, by the next working day:

  1. submit a formal notification to the CAB for cancellation of certification; and

  2. notify ASC of the mass escape event, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Note: Indicator 2.4.9 only applies for species/regions that are classified as ‘Category Moderate (MO)’ in the EICAT Species Factsheet.

  • This Indicator requires a strict limit on mass escape events over a six-year period to ensure that large-scale fish escapes are rare and properly managed. It also requires certification cancellation if the limit is exceeded.

  • An event counts as a ‘mass escape’ if the thresholds are exceeded, regardless of cause (e.g. storm damage, net failure, human error). The thresholds are:

    • For marine salmonids: more than 5,000 individuals escaping at once. The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6.1.

    • For other fish species: More than 6% of the stocked population escaping at once. The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6.1.

  • The UoC is allowed only one mass escape event in a rolling six-year period. If a second mass escape event occurs within six years, the UoC must notify the CAB the next working day and request cancellation of certification.

  • The UoC should have a system, or method, to detect and document mass escape events, including the identification of root cause(s) and determination of corrective action(s) to prevent re-occurrence.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The UoC has a register of known escapes in which exceedance of the set limit is monitored.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records of mass escape events are maintained.

  • Escape limits remain below the set threshold and that calculations are made correctly.

2.4.10 The UoC shall implement appropriate mitigation measures according to the contextualisation of the EICAT category, following the method outlined in Appendix 6 (6.2).

Indicator applicability: fish species with an EICAT Category MO

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Note: Indicator 2.4.9 only applies for species/regions that are classified as ‘Category Moderate (MO)’ in the EICAT Species Factsheet.

  • This Indicator requires that the UoC implements suitable actions to minimise the potential harm to biodiversity by a species, depending on its context as determined in Appendix 6 (following the decision-tree in this Appendix).

  • For situations in which either the species, the production region or the culture system results in a low likelihood of contributing to biodiversity harm, the UoC is not required to implement actions.

  • For situations in which either the species, the production region or the culture system contributes to biodiversity harm, the UoC is required to implement actions that reduce this risk. This could mean, e.g.:

    • Installation of net pens as per technical standards in order to further reduce the likelihood of escapes occurring.

    • Installation of additional screens or barriers in pond/tank culture to further reduce the likelihood of escapes occurring.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents demonstrating to what extent the decision tree in Appendix 6 is applicable, and evidence of a reduction in the harm category (where relevant).

  • In cases where a reduction in the harm category is not possible, the UoC should demonstrate which additional measures have been taken, including the intended outcome of these measures.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Confirmation of the decision-tree results in Appendix 6.
    • In cases where a reduction in the harm category is not possible, confirmation that additional measures have been taken, including the intended outcome of these measures.

  1. submit a formal notification to the CAB for cancellation of certification; and

It does not include unverified or speculative losses.

    • Marine salmonids (e.g., Atlantic salmon, trout): A hard limit of 300 individuals per production cycle. The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6 (6.1).

    • Other fish species: A percentage-based limit of 6% of the total stocked population per production cycle or year (whichever is stricter). The formula for calculation can be found in Appendix 6 (6.1).

  • If the UoC exceeds the set limit, a formal notification to the CAB shall be submitted by the next working day.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

Indicators 2.4.14 – 2.4.15: Additional escape prevention measures

2.4.14 The UoC shall count fish with a minimum of 98% accuracy.

Indicator applicability: fish species with an EICAT Category MO or MR/MV

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to ensure that fish counting procedures achieve a minimum accuracy of 98%, meaning that the error margin must not exceed 2% and applies to both manual and automated counting methods.

  • The total number of fish at key stages of production (e.g. stocking and harvesting) needs to be counted.

  • The actual count should be within 2% of the true number (e.g. if 100,000 fish are stocked, the count must be between 98,000 and 102,000).

  • Acceptable counting methods include e.g.:

    • Automated systems: optical counters, AI-based image recognition or volumetric counting.

    • Manual counting: hand counting, sample-based extrapolation or visual verification.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The UoC shall demonstrate that fish are counted at key stages of production (e.g. stocking and harvesting) using a method that achieves 98% accuracy.
    • If automated systems are used, ensure they are regularly calibrated.
  • Documentation of counting procedures, accuracy checks and error rates.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Results of fish counts at key stages of production have been presented.

  • That calibration of the counting method is conducted.

  • Documents are maintained to record counting procedures, accuracy checks and error rates.

2.4.15 The UoC shall use all-male stock.

Indicator applicability: tilapia with an EICAT Category MO or MR/MV

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires that the UoC only stocks tilapia that is ‘all-male’ if the EICAT Category is set at Moderate (MO), Major (MR) or Massive (MV).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents demonstrating that the UoC is aware of the EICAT
    Category.

  • If the EICAT Category is set at Moderate (MO), Major (MR) or Massive (MV) documents demonstrate that the stocked tilapia is ‘all-male’.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The correct EICAT categorisation is applied.

  • If the EICAT Category is set at Moderate (MO), Major (MR) or Massive (MV), documents have been presented to demonstrate all stocked tilapia are ‘all-male’.

2.4.16 The UoC shall only stock smolts produced in cage culture if the supplier operates in a region where native salmonids of the same species are present.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires that smolts produced in cage culture are only sourced from suppliers operating in regions where native populations of the same species exist to prevent the potential competition with, or displacement of, native species in regions without natural salmonid populations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Demonstrate that the supplier of smolts operates in a region where native salmonids of the same species are present.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Verify that the supplier of smolts operates in a region where native salmonids of the same species are present.

2.4.17 The UoC shall communicate each escape incident to the local fishery trust(s).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This indicator requires the UoC to notify local fishery trusts whenever an escape incident occurs to ensure transparency, facilitate environmental monitoring and support mitigation efforts.

  • For each escape incident, the UoC must report key details such as:

    • Date and time of the escape.

    • Estimated number of escaped fish.

    • Species involved.

  • The UoC should identify the relevant local fishery trust(s) and establish clear communication channels. Fishery trusts are typically regional organisations responsible for managing wild fish populations and aquatic ecosystems. They may include government agencies, conservation groups or local fisheries management bodies.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • In case of escapes, the UoC shall maintain records of communications with fishery trusts (emails, reports or acknowledgments).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Verify that, in case of escapes, the UoC has communicated each escape incident to the fishery trusts.
