2.4.18 The UoC shall collaborate with fishery trust(s) in conducting native salmonid monitoring programme(s) in the waterbody where it operates.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to collaborate with local fishery trusts in conducting native salmonid monitoring programmes within the waterbody where it operates.

    • The purpose is to track the status of native salmonid populations and assess potential impacts from aquaculture activities. ‘Collaborate’ would imply involvement e.g. beyond providing funding or passive support.

  • Collaboration may include:

    • Sharing data on site operations and potential interactions with native salmonids.

    • Assisting in monitoring efforts (e.g. providing access to sites, participating in surveys).

    • Supporting scientific research or environmental assessments.

  • The monitoring programme should address as minimum:

    • Tracking population health, abundance and migration patterns of wild salmonids.

    • Assessing genetic integrity (to detect any impact from escaped farmed fish).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The UoC maintains records (e.g. agreements, partnerships, etc.) of collaboration with fishery trust(s).

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records have been presented to demonstrate collaboration with fishery trust(s).

2.4.19 The UoC shall conduct, in collaboration with the local fishery trust(s), a scientific baseline study to determine the genetic composition of the contemporary native and farmed salmonid population(s) in the waterbody where it operates. The baseline study shall:

  1. use credible methodologies and analysis and undergo peer review; and

  2. include known historical farmed and native salmonid genetic profiles; and

  3. determine if changes in the genetic composition of the contemporary native salmonid population(s) have occurred; and

  4. if changes in the genetic composition of the contemporary native salmonid population(s) are detected, seek to determine if these have occurred through introgression of farmed salmon or through other mechanisms; and

  5. be updated every three years.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This Indicator requires the UoC to conduct a collaborative scientific baseline study on the genetic composition of both native and farmed salmonid populations in the waterbody where it operates.

    • The goal is to assess potential genetic changes in wild populations, particularly from interbreeding (introgression) with farmed salmon, and ensure ongoing monitoring.

  • The study should establish a genetic baseline for comparison over time and should follow rigorous scientific methods and undergo peer review for credibility.

  • The study should use established genetic analysis techniques (e.g. DNA sequencing, microsatellite markers, SNP analysis).

  • The study should, if available, include known historical genetic profiles of both native and farmed salmonid populations in the waterbody.

  • The study should determine if genetic changes have occurred in native populations and identify if this is the result from introgression from farmed fish or other evolutionary pressures.

  • The study must be updated every three years.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The UoC maintains records of the conducted study or demonstrates
    that the study is under development.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Verify that the study has been concluded and has been conducted according to the requirements or is under development.

2.4.20 The UoC shall publicly disclose the scientific baseline study (see Indicator 2.4.19).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

2.4.21 The UoC shall time fallowing periods to occur outside the out-migration period of native salmonids.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This indicator requires the UoC to schedule fallowing periods outside the out-migration period of native salmonids.

  • The UoC should

    • Identify the local out-migration period of native salmonids in its operating region.

    • Schedule fallowing periods so that no fish are present in cages during this time.

    • Work with scientists, local fishery trusts, and regulatory bodies to align fallowing timing with migration patterns.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The out-migration period of native salmonids has been determined.

  • Documents demonstrating fallowing periods have been scheduled outside the out-migration period.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Fallowing periods occur outside the out-migration period of native salmonids.

Type Name
Video Benthic Impact – Cages and Suspended Systems

Benthic impact – Cages and Suspended Systems

2.5.1 The UoC shall1010An exemption applies to sites situated in areas classified as having a ‘hard bottom’. Evidence is required to support the classification ‘hard bottom’. determine benthic status, following the method outlined in Appendix 7 (7.2.1, 7.3.1, 7.4.1, 7.7).

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems

2.5.2 The UoC shall demonstrate an ’Acceptable‘ benthic status1111An exemption applies to cage sites situated in lakes and reservoirs, where determination of benthic status is required (Indicator 2.5.1) but demonstration that the status is ‘Acceptable’ is not required for the first three years of the ASC Farm Standard being effective., following the method outlined in Appendix 7 (7.2.2, 7.3.2, 7.4.2).

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems

2.5.3 The UoC shall ensure that the person conducting sediment sampling and analysis (see Indicator 2.5.1) is independent and has the necessary competencies, experience and training. In cases where regulatory requirements are defined, the UoC shall ensure that the person conducting the sampling and analysis complies with these requirements.

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The method for benthic monitoring for cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems is composed of:

    • Sediment sampling zones and sampling locations across transects.

    • Benthic quality categories and thresholds for defining those categories and the benthic status.

Sampling approach

  • The method uses a three-level sampling approach:

    • The number of transects and sampling locations, as well as the complexity of analysis, may increase based on Level 1 or Level 2 monitoring results:

      • Level 1 requires sampling along one transect in the direction of the predominant current. The samples are to be analysed for redox potential and total free sulphide.

        • Direction of the predominant current is the compass direction in which the water flows the majority of the time.

      • Level 2 requires sampling along three additional transects. The samples are to be analysed for redox potential and total free sulphide.

      • Level 3 requires sampling as per Level 2 (at a minimum, on the two transects in the direction of the predominant current). The samples are to be analysed for three (of the 14) biotic indicators selected from Table 2 of Appendix 7 (7.1).

        • Sites should select biotic indicators that are more appropriate based on their location or based on regulatory requirements.

          • In Scotland, sites should select AZTI’s Marine Biotic Index (AMBI) as one of the biotic indicators since it is a component of the Infaunal Quality Index (IQI) required by the regulation in that country.

    • Sites can choose to commence monitoring at any of the three levels.

      • Previous benthic impact results can provide an indication of the level at which monitoring should commence.

    • The same sediment samples collected for Level 1 or Level 2 sampling can be used for the analysis required by Level 3 sampling.

      • Sites are not required to collect new sediment samples.

    • Transects:

      • In cases where a transect overlaps with another site, the direction of the overlapping transect should be adjusted.

      • The same applies to any transect/sampling station overlapping with land.

      • Transect directions should also be adjusted to avoid sampling in areas where water depth changes rapidly along the transect.

      • In all cases, each transect should be as close to 90 degrees from each other as possible.

      • In cases where multiple cages are located in close proximity, transects should be located at the edge of the last cage site.

    • Given the low complexity associated with Level 1 and Level 2 sampling and analysis, it is advisable for sites to conduct monitoring not only at the required timings by the indicator but also prior to those timings

      • The results can indicate the need for Level 3 sampling at the timings required by the indicator, thereby assisting in monitoring planning.

Ecological Quality Status (EQS) categories

  • Ecological Quality Status (EQS) categories are used to determine the benthic status (see more details on the categories in the Useful Resources section).

Compliance Framework

  • A numerical scoring method that combines all indicator data collected from each sampling zone is used to determine the EQS Category and benthic status:

    • The method requires calculating the mean value for each indicator in each sampling zone to determine the Indicator EQS Score for that zone.

    • Next, an overall Zone EQS Score is calculated by combining the Indicator EQS Scores.

    • The overall Zone EQS Score is used to determine the final EQS Category for each sampling zone and the ‘acceptable’ benthic status.

      • In the case of cages, the EQS Category of the Reference Zone will determine the EQS Categories for ‘acceptable’ benthic status of the sampling zones.

Sampling Timing

  • Sampling is required to be conducted during the period when the benthic impact is expected to be highest, i.e. at peak impact, and uses proxies for determining peak impact:

    • Peak biomass (cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems).

    • Maximum annual bottom water temperature (cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems).

    • Peak feeding (cage culture only).

      • By considering these proxies, cage culture sites shall (see Appendix 7 (7.2.1 and 7.3.1)):

        • Provide the CAB with information on when the highest impact on the benthos is predicted to occur.

        • Determine the timing sampling that applies.

          • For cage sites with multiple peaks in feeding/biomass occurring in any year and for suspended marine mollusc systems, the requirements allow for reducing the sampling frequency as long as there have been no significant changes to farming practices. Examples of significant changes to farming practices are:

            • Modification of the disposition of cages/long lines.

            • Addition of cages/long lines.

            • Increase of biomass.

            • Change in species produced.

    • An independent person is a person who is not an employee of the ASC Certificate Holder.

    • To demonstrate competence, the person conducting sediment sampling and analysis should be able to:

      • Perform requested sampling and/or analysis.

      • Operate equipment

      • Develop, verify and validate methods.

      • Use suitable reference standards.

      • Analyse sampling and calibration results, including statements of conformity and interpretations.

      • Record, review and authorise the release of results.

      • Contribute to, or produce, reports that can clearly and concisely explain how the results are able to meet or otherwise not meet the requirement.

      • Perform internal audits on the sampling, analysis and results

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Production overview information:

    • Biomass (projected and current).

    • Feed delivered (projected and current).

    • Harvest (biomass, time of harvesting).

  • Bottom water temperature data.

  • Visual imagery confirming hard bottom.

  • Records:

    • Sampling activity, including:

      • Timing and person conducting sampling.

      • GPS sampling locations.

      • Competence, experience and training of the person conducting sampling and analysis.

      • Sampling analysis results.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Sampling was conducted according to the method and timing stated in Appendix 7 (7.2, 7.3, 7.4), by cross-checking production overview
    information and records.

  • Competence, experience and training of the person conducting sampling.

    • Adequate level of personnel competence should be verified by observations and interviews.
  • The sampling analysis results that demonstrate an acceptable EQS.

Useful Resources

The benthic monitoring method for cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems uses five Ecological Quality Status (EQS) categories to define abiotic and biotic qualities based on the seabed macrofaunal communities. The EQS categories are outlined in Table 1 below.

Table 1. Descriptions of benthic macrofauna assemblages for each of the five Ecological Quality Status (EQS) categories of the benthic monitoring method for cage culture and suspended marine mollusc systems:

2.5.4 The UoC shall demonstrate that the benthic status does not deteriorate downstream from the site’s effluent point, following the method outlined in Appendix 7 (7.5).

Indicator applicability: freshwater systems discharging into rivers

2.5.5

Indicator applicability: freshwater systems discharging into rivers

The UoC shall ensure that:

  • the person conducting sediment sampling (see Indicator 2.5.3) has the necessary competencies, experience and training; and 
  • the laboratory conducting the analysis of the samples is accredited and has approved the sampling methodology.

In cases where regulatory requirements are defined, the UoC shall ensure that the person conducting the sampling and/or the laboratory conducting the analysis complies with these requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The benthic monitoring method for freshwater systems discharging into rivers:
    • Uses sediment sampling upstream and downstream from the site outflow point to:

      • Determine the presence, composition, abundance and diversity of invertebrate fauna; and

      • Categorise the benthic status upstream and downstream as a measure of assessing the aquatic ecosystem health.

Sampling Timing

  • Should consider the seasonality of the presence of the macroinvertebrate species, e.g. insects in their larval stage of the life cycle.

    • It is recommended that sampling is conducted during summer and winter.

    • In geographical regions like Scandinavia, spring and autumn are recommended as the best times for sampling.

Location

  • Practical considerations should be taken into account regarding the sampling locations midstream (e.g. strong currents, particularly in wide, deep rivers).
    • In cases where it is impossible to collect samples in locations midstream, sites should ensure sampling all available substrate types present along the bank and in areas with slower water flow.

Gear

  • Standard equipment such as a surber sampler, handnet and grab should be used.

Sampling analysis

  • ISO/IEC 17025 is an example of laboratory accreditation.

  • For more guidance, see the section Useful Resources below.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:
  • Sampling activity, including:

  • Scope of the sampling

  • Timing and frequency of the sampling and the person conducting
    sampling.

  • GPS sampling locations.

  • Classification system.

  • Analysis results.

    • Competence, experience and training of the person conducting
      sampling and analysis.

    • Accreditation of the laboratory conducting the analysis of the
      samples.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Sampling was conducted as per the minimum requirements in Appendix 7 (7.5) by cross-checking records.

  • Sampling analysis results demonstrate benthic status downstream from the effluent discharge similar to, or better than, upstream.

  • Sampling frequency agrees with the frequency required by Appendix 7 (7.5).

Useful Resources

  • [ISO 10870:2012, Water quality — Guidelines for the selection of sampling methods and devices for benthic macroinvertebrates in fresh waters.

2.5.6 The UoC shall report to ASC the benthic status, according to ASC data submission procedures.

Indicator applicability: cage culture, suspended marine mollusc systems

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

2.6.1 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific limits on Total Nitrogen (TN) and Total Phosphorus (TP) release, according to Appendix 2(2.1).

Indicator scope: fed systems

2.6.2 (Reporting) The UoC shall annually report to ASC TN and TP release (Indicator 2.6.1), according to ASC data submission procedure.

Indicator scope: fed systems

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • TN and TP in the feed are required for the calculations. TN and TP content in the feed should be obtained from the feed supplier.

  • The suitability of the TN and TP limits per tonne of production should be reviewed if the UoC is in a Type A waterbody and needs to implement corrective actions, in accordance with Indicator 2.6.13.

  • The annual limits may need to be reduced to prevent shifts in trophic status or correct increases in limiting nutrients.

  • Equipment used to measure TN and TP per tonne of production should be calibrated according to the technical specifications. The equipment used will be based on the formula used in Appendix 8 (8.2):

    • Equipment is required for Formula 2 to measure TN and TP concentration in the influent and effluent water and the volume of the effluent water.

    • Equipment is required for Formula 3 to measure TN and TP concentration in the influent and effluent water.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The formula (outlined in Appendix 8 (8.1)) used to determine the TN and TP load per tonne of production.

  • Results of the TN and TP load per tonne of production based on the relevant calculation.

  • Equipment to measure TN and TP load per tonne of production has been calibrated according to the manufacturer’s instructions, based on the formula used in Appendix 8 (8.2).

Auditors should confirm:

  • TN and TP load per tonne of production has been determined.

  • Species-specific limits have been adhered to (where applicable) over the previous 24-month period.

    • TN and TP have been determined and reported where species-specific limits are not available.

  • The UoC has calibrated the equipment used to determine the TN and TP load per tonne of production, based on the formula used in Appendix 8 (8.2).

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.3 The UoC shall ensure that feed used contains <1% fines, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.3).

Indicator applicability: cage-fed systems with feed of a diameter ≥3mm

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Indicator 2.6.3 complements the other water quality indicators by addressing the direct release of uneaten feed in the form of fines into the environment.

  • Setting a maximum percentage of fines in the feed addresses the efficient and proper transport, storage and physical delivery of feed pellets to the site.

  • Poor performance in any of the above phases of feed handling will result in a higher percentage of fines (fine particles of feed) and potentially greater impacts on water quality, due to an increase in suspended organic particles and nutrients released into the environment.

  • Sampling of feed lots includes feed delivered as material in bulk, big bags and small bags to the site.

  • Testing by the feed manufacturer to the UoC is permissible where there is no significant risk of feed deterioration during subsequent handling, storage or application.

    • The UoC should demonstrate that deterioration in feed does not take place during the processes outlined above.

    • The UoC should report the schedule and location of testing of feed if it is not conducted on-site.

    • Rationale for not testing on site should also be reported.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The method used to determine the percentage of fines in feed, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.3).

  • The determination and documentation of a schedule and location for the testing of feed.

  • If testing takes place prior to delivery to the site, the rationale should be documented for not testing on site.

  • Calibration of sieving machines (if used) in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The rationale for the timing and location of feed sampling.

  • The UoC has appropriate testing technology on site and that, if applicable, it is calibrated as required.

  • The method used to determine the percentage of fines in feed, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.3).

  • Review testing results and confirm that results demonstrate feed contains <1% of fines.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.4 The UoC shall ensure that cages are sited under at least one of the following conditions:

Indicator scope: cages

  • In water that is at least twice the cage depth; or,
  • ≥10m above the bottom of the waterbody; or,
  • During periods at >75% peak biomass, the velocity of the current below the cages is >0.1 m/s, measured according to Appendix 8 (8.4)1212An exemption applies to sites situated in areas classified as having a “hard bottom”. Evidence is required to support the classification “hard bottom”..

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should initially determine the depth of the waterbody in comparison to the depth of the cage.

    • Measurements should take place at the lowest water level and from the bottom of the cage.

    • Depth should also be measured from the outer circumference of the culture containment space, i.e. excluding predator nets, mortality collection chambers etc.

    • In tidal systems, the depth should be measured at mean low water spring tide (MLWS).

  • If the depth of the water column (surface to seafloor) is less than 10m or less than double the cage depth, the UoC should measure the current velocity below the cage to determine whether the >0.1 m/s threshold is met.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Results of measurements which demonstrate that all cages in the UoC meet the depth/current velocity requirements in Indicator 2.6.4.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The UoC has provided evidence demonstrating that all cage systems meet the siting requirements outlined in Indicator 2.6.4.

  • If mean current velocity is used to meet the requirement, the UoC has provided evidence that measurements were taken during periods with >75% peak biomass.

Useful Resources

  • An example of how to measure current velocity below cages can be found under Section 2.1 of the following document: Marine Scotland (2015): A Technical Standard for Scottish Finfish Aquaculture.

2.6.5 The UoC shall ensure that the Receiving Waterbody (RW) has been classified per site as Type A, B or C, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.5).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should initially define the boundaries of the Receiving Waterbody (RW) based on hydrological characteristics, which determines its sensitivity to nutrient enrichment.

    • Hydrodynamically isolated embayments (HIEs) should be treated as separate waterbodies during the classification process.

  • Marine waterbodies include:

    • Off-shore and inshore coastal systems.

    • More enclosed waterbodies susceptible to seawater intrusion through tidal exchange or storm surges.

  • Exposed near-shore waterbodies (i.e. not in a bay or channelised system) and offshore waterbodies will be classified as Type C.

  • Once the boundaries of the RW are defined, HRT should be calculated unless the RW is an exposed near-shore or offshore waterbody.
    • The area and average depth of the waterbody need to be determined.
    • The cross-sectional area of the waterbody outflow or channel is required to calculate flow rate.
      • A transect should be determined from one side of the outflow/channel to the other side.
      • The length (in metres) of the transect is multiplied by the average depth of the transect to determine the cross-sectional area.
      • The cross-sectional area in then multiplied by the flow velocity (V). The result of this calculation is the flow rate (Q).
    • If a marine waterbody has HRT ≥5 days, it is a Type A, if it is ≤ 5 days, it is Type C.
  • Determining flow rate and levels of Total Suspended Solids (TSS) will distinguish between Type B and C freshwater bodies.
  • Flow rate can be obtained from regulatory bodies. Low flow then needs to be calculated by plotting the cumulative distribution of the data and calculating the 25th percentile of the cumulative distribution.
    • This can be calculated in Microsoft Excel using the cumulative distribution function. The 25th percentile (or quartile) can then be calculated.
  • Waterbody types designated under national legislation should be used only if the following are met:
    • The classification includes area-based water quality monitoring.
    • Targets are used to determine good ecological status. An example is the Water Framework Directive.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A map of the Receiving Waterbody, which outlines:

    • The area and average depth of the waterbody; and,

    • The location where flow rate (Q) was determined; or,
    • That the site is in a RW which is an exposed near-shore or off-shore marine RW (Type C only).

  • The waterbody classification, which includes outputs from HRT, flow rate and TSS calculations.

    • The methods used to measure flow rate and TSS, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.5 and 8.12).

    • If applicable, evidence that demonstrates alternative methodologies to calculate TSS or flow rate are equivalent to the ones in Appendix 8 (8.5).

Auditors should confirm:

  • A map has been presented by the UoC which outlines the RW, and which supports the classification of the RW.

  • The results of the HRT calculation and flow rate/TSS measurements conducted by the UoC.

    • These results will support the RW classification determined by the UoC.

  • Evidence presented by the UoC, demonstrating the methods used to measure flow rate and TSS, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.5 and 8.12).

Useful Resources

Steps to determine whether the RW is a HIE are as follows:

  1. If the site is in a waterbody that has been identified as a HIE by a regulatory body, this will form the boundaries of the RW.

  2. Review the characteristics of the RW and determine if at least one of the following is identified:

    • The RW has poor connectivity to deep offshore waters, and/or;

    • The RW is sheltered from energetic conditions e.g., inflows, currents, exposure to onshore or monsoonal winds, and/or;

    • The hypolimnion is periodically or permanently poorly flushed.

Where the RW shares these characteristics, it is possible to demonstrate the RW is not a HIE. The steps to demonstrate that the RW is not a HIE are as follows:

  1. Identify the narrowest point in the embayment opening (red line in Figure 1).

  2. Establish two transects of length, which start at the narrowest point and extend in and out of the embayment (red dashed line in Figure 1).

  3. Collect water samples at 0.5m depth from an equal number of equally spaces sites in each transect.

  4. Analyse water samples for concentrations of chloride, conductivity, salinity, TN or TP. Analytical methods for TN and TP can be found in Appendix 8 (8.12).

  5. Plot the concentrations of the parameter analysed in step 4 against their position on the transects.

  6. Based on the results from step 5, determine whether there is a statistically significant increasing or decreasing trend in concentrations moving from the furthest offshore to the most enclosed site.

  7. An embayment is hydrologically isolated when a statistically significant increasing or decreasing trend in concentrations has been determined.

Figure 1. Tracer sampling points along a transect for HIE determination.

  • If measurements of HRT or flow rates are not available, publicly accessible global databases can be used to obtain annual outflow estimates. Data sources include:

    • HydroAtlas, accessed November 22, 2023: https://www.hydrosheds.org/hydroatlas

    • G-RUN: Global Runoff Reconstruction, accessed November 2023: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.9228176

  • Google Earth Pro can be used to estimate the area and average depth of a waterbody to help calculate the HRT, accessed May 2024: Earth Versions – Google Earth and Measure distance & elevation – Google Earth Help

  • Examples of credible secondary sources for flow rates include government flow monitoring and modelling, as well as publicly available databases, including:

    • WWF Risk Filter Suite, accessed November 22, 2023: https://riskfilter.org/

    • Water Risk Atlas, accessed November 22, 2023: https://www.wri.org/aqueduct

  • Guides on how to calculate cumulative distribution (NORMDIST function) and the 25th percentile/quartile (QUARTILE function) for the flow rate data from secondary sources, using Microsoft Excel:

    • NORMDIST function, accessed November 27, 2024: NORMDIST function – Microsoft Support

    • QUARTILE function, accessed November 27, 2024: QUARTILE function – Microsoft Support

2.6.6 The UoC shall define the Waterbody Unit of Management (WUM), following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.6).

An exception applies where a WUM is already defined, in which case the UoC shall provide evidence of the defined WUM.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The following characteristics should be used to define the Waterbody Unit of Management (WUM):

    • The WUM reflects a logical geographic scope, for example, a lake and its catchment area.

    • The boundaries of the waterbody reflect the ability to realistically manage eutrophication risk within it.

    • Boundary setting should consider hydro-morphology, bathymetry, water movement and stratification characteristics.

    • Areas with high risk of adverse impacts due to cumulative effects, for example HIEs in larger waterbodies, should be a separate WUM.

    • Areas established for water quality monitoring at a national or regional level.

    • The Water Quality Advisory Committee (WQAC) can resolve issues with defining the WUM where the WUM boundaries are not clear.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A map of the WUM which includes the components outlined in Appendix 8 (8.6).

    • The map should be updated on an annual basis where required.

  • The results of measurements to confirm if the WUM is a HIE (if applicable).

Auditors should confirm:

  • A map of the WUM has been developed and presented by the UoC, according to the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.6).

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.7 The UoC shall ensure that the person conducting water quality monitoring has the necessary competencies, experience and training.

The UoC shall ensure that the person defining the WUM has the necessary competencies. In cases where regulatory requirements are defined, the UoC shall ensure that the person defining the WUM complies with these requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • To demonstrate competence, personnel responsible for conducting water quality analysis and defining the WUM should be able to:

    • Perform the required sampling and/or analysis.

    • Operate sampling/analytical equipment.

    • Develop, change, verify and validate methods.

    • Use suitable reference standards.

    • Analyse sampling and calibration results, including statements of conformity and interpretations.

    • Record, review and authorise the release of results.

    • Contribute to or produce reports that can clearly and concisely explain whether the results meet the requirements.

    • Have completed relevant training modules.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The personnel responsible for conducting water quality analysis and defining the WUM have competencies to do so, for example a suitable level of education and/or experience.

    • Where applicable, the personnel meet national requirements/qualifications for the spatial definition and/or management of waterbodies.

  • Relevant training modules have been completed by the personnel responsible for conducting water quality analysis and defining the WUM.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The personnel responsible for conducting water quality analysis and defining the WUM have the necessary competencies.

    • Where applicable, national requirements/qualifications are met by the personnel defining the WUM.

  • Evidence has been presented that relevant training modules have been completed.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.8 The UoC shall establish a Water Quality Monitoring Network (WQMN), following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7).

An exception applies where a WQMN is already established, in which case the UoC shall participate in the WQMN.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Evidence of spatial management at a national/regional level for water quality can be used by the UoC to demonstrate that the intent of Indicator 2.6.8 has been met. To use this evidence, the following should be met:

    • The boundaries of waterbodies are defined.

    • Waterbodies are managed to ensure water quality remains at a ‘Good’ or ‘Very Good’ status.

    • Where required, corrective actions are implemented by the regulator and complied with to ensure water quality status improves.

    • Examples of spatial management at a national/regional level include the European Union Water Framework Directive.
  • It is the responsibility of the UoC to conduct outreach to ASC Certified sites and non-certified sites belong to ASC Certificate Holders if a Water Quality Monitoring Network (WQMN) has not been established.
    • Examples of outreach can include:

      • Copies of correspondence (written and email).

      • Agendas and minutes of meetings.

      • Third-party stakeholder testimony.

  • As per Appendix 8, section 8.7, a Terms of Reference (ToR) document shall be drafted and agreed upon by all members of the WQMN upon formation, which includes the following:

    • The membership list and commitments from members to meet the WQMN requirements, as outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7.1).

    • The assignment of a focal point, who will coordinate data sharing, the drafting of the ToR and agreement to the ToR by all members of the WQMN.

      • The focal point should ideally be a rotating position, though determination is left to discretion of the WQMN membership.
    • A commitment to review the ToR on a regular basis (for example every 12 months) or as and when required, such as when changes in membership of the WQMN occur, or when the waterbody demonstrates evidence of excessive nutrient loading, eutrophication or trophic status shifts.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An agreed map of the WUM by members of the WQMN, which includes the components outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7).
    • The map should be updated on an annual basis where required.

  • Evidence of outreach efforts and responses (where applicable) to ASC Certified site and non-certified sites belong to ASC Certificate Holders if a WQMN needs to be established.

  • If a WQMN has been established, the UoC presents evidence that they have joined the WQMN or the UoC can demonstrate the spatial management of water quality at a national/regional level.

  • A ToR has been agreed upon by all members of the WQMN, which includes commitments to the WQMN requirements, as outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7.1).

Auditors should confirm:

  • A map of the WUM has been developed by the WQMN and presented by the UoC, which includes the components outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7).

  • Evidence of outreach efforts and responses to ASC Certified site and non-certified sites belong to ASC Certificate Holders if a WQMN needs to be established.

    • Auditor discretion should be used to determine if sufficient levels of outreach has been conducted, when such outreach has not been reciprocated.

  • Evidence that the UoC has formed/joined a WQMN, or that the UoC presents evidence that water quality is managed at a national/regional level.

  • A ToR has been presented, which has been agreed upon by all members of the WQMN. The ToR includes commitments to the WQMN requirements, as outlined in Appendix 8 (8.7.1).

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.9 The UoC shall conduct a water quality survey and determine the water quality baseline, including the trophic status, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.8).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The data collected as part of the 24-month site level monitoring survey is submitted by the UoC to the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • The water quality baseline is based on 24-months of monitoring data from the site level monitoring survey. However, the following phased approach is permitted when sites do not have sufficient data prior to the initial audit:

  • The water quality baseline is characterised by the ASC Water Quality Calculator, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.8).

  • The baseline should be conducted per site and per waterbody. The results should then be shared with members of the WQMN.

  • The baseline determines whether primary production in the waterbody is limited by nitrogen (N), phosphorous (P), or if it is co-limited. Other factors (than N or P) may be limiting primary productivity in a waterbody.

    • The UoC should present evidence of these other limiting factors (e.g. temperature or altitude) where applicable.
  • Harmful algal blooms (HABs) and Adverse Turnover Events (ATEs) are required to be reported as part of the baseline characterisation. The number of ATEs and HABs that have occurred can be recorded by conducting the following:

    • Reviewing news media and consulting local stakeholders. Alternatively, reviewing data collected by regulatory bodies where available.

    • Reporting the number of ATEs and HABs which have resulted in fish mortality events (farmed or wild) or the mortality of other aquatic species.

    • Reporting instances where fish mortality events or loss of other aquatic species can be attributed to natural phenomena. These instances will not count towards the frequency limits for ATEs and HABs.

    • Reporting the number of ATEs and HABs, as determined by national or regional regulatory/scientific organisations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The methodology and analytical methods used to conduct site level monitoring survey are in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.8).

  • The sampling methodology for collecting 24-months of data for the site level monitoring survey, if this is not available at the initial audit.

  • The results of the site level monitoring survey, as determined by the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • The results of the 24-month baseline characterisation, as determined by the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • Records of HABs and ATEs from the last 10 years.

Auditors should confirm:

  • A water quality monitoring survey has been conducted by the UoC. Results are presented from the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • A sampling methodology has been presented for collecting 24-months of data for the site level monitoring survey, if this is not available at the initial audit.

  • The data collected for the site level monitoring survey followed the methodology and analytical measures outlined in Appendix 8 (8.8).

  • A water quality baseline has been characterised. Results are presented from the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • The results of the review by the UoC into adverse turnover events and harmful algal blooms in the waterbody.

Useful Resources

  • Vollenweider, R.A., Rinaldi, A. and Montanari, G. (1992) Eutrophication, structure and dynamics of a marine coastal system: results of ten-year monitoring along the Emilia-Romagna Coast (Northwest Adriatic Sea). Marine Coastal Eutrophication, Proceedings of an International Conference, Bologna, Italy, 21–24 March 1990, Pages 63-106: https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-444-89990-3.50014-6
  • More information about the equations used for TSI assessment, including the relevant peer-reviewed scientific literature, is provided in Carlson, R.E. and Simpson, J. (1996) A Coordinator’s Guide to Volunteer Lake Monitoring Methods. North American Lake Management Society, 96 p.

2.6.10 The UoC shall, after the determination of the water quality baseline, conduct monitoring of the water quality parameters listed below, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.8)1313An exemption applies if the mean of Secchi Disk (SD) depth calculated over any rolling two-year period remains ≥10m.:

  • Total Nitrogen (TN); and,
  • Total Phosphorous (TP); and,
  • Dissolved Oxygen (DO); and,
  • Secchi Disk (SD) depth; and,
  • Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Quarterly monitoring ensures the UoC can capture any seasonal or inter-annual variations in the data collected.

  • Measurements should be timed to coincide with, or immediately follow, annual turnover events when the waterbody is not permanently stratified (holomictic).

  • The UoC should calibrate equipment used to measure DO, TN, TP, SD and Chl-a according to the technical specifications of the equipment.

  • The UoC should conduct measurements of the parameters in-situ.

    • Samples may be sent for laboratory analysis, however variability with sample maintenance during transit can lead to inconsistent results. This is particularly evident with DO and Chl-a samples.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentation outlining the sampling plan to conduct quarterly monitoring and that is in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.8).

  • Quarterly monitoring data has been collected and submitted to the ASC Water Quality Calculator. Data should be submitted at least annually.

  • Evidence that quarterly monitoring data has been timed with annual turnover events (where applicable).

  • That equipment to measure DO, TN, TP, SD and Chl-a has been calibrated according to technical specifications.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The sampling methodology to conduct quarterly monitoring is in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.8).

  • The UoC has conducted quarterly monitoring of the water quality parameters and submitted data to the ASC Water Quality Calculator at least annually.

  • Evidence has been provided demonstrating the UoC has calibrated equipment to measure DO, TN, TP, SD and Chl-a in accordance with the technical specifications.

Useful Resources

  • Paerl, H.W., Scott, J.T., McCarthy, M.J., Newell, S.E., Gardner, W.S., Havens, K.E., Hoffman, D.K., Wilhelm, S.W. and Wurtsbaugh, W.A., 2016. It takes two to tango: when and where dual nutrient (N & P) reductions are needed to protect lakes and downstream ecosystems. Environmental science & technology, 50(20), pp.10805-10813.

  • Information on the appropriate use of Secchi Disks can be found here: ‘What is a Secchi disk’, accessed November 22, 2023: https://www.nalms.org/s
    ecchidipin/monitoring-methods/the-secchi-disk/what-is-a-secchi-disk/
  • Example of a method for Chl-a measurements made using ethanol extraction followed by spectrophotometric measurement at wavelengths 665 and 750nm (using accredited methods: EPA method 445.0: Method 445.0 In Vitro Determination of Chlorophyll a and Pheophytin ain Marine and Freshwater Algae by Fluorescence, accessed November 22, 2023: https://cfpub.epa.gov/si/si_public_record_report.cfm?Lab=NERL&dirEntryId=309417

  • Cost effective example for measuring using in-situ Chl-a using a field spectroflurometer include the FluoroSense handheld fluorometer manufactured by Turner Designs and the YSI handheld meter with EXO1 (#599080) or EXO2 (#599201) sondes.

  • Hamdhani, H., Eppehimer, D.E., Walker, D. and Bogan, M.T. (2021) Performance of a Handheld Chlorophyll-a Fluorometer: Potential Use for Rapid Algae Monitoring. Water, 13, 1409: https://doi.org/10.3390/w13101409

  • Kuha, J., Järvinen, M., Salmi, P. and Karjalainen, J. (2020). Calibration of in situ chlorophyll fluorometers for organic matter. Restoration of Eutrophic Lakes, 847, 4377-4387: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10750-019-04086-z

2.6.11 The UoC shall, based on the monitoring of the water quality parameters, ensure that there is no decline in trophic status compared to the water quality baseline determined, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.8).

2.6.12 The UoC shall, based on the monitoring of the water quality parameters, ensure that there is no upward rate of change >25% over the previous 24 months, for any of the water quality parameters listed below, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.8):

  • TN; and,
  • TP; and,
  • Chl-a; and,
  • Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD).

2.6.13 The UoC shall implement a nutrient reduction plan when at least one of the following is identified:

  • TN, TP or Chl-a has increased by ≥5 index points according to Table 2 in Appendix 8 (8.8), compared to the water quality baseline; or,
  • TN, TP or Chl-a increased by ≥15% over the past 24 months; or,
  • The distance from the surface to the zone of oxygen depletion or to the zone of anoxia has decreased by ≥25% over the past 24 months; or,
  • BOD has increased by ≥15% over the past 24 months; or,
  • ≥1 adverse turnover event or ≥1 harmful algal bloom within the past 10 years.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Quarterly monitoring of TN, TP and Chl-a will determine whether there has been a change in the status of the limiting nutrients or a decline in trophic status. BOD will also need to be calculated annually. The calculated data will be compared to the water quality baseline.

  • Quarterly monitoring data will be submitted to the ASC Water Quality Calculator at least annually. The ASC Water Quality Calculator will determine rates of change in the limiting nutrient(s) and trophic status compared to the baseline.

  • A decline in trophic status will be determined when the next Trophic Status Index (TSI) breakpoint has been exceeded, in accordance with Table 2 in Appendix 8 (8.8).

    • Exceedance of the next TSI breakpoint will occur when one parameter falls into the next TSI category.
  • The ASC Water Quality Calculator also determines whether one of the scenarios in Indicator 2.6.13 has occurred based on the quarterly monitoring data.

    • If one of scenarios has occurred, an action plan needs to be implemented to reduce nutrients released by the site and/or to have improved the efficiency of the feed used.

    • The action plan should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Monitoring data has been submitted annually to the ASC Water Quality Calculator and results have been obtained.

  • Results will determine the trophic status and status of TN, TP, Chl-a and BOD, in accordance with Indicator 2.6.12. Results will also be compared to the water quality baseline after the first annual submission.

    • Any upward transitions in trophic status at the compared to the water quality baseline will be determined based on the results from the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

    • Results from the ASC Water Quality will determine rate of change for TN, TP, Chl-a and BOD compared to the water quality baseline, specifically whether this exceeds 25% over the previous 24 months.

  • Results from the ASC Water Quality Calculator will be obtained to determine whether one of the scenarios in Indicator 2.6.13 has occurred.

    • This will be based on the TN, TP, Chl-a and BOD data submitted to the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

    • It will also be based on submissions of the number of HABs and ATEs to the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

    • If one of the scenarios has occurred, an action plan will have been documented which will reduce nutrient nutrients released by the site and/or to have improved the efficiency of the feed used.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The UoC presents evidence demonstrating monitoring data has been submitted annually to the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

  • The UoC presents the outputs from the ASC Water Quality Calculator, which demonstrates whether there has been a decline in trophic status or upward rate of change >25% for TN, TP, Chl-a and BOD.

  • The UoC presents evidence which determines whether one or more of the scenarios in Indicator 2.6.13 have occurred.

  • A specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound action plan has been documented by the UoC, and has been presented, if one of the scenarios in Indicator 2.6.13 has occurred.

Useful Resources

  • Trophic status is determined using the Carlson Index values (0-100), with ‘breakpoints’ set at minimum internals of 10 index points.

    • Carlson’s Index is used to classify Type A waterbodies and consists of four separate normalised indices: Chlorophyll-a, Total Phosphorous, Total Nitrogen and Secchi Disk transparency measurements.

    • Normalised TSI values range from 0 (ultra-oligotrophic) to 100 (hypereutrophic). A TSI of less than 40 is indicative of oligotrophic conditions, while TSI values greater than 50 are indicative of eutrophic conditions. TSI values between 40 and 50 are indicative of mesotrophic conditions.

  • More information about the equations used for TSI assessment, including the relevant peer-reviewed scientific literature, is provided in Carlson, R.E. and Simpson, J. (1996) A Coordinator’s Guide to Volunteer Lake Monitoring Methods. North American Lake Management Society, 96 p.

2.6.14 The UoC shall report annually to ASC the WUM hydraulic characteristics, according to ASC data submission procedures.

2.6.15 The UoC shall report annually to ASC the water quality monitoring results and the BOD value, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ASC data collection spreadsheets will be completed with data used to characterise the baseline of the RW, in accordance with Appendix 8 (8.8.4).

  • The data reported will facilitate the implementation of the requirements for sites located in Type A waterbodies.

  • Auditors will have access to the reported data to support with the auditing process.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Complete data collection spreadsheets and results from the ASC Water Quality Calculator that confirm data has been submitted.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Data has been submitted by the UoC and results have been obtained from the ASC Water Quality Calculator.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.16 The UoC shall use a treatment system prior to the discharge of effluent water that ensures:

  • ≥65% of Total Suspended Solids (TSS) are captured; and,
  • concentration of settleable solids in effluent water is <3.3ml/L.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Methods to measure Total Suspended Solids (TSS) can be found in Appendix 8 (8.12).

  • Concentration of settleable solids (ml/L) can be measured by calculating the volume of solids that settles to the bottom of a conical cone (Imhoff cone) in one hour.

  • More sophisticated methods such as spectrophotometer readings can also be used to measure settable solids.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Details and location of the system used to treat effluent prior to discharge.

  • Evidence regular testing of TSS and settleable solids has taken place. Quarterly testing would demonstrate best practice.

  • Results from the testing of point source releases which demonstrate ≥65% of TSS are captured and the concentration of settleable solids in effluent water is consistently <3.3ml/L.

Auditors should confirm:

  • A treatment is in place and located prior to the point of discharge.

  • Results of testing from the UoC which confirm the treatment system captures ≥65% of suspended solids and that the concentration of settleable solids in effluent water is <3.3ml/L.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.17 The UoC shall conduct monitoring of TN, TP and TSS upstream from the inflow point and downstream from the outflow point, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.9), if one of the following conditions applies:

Indicator scope: waterbody Type B

  • The site effluent flow contribution to the receiving water flow is >10%, as calculated following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.10); or,
  • The site effluent enters a river or channel <1km upstream of a Type A waterbody.

2.6.18 The UoC shall, if Indicator 2.6.17 applies, ensure there is <25% increase in TN, TP and TSS concentrations between the measured upstream concentration and the calculated downstream concentration.

Indicator scope: waterbody Type B

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The methods for measuring TN, TP and TSS can be found under Appendix 8 (8.12).

  • The UoC can measure flow contribution, TN, TP and TSS upstream from the inflow point of the first site and immediately downstream of the outflow point of the last site in a waterbody.

    • This may reduce sampling costs when there are multiple sites discharging point source effluent releases to a Type B waterbody near each other.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Maps demonstrating the sampling locations are upstream from the inflow point and downstream from the outflow point.

  • Annual calculation of site effluent flow contribution to the receiving water flow based on the methodology in Appendix 8 (8.10).

  • Results of the site effluent flow contribution calculation, which demonstrate whether the contribution is greater than or less than 10%.

  • If Indicator 2.6.17 applies, results of measurements of TN, TP and TSS upstream from the inflow point and downstream from the outflow point.

  • Results of calculations to demonstrate there is <25% increase in site effluent flow between upstream and downstream sample sites.

Auditors should confirm:

  • A map has been presented which demonstrates the sampling locations are upstream from the inflow point and downstream from the outflow point.

  • The UoC has conducted an annual calculation of the site effluent flow contribution to the receiving water flow.

  • Whether the site effluent flow contribution calculation presented by the UoC exceeds 10%.

  • If Indicator 2.6.17 applies, the UoC has presented quarterly results of TN, TP and TSS measurements from sampling locations upstream from the inflow point and downstream from the outflow point, whilst still following the sampling method in Appendix 8 (8.8 and 8.9).

  • Results of calculations presented to demonstrate there is <25% increase in site effluent flow between upstream and downstream sample sites.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.19 The UoC shall conduct monitoring of DO concentration and DO saturation, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.11).

2.6.20 The UoC shall demonstrate that the weekly average of daily DO saturation is ≥65% in freshwater and ≥70% in seawater1414Waterbodies with salinity levels 30-49 ppt (parts per thousand) shall be considered as seawater for this Indicator..

2.6.21 The UoC shall demonstrate that ≤5% of the weekly averages of daily DO concentrations are <2mg/l.  An exception applies if the UoC cannot demonstrate this, in which case the UoC shall:

  • Demonstrate ≥70% saturation by conducting continuous monitoring using an electronic probe and recorder with a 15-minute sampling frequency for at least one week; or,
  • Ensure percentage saturation results are consistent with results from an ‘upstream, near-field’ non-impacted reference location, at least 500m upstream of the site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For both diffuse-source and point-source effluent releases, the UoC should monitor and record percent saturation of DO.

  • All measurements should be taken using a calibrated oxygen meter or equivalent method.

  • The percent saturations should then be calculated based on the monitoring data.

  • The analytical methods for DO sampling can be found in Appendix 8 (8.12).

  • Any missed samples or deviations in sampling time should be accompanied by a written justification.

  • The UoC can measure DO concentration and saturation immediately downstream of the last site in a waterbody whilst still following the sampling method in Appendix 8 (8.11).

    • This may reduce sampling costs when there are multiple sites discharging point source effluent releases to a Type B waterbody near each other.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The oxygen meter has been calibrated according to the technical specifications.

  • Records of measurement locations, demonstrating monitoring took place immediately downstream from the outflow point, or in the receiving waterbody downstream from the site for diffuse source releases.

  • Records of daily monitoring of DO concentration and saturation, which result in weekly averages of daily DO saturation.

  • ≤5% of the weekly averages of daily DO concentrations are 2mg/l.

  • Written justifications are maintained for any missed samples or deviations in sampling times.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The UoC has calibrated the oxygen meter according to the technical specifications.

  • Measurement locations were immediately downstream from the outflow point, or in the receiving waterbody downstream from the site for diffuse source releases.

  • Weekly averages of daily DO saturation are presented by the UoC and that the averages are ≥65% for freshwater and ≥70% for seawater.

  • The UoC has presented evidence that ≤5% of weekly samples fall under 2 mg/L DO.

  • Written justifications are provided for any missed samples or deviations in sampling times.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.6.22 The UoC shall conduct DO monitoring downstream from the outflow point and shall demonstrate that daily diurnal DO (DDDO) fluctuation is ≤65% saturation, following the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.11).

Indicator scope: point source systems in waterbody types A and B

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For UoCs located in tidal systems, timing of measurements should correspond with high and low tides, to reflect variations related to the tidal regime.

  • The UoC can conduct DO monitoring immediately downstream of the last site in a waterbody whilst still following the sampling method in Appendix 8 (8.11).

    • This may reduce sampling costs when there are multiple sites discharging point source effluent releases to a Type B waterbody near each other.

  • The methods outlined in Appendix (8.11.2 and 8.11.3) shall be used to record DO concentrations used to determine daily diurnal DO (DDDO).

  • Any missed samples or deviations in sampling time should be accompanied by a written justification.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records that DO measurements correspond to high and low tides in tidal systems.

  • The location of the sampling point, demonstrating that measurements have taken place downstream from the outflow point.

  • Results of daily DO monitoring and DDDO fluctuation calculations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • DO measurements have taken place at high and low tides in tidal systems.

  • DO measurements have taken place downstream from the outflow point.

  • The UoC has presented results of the DDDO calculations based on DO measurements collected in accordance with the methods outlined in Appendix 8.11.1 and 8.11.2.

  • Confirm the fluctuation level based on the DDDO calculation is ≤65% saturation level.

  • Written justifications were provided if there were any missed samples or deviations in the sampling time.

Useful Resources

N/A

Salinisation 2.7

2.7.1 The UoC shall1515An exemption applies where ponds are located in naturally brackish or saline environments. use low permeable liners.

Indicator applicability: brackish or saltwater pond culture

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Brackish water has a salinity of 0.5-29.9 ppt, while seawater has a salinity of > 29.9 ppt.

  • Low permeable liners include liners made from:

    • Plastic,

    • Imported clays,

    • Ripping and re-compaction of in situ clays, mixing with bentonite,

    • Geo-membranes, and

    • Composite liners.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records demonstrating the installation and maintenance of low permeable liners in ponds.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Low permeable liners have been installed and maintained in ponds.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.7.2 The UoC shall not discharge brackish or saltwater effluent over land.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The location and/or route of the discharge of brackish or saltwater effluent to demonstrate discharge does not take place over land.
    • Examples of evidence may include maps/plans of the discharge locations/routes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Evidence has been presented, such as maps/plans, to demonstrate brackish or saltwater effluent is not discharged over land.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.7.3 The UoC shall only discharge effluent water of a salinity level equal to or lower than the salinity level of the receiving waterbody or natural wetland. An exception applies to waterbodies and natural wetlands that have naturally periodic varying salinity levels, in which case the salinity level of the effluent water shall be within range of the natural variation.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Salinity levels are: Freshwater (limnetic; <0.5 ppt), slightly saline (oligohaline; 0.5-4.9 ppt), moderate saline (mesohaline; 5-17.9 ppt), highly saline (polyhaline; 18-29.9 ppt) and seawater (euhaline; 30-34.9 ppt).

  • River estuaries are an example of a waterbody that have periodic varying salinity levels. These can also be referred to as poikilohaline waterbodies.

  • Salinity testing of effluent water in the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands should be conducted.

    • Salinity levels in the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands may be obtained from credible sources, e.g. results of government monitoring.

  • To comply with the exception in the indicator, salinity testing in the waterbody or natural wetland should take place. Alternatively, test results can be obtained from credible sources, e.g. scientific or government body.

    • Results should then be compared to the salinity level of the effluent water to determine whether it is within the range of natural variation for the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Results of salinity testing for effluent water and in the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands.

  • If applicable, reports or measurements determining whether waterbodies and natural wetlands have naturally varying salinity levels.

    • Reports or measurements determining whether the salinity level of the effluent water is within the range of the natural variation for the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Salinity test results have been presented which determine one of the following:
    • Salinity level of the effluent water is equal to or lower than the salinity level of the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands.

    • Salinity level of the effluent water is within the range of natural variation for the receiving waterbody or natural wetlands that have naturally varying salinity levels.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.7.4 The UoC shall ensure that freshwater-wells used for culture water do not exceed a conductivity of 1,500 micro-mhos per centimeter (µmho/cm) or chloride concentration of 300mg/L.

An exception applies where well-monitoring is not permitted by applicable law, in which case regulatory records shall be obtained to provide evidence of conductivity levels.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Freshwater wells with a conductivity or chloride concentration above the thresholds in Indicator 2.7.4 will demonstrate that salinisation has taken place.

  • Specific conductance or chloride concentration should be monitored at a frequency adapted to fluctuations due to natural factors, such as seasonal rains.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records of specific conductance of freshwater wells on, or in proximity to the site (within 1km radius).

    • Records should demonstrate monitoring has taken place at least every six months and considered natural factors, such as seasonal rains.

  • Regulatory records obtained where applicable, to demonstrate well-monitoring is not permitted by law.

    • Records shall contain evidence of conductivity testing.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Monitoring records are available for freshwater wells in proximity to the site, which demonstrate either conductivity or chloride concentration is below the relevant threshold specified in Indicator 2.7.4.
    • Monitoring has taken place at least every six months and considered natural factors, such as seasonal rains.

  • Regulatory records are available for instances where well-monitoring is not permitted by law.

  • The records demonstrate conductivity testing has taken place.

Useful Resources

  • Hand-held refractometers can be used to measure salinity. These devices are appropriate for salinities of approximately 2 or 3 ppt, but they are not sensitive enough to determine if sites are causing the salinisation of freshwater bodies.

  • The quickest and easiest method to evaluate salinity of water is to measure specific conductance with a conductivity meter. An alternative method is a chloride test kit, which is typically cheaper.

Biosolids 2.8

2.8.1 The UoC shall ensure that biosolids are appropriately contained.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should develop and implement a biosolids management plan, which includes procedures relating to the containment of biosolids.

  • The appropriate containment of biosolids should consider the risk of runoff during anticipated and/or recurring extreme weather events, such as tropical storms or flooding.

    • This risk is higher when biosolids are removed from culture systems, canals and/or treatment systems.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents demonstrating the appropriate containment of biosolids. An example may be a biosolids management plan.
    • The management plan may include a flow diagram that outlines key steps for the containment of biosolids.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documents, for example a biosolids management plan, have been presented which demonstrate the appropriate containment of biosolids.

  • Conformance should be confirmed through a visual inspection of the site.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.8.2 The UoC shall ensure that biosolids are not disposed or released into receiving waterbodies, natural wetlands or other ecosystems.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This requirement will mitigate impacts on water quality and the risk of salinisation, therefore supporting the implementation of Criterion 2.6 and 2.7 respectively.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records which demonstrate:

  • Information on the disposal and/or release of biosolids.

    • The location where biosolids are disposed and/or released, which confirm they are not disposed of and/or released into receiving waterbodies, natural wetlands or other ecosystems.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records have been presented which demonstrate biosolids are not disposed of and/or released into receiving waterbodies, natural wetlands or other ecosystems.

  • There is no evidence of the discharge and/or release of biosolids into receiving waterbodies, natural wetlands or other ecosystems during the audit.

    • This may be carried out through a visual inspection of the site and any surrounding waterbodies.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.8.3 The UoC shall only re-use uncontaminated biosolids.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The following outlines examples of the purposes for uncontaminated biosolids re-use:

    • Fertiliser in agriculture.

    • Maintenance and building of dykes.

    • Maintenance of roads or infrastructure.

    • Biogas.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents demonstrating the appropriate treatment and re-use of biosolids.
    • An example may be a biosolids management plan.
      • The management plan may include a flow diagram that outlines key steps for the treatment of biosolids prior to re-use to ensure they are uncontaminated.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documents, for example a biosolids management plan, have been presented which demonstrate only uncontaminated biosolids are re-used.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.8.4 The UoC shall dispose of biosolids responsibly if they cannot be re-used.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The responsible disposal of biosolids mitigates impacts on natural ecosystems and waterbodies.

    • Impacts may include salinisation or eutrophication.

  • The UoC should develop and implement a biosolids management plan which procedures relating to the responsible disposal of biosolids.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documents outlining the process and location of biosolids disposal.
    • The documents should demonstrate biosolids are disposed of responsibly. An example may be a biosolids management plan.
      • The management plan may include a flow diagram that outlines key steps for the disposal of biosolids.
  • If biosolids are transferred to a third party, evidence should be available to confirm that the third party has disposed of biosolids responsibly.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documents, for example a biosolids management plan, have been presented which demonstrate the responsible disposal of biosolids.

  • If biosolids are transferred to a third-party, evidence has been presented to confirm that the third-party has responsibly disposed of biosolids.

Freshwater Use 2.9

2.9.1 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a Water Efficiency Management Plan (WEMP) in areas identified as having ‘high’ or ‘extremely high’ water stress according to the Aqueduct ‘Water Risk Atlas1616https://www.wri.org/applications/aqueduct/water-riskatlas/#/?advanced=false&basemap=hydro&indicator=w_awr_def_tot_cat&lat=-14.445396942837744&lng=-142.85354599620152&mapMode=view&month=1&opacity=0.5&ponderation=DEF&predefined=false&projection=absolute&scenario=optimistic&scope=baseline&timeScale=annual&year=baseline&zoom=2View More, with the intent to reduce water consumption.

2.9.2 The UoC shall ensure the WEMP is annually reviewed and revised as necessary.

Indicator applicability: areas identified as having ’high‘ or ’extremely high‘ water stress

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Aqueduct ‘Water Risk Atlas’ measures all water-related risks. Higher values indicate higher water risk.

    • ‘Water Stress’ is an indicator under ‘Physical Risks Quantity’ and measures the ratio of total water demand to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies.

    • The site needs to check whether its location is classified as being in an area of ‘high’ or ‘extremely high’ water stress.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The ‘Water Stress’ classification of the area in which the site is located. This must match the coordinates of where the site is located.

  • A Water Efficiency Management Plan (WEMP) has been developed, implemented and maintained if the site is in an area identified as having ‘high’ or ‘extremely high’ water stress.

    • The WEMP should have specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound objectives and targets to reduce water consumption.

  • Documents demonstrating the WEMP has been reviewed annually, to determine whether it is meeting the objective of reducing water consumption.

  • Data or documents to demonstrate the WEMP is effective at reducing water consumption.

  • Revisions to the WEMP if it has not been deemed effective at reducing water consumption.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The risk of water stress according the ‘Water Risk Atlas’.

  • Evidence that a WEMP has been developed, implemented and maintained, if the site is in an area identified as having ‘high’ or ‘extremely high’ water stress.

    • Objectives and targets are in place in the WEMP which aim to reduce water consumption.

    • Evidence of an annual review of the WEMP.

    • Evidence has been presented to demonstrate the WEMP is effective at reducing water consumption.
    • Revisions to the WEMP have been made if the WEMP has not been effective at reducing water consumption.

Useful Resources

  • Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas: Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas.

2.9.3 The UoC shall monitor and record water levels in groundwater wells, and shall include the results in the WEMP.

Indicator applicability: areas identified as having ’high‘ or ’extremely high‘ water stress

An exception applies where monitoring is not permitted by applicable law, in which case regulatory records shall be obtained to provide evidence of recording of water levels.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Water levels in groundwater wells should be tested and recorded at similar times during the year.

  • Monitoring of water levels in groundwater wells determines whether water is being replenished in the ground. When water abstraction increases beyond the rate of replenishment, the result is a reduction in the water table.

    • A reduction in the water table would demonstrate that the WEMP is not effective at reducing water consumption.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Results from the monitoring of water levels in groundwater wells.

  • Documents demonstrating the monitoring results have been included in, and informed revisions of, the WEMP (where required).

  • Regulatory records which provide evidence of the recording of water levels, if monitoring is not permitted by law.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Monitoring results have been presented which demonstrate the recording of water levels in groundwater wells.

    • Results can either be from testing conducted by the site or a regulatory body if monitoring is not permitted by law.

  • Monitoring results have informed the drafting or revision of the WEMP.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.9.4 The UoC shall not use freshwater to reduce the salinity of culture water. An exception applies if discharged effluent water is desalinated.

2.9.5 The UoC shall not use salt to increase the salinity of fresh culture water. An exception applies if discharged effluent water is desalinated.

No additional guidance is provided for these indicators.

2.9.6 The UoC shall not abstract >50% volume of surface water. An exception applies if the UoC can demonstrate that the water abstraction is based on a minimum Vital Flow determined by a regulatory permit or scientific study.

2.9.7 The UoC shall return >90% of the abstracted surface water volume to its source.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Abstraction of water refers to the process of taking water from a natural source, in this case surface water.

  • Responsible abstraction, or a minimum vital flow, is important for mitigating impacts on freshwater ecosystems and water quality.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records demonstrating the volume of water abstracted from surface water and the volume returned to the source from which the water was originally abstracted.

  • A minimum vital flow has been determined by a regulatory permit or scientific study, if the exception in Indicator 2.9.6 applies.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records have been presented which demonstrate the volume of water extracted from surface water and the volume returned to the source from which the water was originally extracted.

  • Evidence of a minimum vital flow determined by a regulatory permit or scientific body, if the exception in Indicator 2.9.6 applies.
