2.10.1 The UoC shall calculate the energy use of production following the method outlined in Appendix 9 (9.3).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Tracking use of energy inputs is a necessary step in calculating the GHG emissions associated with aquaculture production and products.
    • Energy inputs include all those sources of energy used for the purpose of production, including electricity and energy carriers such as diesel or natural gas.
  • To the extent possible, Certificate Holders are encouraged to calculate energy use specific to the certified site. However, in some cases, this may be difficult to do. For example, fuel purchased may be used to supply vessels servicing many sites, potentially both certified and non-certified sites or even multiple sites or companies.
    • In these cases, a portion of the overall input may be allocated to the certified site based on a logical allocation basis.
      • For example, dividing energy inputs between sites based on the relative number of vessel trips or using the site’s relative share of production among the group of sites serviced.
  • Energy inputs to hatcheries are not included in calculations of on-site energy use. However, in cases where the juvenile stage of the supply chain is integrated with grow-out, sites may choose to include this stage in their calculations to simplify calculations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentation of energy intensity factors (e.g., MJ of energy per L of diesel) used if they are different to the default values used in the ASC Farm Standard Energy Use Data Submission Template.

  • Evidence to support the quantity of each energy input specified in calculations is available on request, along with any allocation of energy inputs between multiple sites if applicable.

    • This may be, for example, fuel purchase invoices or electricity use records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The energy use value is calculated and reported in MJ of energy per tonne of live weight production.

  • Energy use of production is calculated for either (a) the most recent completed production cycle; or (b) three consecutive years of production.

  • Documentation is provided to support input variables and calculations.

  • The ASC Farm Standard Energy Use Data Submission Template is used to demonstrate results.

Useful Resources

  • Certificate Holders are encouraged to use the ASC Farm Standard Energy Use Data Submission Template for calculating the energy intensity of production after energy inputs are quantified.

  • Additional energy intensity factors for a range of energy inputs are available from the UK Department of Energy Security and Net Zero1717DESNZ (2022). Greenhouse gas reporting: Conversion factors 2022. United Kingdom Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Available at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/greenhouse-gas-reporting-conversion-factors-2022.

2.10.2 The UoC shall calculate the feed and farm-related GHG emissions of production following the method outlined in Appendix 9 (9.4).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Consistent and transparent measurement of GHG emissions following a life cycle assessment approach is necessary to underpin effective GHG reduction and management and to inform broader efforts to understand and reduce the GHG impact of global food systems.
    • This indicator ensures that all ASC certified sites undertake this important first step in contributing to efforts to combat climate change.
  • ASC does not require the use of any particular GHG calculation framework or tool or conformance with any particular GHG methodology or standard. However, some methodological requirements are stipulated in Appendix 9 to ensure a sufficient level of consistency, completeness and accuracy of GHG calculations.
  • Certificate Holders should consider the reporting format of the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template in undertaking their calculations.
    • This includes the characterisation of GHG emissions in three distinct ways:
      • By scope (based on Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 GHG emissions as defined in the GHG Protocol),
      • By category (e.g., land use change emissions, if known; if unknown, emissions may be characterised as ‘unspecified’), and
      • By input (e.g., broad categories of feed ingredients, energy inputs, etc.).
  • To the extent possible, Certificate Holders are encouraged to calculate GHG emissions specific to the certified site. However, in some cases, this may be difficult to do. For example, fuel purchased may be used to supply vessels servicing many sites, potentially both certified and non-certified sites, or even multiple sites or companies.
    • In these cases, a portion of the overall input may be allocated to the certified site based on a logical allocation basis.
      • For example, dividing energy inputs between sites based on the relative number of vessel trips or using the site’s relative share of production among the group of sites serviced.
      • For feed inputs, because the certified site’s feed use records are needed for certification, data used for GHG calculations should be specific to the certified site.
  • GHG profiles from hatcheries are not required.
    • The hatchery or juvenile stage of the aquaculture supply chain typically accounts for a very small percentage of overall GHG emissions, and due to the varied nature of sourcing juveniles, requiring their inclusion in calculations could result in confusion and unnecessary burden. 
      • Instead, sites may account for juvenile inputs as described in Appendix 9.
    • GHG calculations may optionally still include hatchery-specific data, and efforts to reduce GHG emissions at the hatchery stage may also be included to demonstrate efforts in the site’s GHG management plan for Indicator 2.10.4.
  • GHG emissions should first be calculated relative to live weight production, as kg CO2-equivalent (CO2e) emissions per tonne of live weight production. As a final step, emissions are converted to an edible weight basis. 
    • This step is facilitated by the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template.
    • By default, the muscle fraction of the animal is the conversion factor, such that a muscle fraction of 0.5 results in an edible weight GHG value double that of the live weight basis value.
    • If, however, a portion of the non-edible fraction of the animal is used for other purposes (e.g., by-product meal), a portion of emissions may be allocated to the non-edible product.
      • In these cases, the allocation is undertaken directly within the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template following both allocation methods: dividing emissions between edible and non-edible product on the basis of their relative mass, and on the basis of their relative economic value as expressed by their revenue generation.
        • This allocation step is not applicable to bivalve and abalone shells; for these species, the muscle fraction alone is used for converting results to an edible weight basis.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • GHG profiles for feeds used, specific to the feed supplier and species or species group and updated on an annual basis, as required to be shared by the feed supplier according to Criterion 1.21 of the ASC Feed Standard and using the format of the ASC Feed Standard GHG Data Submission Template.

  • For marine salmonids only: GHG profiles for any supplying grow-out site(s) as required to be shared by the previous grow-out site(s).

  • Documentation of the source of any GHG emission factors used.

    • This may be documentation of calculation tools (e.g., the ASC GHG Calculator) or documentation of specific emission factors and their source if calculating emissions manually.
  • Documentation of the input variables used (e.g., quantity of electricity).
    • Inputs of energy should reflect those calculated in Indicator 2.10.1. All input variables should be supported by evidence such as invoices or feed use records if requested.

  • Documentation of conversion factor and, if applicable, allocation factors, used to convert GHG calculations from a live weight basis to an edible weight basis.

  • Documentation of power purchase agreements, if applicable, to demonstrate use of electricity from specific dedicated sources rather than the national or regional electricity grid.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records of GHG profiles from feed suppliers and (for marine salmonids) prior grow-out sites are available.

  • GHG emissions are calculated in kg CO2e relative to live weight production and edible weight product and recorded using the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template.

  • If using a tool other than the ASC GHG Calculator, documentation showing how the tool conforms to the methodological requirements outlined in Appendix 9;

    • This may be a signed declaration from the tool provider or highlighted elements in the tool’s user documentation.

  • Values input into the ASC GHG Calculator, another tool, or manual calculations are supported with evidence (e.g., fuel purchase invoices).

  • If undertaking calculations manually, demonstration of the calculations undertaken, including the use of GHG data from feed suppliers and (for marine salmonids) prior grow-out sites in conformance with the requirements of Appendix 9.

  • The scope of included activities reflects the requirements outlined in Appendix 9.

  • GHG emissions are not adjusted using carbon credits or offsets.

Useful Resources

  • Certificate Holders are encouraged to use the ASC GHG Calculator, available at https://ghg.asc-aqua.org, to ensure compliance with regards to calculation scope, methods, data sources and reporting format. Use of this tool is voluntary; other tools, consultants, or internal procedures may be used if documentation is available to demonstrate compliance with the requirements in Appendix 9.

  • Recommended factors for converting GHG emissions from a live weight basis to an edible weight basis may be sourced from supplemental material of Gephart et al. (20211818Gephart, J. A., Henriksson, P. J., Parker, R. W., Shepon, A., Gorospe, K. D., Bergman, K., … & Troell, M. (2021). Environmental performance of blue foods. Nature, 597(7876), 360-365. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03889-2). Other conversion factors may be used if they reflect the actual edible yield (i.e., muscle fraction) of the animal.

  • A range of methodological frameworks and standards are available to guide life cycle assessments and GHG accounting. Use of any of these is optional, provided that calculations are still in compliance with the requirements of Appendix 9. Examples include:

    • General life cycle assessment methods in ISO 140401919ISO. (2006). ISO 14040 — Environmental management — Life cycle assessment — Principles and framework. Geneva, Switzerland: ISO. and ISO 140442020ISO. (2006). ISO 14044 — Environmental management — Life cycle assessment — Requirements and guidelines. Geneva, Switzerland: ISO.
    • The GHG Protocol from the World Resources Institute2121WRI. (2004). The greenhouse gas protocol: A corporate accounting and reporting standard. Washington, D.C., USA: World Resources Institute.
    • ISO 140672222ISO. (2013). ISO 14067 — Greenhouse gases — Carbon footprint of products — Requirements and guidelines for quantification and communication. Geneva, Switzerland: ISO. and marine fish product category rules in ISO 229482323ISO. (2020). ISO 22948 — Carbon footprint for seafood — Product category rules (CFP–PCR) for finfish. Geneva, Switzerland: ISO.
    • The Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) marine fish product category rules2424Marine Fish PEFCR. (2024). Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR) for unprocessed Marine Fish Products. In draft available at: https://www.marinefishpefcr.eu/
    • PAS 20502525BSI. (2011). PAS 2050:2011 – Specification for the assessment of the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions of goods and services. London, UK: British Standards Institution. and seafood product category rules in PAS 2050-22626BSI. (2012). PAS 2050-2:2012 – Assessment of life cycle greenhouse gas emissions. Supplementary requirements for the application of PAS 2050:2011 to seafood and other aquatic food products. London, UK: British Standards Institution.

2.10.3 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a GHG Management Plan, and shall ensure the plan is annually reviewed, and revised as necessary, following the targets set out in Appendix 9 (9.5).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • After calculating GHG emissions and identifying major contributors (‘hot spots’) to overall emissions, a Management Plan allows a site to identify actions to reduce, minimise and/or avoid GHG emissions.
  • Actions proposed in a GHG Management Plan should demonstrably relate to emissions identified during GHG calculations. Actions may also relate to GHG emissions beyond the scope of ASC’s GHG calculation requirements if evidence is shown that these emissions are substantial. 
    • For example, efforts to reduce GHG emissions from product transport can have a significant effect in some cases, particularly if air freight is used.
  • Actions proposed in a GHG Management Plan should be accompanied with means to track implementation and effectiveness.
  • Not all GHG emission reduction efforts require major changes to operations or large new infrastructure investments. 
    • Incremental improvements to feed conversion ratios, mortality rates, and energy efficiency can also be effective ways to reduce GHG emissions.
  • GHG targets, relative to both live weight production and edible weight product, are provided in Appendix 9. 
    • These targets are not intended as thresholds for standard conformance. 
      • Rather, they provide a guide for Certificate Holders to assess their performance against established benchmarks, support efforts in their GHG Management Plan and facilitate tracking over time.
  • By calculating and reporting emissions on an annual basis, sites will be able to track their GHG performance over time and assess the effectiveness of actions taken in their GHG Management Plan. 
    • If emissions relative to production are increasing, the GHG Management Plan should be reviewed and, if needed, revised.
  • Reporting of GHG emissions to ASC, with a consistent approach across certified sites, will also support ASC’s efforts to provide guidance back on the types of actions that are achieving significant improvements in GHG performance.
  • While calculation and reporting of GHG emissions requires the use of two allocation methods to promote transparency and consistency across certified sites, Certificate Holders may select either allocation method as the basis for identifying actions in their GHG Management Plan and tracking emissions over time.
  • For many sites, emissions may come primarily from the production and use of feed.
    • Coordinating with feed suppliers may be an effective way to target improvement of GHG emissions in these cases. 
      • This may take the form of identifying lower GHG ingredients, transitioning to ingredients associated with lower rates of deforestation and land conversion, or improving feed conversion ratios through improved feed compositions.
  • The GHG Management Plan may be site-specific or may be applicable across many sites or developed at a corporate level, provided that the GHG tracking and actions taken are demonstrated to be relevant to the site and to reflect identified hot spots of emissions. 

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Copies of current and previous versions of the GHG Management Plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Presence of a GHG Management Plan.

  • The GHG Management Plan is maintained by a designated member of staff and is regularly reviewed and updated.

  • Actions proposed in the GHG Management Plan reflect identified sources of GHG emissions.

  • The GHG Management Plan includes tracking of GHG emissions over time relative to the targets set out in Appendix 9.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.10.4 The UoC shall report annually to ASC the energy use and GHG emissions per site according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Public disclosure of energy use and GHG data are not required by the ASC Farm Standard. Instead, reporting to ASC is required.
    • This ensures that energy use and GHG performance of ASC certified production can be tracked and communicated in an aggregated form and also supports assessment of the requirements and identification of common issues, errors or need for improved guidance.
      • Data submitted to ASC is used in accordance with ASC’s data use policies.

  • There are two data submission templates: one for energy use and one for GHG emissions.

  • Data submitted to ASC should reflect the same calculation results as demonstrated during the audit in compliance with Indicators 2.10.1 and 2.10.2.

  • Data submission for both energy use and GHG emissions is on an annual basis. However, in some cases, sites may not have new data to submit in a given year.

    • If the site is calculating values relative to a production cycle and a new production cycle has not completed since the prior year’s data submission. In this case, data submission is still required but may reflect the same submission as the prior year.

    • If calculating values for three consecutive years of production and previous records are not available, data submissions in the first and second years may reflect one or two years of production, respectively.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Demonstration of successful data submission on an annual basis.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Successful annual data submissions using the ASC Farm Standard Energy Use Data Submission Template and the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template.

  • Data reported in data submissions reflect results shown in audit for Indicators 2.10.1 and 2.10.2.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.10.5 The UoC shall provide GHG emissions data to any subsequent ASC certified site to which it supplies fish for grow-out.

Indicator applicability: Marine salmonids

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • In the case of marine salmonids, grow-out sites that supply fish to subsequent grow-out sites are required to be certified under the ASC Farm Standard.
    • This necessitates that they calculate and report GHG emissions as per Indicator 2.10.2.
      • This facilitates the sharing of data with subsequent grow-out sites to ensure that GHG calculations at the point of harvest include relevant inputs from the prior site.
  • Specific data on the energy inputs and feeds used from the prior site are not required. Only the GHG profile, reflecting the format of the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template, is needed.
    • This does not apply to other species which do not require full certification of prior sites.
  • GHG profiles from hatcheries are not required, as explained above for Indicator 2.10.2.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

N/A

Auditors should confirm:

  • Subsequent grow-out sites are provided a GHG profile reflecting the format of the ASC Farm Standard GHG Data Submission Template either as part of regular process or upon request.

Useful Resources

N/A

Material Use, Waste and Pollution Control 2.11

2.11.1 The UoC shall assess and, where feasible, implement measures to reduce, reuse and recycle waste materials.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ‘Reducing’ refers to using fewer materials, like fewer plastic bottles or buying materials, like products or equipment, with less packaging.
    • This will cut down on waste from the start.

  • ‘Reusing’ refers to using materials again instead of disposing of them.

    • This produces economic savings and reduces the amount of materials that end up as waste.

  • ‘Recycling’ refers to collecting and processing materials to be turned into new materials.

    • As a means of giving materials a new use instead of disposing of them as waste in landfills.
  • Sites should identify the materials used and assess whether it is reasonably practical to prioritise reduction, reuse and recycling over disposal.

    • The assessment should consider, for example, the availability of recycling facilities in the area.

    • If applicable, the outcome of the assessment should be turned into policies or procedures.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Identification of materials used and an assessment of the feasibility of reducing, reusing and recycling.

  • Policies and procedures outlining the steps to handle materials deemed feasible for reduction, reuse and recycling.

    • Employees should be aware of these policies or procedures.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The site identified the material used and assessed the feasibility of reducing, reusing and recycling.

  • Materials identified as feasible to reduce, reuse or recycle are effectively and appropriately reduced, reused or recycled.

  • Employees’ awareness of the policies and procedures that outline the steps to handle materials deemed feasible for reduction, reuse and recycling.

    • This may be demonstrated through training conducted by the site or the presence of signs/posters regarding the appropriate reduction, reuse and recycling of materials.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.11.2 The UoC shall capture non-biological solid waste, including plastics, prior to effluent discharge.

Indicator applicability: point-source discharge

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Filters or screen barriers installed in the effluent pipe/channel prior to discharge are examples of methods for capturing non-biological solid waste.

  • Based on their context, sites should identify and assess non-biological solid waste that could end up in the effluent to determine the most appropriate method for its capture.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Identification (e.g. a list) of non-biological solid waste generated at the site.

  • An assessment of the characteristics of non-biological solid waste to determine the most appropriate method for capturing it in case it ends up in the effluent.

  • Records of maintenance of the method used to capture non-biological solid waste (if applicable, e.g. filter or screen barriers).

Auditors should confirm:

  • The site has identified and assessed non-biological solid waste generated.

  • Through site inspection, the method to capture non-biological solid waste prior to effluent discharges and its suitability.

Useful Resources

N/A

2.11.3 The UoC shall dispose of waste responsibly.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Sites should identify and classify waste based on where it will be disposed of. This includes the following types of waste:

    • Recyclables: e.g. plastics, metals and paper.

    • Hazardous: e.g. chemicals, batteries and medical waste.

    • Non-recyclable: e.g. biological and non-biological waste
  • Based on the classification, sites should determine the facilities to use for waste disposal, for example:

    • Recycling facility.

    • Landfill.

    • Waste management company.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Identification and classification of waste.

  • Records confirming that waste is disposed of in appropriate facilities according to its classification and the legality of those facilities.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The site:

    • Has identified and classified the waste it generates.

    • Uses facilities that are appropriate for the type of waste and that they legally operate.

2.11.4 The UoC shall not use pesticides that are banned or restricted by any of the following conventions or organisations:

  • The Rotterdam Convention on Prior Informed Consent (PIC)2727http://www.pic.int/TheConvention/Chemicals/AnnexIIIChemicals
  • The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)2828http://chm.pops.int/TheConvention/ThePOPs/ListingofPOPs/tabid/2509/Default.aspx
  • The World Health Organisation (WHO), for products classed as ’extremely hazardous‘ or ’highly hazardous‘ (classes Ia and Ib).2929https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240005662

2.11.5 The UoC shall only use net antifouling agents containing biocides that are approved by local regulations in either Australia, the European Union, Japan or the United States of America.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Pesticides: The Rotterdam Convention on Prior Informed Consent (PIC) defines pesticides as chemicals used to destroy, prevent, or control pests, including vectors of human or animal disease, and unwanted species of plants or animals causing harm during or otherwise interfering with the production, processing, storage, transport, or marketing of food, agricultural commodities, wood, and wood products or animal feedstuffs.

  • Biocides: The Biocidal Products Regulation (BPR, Regulation (EU) 528/2012) defines biocides as any substance or mixture, in the form in which it is supplied to the user, consisting of, containing or generating one or more active substances, with the intention of destroying, deterring, rendering harmless, preventing the action of, or otherwise exerting a controlling effect on, any harmful organism by any means other than mere physical or mechanical action.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • List of pesticides and biocides used by the site.
    • Including purchase records.

  • Copy of the list of banned or restricted pesticides by the conventions or organisations stated by the indicator.

  • Copy of the list of biocides approved by local regulations in either Australia, the European Union, Japan or the United States of America.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Pesticides used by the site are not on the list of banned or restricted pesticides by the conventions or organisations stated by the indicator.

  • Biocides used by the site are not on the list of net antifouling agents containing biocides approved by local regulations in either Australia, the European Union, Japan or the United States of America.

Useful Resources

  • REGULATION (EU) No 528/2012 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 22 May 2012 concerning the making available on the market and use of biocidal products.

2.11.6 The UoC shall hold water containing hormones for at least 48 hours or as per product specifications, whichever is greater, prior to discharge.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

2.11.7 The UoC shall ensure that all processing effluent is treated to minimise biosecurity and environmental risks.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • An appropriate effluent treatment should be able to eliminate or reduce to acceptable levels the discharge of (amongst others):

  • Organic matter: measured, for example, as the reduction of Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD), Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) or Total Suspended Solids (TSS) after treatment.

  • Nutrients: measured, for example, as the reduction of nitrogen and phosphorous after treatment.

  • Pathogenic microorganisms: measured, for example, as the reduction of microbial counts after treatment.

  • Oils and greases.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • An effluent monitoring plan appropriate for the type and amount of processing effluent discharged.
    • Including the parameters, frequency of monitoring and acceptable limits.
  • Analysis results of the parameters included in the effluent monitoring plan.

  • Corrective actions when analysis results exceed acceptable levels.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Effluent monitoring plan has been developed and implemented.
    • This includes monitoring analysis results.
  • Corrective actions taken when analysis results exceed acceptable levels.

Useful Resources

  • V. Venugopal, A. Sasidharan (2021). Seafood industry effluents: Environmental hazards, treatment and resource recovery. Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering.

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended culture not using copper-treated gear or infrastructure

2.11.9 The UoC shall not treat or clean aquaculture gear or infrastructure in situ.

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended culture using copper-treated gear or infrastructure

2.11.10 The UoC shall clean aquaculture gear or infrastructure in land-based facilities that treat effluents, including the capturing of copper.

Indicator applicability: cage culture and suspended culture using copper-treated gear or infrastructure

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documentation confirming land-based facilities treat effluents.
    • Including verification that the facility captures copper in its effluent treatment, if applicable.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documentation confirming land-based facilities treat effluents.

2.11.11 The UoC shall demonstrate that copper levels in the sediment are £ 34 mg Cu/kg dry sediment weight, following the method outlined in Appendix 7 (7.6).

An exception applies where copper levels in sediment > 34 mg Cu/kg dry sediment weight, in which case the UoC shall demonstrate that the levels fall within the range of background concentrations measured following the method outlined in Appendix 7 (7.6).

Indicator applicability: cage culture in marine/brackish waters using copper nets or copper-treated nets

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

2.11.12 The UoC shall handle, use, store and dispose of chemicals according to the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) provided by the supplier.

2.11.13 The UoC shall not discharge effluent containing chemicals without adequate treatment.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The adequacy of a treatment depends on the types of chemicals found in the effluent, such as heavy metals, organic compounds, acids and bases.
    • To determine the most adequate treatment, it is essential to understand the following characteristics of the effluent:
      • Chemical composition (organic vs. inorganic, hazardous vs. non-hazardous).
      • pH levels (acidic, neutral or alkaline).
      • Solubility (dissolved, suspended or emulsified).
      • Toxicity (bioaccumulative, carcinogenic, etc.).
    • Based on the above characteristics, examples of treatments that might be used are:

      • Physical-Chemical Treatment: pH neutralisation, coagulation and flocculation, chemical precipitation, adsorption, membrane filtration, electrochemical treatment, solvent extraction.

      • Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOPs): ozonation, ultraviolet + hydrogen peroxide.

      • Biological Treatment: aerobic and anaerobic treatment, bioaugmentation.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Presence of treatment method for effluents containing chemicals.
    • Including the rationale for determining the most adequate method.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Through site inspection the presence of a treatment method for effluents containing chemicals.
    • Including the rationale for determining the most adequate method

2.11.14 The UoC shall adequately contain hazardous materials to prevent spillage, contamination and pollution.

2.11.15 The UoC shall implement spill prevention and emergency response procedures for hazardous materials.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Sites should consider their context and external circumstances when determining the most adequate containment method.
    • Examples of external circumstances are natural disasters and sabotage. 
  • Containment should be:
    • Impervious.
    • Capable of containing at least 110% of the volume of the largest container stored within it.
  • The spill prevention and emergency response procedures for hazardous materials should:
    • Outline the preventative maintenance of equipment destined to prevent and respond to spills from, for example, vehicles, winches, cranes, and mechanical equipment on land and water.
    • Be tested for adequacy at established frequencies.
      • Depending on the test results, the plan should be revised.
  • Employees should be trained on the spill prevention and emergency response procedures.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • List of hazardous materials present or used on the site.

  • Records of employee training on the spill prevention and emergency response procedures.

Auditors should confirm:

  • List of hazardous materials present or used on the site.

  • Employees have been trained on the spill prevention and emergency response procedures.

    • Cross-check during employees’ interviews.

  • Through site inspection:

    • That hazardous materials are adequately contained.

2.11.16 The UoC shall adequately store perishable materials to minimise spoilage, spillage, contamination or pest damage.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

2.11.17 The UoC shall adequately maintain machinery, aquaculture gear and infrastructure to minimise performance degradation and failure.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The site should develop a maintenance plan that identifies the schedule for regular maintenance of machinery, aquaculture gear and infrastructure.

  • The person(s) conducting maintenance should have an adequate level of competence based on the type of maintenance required.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Maintenance plan that identifies the schedule for regular maintenance of machinery, aquaculture gear and infrastructure.

  • Records to demonstrate maintenance was performed according to the schedule outlined in the maintenance plan.

    • Written justification should be in place in cases of deviation from the schedule outlined in the maintenance plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The site has a maintenance plan covering regular maintenance of machinery, aquaculture gear and infrastructure.

  • Records that the schedule has been adhered to.

2.11.18 The UoC shall mark and record substantial aquaculture gear.

Indicator applicability: water-based UoC

2.11.19 The UoC shall retrieve lost aquaculture gear.

Indicator applicability: water-based UoC

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Intent of Indicator 2.11.18 is that substantial aquaculture gear is identifiable as belonging to the site.
    • So, it can be attributable to the site in case of gear loss and facilitate retrieval (see Indicator 2.11.9).
  • Substantial gear includes:
    • Floats.
    • Cages.
    • Bags.
    • Predator nets.
    • Racks.
  • The site should maintain equipment and/or mechanisms for retrieving lost aquaculture gear, for example, scoop nets and grapple hooks (Indicator 2.11.19).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A record, or log, of substantial aquaculture gear should be maintained.

    • At a defined frequency, the substantial aquaculture gear record should be contrasted with the physical inventory present at the site to determine whether any gear has been lost.

  • Policies or procedures for locating and retrieving substantial aquaculture gear.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Record, or log, of substantial aquaculture gear.

  • Through site inspection:

    • That substantial aquaculture gear is attributable to the site and recorded.

    • That the site maintains equipment and/or mechanisms for retrieving lost aquaculture gear.

  • Policies or procedures are in place to locate and retrieve substantial aquaculture gear.

Useful Resources

N/A

Auditors should confirm:

Criterion 2.11 – Material Use, Waste and Pollution Control

Feed 2.12

2.12.1 The UoC shall only use ASC-conforming compound feed.

Indicator scope: every UoC using compound feed.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ASC-conforming compound feed is sourced from feed mills certified to the ASC Feed Standard.
    • It includes feeds produced under the mass balance model, as well as feeds produced under the segregation model.
  • This requirement does not apply to non-certifiable species (e.g., cleaner fish).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Documented process to confirm feed is ASC-conforming that includes verification of (see Indicator 1.4.3):
    • The feed mill certification against the ASC Feed Standard.
    • The documentation that identifies:
      • The feed as ASC-conforming.
      • The feed production model applied (i.e., mass balance or segregation).
      • In the case of segregated feed, a distinct feed name which is also listed on the schedule to the feed mill certificate.
      • Whether the feed is traceable as ASC-conforming throughout all steps between the feed mill and site.
  • Records:
    • Feed purchased and type.
    • Feed delivery notes – confirming traceability between feed mill and site.
    • Feeding records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Documented process to confirm feed product is ASC-conforming that includes verification of (see Indicator 1.4.3):
    • The feed mill certification against the ASC Feed Standard.
    • The documentation identifies:
      • The feed as ASC-conforming.
      • The feed production model applied (i.e., mass balance or segregation).
      • In the case of segregated feed, a distinct feed name which is also listed on the schedule to the feed mill certificate.
      • Whether the feed is traceable as ASC-conforming throughout all steps between the feed mill and site.
  • Records 
    • Feed purchased and type.
    • Feed delivery notes – confirming traceability between feed mill and site.
    • Feeding records.

N/A

2.12.2 The UoC shall only use seaweed from regulated sources.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using seaweed as a direct feed source.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Regulated source means that there are national/international laws, agreements or policies governing the harvesting or farming of seaweed and that these are complied with, or the seaweed is from a certification scheme which addresses the responsible management of seaweed, whether wild-harvested or farmed.
    • Seaweed certified to the following standards meet this ASC requirement on regulated sources:

      • ASC-MSC Seaweed Standard

      • FairWild Standard

      • Standards approved in the IFOAM Family of Standards Organic Standards

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Legislation which stipulates responsible harvesting or farming.

  • Supplier harvesting or farming permits.

  • Certification documentation.

  • Records:

    • Harvest.

    • Transport to the UoC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Legislation which stipulates responsible harvesting or farming.

  • Presence and validity of permits.

  • Certification documentation.

  • Records.

    • Harvest.

    • Transport to the UoC.

2.12.3 The UoC shall not use feed containing protein derived from the same genus as the species being farmed. An exception applies where it can be demonstrated that same-species protein hydrolysates are verified to be <10,000 daltons, in which case use is allowed.

How do I interpret this requirement?

N/A

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:
    • Feed purchased (including information on species/genus used as marine ingredients for fishmeal).
    • Feed fed.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records:

Useful Resources

  • Although the science behind prion diseases, infectivity and pathogenicity in fish in association with Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSEs) is not very well developed, ASC has taken a precautionary approach and followed the guidelines of FAO (2011) Aquaculture Development. 5. Use of Wild Fish as Feed in Aquaculture Principle 9.1 “For biosecurity reasons, intraspecies recycling is an unacceptable practice that should be prohibited”3030FAO. Aquaculture development. 5. Use of wild fish as feed in aquaculture. FAO Technical Guidelines for Responsible Fisheries. No. 5, Suppl. 5. Rome, FAO. 2011. 79p..
  • Protein hydrolysates verified to <10,000 daltons are allowed as controlling the molecular weight provides a good verification of the appropriateness of an applied transformation process. This is in line with Regulation (EU) 142/2011 regarding the use of animal by-products.

2.12.4 The UoC shall not feed wet feedstuffs, moist pellets, or uncooked/ unprocessed marine raw materials.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Wet feedstuffs can be used as carbon sources for water quality control i.e., anaerobic fermentation or biofloc technology.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Records:
    • Feed purchased.
    • Feed fed.

Principle 3

The aquaculture industry is committed to respecting and promoting human rights

Rights Awareness 3.1

3.1.1 The UoC shall have a written human rights policy, approved by senior management, with the intent of publicly demonstrating its commitment to at least the following:

  • freedom of association and the effective recognition of the right to collective bargaining; and
  • the elimination of all forms of forced or compulsory labour; and
  • the effective abolition of child labour; and
  • the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation; and
  • a safe and healthy working environment; and
  • being a good neighbour and respecting the rights of surrounding communities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A human rights policy:
    • is the “company’s public expression of its commitment to meet its responsibility to respect internationally recognized human rights standards”3131United Nations Global Compact (2015), A Guide for Business: How to Develop a Human Rights Policy. Available at: How to Develop a Human Rights Policy 20151013.indd (ohchr.org)
    • is appropriate to the strategic direction, context and purpose of the organisation
    • provides a framework for setting quality objectives
    • includes an explicit commitment to respect all other internationally recognised human rights standards3232International Bill of Human Rights, A Brief History and the two International Covenants. Available at: International Bill of Human Rights | OHCHR that apply to people that may be impacted by the UoC’s operations
    • includes stipulations concerning the company’s expectations of personnel, business partners and other relevant parties
    • includes information on how the company will implement its commitment
    • is aligned with the requirements in the ASC Farm Standard, and local and international human rights laws and standards 
    • is signed by senior management
    • is understood by all employees.
  • Each company will need to determine for itself which human rights may need to be prioritised in its policy because this will depend on the risks associated with the:
    • company’s location
    • type of farming practices
    • composition of the workforce.
  • The content of the human rights policy may vary according to the UoC’s size and national legal frameworks, and could also include the following topics:
    • recruitment and termination (see Indicators 3.2.3-3.2.8, 3.3.3-3.3.6, 3.4.1, 3.4.3, 3.4.4, 3.7.1-3.7.4)
    • employee representation (see Indicator 3.1.3)
    • loans and advances (see Indicator 3.2.9)
    • remediation (see Indicators 3.2.2, 3.3.2)
    • anti-discrimination (see Criterion 3.4)
    • training (see Indicators 3.1.4, 3.5.5)
    • freedom of association and collective bargaining (see Criterion 3.6)
    • transparent contracts (see Criterion 3.7)
    • fair wages (see Indicators 3.8.1, 3.8.4, 3.8.5, 3.8.6)
    • working hours (see Criterion 3.9)
    • performance and workplace conduct (see Criterion 3.10)
    • employee accommodation (see Criterion 3.11)
    • grievance mechanisms (see Criterion 3.12)
    • community relations and Indigenous rights (see Criterion 3.13).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • human rights policy
  • evidence that senior management have signed it off

Auditors should confirm:

  • that the human rights policy is in place, approved by a member of senior management;

  • where the policy is communicated and available publicly;

  • whether the policy is available to all relevant stakeholders;

  • that the human rights policy is consistent with other company policies and procedures.

Useful Resources

  • Some examples of human rights policies can be found here.
  • United Nations (2011), Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. Available at: https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/guidingprinciplesbusinesshr_en.pdf
  • ILO (2022), ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and its Follow-up. Available at: wcms_716594.pdf (ilo.org)
  • International Bill of Human Rights, A Brief History and the two International Covenants. Available at: International Bill of Human Rights | OHCHR
  • United Nations Global Compact (2015), A Guide for Business: How to Develop a Human Rights Policy. Available at: How to Develop a Human Rights Policy 20151013.indd (ohchr.org)
  • OECD (2023), OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct. Available at: https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/81f92357-en.pdf?expires=1729687419&id=id&accname=guest&checksum=62CA2A98BB5F19532709D450D88B4404

3.1.2 The UoC shall have at least one named member of management who is responsible for the implementation and maintenance of the human rights policy.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Implementing and maintaining the human rights policy means that the named member of management is responsible for:

    • translating the policy statement into practical actions and initiatives within the UoC and in day-to-day operations

    • monitoring the UoC’s human rights performance, including:

    • identifying areas of improvement

    • reporting progress or issues to senior management or relevant stakeholders

    • overseeing continuous improvement

    • overseeing training and awareness programmes aimed at educating employees and stakeholders about human rights principles, policies, and procedures

    • updating the policy regularly or when there are changes at the UoC.

  • The named member of management should also commit to working with employee representation in the implementation of the policy, ensuring that employees’ views are taken into account.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records that allow for the verification of the named member of management

  • plan of actions involved in implementing the policy

  • plans for monitoring implementation of the policy

  • evidence of any remediation or corrective actions that have taken place

  • plans for regularly updating and revising the policy.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that the named member of management understands their responsibilities in implementing and maintaining the policy;

  • that employees are aware of the named member of management responsible for the human rights policy;

  • that the human rights policy is being implemented, which can include checking:

    • progress against any action plans and monitoring plans,

    • if employees are aware of and understand the contents of the policy,

    • evidence of any remediation or corrective actions where there are negative human rights impacts.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.1.3 The UoC shall facilitate the establishment of employee representation to support the implementation and maintenance of the human rights policy.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Employee representation:

    • can vary with the size and context of the UoC. It can be a committee or nominated representatives

    • ensures that the voices and perspectives of employees are heard and considered in matters related to human rights.

  • A committee structure preferably:

    • represents the composition of employees, enhancing inclusivity

    • holds elections for the employee committee, allowing all employees to nominate and vote for members.

    • Meets on a regular basis and occasionally on a more ad-hoc basis, where need arises.

  • A committee’s role includes:

    • assisting in the development of strategies, initiatives, and activities that promote human rights within the organisation

    • helping to monitor the UoC’s human rights performance

    • identifying areas where the policy might not be effectively implemented or where issues arise

    • engaging in dialogue with management to address concerns, propose improvements, and ensure that the policy remains relevant and effective

    • raising awareness among their colleagues about the UoC’s human rights policy, principles, and procedures.

  • The UoC should ensure that any employee representative or committee:

    • has knowledge about the human rights policy

    • understands what their role involves. This can include ensuring that they have access to training.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • list of members of the employee committee or employee representation

  • records of meetings and actions

  • records of election procedures.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees are aware of who represents them and how to contact them;

  • the employee representation understands their role and the human rights policy.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.1.4 The UoC shall ensure that employees are trained on the human rights policy.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The policy is:

    • distributed to all employees

    • available for all employees to access

    • in a format and language that they can understand, with provisions for illiteracy, if necessary.

  • Informing employees about their human rights can help:

    • prevent issues such as harassment, discrimination, or other human rights abuses within the workplace

    • demonstrate transparency and commitment to the human rights policy to employees and stakeholders

    • develop a more inclusive, equitable and ethical work environment.

  • Training for employees on the policy should include:

  • an understanding of the significance of the human rights policythe rights and responsibilities that the policy includeshow to report human rights violations or concerns through the UoC’s grievance mechanism

    information in a format that is understandable and accessible to all employees, including those who may have language or literacy barriers.

  • Training should take place annually or when there are new employees

  • Records of training attendance and content should be maintained.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of the training, including attendees and topics covered

  • policy available for employees in an accessible format.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the purpose and contents of the policy;

  • training is taking place annually and all employees are trained.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.1.5 The UoC shall publicly disclose the human rights policy and actively communicate it to all suppliers, buyers and other relevant stakeholders.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The policy can be published:

  • on the UoC’s websitein annual reports anywhere where it is easily accessible to anyone interested in learning about the UoC’s commitment to human rights

    • in written (printed) materials to distribute to employees, suppliers, and communities

    • through local media or social media

    • through letters to suppliers

    • in collaboration with local organisations (such as NGOs).

  • The policy should be:

    • actively communicated to all suppliers, including subcontractors and business partners

    • included in contracts and agreements with suppliers.

  • For some specific target groups, such as local communities, it may be necessary to communicate more actively about (parts of) the policy, for example, during stakeholder meetings.

  • ‘Other relevant stakeholders’ can include anyone who is interested in or impacted by the operations of the UoC, for example:

    • anyone in the supply chain

    • local community members

    • local NGOs and community organisations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • publication of the policy

Auditors should confirm:

  • that the policy is publicly available and easily accessible;

  • that stakeholders are aware of the existence and contents of the policy.

Forced Labour 3.2

Training Content

Our training content is designed to help you better understand key requirements of the ASC Farm Standard.

Videos are publicly accessible, and most offer subtitles in multiple languages.
