Type Name
Video Preventing Forced Labour Under the ASC Standards

3.2.1 The UoC shall not engage in or support forced labour.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Forced labour can take many forms and can include:
    • work that is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty:
      • penalties do not need to actually take place for forced labour conditions to occur. The threat itself of the penalty or any other type of retaliation, as well as the penalty itself, constitutes forced labour
      • penalties and other types of retaliation include but are not limited to the following (adapted from ILO Handbook on Forced Labour3333ILO (2015), Combating Forced Labour: A Handbook for Employers and Business. Available at: https://www.ilo.org/media/441596/download):
        • isolation, restriction of movement, confinement or imprisonment
        • physical and sexual violence against employees, family or close associates 
        • abusive working and living conditions
        • excessive overtime 
        • financial penalties, withholding of wages 
        • shift to even worse working conditions, removal of rights or privileges 
        • exclusion from future employment 
        • deprivation of food, shelter or other necessities 
        • denunciation to authorities such as police or department of immigration, deportation 
        • any other type of physical, mental or social harm
    • work for which the person has not offered himself or herself voluntarily, including where employees are not allowed to terminate employment at any time
    • the use of deception or other forms of coercion, including where employees are not informed of working conditions prior to or during employment
    • the use of exploitative loans to prevent employees from leaving their jobs. This is also referred to as debt bondage, which can occur when employees:
      • incur debts related to employer loans with high interest rates
      • are forced to pay off recruitment fees or associated costs 
      • are forced to pay high portions of their salaries towards employer provided accommodation or supplies purchased at an inflated cost at employer-run stores.
  • The wording ‘or support’ in the indicator means that the UoC:
    • does not use any suppliers, subcontractors or other workers who are in any way involved in a system of forced labour
    • does not engage in forced labour through any other third parties or business relationships.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts

  • licences or certificates of any recruitment agencies used (see Indicator 3.2.3)

  • evidence that any recruitment agencies used are complying with relevant regulations (see Indicator 3.2.3)

  • records from internal audits.

Auditors should confirm:

  • general risk factors for forced labour in a country (see useful resources section);

  • NGOs’ or other local organisations’ knowledge of any reports of forced labour in the sector in this region;

  • human resources personnel’s awareness of any issues in the workplace;

  • worker or union representative’s awareness of any issues in the workplace;

  • whether or not any migrant workers are working at the UoC whether local or international, as a heightened risk factor for forced labour;

  • whether or not recruitment agencies are being used, as a heightened risk factor for forced labour;

  • that employees are not threatened with any penalties or retaliation;

  • that employees are not in any form of debt bondage;

  • that employee contracts are clear and up-to-date and employees understand their terms and conditions of employment;

  • consistency with records related to other parts of the ASC Farm Standard that represent risk factors for forced labour, e.g.:

    • recruitment and workplace policies

    • wage and payroll records

    • overtime records

    • employee committee records

    • grievance mechanism records.

Useful Resources

  • ILO (2015), Combating Forced Labour: A Handbook for Employers and Business. Available at: https://www.ilo.org/media/441596/download

  • US State Department country reports for human trafficking: https://www.state.gov/trafficking-in-persons-report/

3.2.2 If forced labour is identified, the UoC shall implement remediation processes that prioritise the best interest of the person, following the method outlined in Appendix 10.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The remediation framework is set out in Appendix 10, including timelines, corrective action and reporting obligations.
  • Remediation of forced labour:
    • will vary depending on the situation and the needs of the employee in question
    • always takes into account the best interest of the employee, respecting their wishes and protecting their privacy
    • is ideally carried out in consultation with local experts, such as NGOs.
  • When remediating a case of forced labour, there can be different steps in the process, which can include:
    • immediate actions to safeguard the employee, for example removing them to a safe location
    • medium term actions to develop a plan to provide appropriate remedy to the victim, including but not limited to:
      • restoration of original job terms
      • wage repayment or other compensation
      • medical or other care as necessary
      • repatriation or other steps deemed necessary
    • long term actions to enact and monitor the plan, which can take up to several years.

  • The UoC should then engage in a process of developing corrective actions to prevent forced labour reoccurring. This can include:

    • performing an analysis of what went wrong in their system to prevent it

    • implementing measures to prevent future recurrence

    • considering working with local experts on this corrective action.

  • Given the complexity of human rights issues, partnership with external partners is often necessary to provide effective remediation. They can:

    • provide support for the development of a remediation plan
    • help in implementing the remediation plan
    • help to implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence.
  • These potential partners can include:
    • local NGOs
    • individual experts
    • community liaisons/leaders
    • government offices
    • supply chain partners, or others.
  • Potential support that these partners can provide could include:
    • training
    • improved access to social services and education
    • advocacy
    • direct financial support or other support for the affected person and their families to find other sources of income.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented remediation procedures
  • records and documents of any remediation process that has taken place
  • records and documents of any corrective actions that have been put into place
  • documented monitoring system in place.

Auditors should confirm:

  • existence of remediation procedures;
  • knowledge and capacity of staff to implement remediation procedures, or availability of external capacity;
  • the ability of the site to monitor any corrective actions within their management system;
  • knowledge and capacity of staff to develop corrective actions, where necessary;
  • amended contracts with recruitment agencies, where relevant.

Useful Resources

  • Bureau of International Labor Affairs, Forced Labor Remediation Guide. Available at: https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ilab/comply-chain/steps-to-a-social-compliance-system/step-6-remediate-violations/key-topic-forced-labor-remediation-guide#:~:text=REMEDIATION%20ACTION%3A,-Ensure%20that%20wages&text=Ensure%20that%20payment%20schedules%20are,receive%20their%20full%20wages%20due.

  • ILO (2015), Combating Forced Labour: A Handbook for Employers and Business. Available at: https://www.ilo.org/media/441596/download

3.2.3 The UoC shall ensure that where recruitment agencies are used, they comply with applicable legal requirements and are licenced or certified by the relevant authority, where such licensing or certification exist.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC is responsible for initial screening of recruitment agencies, including:
    • checking that they comply with relevant regulations, which includes:
      • national labour laws
      • employment rights
      • applicable laws in the country of operation, for example, some countries have specific regulations for recruitment and employment agencies
    • verifying their licence or certificate to operate, where these systems exist:
      • in some countries and sectors, licensing rules apply. For example, in the UK, an agency supplying labour in agriculture, horticulture, shellfish gathering or food processing and packaging may need to be licensed by the Gangmasters & Labour Abuse Authority (GLAA)3434NIBusinessInfo.co.uk, Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses. Available at: https://www.nibusinessinfo.co.uk/content/licences-employment-agencies
    • checking that they comply with the indicators directly addressing recruitment agencies in the ASC Farm Standard:
      • indicator 3.2.4: employees’ original identity documents are not retained
      • indicator 3.2.5: employees are allowed to terminate their employment
      • indicator 3.2.6: employees do not have any part of their salary, property or benefits unlawfully withheld
      • indicator 3.2.7: employees are not charged any fees associated with recruitment
      • indicator 3.2.8: prison labour is not used
      • indicator 3.4.1: no discrimination in recruitment
      • indicator 3.4.3: not testing for pregnancy or virginity
      • indicator 3.4.4: medical tests are only conducted during recruitment if required for the function of the job or by national law;
    • verifying their compliance with any contractual agreements in place between the UoC and the recruitment agency.
  • The UoC is also responsible for continued monitoring of recruitment agencies, including annually reviewing their:
    • licence to operate
    • compliance with applicable regulations
    • compliance with the relevant ASC Farm Standard indicators
    • compliance with any contractual agreements in place.
  • The UoC can outsource this screening and monitoring to subcontracted professionals, such as acknowledged NGO licensing programmes.
  • When recruitment agencies are used for hiring migrant employees, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and terms and conditions can be agreed between the UoC and recruitment agency detailing the conditions under which foreign migrant employees will be hired.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of screening of recruitment agencies, both upon engagement of the agency and also on an ongoing basis
  • copies of valid, up-to-date licences of recruitment agencies
  • contracts with recruitment agencies
  • employee contracts for those who have been recruited by recruitment agencies.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether or not recruitment agencies have been used by the UoC;
  • that a recruitment agency screening process is in place;
  • terms and conditions of employment for those who have been recruited through recruitment agencies;
  • if any foreign migrant employees have been recruited through agencies;
  • if terms and conditions and an MoU are in place for the recruitment of migrant employees;
  • employees’ perceptions of the recruitment process;
  • that recruitment agencies used have not been associated with any bad practices by local labour unions or other organisations.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.4 The UoC shall ensure that original identity documents are not retained, including by any recruitment agencies used. If a secure storage option for identity documents is provided, the UoC shall ensure that:

  1. it is the choice of the employee to use the storage, and;
  2. stored items are logged, and;
  3. employees have free access to the storage.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The retention of identity documents is a violation of employees’ basic rights.
  • When employees cannot easily prove their identity or citizenship status or have the documents required to travel, they become more vulnerable to exploitation.
  • Employees should always either possess or have access at any time to their original personal documentation, including documentation needed to terminate employment, and to leave the country and travel freely. For example:
    • ID cards
    • passports
    • visas
  • If a recruitment agency is involved and stores employees’ personal documentation there, it is still the responsibility of the UoC to ensure that the conditions outlined in the indicator are met.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • storage solutions for personal documents
  • policies about the retention of employee documents.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether or not employees store personal documents anywhere at the UoC;
  • that employees are not asked to hand over any personal documents.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.5 The UoC shall ensure that employees, whether employed directly or through a recruitment agency, are allowed to terminate their employment according to their employment terms and conditions.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The word ‘directly’ means an employee who is employed by the UoC, rather than by a recruitment agency.
  • The UoC is responsible for ensuring that any employees who are working at the UoC, but recruited and/or contracted by a recruitment agency are also allowed to terminate their own employment.
  • The UoC should also be aware of and comply with local labour laws and regulations related to employment termination.
  • The UoC has fair and transparent employment agreements (see Criterion 3.7) that are:
    • documented
    • specify termination conditions, which may include:
      • providing written notices
      • maintaining records of the process.
  • Examples of unacceptable terms and conditions relating to terminating employment are:
    • a defined period where employees are not allowed to resign or terminate their employment
    • employees are not allowed to resign without permission from management
    • employees are required to pay fees in order to resign or terminate their employment
    • anything in the terms and conditions that is contrary to local labour laws and regulations.
  • To ensure that any disagreements or conflicts about termination are reported without fear of retaliation, and resolved, it is also important that there are accessible and effective grievance mechanisms in place (see Criterion 3.12).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts that include conditions for termination of employment
  • records of resignation
  • evidence that recruitment agencies allow employees to terminate their employment.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether or not employees are aware of how they can terminate their employment if they wish, and what the terms and conditions are for doing so.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.6 The UoC shall ensure that employees, whether employed directly or through a recruitment agency, do not have any part of their salary, property, or benefits unlawfully withheld.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A common tactic in forced labour situations can be to withhold salary, property or benefits, to pressure an employee to stay in employment.
  • Benefits can be:
    • those allowed by law
    • defined by contract
    • defined by collective bargaining agreement
    • inclusive of, for example:
      • paid time off
      • sick leave
      • health insurance
      • private pensions scheme
    • can include bonuses.
  • There are situations where withholding salary, property or benefits are legally required, and so allowed under this indicator. For example:
    • Salary withholdings, as required by the government. For example, part of a salary is sometimes withheld by a government for:
      • statutory pensions
      • health insurance
      • taxes
      • or a government can sometimes require the withholding of salary to pay overdue childcare support costs to another parent
      • or a government can require the withholding of salary to pay overdue taxes.
    • Salary deductions, as defined in a contract or collective bargaining agreement, that are agreed by both parties. For example, an agreed voluntary deduction for housing costs could be allowable.
    • Bonuses, which are considered optional and additional to the agreed salary and benefits. However, if clearly defined performance targets related to a bonus payment have been achieved, then the bonus cannot be withheld.
  • The UoC is responsible for ensuring that any employees who are working at the UoC but recruited and/or contracted by a recruitment agency do not have any parts of their salary, property or benefits withheld unlawfully.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts that include information about any wage deductions
  • payslips and payroll records
  • evidence that recruitment agencies do not unlawfully withhold any salary, property or benefits.

Auditors should confirm:

  • contracts do not contain any unlawful deductions;
  • wage terms listed in contracts match payslips or payroll records;
  • any deductions made from wages such as taxes, or social security, are lawful, transparent, and authorised by the employee;
  • employees are aware of the purpose of any deductions being made.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.7 The UoC shall ensure that employees, whether employed directly or through a recruitment agency, are not charged any fees associated with recruitment, employment or travel and repatriation.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Charging employees fees for recruitment or during employment can lead to debt bondage and makes employees vulnerable to exploitation and coercion.
  • If fees are found, the UoC shall reimburse them as soon as possible.
  • Following are a list of recruitment fees and related costs as determined by the ILO and adapted from their guidance3535ILO (2019), General Principles and Operational Guidelines for Fair Recruitment and Definition of Recruitment Fees and Related Costs. Available at: https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@ed_protect/@protrav/@migrant/documents/publication/wcms_703485.pdf that may be incurred as a result of the recruitment process and that are not to be charged to potential or actual employees:
    • recruitment fees:
      • payment for services provided by a recruitment agency to match employers with applicants for employment
      • payment for the recruitment of potential employees for the purpose of employing them to perform work for a third party
      • payments to sub-agents as a finder’s fee
      • payments required to cover costs of recruitment fees from employees
      • payments to cover costs of recruiting referral and placement services, for example advertising positions or conducting interviews.
    • related costs are expenses related to recruitment and placement within or across national borders, and when related to the recruitment process and initiated by a recruitment agency or employer or an agent acting on behalf of those parties, are not paid by the employee or potential employee. These can include:
      • medical costs: payments for medical examinations, tests or vaccinations
      • insurance costs: costs to insure the life, health or safety of an employee, including enrolment in migrant welfare funds
      • costs for skills and qualification tests, for example: language tests
      • costs for training and orientation: including on-site and pre-departure or post-arrival orientation of new employees
      • travel and lodging costs within the recruitment process, including for training, interviews, consular appointments, relocation, and return or repatriation
      • application and service fees that are required for the recruitment process, including fees for services in preparing, obtaining or legalising workers’ employment contracts, identity documents, passports, visas, background checks, security and exit clearances, banking services, and work and residence permits
      • equipment costs: for tools, uniforms, safety gear and other equipment needed to perform assigned work safely and effectively
      • this list of costs is not exhaustive.
  • Undisclosed costs are also never allowed, such as previously undisclosed cost recovery-fees for expenses after they occur.
  • The UoC is responsible for ensuring that any employees who are working at the UoC but recruited and/or contracted by a recruitment agency have not been charged any fees or costs, as outlined above.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts
  • contracts with any recruitment agencies that contain an agreement that workers will not be charged any fees towards recruitment at any stage of recruitment
  • payslips and pay records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether a recruitment agency has been used for recruitment;
  • that wage terms listed in contracts match payslips or payroll records and there are no hidden fees being deducted;
  • whether contracts of migrant workers contain clauses about repatriation;
  • employees’ perceptions of the nature and conditions of their recruitment process.

Useful Resources

  • ILO (2019), General Principles and Operational Guidelines for Fair Recruitment and Definition of Recruitment Fees and Related Costs. Available at: https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@ed_protect/@protrav/@migrant /documents/publication/wcms_703485.pdf

3.2.8 The UoC shall not engage in prison labour, including where any recruitment agencies are used.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Prison labour often involves the use of incarcerated individuals under conditions that can amount to forced labour.
  • Such employees may not have the freedom to choose their employment, which may be assigned as a condition of their incarceration or reintegration.
  • This indicator applies to any person held involuntarily, which includes:
    • unauthorised immigrants
    • refugees
    • people awaiting trial or sentence
    • prisoners
    • people in drug rehabilitation programmes
    • people held for retraining
    • people held for political reorientation.
  • This indicator also applies to reintegration programmes where work may be voluntary and persons held/prisoners may receive a salary.
    • Although the intention of such programmes is to facilitate an inmate’s transition back into society, ASC does not allow such programmes under the ASC Farm Standard as it is not in a position to monitor the fairness of such practices and ensure that there is no exploitation of people on a global scale.
  • The UoC is responsible for ensuring that any recruitment agencies used are not engaged in prison labour for employees working at the UoC.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts
  • written agreements with any recruitment agencies.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether any recruitment agencies are used, and where they source employees from.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.9 The UoC shall have a policy if providing loans and advances, in which the terms and conditions are not used to bind employees to employment. The policy shall be communicated to employees in an understandable manner.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This indicator only applies if loans and/or advances are provided by the UoC to its employees.
  • The policy should be documented and accessible and could for example include the following items:
    • eligibility
    • types of financial assistance available (for example, loans for specific purposes such as medical emergencies, education, or unexpected expenses and advances)
    • approval process
    • repayment terms
    • applicable interest and fees (note: interest cannot be charged on advances)
    • confidentiality
    • transparency.
  • Communicating in an understandable manner means that the UoC ensures that all
    employees understand the policy.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • loans and advances policy
  • payslips and pay records
  • signed agreements with the employees who are entering into the loan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that employees understand the conditions around loans and advances.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.10 The UoC shall allow employees to move around the workplace to freely access sanitary
facilities and have access to drinking water during their shift.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should ensure that employees’ access to drinking water is unrestricted.
  • Free movement of employees to use sanitary facilities and access water:
    • helps prevent:
      • dehydration
      • heath stress
      • related health issues that can arise when workers are denied access to water
      • accidents and injuries caused by discomfort or dehydration.
    • is sometimes guided by health and safety or food safety procedures. For example, the farm may need employees to change clothes for food preparation or move to a designated area for health and safety reasons.
  • Where employees have special needs, for example health needs that require frequent food and water, these needs are accommodated.
  • Employee representation and clear grievance mechanisms (Criterion 3.12) can support these practices.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • clearly labelled sanitary facilities and drinking water.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that employees are aware of this requirement and feel able to access these basic needs.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.11 The UoC shall not keep employees involuntarily at the site outside of a shift, including confining them in employee accommodation.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Keeping employees trapped at the workplace is a key indication that there is forced labour.
  • Preventing this can include that employers communicate to employees that they are allowed to:
    • leave the worksite
    • leave their accommodations when living on site, when they are not on their shift.
  • This does not apply where staying on site is part of the agreement of contracts, for example a two-week shift on a feed barge followed by one-week off.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts
  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that employees understand that they are free to leave the site when they are not on their shifts;
  • that there are no restrictions evident, such as locked gates, or external locks on dormitories.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.12 The UoC shall offer employees free-of-charge and safe transportation for employees to leave the site when it is not easily accessible.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • In order to ensure that the employee is freely able to leave the workplace as per Indicator 3.2.11, the UoC provides reasonable transportation for employees to reach nearby communities when:
    • there is no public transportation
    • there are no easily accessible, available and affordable private transportation options.
      • the UoC should agree with employees about what easily accessible and affordable means in their context. Employee representation can support with this.
  • An example of reasonable transportation to leave the premises would be the provision of a free shuttle at the start and end of each shift to the nearby towns where employees live, in areas where there is no public transport.
  • Where the workplace is remote, transportation may only be necessary at the end of an agreed upon time period, such as a shift.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • company policy about transport for remote sites
  • transport logs / schedules
  • vehicle maintenance logs
  • third party transport contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether there are public transport options to the site;
  • how employees travel to and from the work site;
  • available vehicles for transport appear safe and sufficient;
  • there are no transport fees in wage records.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.13 The UoC shall not require employees to reside in employee accommodation as a
condition of employment for easily accessible sites.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC may provide housing for employees that meets the terms of Criterion 3.11: Employee Accommodation.
  • When the UoC provides housing, whether it owns, leases or contracts the accommodation from a service provider, the UoC communicates to employees that living in this housing is optional for them.
  • The freedom for employees to choose where they live respects employees’ dignity and autonomy and prevents coercion and potentially trapping them in exploitative conditions.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether the worksite is easily accessible via public or private transport
  • how many employees live in accommodation provided by the UoC
  • that the decision to reside in accommodation provided by the UoC is the employee’s own choice

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.14 The UoC shall not require family members of owners or employees to work. Where family members have the opportunity to work, the UoC shall ensure they are separately and voluntarily contracted.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • If family members wish to be employed, the UoC respects their right to make independent employment decisions by contracting them separately.
  • This indicator can be met by:
    • implementing independent recruitment processes for family members, similar to how one would hire any other employee
    • avoiding any forms of coercion or pressure to compel family members to work for the farm.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether family members live on site, which can increase the likelihood that they may work at the UoC;
  • everyone working at the UoC has an employment contract.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.2.15 The UoC shall not require employees to purchase from employer-operated stores or services as a condition of employment. Where alternative stores or services are not available due to the remote location, the UoC shall ensure that goods and services are sold at fair and reasonable prices.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The words ‘employer-operated’ here includes the UoC itself and any services that they may contract to operate a store or service.
  • Requiring employees to purchase goods or services from employer-operated stores or services is a form of economic coercion and can limit their economic freedom and choices.
  • Prices of goods and services should be based on an understanding of reasonable pricing of the same goods and services in the local market. Employers can also make this transparent by providing a cost breakdown of these goods and services.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts
  • payslips and pay records
  • any cost breakdown of goods and services in the local market.

Auditors should confirm:

  • if there are employer-operated stores and services on site;
  • the prices of goods at these facilities;
  • if any deductions are made from wages for goods purchased on site;
  • employees’ perception of their ability to choose where to purchase goods or services.

Video Preventing Child Labour Under the ASC Standards

Child Labour Under the ASC standards

Criterion 3.3 – Child Labour

Throughout this criterion, when we refer to the age of the child, we are referring to a full Western calendar year, where the child is 0 at birth.

3.3.1 The UoC shall not engage in child labour. Child labour is work that:

  • is mentally, physically, socially or morally dangerous and harmful to children; or
  • interferes with their schooling.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ‘No engagement’ means that child labour does not occur:

    • within the UoC’s production sites and facilities

    • as a result of actions taken by recruitment agencies for the UoC

    • within the UoC’s supply chain.

  • A child is anyone under the age of 18.

  • Child labour is any unacceptable form of work carried out by children and is prohibited by ASC, including the following:

    • all children under the age of 13 taking part in any economic activity;

    • all children aged 13 and 14 years old engaged in more than light work as stipulated by national, regional and/or local regulations;

    • all children under the age of 18 involved in work that is mentally, physically, socially or morally dangerous and harmful to children or interferes with their schooling.

  • Table 2 below shows the ages of children and the type of work that they are permitted to engage in:

Table 2. Ages of children and type of work permitted:

  • ILO notes: ‘Not all work done by children should be classified as child labour that is to be targeted for elimination. The participation of children or adolescents above the minimum age for admission to employment in work that does not affect their health and personal development or interfere with their schooling, is generally regarded as being something positive. This includes activities such as assisting in a family business or earning pocket money outside school hours and during school holidays. These kinds of activities contribute to children’s development and to the welfare of their families; they provide them with skills and experience, and help to prepare them to be productive members of society during their adult life.’3636ILO, What is Child Labour? Available at: https://www.ilo.org/international-programme-elimination-childlabour-ipec/what-child-labour
  • If children are assisting at the UoC as part of it being a family business, this would be covered by the scope of this Criterion.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records
  • employee contracts
  • job descriptions of all employees.

Auditors should confirm:

  • presence of general risk factors for child labour in a country;

  • NGOs’ or other local organisations’ knowledge of any reports of child labour in the sector in this region;

  • human resources personnel’s awareness of any issues in the workplace;

  • worker or union representatives’ awareness of any issues in the workplace;

  • whether or not any children are present at the UoC;

  • that employees and managers have an understanding of what is hazardous work and what is light work;

  • confirm life or work histories of employees, when a suspicion exists that the age of an employee does not match the records.

Useful Resources

  • What is Child Labour? What is child labour | International Labour Organization (ilo.org)
  • Supplier Guidance on Preventing, Identifying and Addressing Child Labour, ILO https://www.ilo.org/ipec/Informationresources/WCMS_792211/lang–en/index.htm
  • Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil Guidance on Child Rights for Palm Oil Producer https://rspo.org/wp-content/uploads/RSPO-GUI-T08-007_V1_ENG_Guidance_on_Child_Rights_for_PO_Producers.pdf#:~:text=The%20RSPO%20standards%20require%20palm,for%20employees%20and%20their%20families.
  • Rainforest Alliance Child Labor Guide https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/resource-item/child-labor-guide-an-introduction/
  • FAO Guidance on addressing child labour in fisheries and aquaculture: https://www.fao.org/3/i3318e/i3318e.pdf

3.3.2 If child labour is identified, the UoC shall implement remediation processes that prioritise the best interest of the child, following the method outlined in Appendix 10.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The remediation framework is set out in Appendix 10, including timelines, corrective action and reporting obligations.
  • Remediation of child labour:
    • will vary depending on the situation and the needs of the child in question
    • always takes into account the best interest of the child
    • is ideally carried out in consultation with local experts such as NGOs.
  • When remediating a case of child labour, there can be different steps in the process, which can include:
    • immediate actions to safeguard the child, for example removing them from the work situation to a safe location and locating their parents;
    • medium-term actions to develop a plan to protect the child both in the short and longer term and provide appropriate remedy to the victim, including but not limited to:
      • medical or other care as necessary
      • ensuring they are being safely looked after
      • access to adequate resources for the child and for their education;
    • long-term actions to enact and monitor the plan, which can take up to several years.
  • The UoC should engage in a process of developing corrective actions to prevent child labour reoccurring. This can include:
    • performing an analysis of what went wrong in their system to prevent it
    • implementing measures to prevent future recurrence
    • considering working with local experts on this corrective action. 
  • Potential measures to prevent child labour include:
    • robust age verification system prior to employment
    • facilitate children’s access to school
    • employee education about child labour and child rights
    • facilitate access to childcare for employees
    • pay workers a living wage
    • promote community awareness on child labour
    • provide literacy and numeracy training for employees
    • birth registration campaign.
  • Given the complexity of human rights issues, partnership with external partners is often necessary to provide effective remediation. They can:
    • provide support for the development of a remediation plan
    • help in implementing the remediation plan
    • help to implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence.
  • These potential partners can include:
    • local NGOs
    • individual experts
    • community liaisons/leaders
    • government offices 
    • supply chain partners, or others.
  • Potential support that these partners can provide could include:
    • training
    • improved access to social services and education
    • advocacy
    • directly financial support or other support for the affected person and their families to find other sources of income.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented remediation procedures

  • records and documents of any remediation process that has taken place

  • records and documents of any corrective actions that have been put into place

  • documented monitoring system in place.

Auditors should confirm:

  • existence of effective and appropriate remediation procedures;

  • knowledge and capacity of staff to implement remediation procedures;

  • the ability of the site to monitor any corrective actions within their management system;

  • knowledge and capacity of staff to develop corrective actions, where necessary.

Useful Resources

  • Eliminating Child Labor, Best Practice for Remediation, GoodWeave  https://goodweave.org/best-practice-briefs/#:~:text=The%20GoodWeave%20System%20is%20a,root%20causes%20of%20child%20labor

3.3.3 The UoC shall implement an age verification mechanism for all employees and shall maintain records of verified ages.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • An employment process that includes an age verification mechanism helps to confirm that employees are of the age category indicated, thereby enabling the UoC to prevent all forms of child labour.

  • Age is verified by legal documentation in a robust age identification process where the UoC requires proof of identity:

    • preferably an official photo ID card such as a national ID or passport, or

    • birth documentation.

  • If there are concerns that the identification may not be authentic, the employer can interview the applicant including information on their background (for example about schooling history, family and family members) to make sure that the potential employee is being honest about their age, and the information provided is plausible.

  • If there is no identification available, the employer can interview family members and community members, using significant events to help to place the year of the person’s birth. For example, finding out if the person was born before or after the big flood in the village.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • how management implements age verification

  • the ages of employees.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.3.4 The UoC shall report to ASC if the UoC is a family farm and if any children work on the site, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This is a reporting requirement, not a disclosure requirement, which means that all data is held confidentially by ASC, who does not share it publicly.

  • Companies should never publicly share personal employee data.

  • The information collected through this reporting requirements will enable ASC to:

    • gain insights into family farms where children may help out their parents, which will inform the future development of ASC’s child labour requirements

    • foster open discussions about the challenges of family farms.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • confirmation of data uploaded to MyASC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that data uploaded to MyASC is consistent with results of the wage gap analysis.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.3.5 The UoC shall not employ children under the age of 13 under any circumstances.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Employing children under the age of 13 carries risks for their physical, mental, social and moral development and wellbeing.

  • There are no circumstances in which employing a child under the age of 13 is permitted under the ASC Farm Standard.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • employee contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether there are any children living at the site or otherwise present;

  • whether employee contracts match the age verification records;

  • employees’ knowledge of any children having been on site.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.3.6 The UoC ensure any child employed aged 13 and 14, or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling, only conducts light work if permitted by applicable law and where the following conditions are met:

a)

a risk assessment is conducted to determine that the work is non-hazardous; and

b)

the child receives appropriate training prior to work; and

c)

the child receives appropriate supervision; and

d)

parental/guardian consent is given; and

e)

the work does not interfere with schooling; and

f)

the work is for limited hours (see Indicators 3.3.9 and 3.3.14)

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The age of completion of mandatory schooling refers to the national, legal age at which children are allowed to leave school.

  • If children are below this age, they cannot be employed as young employees and come under the category of only being allowed to conduct light work. For example, if school is mandatory in a country until the age of 16, a 15-year-old child may not be employed as a young employee, but only employed for light work.

  • Allowing children to conduct light work means that there are stricter working conditions in place than for other employees, including:

    • the type of work they are able to do

    • the hours they can work

    • the extra support that they need

    • the place that work must have in the wider context of their lives.

  • Children aged 13 and 14 may be employed by the UoC for light work when:

    • they are appropriately supervised and trained by adults

    • the work is non-hazardous

    • the work does not interfere with their schooling

    • the work does not take place during normal school hours

    • they have parental/guardian consent to work

    • work is limited to specific times of the day.

  • Children helping parents at home with daily chores or participating in other activities unrelated to the function of the UoC are not covered in the scope of the ASC Farm Standard.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • job and activity descriptions

  • training records

  • working hours records

  • evidence of parental/guardian consent.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the kinds of tasks that all employees are carrying out;

  • whether there are any children employed by the UoC;

  • whether there are any children living at the UoC with their families;

  • who provides supervision of young employees and how;

  • young employees’ description of their tasks and working hours.

Useful Resources

  • United States Department of Labor: The Findings on the Worst Forms of Child Labour report (updated annually): https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ilab/resources/reports/child-labor/findings

3.3.6 The UoC shall ensure any young employees only conduct work where the following conditions are met:

a)

a risk assessment is conducted to determine that the work is non-hazardous; and

b)

the young employee receives appropriate training prior to work; and

c)

the young employee receives appropriate supervision; and

d)

parental/guardian consent is given; and

a)

work is for limited hours (see Indicators 3.3.9, 3.3.10, 3.3.15-3.3.18).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC:

    • understands whether a child is allowed to be classed as a young employee

    • understands the legal requirements for children to attend school in their country of operation

    • ensures that young employees do not engage in work that is hazardous

    • complies with the working hours limits set out in this criterion.

  • Children aged 15, 16 and 17 may be employed by the UoC as young employees, as long as:

    • the work is not hazardous

    • they are appropriately supervised and trained

    • they are above the age of mandatory schooling

    • they have parental/guardian consent to work

    • the national, regional, and/or local law permits children to work.

  • Children below the age of completion of mandatory schooling are not allowed to be employed as young employees but may be permitted to
    conduct light work. For example, if school is mandatory in a country until the age of 16, a 15-year-old child may not be employed as a young employee, but only employed for light work.

  • Children are prohibited not only from any work that has been deemed hazardous for adults, but also from work that may not be hazardous for adults but that may be for children, for example:

    • a job that requires long periods of isolation without human contact, which can cause mental harm such as stress, anxiety and depression to a child;

    • physical work carrying heavy loads, which can lead to physical injury and permanent damage to a body that is still developing.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • risk assessment documents

  • training records

  • age verification records

  • job and activity descriptions

  • evidence of parental/guardian consent.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the kinds of tasks that all employees are carrying out;

  • whether there are any children employed by the UoC;

  • whether there are any children living at the UoC with their families;

  • who provides supervision of young employees and how;

  • young employees’ description of their tasks and working hours.

Useful Resources

  • United States Department of Labor: The Findings on the Worst Forms of Child Labour report (updated annually): https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ilab/resources/reports/child-labor/findings

3.3.8 The UoC shall facilitate school attendance for any children living at the site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Ensuring access to education helps prevent child labour.

  • No child under 18 working at the UoC may be:

    • deprived of educational opportunities (including attending school during school hours or after school activities)

    • forced to leave, drop out, or otherwise depart school early

    • forced to combine school attendance with long working hours.

  • When employees and their families live on site, the UoC supports access to schools for employees’ children. This may mean, for example:

    • providing parents the time to drop off and pick up their children

    • providing a bus service or bicycles to reach school when the nearest school is outside walking distance

    • raising awareness among employees about the importance of children attending school.

  • If children live off the UoC site, but on another site or at accommodation provided by the UoC, this indicator applies.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • information about which children live on the site.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether there are any children living on the site with their families;

  • the availability of schools in the local area

  • whether children living on site are attending school and how they get there.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Excessive working hours can have a detrimental physical and mental impact on all people, but particularly on children under the age of 18 who have not yet reached adulthood.

  • Protecting children from excessive working hours is an important part of the prevention of child labour.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • young employee contracts.

3.3.10 The UoC shall not allow overtime hours for employees under the age of 18.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Any hours over and above the standard contracted hours are considered overtime. For example, an employee could be contracted to a standard four hour week and if they were to work the fifth hour, this would be deemed as overtime.

  • Employees under the age of 18 are not allowed to work any hours over their standard contracted hours.

  • Excessive working hours can have a detrimental physical and mental impact on all people, but particularly on children under the age of 18 who have not yet reached adulthood.

  • Protecting children from excessive working hours is an important part of the prevention of child labour.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • working hours records

  • payslips and pay records

  • young employee contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether anyone under the age of 18 is employed at the UoC;

3.3.11 The UoC shall ensure that children conducting light work:

a)

do not work more than 14 hours per week (excluding breaks); and

b)

do not work more than 2 hours per day on a school day (excluding breaks); and

c)

do not work more than 3 hours per day on a non-school day (excluding breaks); and

d)

have a combined time for school, work and transportation to and from school and work totalling less than 8 hours per day (excluding breaks).

Indicator applicability: children aged 13 or 14, or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Excessive working hours can have a detrimental physical and mental impact on all people, but particularly on children under the age of 18 who have not yet reached adulthood.

  • Protecting children from excessive working hours is an important part of the prevention of child labour.

  • Children engaged in light work have restrictions on the number of hours that they can work:

    • on a school day to ensure that work does not interfere with their schooling

    • on a non-school day and across a week to ensure that they:

      • are not working an excessive number of hours

      • have adequate time for education, rest and play.

  • Requiring that a child conducting light work spends no more than 8 hours per day at school, work and on transportation is important for allowing them to have adequate rest and leisure time.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • working hours records

  • payslips and pay records

  • young employees’ contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether anyone under the age of 15 or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling is employed at the UoC;

  • working hours and rest hours of employees under the age of 15 or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling;

  • that information in contracts, age verification records and payslips match;

  • young employees’ description of their working hours.

3.3.12 The UoC shall ensure that where children conduct light work for more than 2 hours on a non-school day, an additional 0.5-hour break period is included within the shift.

Indicator applicability: children aged 13 or 14, or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Excessive working hours can have a detrimental physical and mental impact on all people, but particularly on children under the age of 18 who have not yet reached adulthood.

  • Protecting children from excessive working hours is an important part of the prevention of child labour.

  • Children engaged in light work should have regular breaks.

  • Where a child is conducting light work for a period of more than 2 hours (only applicable on a non-school day under the ASC Farm Standard), they shall be given a 0.5-hour break period.

  • Some examples that demonstrate compliance with the ASC Farm Standard:

    • Child A works on a Saturday morning from 9:00 – 11:00. She has a 30-minute break and works again from 11:30 – 12:30.

      • Child A’s example is compliant because she is working no more than 3 hours on a non-school day, and she is given a break of 0.5 hours within the work shift.

    • Child B works on a Tuesday afternoon from 15:00 – 17:00 and then goes home.

      • Child B’s example is compliant because he is working no more than 2 hours on a school day.

  • Some examples that demonstrate non-compliance with the ASC Farm Standard:

    • Child C works on a Saturday morning from 9:00 – 11:30 and then goes home.

      • Child C’s example is non-compliant because she has worked more than 2 hours without a break.

    • Child D works on a Tuesday afternoon from 15:00 – 17:30 and then goes home.

      • Child D’s example is non-compliant because he has worked more than 2 hours on a school day.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • working hours records

  • payslips and pay records

  • young employees’ contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether anyone under the age of 15 or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling is employed at the UoC;

  • working hours and rest hours of employees under the age of 15 or below the age of completion of mandatory schooling;

  • that information in contracts, age verification records and payslips match;

  • young employees’ description of their working hours.

3.3.16 The UoC shall ensure that young employees have a total break time of at least 1 hour within 8 consecutive hours of work, with at least 0.5 hours break within any 4.5 consecutive hours of work.

Indicator applicability: young employees aged 15 or above and above the age of completion of mandatory schooling.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Excessive working hours can have a detrimental physical and mental impact on all people, but particularly on children under the age of 18 who have not yet reached adulthood.

  • Protecting children from excessive working hours is an important part of the prevention of child labour.

  • Young employees should have regular breaks.

  • A young employee should have at least 1 hour break within 8 hours of work, and at least 0.5 hours break within 4.5 hours of work.

  • Some examples that demonstrate compliance with the ASC Farm Standard:

    • A works on a Monday from 9:00 – 17:00 and has a break for lunch from 12:00 -13:00.

      • A’s example is compliant because her workday is no more than 8 hours long and within those 8 hours, she has 1 hour break.

    • B works on a Thursday afternoon from 10:00 – 14:30 and has a break from 12:00 – 12:30.
      • B’s example is compliant because he is working 4.5 hours with a 0.5-hour break in that time.

  • Some examples that demonstrate non-compliance with the ASC Farm Standard:

    • C works on a Friday from 9:00 – 18:00 and has a break for lunch from 12:00 -13:00.

      • C’s example is non-compliant because, even though she has a 1-hour break, her workday is 9 hours long.

    • Child D works on a Tuesday afternoon from 13:00 – 18:00 and then goes home.
      • Child D’s example is non-compliant because he has worked more than 4.5 hours without a break.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • age verification records

  • working hours records

  • payslips and pay records

  • young employees’ contracts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether anyone under the age of 18 is employed at the UoC;

  • working hours and rest hours of employees under the age of 18;

  • that information in contracts, age verification records and payslips match;

  • young employees’ description of their working hours.

Discrimination and Harassment 3.4

3.4.1 The UoC shall not engage in or tolerate any form of discrimination, and shall ensure that all employees and applicants receive equal treatment and opportunities in all employment and recruitment practices.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Discrimination is the unequal treatment of different of people, based on their personal characteristics, such as:

    • age

    • caste

    • colour

    • disabilities

    • ethnicity

    • gender

    • legal status

    • marital status

    • nationality

    • parental status

    • participation in trade unions

    • political opinion

    • pregnancy

    • race

    • religion

    • sexual orientation.

  • Discrimination:

    • is a global and pervasive problem

    • causes negative impacts on many levels

    • can lead to individuals suffering unequal treatment, stress and harm, at home, in society and in the workplace

    • can perpetuate poverty

    • can stifle development and productivity.

  • Sometimes discrimination can be obvious and clear, but at other times it can be difficult to detect and consequently, hard to address.

  • Equal opportunities means:

    • equal pay for equal work

    • equal living standard for equal work

    • equal employment possibilities for equal ability/engagement

    • equal promotion possibilities for equal ability/engagement.

  • Equal opportunities at work means that all employees in an organisation, regardless of their sex, race, language, religion, economic or family situation, and other characteristics, have the same opportunities for:

    • education

    • training

    • career development

    • chances to apply for and be selected for posts

    • chances to be promoted.

  • Table 3 below shows some examples of situations considered and not considered discrimination.

Table 3. Examples of discrimination situations:

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • terms of service between recruitment agencies and the UoC

  • documents from recruitment processes

  • payslips and pay records

  • employee contracts and terms and conditions

  • anti-discrimination policies

  • hiring and promotion policies

  • diversity and inclusion policies

  • training records for employees and managers related to non-discrimination

  • termination and disciplinary records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether employees feel that they and their colleagues receive equal treatment, and that promotions are based on merit;

  • whether the composition of the workforce at different levels suggests there are no barriers for certain groups to be promoted.

Useful Resources

  • The Equal Opportunities Commission: www.eoc.org.uk

  • European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions: https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/observatories/eurwork/industrial-relations-dictionary/equal-opportunities

3.4.2 The UoC shall not engage in or tolerate any form of violence or harassment.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • ‘The term ‘violence and harassment’ in the world of work refers to a range of unacceptable behaviours and practices or threats thereof, whether a single occurrence or repeated, that aim at, result in, or are likely to result in physical, psychological, sexual or economic harm, and includes gender-based violence and harassment.’3737Convention C190 – Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) (ilo.org)
  • Violence and harassment can come in many forms, including:
    • sexual
    • mental
    • verbal
    • physical.
  • Examples of harassment in the workplace can include the following3838Workplace bullying and harassment – GOV.UK (www.gov.uk).
    • spreading malicious rumours
    • unfair treatment
    • picking on or regularly undermining someone
    • denying someone training or promotion opportunities.
  • Harassment can happen in many forms:
    • in person (face to face, by phone)
    • in writing (email, letter, text)
    • online (on social media).
  • It can be:
    • undertaken by a single person or group of people
    • hidden (for example, gossiping about someone in their absence)
    • overt (for example, an unwanted nickname that undermines someone).
  • One widespread form of harassment is sexual harassment, which can also take place in the workplace and is any unwanted behaviour of a sexual nature. Examples can include3939What sexual harassment is – Sexual harassment – Acas:
    • anything that violates someone’s dignity
    • inappropriately and uncomfortably crowding someone else
    • telling sexually offensive jokes
    • making sexual remarks or gestures about someone’s body, clothing or appearance
    • making sexual comments or jokes about someone’s sexual orientation or gender reassignment
    • asking questions about someone’s sex life
    • displaying or sharing pornographic or sexual images, or other sexual content
    • touching someone against their will 
    • sexual assault or rape.
  • Power dynamics can play a part in harassment, for example:
    • something that could be a joke between two friends outside the workplace can be a case of harassment in the workplace if there is an unequal balance of power;
    • someone in management making a flirtatious comment to a junior colleague is not appropriate, whereas the same comment between two friends might be acceptable. 
  • Responsible management includes being aware of a manager’s position in relation to the people who they manage.
  • Abusive behaviour can include4040CCOHS: Violence and Harassment in the Workplace:
    • threatening behaviour (such as shaking fists, destroying property or throwing objects)
    • verbal or written threats (any expression of an intent to inflict harm)
    • verbal abuse (swearing, insults or condescending language)
    • physical attacks (hitting, shoving, pushing or kicking).
  • The workplace includes not just the physical place of work, but anywhere where work-related events or interactions occur. 
  • Workplace violence and harassment can occur not only in the workplace but also off-site at social events related to work, business meetings away from the UoC, or outside the workplace and away from work.
  • Some steps towards the prevention of harassment and discrimination can include:
    • employees and management are trained and know and understand what harassment and discrimination are 
    • the UoC clearly states its position on discrimination through an internal code of conduct, policy or in a statement
    • the UoC assesses where there is potential for discrimination. For example, the UoC acknowledges the high number of migrant employees and understands that this is potentially a group who are at risk of being discriminated against
    • the UoC develops an action plan to prevent discrimination, which includes monitoring where there is a risk of discrimination.
  • Providing good communication of what these behaviours look like and why they are not permitted creates awareness among employees in the workplace. 
  • Regular dialogue with employees and with employee representatives can be an effective way of monitoring what is going on.
  • An accessible, safe and anonymous reporting system (grievance mechanism) can give employees the ability to report violence or harassment.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • anti-harassment policy that includes the prohibition of abusive and exploitative behaviour

  • training records

  • disciplinary records

  • health and safety incident reports

  • grievances that have been reported.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand what they should do if any violence or harassment takes place;

  • employees are familiar with the UoC’s position on violence and harassment;

  • employees’ perceptions of how they or their colleagues are treated;

  • any instances of violence and harassment that have taken place and how they have been dealt with;

  • there are no unusually high staff turnover rates;

  • human resources personnel are aware of any issues in the workplace;

  • worker or union representatives are aware of any issues in the workplace.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.4.3 The UoC shall ensure that employees, whether employed directly or through a recruitment agency, are not tested for pregnancy or virginity and are not forced or coerced into involuntary contraception.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Tests for virginity sometimes take place in some parts of the world as a custom and practice, with the social expectation that women and girls should remain ‘virgins’ until they are married.

  • The term ‘virginity’, as used in this way, is not a medical or scientific term, but a social and cultural construct that reflects discrimination against women and girls.

  • It is discrimination if a woman is tested for pregnancy during recruitment.

  • This indicator helps:

    • prevent this kind of discrimination by ensuring that testing for pregnancy or virginity is not permitted

    • protect women against unnecessary and potentially invasive tests.

  • The ASC Farm Standard does not permit testing for pregnancy during recruitment or ongoing employment but having a company policy that states that pregnancies need to be declared from a certain point onwards, for health and safety reasons, is appropriate and can be necessary for safeguarding a mother and baby’s health.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • terms of service between recruitment agencies and the UoC

  • documents from recruitment processes

  • information about which, if any, medical tests are conducted

  • hiring and medical examination policies.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the experiences of female employees during the hiring process;

  • medical tests are only carried out based on a risk assessment (see also 3.4.5).

Useful Resources

  • https://www.who.int/news/item/17-10-2018-united-nations-agencies-call-for-ban-on-virginity-testing

3.4.4 The UoC shall ensure that medical tests are only conducted during the recruitment process if required for the function of the job or by applicable law, including where any recruitment agencies are used.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • There are occasional situations where the UoC, or the agency involved in recruitment may need to perform medical tests. For example:

    • it is required by law.

    • if the function of the job requires it.

    • for health and safety reasons.

    • determining whether a medical test is necessary happens through a
      health and safety risk assessment (Indicator 3.5.4).

  • Examples of when medical tests may be allowed are:

    • when the function of a job might require a medical test, such as in the recruitment of divers. A diver may have to undergo a chest x-ray to demonstrate that they are fit enough to dive regularly.

    • when an employee is asked to test for COVID-19 before coming into the workplace, to avoid the spread of the disease.

    • when a test may be required by national law, such as the existence of laws in 25 countries that make HIV testing mandatory to obtain a work or residence permit: https://lawsandpolicies.unaids.org/topicresult?i=25&lan=en.

  • Examples of when medical tests may not be allowed are:

    • a test for sexually transmitted infections (STI), which could lead to discrimination about someone’s sexual practices and/or ability to work.

    • when an HIV test is given outside of the 25 countries that make HIV testing mandatory to obtain a work or residence permit, as they are not relevant for the function of any jobs in aquaculture.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • terms of service between recruitment agencies and the UoC

  • documents from recruitment processes

  • health and safety and food safety risk assessments that require medical testing

  • information about which medical tests are required.

Auditors should confirm:

  • where medical tests are required, the decision for these tests has been based on the outcome of a risk assessment;

  • employees understand the reasons for the medical tests.

N/A

3.4.5 The UoC shall only require medical tests during employment if justified by a healthy and safety or food safety risk assessment.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • There are occasional situations where the UoC, or the agency involved in recruitment may need to perform medical tests. For example:

    • it is required by law

    • if the function of the job requires it

    • for health and safety reasons.

  • Determining whether a medical test is necessary happens through a health and safety risk assessment (Indicator 3.5.4).

  • Examples of when medical tests may or may not be allowed are:

    • An example of when the function of a job might require a medical test is the recruitment of divers, a diver may have to undergo a chest x-ray to demonstrate that they are fit enough to dive regularly.

    • An example of when a medical test might be necessary is if an employee is asked to test for Covid-19 before coming into the workplace, to avoid the spread of the disease.

    • An example of when a medical test is not allowed is an STI test, which could lead to discrimination about someone’s sexual practices and / or ability to work.

    • An example of when a test may be required by national law is the existence of laws in 25 countries that have a law that makes HIV testing mandatory to obtain a work or residence permit: https://lawsandpolicies.unaids.org/topicresult?i=25&lan=en. Outside of these 25 countries, an HIV test is not necessary and would not be conducted as it is not relevant for the function of any jobs in aquaculture.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • terms of service between recruitment agencies and the UoC

  • documents from recruitment processes

  • health and safety and food safety risk assessments that require medical testing

  • information about which medical tests are required.

Auditors should confirm:

  • where medical tests are required, the decision for these tests has been based on the outcome of a risk assessment;

  • employees understand the reasons for the medical tests.

3.4.6 The UoC shall, when requiring medical tests (see Indicators 3.4.4 and 3.4.5), ensure that:

a.

employees understand the reasons for the tests; and

b.

employees’ medical information is confidential; and

c.

employees have access to their test results; and

d.

employees have the right to use a medical professional of their own choosing, if preferred; and

e.

employees are not charged for the tests.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Any reasons for medical tests are clearly communicated to the employee or prospective employee, at time of recruitment where necessary.

  • The employee or prospective employee has the right to their test results and the UoC ensures that the results are kept confidential.

  • The cost of medical tests is paid by the UoC and is not a cost that is charged to the employee or prospective employee.

  • In some situations, the UoC may have an on-site doctor, or a doctor that there is an established relationship with, who regularly conducts the necessary medical tests. However, an employee or prospective employee is allowed to choose to consult an independent doctor, who could be their own doctor, or someone completely unrelated to the UoC.

  • Costs incurred by employees or prospective employees towards medical tests, if using an independent doctor, are to be reimbursed within an agreed time period.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • terms of service between recruitment agencies and the UoC

  • documents from recruitment processes

  • information about which medical tests are required

  • evidence of provision of copies of medical tests to employees.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the reasons for the medical tests;

  • employees have access to their test results and they are confidential;

  • employees understand that they are able to use an independent doctor if they prefer;

  • there are no costs incurred by employees for any medical tests.

Health and Safety 3.5

3.5.1 The UoC shall carry out a site-specific health and safety risk assessment, approved by a member of senior management, following the method outlined in Appendix 3 (3.4).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • “A risk assessment is simply a careful examination of what, in the workplace, could cause harm to people”4141https://www.ilo.org/media/453896/download#:~:text=A%20risk%20assessment%20is%20simply,and%20members%20of%20the%20public..
  • The ILO identifies five steps in a risk assessment:
    • Step 1: Identify the hazards
    • Step 2: Identify who might be harmed and how
    • Step 3: Evaluate the risk – identify and decide on the safety and health risk control measures
    • Step 4: Record who is responsible for implementing which risk control measures and the timeframe
    • Step 5: Record the findings, monitor and review the risk assessment and update when necessary.
  • The risks assessment should:
    • cover all site activities;
    • result in contingency or prevention measures for all risks identified.
  • The risk assessment should be reviewed and revised:
    • prior to starting a new activity;
    • following feedback on major issues from employees;
    • when a new site is added to the UoC;
    • when there has been a significant change to the process;
    • following accidents or near misses;
    • annually.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented health and safety risk assessments

  • list of contingency and preventative measures to mitigate the risks.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the member of staff that is responsible for conducting and maintaining the risk assessment has a good understanding of the different risks on site, and the actions taken to mitigate them.

  • https://www.ilo.org/media/453896/download#:~:text=A%20risk%20assessment%20is%20simply,and%20members%20of%20the%20public

3.5.2 The UoC shall ensure that the person conducting the site-specific health and safety risk assessment has the necessary competencies, experience and training. In cases where regulatory requirements are defined, the UoC shall ensure that the person conducting the site-specific health and safety risk assessment complies with these requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • To demonstrate competence, the person carrying out the health and safety risk assessment should:

    • understand the:

      • different steps of a risk assessment process

      • health and safety risks inherent in aquaculture operations

      • context of the UoC

      • number of employees and their roles

      • variety of different activities carried out across the site and what they involve;

    • be able to:

      • record risks in a clear and consistent way

      • identify risks in all of the different areas of the site and operations of the UoC

      • identify preventative measures for risks

      • identify mitigation measures for risks

    • have experience conducting health and safety risk assessments

    • have undergone training on conducting health and safety risk assessments. This training can be:

      • ASC training

      • training from an external provider

      • on-the-job training from someone experienced in conducting health and safety risk assessments.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • training records

  • qualifications of the person conducting the health and safety risk assessment

  • health and safety risk assessment.

Auditors should confirm:

  • what applicable legal requirements there are for health and safety risk assessments;

  • the qualifications and experience of the person conducting the health and safety risk assessment;

  • how effective and thorough the risk assessment is that is in place.

3.5.3 The UoC shall allow any person the freedom to remove themselves from an unsafe situation without seeking permission and without fear of retribution.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This requirement is applicable to both the workplace and any accommodation facilities provided by the UoC.

  • An employee could decide that a workplace is unsafe if there are significant risks to health or safety due to, for example:

    • inadequate safety measures

    • faulty equipment

    • lack of training

    • hazardous substances

    • non-compliance with safety laws

    • anything that makes the employee feel unsafe.

  • If an employee feels unsafe, they do not need to ask prior permission to remove themselves from the situation.

  • Retribution can take many forms and can be:

    • obvious punishment, for example:

      • physical threats

      • verbal threats or warnings

    • hidden punishment, for example:

      • being ignored for a promotion

      • being refused requests that are unrelated to the unsafe situation

      • hostile treatment.

  • Management can communicate to employees that they are able to remove themselves from any unsafe situations, for example through:

    • training

    • information in their contracts

    • verbal explanations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts

  • health and safety training records

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand that they are able to remove themselves from unsafe situations without fear of retribution;

  • employees understand what unsafe situations may occur and are aware of escape routes and emergency procedures;

  • management understand that employees have the right to remove themselves from unsafe situations without fear of retribution.
