N/A

3.5.4 The UoC shall ensure that any person with a medical condition, or who is pregnant, does not conduct hazardous work as determined by the health and safety risk assessment (see Indicator 3.5.1).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Hazardous work can include:
    • working with chemicals or dangerous substances
    • working at heights or in dangerous situations
    • heavy lifting or work that is physically challenging
    • working with heavy machinery.
  • Examples of adjusting working conditions for pregnant women can include:
    • reducing physical stress, this includes limiting the weight that employees are lifting:
      • week 1-19 of the pregnancy: maximum of 10 kilos at a time
      • week 20-29 of pregnancy: maximum of 5 kilos up to 10 times a day 
      • from week 30 of pregnancy, maximum of 5 kilos up to 5 times a day 
      • from week 28 of pregnancy, the employee also shouldn’t bend or kneel more than once an hour
      • up to 6 months after giving birth, any work involving lifting, carrying, pulling, and pushing objects should be slowly built up
  • avoiding pregnant women performing tasks under environmental (atmospheric) pressure, such as diving
  • not exposing pregnant and breastfeeding mothers to hazardous substances and bacteria that can harm the (unborn) child.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented health and safety risk assessments.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether there are pregnant women or people with medical conditions working at the UoC;

  • whether or not they have been included in the health and safety risk assessment;

  • that staff responsible for health and safety have an understanding of the particular risks that face pregnant women and people with a medical condition, and how to mitigate those risks.

3.5.5 The UoC shall ensure that any person working on the site receives health and safety training as required to carry out their job. The UoC shall ensure that training is:

a)

free of charge; and

b)

provided in a timely manner; and

c)

repeated on a regular basis; and

d)

conducted during regularly remunerated working hours, or the person is compensated for their time; and

e)

updated as necessary based on new procedures or equipment; and

f)

documented, and records maintained.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Training is important because it contributes to shared responsibility for health and safety, and a workplace where everyone is protected.

  • Training is delivered in a format and language that all employees can understand:

    • provisions are made for anyone who is illiterate

    • the UoC is responsible for ensuring that all employees have understood the training.

  • Training is documented so that it is clear who has attended and what they were trained on.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • training records demonstrating regular training sessions and content trained on

  • attendance records confirming that all employees have been trained.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the different health and safety risks present at the site;

  • employees understand good practices around health and safety at the site;

  • employees have not paid for the training and it has taken place either during working hours, or they have been paid for the time that they have given to the training.

3.5.6 The UoC shall maintain written records of health and safety accidents and near misses, determine the cause and implement appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • An accident is an unexpected event that causes damage, injury or harm.
  • A near miss is an incident that had the potential to cause damage, injury or harm, but was prevented4242https://www.reengage.org.uk/about-us/policies-guidelines/accident-incident-and-near-miss-policy. 
  • The recording and investigation of both of these is important. By investigating to determine the root cause, the UoC is able to:
    • take corrective actions that will allow the incident not to reoccur
    • spot potential problems and prevent them from occurring in the first place.
  • Corrective actions are actions that the UoC can put in place to ensure that the incident does not occur again. Examples are in Table 4 below:

Table 4. Examples of incidents, their cause and the resulting corrective actions:

  • There is a difference between immediate corrective action and the corrective actions to take once the root cause has been determined. For example: a fire extinguisher is blocked by a bin being placed in front of the extinguisher:

    • staff take immediate corrective action and move the bin

    • however, the next day they find that someone has moved the bin back. The immediate corrective action did not prevent reoccurrence

    • staff investigate to determine the root cause and find out why the bin was placed there

    • the investigation shows that this is the most ergonomic layout of the workstation and the bin will always be moved back to that location by whoever is using the workstation

    • staff take long-term corrective action and move the fire extinguisher. This stops the issue from reoccurring.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of accidents or near misses

  • records of corrective actions taken

  • training records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees feel comfortable to report any accidents or near misses;

  • employees understand what the process is for reporting any accidents or near misses.

3.5.7 The UoC shall report to ASC any accidents, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This is a reporting requirement, not a disclosure requirement, which means that all data is held confidentially by ASC, who does not share it publicly.

  • Companies should never publicly share personal employee data.

  • The information collected through this reporting requirements will enable ASC to:

    • gain insights into common incidents and accidents and health and safety risks, which will inform the future development of ASC’s health and safety requirements

    • foster open discussions about health and safety risks and how to prevent them.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • confirmation of data uploaded to MyASC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that data uploaded to MyASC is consistent with results of the wage gap analysis.

3.5.8 The UoC shall ensure that appropriate and understandable health and safety notices, instructions, and warning signs are visibly displayed.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Potential hazards and risk areas around the site are clearly identified by warning signs.

  • The choice of signs, notices and instructions are informed by the health and safety risk assessment.

  • Written safety instructions for equipment use are accessible to all employees who need to use that equipment and are in a language that employees understand.

  • Written safety procedures are available to employees and:

    • include details on:

      • accident prevention and response

      • emergency procedures

    • are in a language that they understand

    • can include pictures or diagrams, which can be helpful.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • warning signs around the site

  • written safety instructions and procedures that are accessible for employees.

Auditors should confirm:

  • warning signs are clearly visible and potential hazards are clearly marked;

  • employees understand where they can access safety instructions and procedures;

  • employees understand what the warning signs mean and what they refer to.

3.5.9 The UoC shall ensure that clear and understandable emergency and fire safety procedures are in place.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should have procedures in place for emergencies that can have a significant impact on people on the site, including:
    • serious injuries
    • fire
    • explosion
    • flood
    • poisoning
    • electrocution
    • hazardous chemical spill.
  • Emergency procedures can include:
    • outlining what might happen and how to raise an alarm
    • what to do if an alarm goes off
    • a plan showing the location of hazardous items
    • a plan for emergency shutdown, isolation or making processes safe
    • how to call the emergency services
    • where the escape routes are located
    • where the assembly points are
    • what the responsibility is of each employee and the management.
  • Drills should be conducted regularly to ensure that employees understand the emergency procedures.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented fire and emergency safety procedures

  • list of equipment and information about maintenance schedules

  • list of hazardous items

  • relevant signs around the workplace.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees have taken part in a drill;

  • employees understand what to do in case of a fire or other emergency;

  • equipment is up-to-date and in good working order.

3.5.10 The UoC shall ensure that escape routes, fire exits, firefighting equipment and fire alarms are clearly marked and maintained in good working order.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Fire safety and other emergency measures are in place, for example:

    • fire alarms

    • marked fire exits

    • marked, well-lit and well-maintained emergency escape routes

    • assembly points

    • firefighting equipment that is maintained annually or as required.

  • Fire drills are conducted regularly to ensure that employees understand the emergency procedures.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented fire and emergency safety procedures

  • list of equipment and information about maintenance schedules

  • list of hazardous items

  • relevant signs around the workplace.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees have taken part in a drill;

  • employees understand what to do in case of a fire or other emergency;

  • equipment is up-to-date and in good working order.

3.5.11 The UoC shall ensure that escape routes, fire exits and firefighting equipment are accessible and clear of obstacles.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC is responsible for:

    • removing any obstacles around escape routes and fire exits

    • ensuring that emergency doors are not locked

    • ensuring that emergency equipment is not blocked by any obstacles.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • information about locations of emergency equipment.

Auditors should confirm:

3.5.12 The UoC shall provide and maintain appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) free of charge and monitor its proper use.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC assesses:

    • what Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is needed (meeting legal stipulations if applicable)

    • for which functions it is needed

    • in which situations it should be used

    • how PPE is well maintained.

  • The use of PPE should be the final option in protecting employees from hazards and the steps below are what comes before the use of PPE:

    • Elimination: Physically remove the hazard

    • Substitution: Replace the hazard with a non-hazardous process

    • Engineering controls: Isolate people from the hazard

    • Administrative controls: Change the way people work

    • PPE: Protect the worker with PPE.

  • PPE often comes with manufacturers’ instructions, which explain how to maintain equipment, and when equipment needs replacing.

  • Providing appropriate storage for the PPE, where it is protected from adverse weather conditions, will prolong the life and useability of the PPE.

  • Training for employees on the correct use of PPE is necessary for ensuring that PPE is used effectively.

  • When new PPE is introduced, or the method of using it changes, updated training helps to ensure the safety of all employees.

  • The list below is adapted from the EU’s Compliance Help Centre4343https://support.ce-check.eu/hc/en-us/articles/360021707072-8-Types-of-Personal-Protective-Equipment-PPE. PPE can include:

  • Employees need somewhere for PPE with:

    • adequate privacy to change into the PPE

    • somewhere to store their belongings

    • a designated place to store or return (e.g. laundry) the PPE after use.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • a record of available PPE, what it is used for and how it is maintained

  • health and safety risk assessment demonstrating when PPE is needed.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees are using PPE correctly and consistently;

  • the PPE is well maintained and in good working condition;

  • employees understand the reasoning behind the use of PPE and why it is important.

3.5.13 The UoC shall provide appropriate first aid in the event of a work-related injury, including access to professional medical assistance.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The supplies needed for first aid at the UoC can be determined by the health and safety risk assessment.
  • Professional medical assistance can include ensuring that the UoC is able to access doctors and an ambulance, where necessary.
  • The following list of first aid kit supplies is adapted from the UK government Health and Safety Executive website4444https://www.hse.gov.uk/simple-health-safety/firstaid/what-to-put-in-your-first-aid-kit.htm:
    • general guidance on first aid (an example from the UK government Health and Safety Executive can be found here: https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/indg347.pdf)
    • individually wrapped sterile plasters of assorted sizes 
    • sterile eye pads/eye wash
    • individually-wrapped triangular bandages, preferably sterile 
    • safety pins 
    • large and medium-sized sterile, individually-wrapped, unmedicated wound dressings
    • disposable gloves 
    • scissors or cutting tool.
  • First aid kits are:
    • checked regularly, to ensure that any items that are past their expiry date are safely disposed of and replaced
    • kept at several locations around the site
    • easily accessible 
    • located near potential hazards or areas of risk.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • complete and well maintained first aid kits in easily accessible locations

  • information about what the first aid kits contain and how to use them.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees know where the first aid kits are kept and how to use them;

  • the UoC has a process in place to ensure first aid kits remain fully stocked and serviceable.

3.5.14 The UoC shall, where not provided by a state or national social security or health system, provide and pay for insurance or have a system to cover costs for all employees for all work-related accidents or injuries. This shall include at least the following:

a)

the cost for transport and medical treatment and medication needed to treat the accident or injury; and

b)

the cost for transport and medical treatment and medication needed for recovery; and

c)

compensation for lost working hours; and

d)

cost for any required repatriation in case of migrant workers.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC is responsible for caring for its employees and protecting them from any financial impacts of an accident or injury.

  • The UoC should ensure that employees are protected from unfair dismissal if they are unable to work for long periods.

  • Depending on the level of the national social security of the country where the site is located, there are likely to be different costs that the UoC is responsible for.

  • For example: an employee injures his back lifting boxes of feed from a truck. He suffers an acute injury, falls down and struggles to stand. The site manager provides him with some painkillers from the first aid kit and takes him in a site vehicle to the nearest hospital. The employee receives some x-rays and is diagnosed as having strained his back and is given pain relief and told he cannot work for 3 weeks. The site manager does not charge the employee for the painkillers from the first aid kit, or the transport to the hospital. The UoC pays the full hospital bill and continues paying the employee’s salary for the 3 weeks that he is off work.

    • If this incident took place in Country A, where there is a social security and healthcare system, the site manager does not charge the employee for the painkillers from the first aid kit, or the transport to the hospital. The UoC does not have to pay any hospital bill because the national health system pays for that. The UoC does not have to pay any of the employee’s salary for the 3 weeks that he is off work because that is covered by the national social security system.

    • If this incident took place in Country B, where there is no social security and healthcare system, the UoC pays all of the costs, as outlined above.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • information about what is provided by the national government

  • documentation showing how the site will cover or pay for any costs that are not covered by the national government, for example, insurance documents.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the UoC has the right plans in place for paying costs of workplace injuries;

  • management understands their role and responsibility in covering these costs;

  • employees understand what happens financially if they have a workplace injury.

3.5.15 The UoC shall ensure that any person who handles or comes into contact with hazardous substances has access to appropriate changing and washing facilities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Hazardous substances that are often used in aquaculture can include4545Microsoft Word – GUIDE_June_2019.docx (syndel.com):
    • disinfectants as part of biosecurity protocols
    • herbicides and pesticides used in pond maintenance
    • spawning aids
    • vaccines used in disease prevention
    • marking agents used in resource management.
  • Contact with some substances can be harmful to employees and can cause ill health or injury, but this is preventable through:
    • the correct use of PPE
    • providing changing and washing facilities, including soap, for:
      • washing hands or skin that has come into contact with hazardous substances
      • washing out eyes
      • changing out of clothes that have come into contact with hazardous substances.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • availability of changing and washing facilities in easily accessible places.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the risk of working with different hazardous substances;
  • employees are aware of the correct procedures to handle hazardous substances;
  • employees understand what to do if they come into contact with hazardous substances.

3.5.16 The UoC shall provide access to appropriate sanitary facilities that:

a)

are clean and hygienic; and

b)

include adequate privacy measures; and

c)

include separation by gender if required; and

d)

are sufficient for the number of people using them.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Sanitary facilities:
    • are clean
    • are dry
    • are warm
    • have a source of ventilation (e.g. a window or fan)
    • have adequate lighting
    • have doors that close and lock for privacy.
  • Facilities include one of the following:
    • pit latrines
    • flush toilets
    • urinals.
  • Taps and running water are also available.
  • For women, facilities for safe disposal of sanitary products are provided.
  • Facilities are constructed of hard materials that are easy to clean.
  • Waste and wastewater are regularly disposed of in accordance with Criterion 2.11: Material Use, Waste and Pollution Control.
  • They are separated by gender, where required.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • presence of clean and appropriate sanitary facilities that are accessible to all employees
  • records of cleaning services.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees report that sanitary facilities are appropriate and they are able to access them without issue;
  • it is clear who has the responsibility for cleaning the facilities and that this happens on a regular basis.

3.5.17 The UoC shall provide access to free, clearly labelled, drinking water.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Access to drinking water is essential for employees’ health and the UoC is responsible for ensuring that:

    • employees know where they can access water

    • the water is clean and appropriate for drinking

    • employees are not charged for drinking water.

  • Access to drinking water is particularly important in extreme heat and the UoC should be aware that they may need to provide more regular breaks and more opportunities for drinking water in hot weather.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • available drinking water stations around the site.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand that they are free to access drinking water and they know where they can find it.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The provision of a clean area to prepare food is important for employees’ health and for reducing the risk of illness.

  • In warm climates, there should be adequate shade for employees to have their breaks in.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • available place to prepare food and eat.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees are able to prepare food and eat in a clean and hygienic space.

3.5.19 The UoC shall ensure that all buildings and structures on the site are safe to use through adequate construction, maintenance and repair.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Without adequate construction, maintenance and repair, buildings could collapse if subjected to external forces, which could have devastating results.

  • Materials can wear out over time, so continuous inspection and testing structures is important.

  • Ensuring adequate construction, maintenance and repair involves regular monitoring by a knowledgeable, designated person, and maintenance and repair.

  • Understanding when and by whom construction, maintenance and repair should be checked is a result of the health and safety risk assessment (Indicator 3.5.1).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documentation about any surveys or construction carried out at the UoC

  • maintenance records.

3.5.20 The UoC shall ensure that machinery and equipment:

a)

is compliant with applicable legal regulations or other recognised standards; and

b)

is safely installed, maintained and safeguarded; and

c)

is only operated by trained employees.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Accidents and injuries involving machinery and equipment can arise from:

    • misuse

    • malfunctioning

    • bypassing, disabling or malfunctioning safety features.

  • All machinery and equipment should be:

    • compliant with national or other recognised health and safety standards

    • appropriately installed, maintained and safeguarded.

  • Only employees trained to use machinery and equipment are permitted to operate it.

  • Examples of improper use of machinery may include:

    • bypassing or disabling emergency stop buttons, guards or interlocks to speed up processes

    • overloading equipment and machinery beyond its capacity

    • using equipment for a purpose it is not intended for

    • making unauthorised modifications

    • ignoring or disabling safety signals.

  • Safely installed usually includes being installed according to manufacturer’s instructions.

  • Safeguarded means that any warning notices and operational guidance are in place for the machinery and equipment.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of who is trained to use the machinery or equipment

  • maintenance records for machinery and equipment

  • instruction manuals for the use of equipment.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand who is allowed to operate the machinery and equipment;

  • the UoC has a process in place to ensure the maintenance and upkeep of the machinery and equipment.

3.5.21 The UoC shall log all commercial diving activities and maintain records, including a list of any persons involved.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Commercial divers are professional divers who engage in underwater operations and have specific skills and qualifications.
  • Through keeping records of commercial diving activities, the UoC can:
    • monitor time spent diving
    • ensure qualifications of commercial divers
    • ensure that appropriate health and safety measures are in place.

  • The types of records to keep depends on local regulations and the type of dive certification. At a minimum, records include:

    • dives
    • time
    • depth
    • surface time
    • associated dive table records.
  • This is usually recorded with a dive safety checklist.
  • These records are also used for the daily diving plan.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • complete diving records

  • list of persons involved in diving at the UoC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • diving records are properly maintained for each dive and are up-to-date.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Different countries have different certifications for commercial diving, but a normal scuba certification is not and should never be accepted as adequate commercial diver training.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • commercial diver certificates for all commercial divers working at the UoC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • management understand the relevant qualifications that divers should have to be allowed to dive commercially;

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • If a diver has been subcontracted from a diving company, the UoC can ensure that the diving company have taken responsibility for the medical tests.

  • Some countries have requirements that medical professionals have to undergo particular training or have particular qualifications to confirm someone’s fitness to work as a commercial diver.

Collective Bargaining and Freedom of Association 3.6

3.6.1 The UoC shall allow all employees to join or form a trade union or worker organisation. An exception applies where this is restricted by applicable law, in which case the UoC shall allow alternative lawful mechanisms for employee engagement.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A trade union or worker organisation represents workers’ labour interests and concerns.

  • Employees are allowed to choose:

    • whether or not to become a member of a trade union or worker organisation

    • which organisation they choose.

  • Freedom of association enable employees to:

    • collectively advocate for their rights

    • negotiate employment terms and conditions

    • address workplace grievances effectively.

  • These practices make them less vulnerable to unfair and exploitative practices in the workplace.

  • Allowing employees to engage in this process includes ensuring that they understand:

    • what freedom of association is

    • that they have the right to engage in it.

  • In cases in which national regulation does not reference migrant employees or does not allow them to join trade unions, the UoC must allow and should encourage them to form an internal employees’ committee that meets periodically and represents migrant employees.

  • The term ‘lawful mechanism’ means a legal process.

  • In countries where the right to freedom of association is restricted by law, the management must allow employees to choose to have parallel means of association.

    • For example, employees can develop an internal employee committee that meets periodically and represents the diversity of employees.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documents, records or other evidence that show how sites have informed their employees that they are free to join or form workers’ organisations of their own choosing, such as:

    • employee contracts

    • employee handbook

    • training records

    • written policy

    • displayed information on the site

  • documents that show how sites have informed their employees of the right to join an alternative organisation

  • meeting minutes of alternative organisations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether local laws and regulations permit freedom of association;

  • employees’ awareness and knowledge of their right to join trade unions and other workers organisations;

  • information from documents and records match with information from employee interviews;

  • employee knowledge and awareness on:

    • their right to form or join an alternative worker organisation

    • their ability to form or join a workers’ organisation, and/or any barriers to doing so.

Useful Resources

  • FOA & worker representation: company guidance. Ethical Trading Initiative.

  • Q&As on Business and freedom of association. International Labour Organisation (ILO).

3.6.2 The UoC shall allow all employees to engage in collective bargaining. An exception applies where this is restricted by applicable law, in which case the UoC shall allow alternative lawful mechanisms for employee engagement.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Collective bargaining:

    • is a voluntary negotiation between employers and workers organisations to establish the terms and conditions of employment by means of written collective agreements

    • aims to reach a collective agreement, however, if bargaining is undertaken in good faith but an agreement cannot be reached, this may still comply with the requirement

    • includes mutually agreed conditions that may be beneficial to workers and/or the management, for example, collective bargaining may mean that workers are:

    • paid a higher wage other than the minimum prescribed by law

    • work a different shift pattern that both workers and management agree is more appropriate to their context.

  • Allowing employees to engage in this process includes ensuring that they understand:

    • what collective bargaining is

    • that they have the right to engage in it.

  • Ensuring employees understand this can form part of training on the human rights policy (Indicator 3.1.4).

  • The term ‘lawful mechanism’ means a legal process.

  • In countries where collective bargaining is restricted by law, the management must allow workers to have parallel means to engage in discussion and negotiation between employees and employers.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documents, records or other evidence that show how sites have informed their employees that they are free to bargain collectively, such as:

    • employee contract

    • employee handbook

    • training records

    • written policy

    • displayed information on the site

  • any collective bargaining agreements that are in place

  • meeting minutes of collective bargaining negotiations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • documents, records or other evidence allow for verifying that sites have informed their employees that they are free to bargain collectively;

  • any collective bargaining agreements in place are being followed;

  • employees’ awareness and knowledge of their right to bargain collectively;

Useful Resources

N/A

3.6.3 The UoC shall not interfere with collective bargaining processes or the establishment, operation, or administration of trade unions or worker organisations.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC:

    • does not disrupt any employees looking to form or join an organisation

    • does not interfere in the election of representatives

    • allows representatives access to employees and workplaces during working hours

    • engages in meaningful negotiations when approached by worker organisations.

  • Interference by employers can take many forms, such as making use of their positions of power and influence to:

    • coerce or intimidate employees into not participating in workers’ organisations or collective bargaining

    • compromise the independence and effectiveness of these organisations and bargaining processes.

  • An employee committee or union shall make decisions independently from the management. For example:

    • representatives are not appointed or supervised by management when executing their union or employee committee duties

    • participation is voluntary

    • there is no limitation to the number of employee organisations that can be set up.

  • Management should be willing to enter into dialogue with employee organisations.

  • Engagement in meaningful negotiations with employee organisations means that the UoC bargains in good faith and does not engage in actions to slow, stop or limit the bargaining process.

  • Employee organisations are allowed to hold meetings at the UoC, if that is what they choose to do, but management cannot ask them to do so.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documents related to the representative election process

  • list of current representatives.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employee knowledge and awareness on:

    • how employee representatives were elected, and if any candidates were chosen by the management

    • whether management interferes with the establishment, functioning and administration of employee organisations

    • whether employee organisations’ meetings can be held freely and without management interference.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.6.4 The UoC shall report to ASC if there are any collective bargaining agreements in place and if there is any engagement with local trade unions, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This is a reporting requirement, not a disclosure requirement, which means that all data is held confidentially by ASC, who does not share it publicly.

  • Companies should never publicly share personal employee data.

  • The information collected through this reporting requirements will enable ASC to:

    • gain insights into collective bargaining practices and contact with local trade unions, which will inform the future development of ASC’s collective bargaining and freedom of association requirements, and worker voice programme.

    • foster open discussions about collective bargaining, and worker voice.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • confirmation of data uploaded to MyASC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that data uploaded to MyASC is consistent with results of the wage gap analysis.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.6.5 The UoC shall uphold any collective bargaining agreements developed.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A collective bargaining agreement is a labour contract usually set out between a union representing employees and management.

  • It can set terms and conditions of employment, including:

    • wages

    • working hours

    • working conditions

    • grievance procedures

    • rights and responsibilities of the worker representatives and management.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documented collective bargaining agreements and which employees are covered by them.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees’ and managers’ understanding of the right of collective bargaining

  • any collective bargaining agreements in place are upheld.

Useful Resources

N/A

Transparent Contracts 3.7

3.7.1 The UoC shall ensure that all employees have received, understood and agreed upon, written information about their employment terms and conditions before starting employment and, where applicable, prior to migration. This information shall include, at least the following:

a)

a description of the role and any responsibilities; and

b)

the type of contract (e.g. permanent, fixed-term, contractor); and

c)

working hours, including allowance for breaks, paid annual leave, allowance for days off on public holidays, and sick leave; and

d)

wages, any agreed wage deductions (e.g. accommodation, meals), compensation for overtime, and loans and advances; and

e)

social benefits (e.g. insurances); and

f)

termination terms and conditions, notice period; and

g)

relevant human rights and labour-related policies; and

h)

information on labour rights (see Indicator 1.1.2).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This indicator applies to all employees.

  • Copies of contracts should be available on file in the language of the employee, and provisions should be made for cases where people have low literacy levels. For example:

    • a colleague verbally communicates the information.

  • In the case of any changes to the contract during employment, the UoC should:

    • discuss the changes with the employee

    • ensure that the employee agrees with the changes

    • records the agreed upon changes

    • provides the employee with a copy of the changes.

  • Examples of changes to terms and conditions can include where employees have:

    • been given a different role or been promoted

    • had changes in their working conditions, for example:

      • wages

      • working hours

      • location.

  • Migrant workers should have contracts that:

    • are written, agreed to, and signed at the time of hiring in the country of origin of the employee

    • state that the employer will pay for travel from the employee’s country and repatriation, and what arrangements are made for that (information about fees and costs related to employment are outlined in Criterion 3.2)

    • do not violate the national laws of the host country, as well as other laws and regulations that apply to migrant employees in their country of origin.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts and contract amendments

  • evidence of the contract being explained to the employee in their language and in a way they understand

  • contracts, Memorandum of Understanding or terms and conditions agreed between the UoC and the labour or recruitment agency.

Auditors should confirm:

  • whether contracts meet national legal requirements for labour contracts;

  • that contract terms and conditions match with working hour records and payroll and wage records and/or the Salary Matrix (see Criterion 3.8);

  • employees’ understanding of the terms and conditions of their contract;

  • whether employees are in possession of a copy of their contract and documented changes;

  • for migrant employees: whether they were required to pay recruitment fees, and any costs incurred for travel to the host country by assessing the process of recruitment. See also Criterion 3.2.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.7.2 The UoC shall ensure that if family members are working on the site they are either subject to Indicator 3.7.1 or they receive compensation or benefits for work done that is proportional to the productivity or profit of the site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • While the ASC Farm Standard requires that all employees working at the UoC are employed through contracts with agreed upon terms and conditions, and fair wages, ASC recognises that:

    • some sites are small businesses that are run with the support of close family members

    • where businesses are supported by family members, it is not always possible to contract and pay those family members in the usual practice outlined in the ASC Farm Standard.

  • This indicator allows for small sites to receive help in operating the business from close family members in a more informal manner and in exchange for some compensation or benefits. These can include:

    • payment in money

    • payment in kind (exchange of goods or other services)

    • a share of the profits of the business.

  • The compensation or benefits is proportional to the productivity or profit of the site, implies fair compensation for the work given.

  • Family members is defined as first or second-degree blood relatives, or those adopted.

    • First-degree blood relative is someone’s:

      • parent

      • sibling

      • child.

    • Second-degree blood relative is someone’s:

      • grandparent

      • grandchild

      • uncle or aunt

      • niece or nephew

      • cousin.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • agreement with the family member about work, working conditions, compensation and benefits

  • evidence of first or second-degree blood relative of the owner or spouse of the owner.

Auditors should confirm:

  • everyone working at the UoC understands their role and how they are compensated;

  • everyone working at the UoC is fairly compensated for their work;

  • everyone working at the UoC is either an employee with a contract or a first or second-degree blood relative of the owner or spouse of the owner.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.7.3 The UoC not engage in false-apprenticeships.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The indicator does not permit false apprenticeships but apprenticeships may be legitimately used within employment relationships if they are:

    • legally permitted

    • adequately documented

    • not used to avoid social or labour obligations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • apprenticeship agreement

  • contracts

Auditors should confirm:

  • that any apprentices at the UoC are aware of the terms agreed in their apprenticeship agreement and that their work fits in the scope of that agreement.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.7.4 The UoC shall ensure that no employment arrangements are used to avoid obligations to employees under applicable national labour and social security laws, and social security for all employees is paid according to applicable legal requirements.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Systematic use of home working, labour-only contracting, sub-contracting, and fixed-term contracts is often an indication of attempts to avoid social or labour obligations.

  • Such employment arrangements can be legitimately used within employment relationships if:

    • they are legally permitted

    • adequately documented

    • not used to avoid social or labour obligations.

  • Home working carries risks that:

    • employees do work that is hidden and not paid for

    • employees miss out on benefits that they are entitled to because they are not present at the workplace.

  • Ongoing, routine tasks necessary for the UoC to operate should be carried out by contracted employees.

  • Temporary employees, such as day labourers, should only be hired for unanticipated peak work or seasonal work. For example, routine feeding is an ongoing task that is carried out by an employee. A day labourer could be hired to support a busy harvest period or to handle an unexpected feed delivery.

  • Fixed-term contracts should have a clearly defined or predictable duration.

    • excessive use of these contracts, or when employees are continuously required to reapply for positions lasting less than six months, should be avoided.

  • Examples of when sub-contracting is used at a UoC are:

    • production

    • fish transfer

    • veterinary treatment

    • diving

    • maintenance

    • harvest

    • slaughter

    • storage

    • transport of fish

    • cleaning

    • catering.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts with contract-workers, sub-contractors and recruitment agencies

  • documentation regarding social security.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees are paid social security according to national legal requirements;

  • employees understand their right to social security and how that applies to their contracts.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.7.5 The UoC shall report to ASC the employee composition, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This is a reporting requirement, not a disclosure requirement, which means that all data is held confidentially by ASC, who does not share it publicly.

  • Companies should never publicly share personal employee data.

  • The information collected through this reporting requirements will enable ASC to gain insights into employee composition, which will inform the future development of ASC’s requirements related to employees.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • confirmation of data uploaded to MyASC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that data uploaded to MyASC is consistent with results of the wage gap analysis.
