Wages 3.8

Training

Training Content

Our training content is designed to help you better understand key requirements of the ASC Farm Standard.

Videos are publicly accessible, and most offer subtitles in multiple languages.

Our online courses and learning pathways require you to log in to the ASC Training Centre. They are currently available in English, with additional languages coming soon.

Type Name
Video Series Implementing ASC Farm Standard Requirements on Living Wage

Minimum and Living Wages
Understanding Living Wages
Calculating Wage Gaps

3.8.1 The UoC shall set wages, before overtime and bonuses, at or above the legal minimum wage. An exception applies where a minimum wage has not been established by applicable law, in which case the UoC shall calculate wages in consultation with employees or their representative organisations.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The following countries do not have a minimum wage established by law:
    • Denmark
    • Finland
    • Italy
    • Norway
    • Sweden
    • Iceland
    • Singapore
    • La Reunion
    • Tonga
    • Tuvalu
    • North Korea
    • South Sudan
    • Brunei
    • Zimbabwe
    • Djibouti
    • Somalia
  • In these countries wages should be negotiated:
    • through collective bargaining or 
    • other consultation with employees and their representative worker organisations.
  • Further guidance on collective bargaining and worker organisations can be found in Criterion 3.6.
  • In-kind benefits provided by the UoC should not be used as a way to pay less than the legal minimum wage to any employee.
  • In-kind benefits can include:
    • housing
    • subsidised rations, food, meals
    • transport
    • utilities such as water and electricity, etc.
  • Some of these in-kind benefits can be included in the living wage calculation, as described in Appendix 11: Methodology for Wage Measurement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • employee contracts

  • payslips

  • working hours records

  • payment transaction records

  • any collective bargaining agreements that are in place.

Auditors should confirm:

  • national legal requirements on minimum wage;

  • relevant collective bargaining agreements on wages in the sector (recommended prior to audit visit);

  • that no in-kind benefits have been paid in place of the legal minimum wage.

Useful Resources

  • Regularly updated list of minimum wages by country: https://wageindicator.org/salary/minimum-wage/minimum-wages-per-country

3.8.2 The UoC shall annually calculate employee remuneration following the method outlined in Appendix 11, and shall assess this against the living wage benchmarks listed on the ASC website to identify if there is a gap between employee remuneration and the living wage benchmark.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A living wage is: ‘the remuneration (wages, bonuses and benefits) received for a standard workweek by a worker in a particular place sufficient to afford a decent standard of living for the worker and their family. Elements of a decent standard of living include food, water, housing, education, health care, transportation, clothing, and other essential needs including provision for unexpected events.’4646Global Living Wage Coalition: https://www.globallivingwage.org/
  • A living wage is different to the national minimum wage: it is usually higher and is adjusted yearly for inflation and is voluntary rather than required by law. 
  • Living wage benchmarks are location-specific monetary amounts calculated by the  Anker Research Institute (ARI) and the Global Living Wage Coalition designed to ensure employees receive sufficient income for a living wage. Sites can find relevant benchmarks in the ASC Living Wage Benchmarks document found online, which is regularly updated. 
  • The living wage gap is defined as the difference between the local living wage and the actual remuneration (wages, bonuses, and benefits) provided to employees.
  • ASC’s requirements on living wage are focused on measuring and reporting wages:
    • helping the UoC assess whether or not they are paying a living wage to employees
    • helping the UoC identify any gap between current wages and the living wage in a particular location.
  • These requirements do not require the UoC to:
    • close any gaps between current wages and the living wage
    • immediately start paying a living wage.
  • Appendix 11 outlines the calculation that the UoC can use to understand how much employees are being paid, which is based on a methodology developed by the Anker Research Institute.
    • The replacement cost for in-kind benefits such as food and housing for the worker has been set by researchers in local living wage benchmarks, which can be found in the reports linked here: ASC Living Wage Benchmarks.
  • ASC recommends the use of a tool called the Salary Matrix developed by IDH, for this calculation, which can help simplify and clarify the process.
    • Guidance for completing the upload of employee payroll, bonus and benefit information is embedded in the tool.
  • The list of local living wage benchmarks is found on ASC’s website here.
    • ASC uses the Anker Research Institute living wage benchmarks. Where one of these is not available, benchmarks from the Wage Indicator Foundation are linked.
  • Through the results of this calculation, the UoC should be able to:
    • develop the wage improvement plan required by Indicator 3.8.4
    • report to ASC, required by Indicator 3.8.5.
  • An example of a possible result from the calculation is:
    • the living wage benchmark in Country X is $980 per month
    • the UoC’s remuneration calculation shows that:
      • fish health technicians are paid $940 per month
      • farm workers are paid $900 per month.
    • The analysis of this calculation shows a living wage gap of:
      • 4% for fish health technicians
      • 8% for farm workers.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • completed Salary Matrix or similar wage measurement analysis calculation

  • employee contracts

  • payslips

  • payment transaction records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the accuracy and completeness of wage measurement analysis;

  • what bonus payments, and in-kind benefits have been paid, through employee and management interviews and document review;

  • the value and benefit of in-kind benefits recorded in the wage measurement analysis, through employee interviews;

  • calculations used in calculating in kind-benefits used for wage calculation, including document review, through management interviews;

  • wage payments.

Useful Resources

  • Living Wages Around the World, Manual for Measurement by Richard Anker and Martha Anker, Chapter 15 Comparing Prevailing Wages to a Living Wage: https://www.elgaronline.com/monobook-oa/9781786431455/9781786431455.xml
  • Wage measurement tool: IDH Salary Matrix
  • List of living wage benchmarks on ASC website

3.8.3 The UoC shall annually report on the gap between employee remuneration and the living wage benchmark, according to ASC data submission procedures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This is a reporting requirement, not a disclosure requirement, which means that all data is held confidentially by ASC, who does not share it publicly.

  • Companies should never publicly share personal employee data.

  • Wage gap data is generated by the UoC through their remuneration calculation (Indicator 3.8.2), and is uploaded by the UoC to MyASC on an annual basis.

  • The information collected through wage gap reporting will enable ASC to:

    • gain insights into national and regional wage gaps, which will inform the future development of ASC’s living wage requirements

    • foster open discussions about the challenges of paying a living wage

    • discuss the role in the payment of living wage of the collaborative effort and shared responsibility of participants in the whole supply chain

    • develop strategies to raise wages and enhance benefits over time.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • confirmation of data uploaded to MyASC.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that data uploaded to MyASC is consistent with results of the wage gap analysis.

Useful Resources

  • Living Wage Data Reporting Template

3.8.4 The UoC shall, where employee remuneration is below the living wage benchmark (see Indicator 3.8.2), develop and implement a wage improvement plan towards payment of a living wage.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The wage improvement plan should:

    • list all categories of employees who are paid below a living wage

    • include targets and timelines for improvements for all categories of employees who are not receiving a living wage

    • be developed for a three-year period

    • include reporting on progress towards the previous year’s goal and where goals have not been met, a justification should be provided.

  • A wage improvement plan template has been developed to support the UoC’s compliance with this Indicator.

  • The UoC may also choose to develop their own wage improvement plan format, as long as it includes all of the elements listed above.

  • The UoC may choose to use a tool such as the GIZ Living Wage Costing Tool to develop the improvement plan.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • completed wage improvement plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the presence of the completed wage improvement plan including reporting towards previous year’s goal;

  • that the plan provides a clear rationale and explanation where no progress has been made towards closing any living wage gap.

Useful Resources

  • ASC’s Wage Improvement Plan template

  • GIZ Living Wage Costing Tool: offers various simulations to analyse the direct cost implications for producers to pay workers a living wage: https://www.nachhaltige-agrarlieferketten.org/en/tips-tools

3.8.5 The UoC shall pay wages in full directly to employees in legal tender or into a bank account in their name at regular intervals, at least monthly. Wages shall not be delayed, deferred or in any way withheld.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • Legal tender does not include:
    • notes which banks no longer exchange
    • notes which are not accepted (for example, too small)
    • currency which is unusable due to inflation
    • in-kind benefits (food, housing, etc) of any kind.
  • There are situations where withholding salary, property or benefits are legally required, and so allowed under this indicator. For example: 
    • salary withholdings, as required by the government. For example, part of a salary is sometimes withheld by a government for:
      • statutory pensions
      • health insurance
      • taxes.
    • a government can sometimes require the withholding of salary to pay overdue child-care support costs to another parent or pay overdue taxes 
    • salary deductions, as defined in a contract or collective bargaining agreement, that are agreed by both parties. For example, an agreed voluntary deduction for housing costs could be allowable.  
    • bonuses, which are considered optional and additional to the agreed salary and benefits. However, if clearly defined performance targets related to a bonus payment, as defined in a contract have been achieved, then the bonus cannot be withheld.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • employee contracts

  • payslips

  • payment transactions.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • direct, regular, and accurate payment to employees through records review and interviews with employees and management;

  • if there are any instances when wages were delayed, deferred or withheld in the past and why;

    • employees understand the process for raising grievances if wages are delayed or inaccurate;

    • when foreign migrant employees are employed, apart from legally required deductions, no other deductions shall be made from their wages before payment, for example:

      • recruitment or agency fees

      • cost of airfare

      • employment visas

      • any fees or costs incurred in the recruitment process for employees to secure employment or placement, regardless of the manner, timing or location of their imposition or collection4747https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@ed_protect/@protrav/@migrant/documents/publication/wcms_536755.pdf.

Useful Resources 

  • General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs: https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@ed_protect/@protrav/@migrant/documents/publication/wcms_536755.pdf

3.8.6 The UoC shall document wage payment and receipt by all employees.

Documentation shall be understandable and made available to the employees and shall include information on at least the following:

a)

wages; and,

b)

advances; and,

c)

loans; and,

d)

hours worked including overtime; and,

e)

calculation of any withholdings.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • Wage payment can be documented in several ways, often through a payslip including all wage information. This can be given to the employee:

    • electronically

    • through a printed copy

    • on or before the payday.

  • Loans provided by an employer can be an important source of funds for employees in some places.

  • Clarity of loan calculations and repayment are particularly important, as loans can be an element driving forced labour if employees are not able to repay within a reasonable amount of time based on their wages.

  • If loan interest rates are charged by the UoC, they should be:

    • at or below bank rates

    • included in receipt of information on advances, loans, hours worked, pay and the calculation of any deductions.

  • For each payment cycle, the UoC should provide a written pay record (such as a payslip) to each employee detailing the following:

    • employee name

    • ID/roll/employee number

    • month/week/pay period

    • number of regular hours worked

    • number of overtime hours worked

    • mandatory deductions towards social security, health insurance and taxes, etc.

    • deductions towards repayment of advances or loans taken by the employee (see also Indicator 3.2.9).

  • The pay record should:

    • be provided in paper or digital form.

    • be provided in a language and format easily understandable to employees.

    • be countersigned by employees unless the payment is traceable by bank transfer.

  • It is particularly important that employees understand the calculation of hourly premium wages for overtime work.
  • Employees should be able to raise any issues they may have related to doubts on calculations on wages, including overtime wages. The UoC should communicate a clear process on how employees can raise such issues.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • employee contracts

  • payslips

  • any loan agreements in place

  • working hours records

  • documented wage information, including advances or any withholdings.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • records of wage payments;

  • accuracy of wage payments;

  • employees’ access to wage information through employee interviews.

Useful Resources 

N/A

3.8.7 The UoC shall ensure that employees are entitled to maternity leave of a minimum of 14 weeks that includes a guarantee of return to the job.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • Many countries have legal requirements for the provision of maternity protection for women employees. These typically include:

    • maternity leave

    • cash benefits

    • employment security, which includes a return to the same or a similar position after taking maternity leave.

  • This requirement extends some or all of these benefits to employees at the UoC.

  • Some countries also have similar legal requirements for the provision of paternity protection for male employees.

  • Maternity leave can include both pregnancy leave and leave following the birth of the child. 

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • written confirmation (either in contracts or a company policy or information document) that maternity provisions have been included that meet the requirements of local legislation

  • evidence of maternity leave being paid, where national law requires.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • employees’ understanding of maternity or paternity leave rights;

  • employees who have taken maternity/paternity benefits have rejoined work at the same or similar position without a reduction in wages;

  • the UoC does not discriminate in hiring between genders so that they can avoid being obligated to pay maternity (or paternity) benefits to employees, see ASC Farm Standard Criterion 3.4 (Discrimination).

Useful Resources 

  • International Labour Organization (ILO) V. Maternity Protection Convention, 2000 (No. 183)
Footnotes

Criterion 3.8 – Wages

Working Hours 3.9

Throughout this criterion, when we refer to ‘week’, it is a reference to a full 7-day calendar week.

3.9.1 The UoC shall ensure that working hours comply with applicable legal requirements and any collective bargaining agreements in place on premium rates, working hours, shift patterns, breaks, daily rest, weekly rest and annual leave.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • National legal requirements on working hours, premium rates, rest times, shift patterns and annual leave can vary according to the country where the UoC is located.

  • National legal requirements should always form the minimum requirement for the UoC.

  • Collective bargaining:

    • is a voluntary negotiation between employers and organisations of employees to establish the terms and conditions of employment by means of a written collective bargaining agreement (CBA)

    • typically covers wages, working hours and working conditions.

  • In the event that national legal requirements, collective bargaining agreements and the ASC Farm Standard differ, the strictest rule always applies.

  • Annual leave:

    • is the longest period of rest available to employees

    • allows physical and mental recuperation, and a break from the workplace

    • is paid with normal wages or with additional holiday pay on top of the normal wage (e.g. 13th month)

    • can be taken in days or weeks, with employees being allowed at least a 2-week block, as suggested by ILO standards.

  • Laws in many nations set fixed monthly and yearly minimum leave days.

  • ILO Convention No. 132 (Holidays with Pay Convention, 1970) specifies that annual leave is:

    • 3 weeks of leave for 1 year of service

    • typically accrued monthly

    • calculated pro-rata to their contracted working hours,

  • ILO Convention No. 146 (Seafarers’ Annual Leave with Pay Convention, 1976) can apply in aquaculture when vessels used by the site and subcontractors travel between sites in open water. This convention specifies:

    • 30 days of annual leave for 1 year of service.

  • Annual leave days are not the same as public holidays, which are:

    • set by governments for cultural or historical reasons

    • not counted as part of annual leave days.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • any written collective bargaining agreements that are in place

  • information about national legal requirements regarding premium rates, working hours, shift patterns, rest breaks and annual leave.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand that they have the right to engage in collective bargaining about their terms and conditions;

  • employees have been provided the opportunity to engage in collective bargaining

  • any collective bargaining agreements in place meet national legal requirements or the ASC Farm Standard, whichever is stricter, at a minimum.

Useful Resources

  • https://ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/—ed_protect/—protrav/—travail/documents/publication/wcms_491374.pdf

3.9.2 The UoC shall maintain records of the hours worked by every employee.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC’s working hours recording system:
    • can help the UoC to protect employees against excessive working hours
    • is accessible to employees to verify the record of their hours
    • may include the use of:
      • time clocks with punch cards
      • digital recording systems
      • recording hours manually
      • or other systems.
  • The records should indicate
    • the start and finish time each day of the week
    • cumulatively add up to the total hours of regular work for the week
    • any overtime hours worked.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • working hours records, which include:

    • start and finish time

    • cumulative working hours

    • any overtime hours worked.

  • payslips

  • employee contracts.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • employees are aware that their working hours are being recorded;

  • employees are able to access their working hours records;

  • employees are able to confirm the accuracy of the working hours records;

  • pay slips, employee contracts and working hours records are all aligned.

Useful Resources 

N/A

3.9.3 The UoC shall ensure that working hours do not exceed 8 hours per day and 48 hours in a week (excluding overtime).

An exception applies where the operations of the UoC require a different working pattern, in which case the UoC may use averaging of working hours if permitted by applicable legal requirements, calculated over a maximum 17-week reference period.

When more than 48 hours are worked in a week as a result of averaging, the UoC shall ensure that the following conditions are met:

a.

it is in line with applicable legal requirements; and

b.

it is in line with collective bargaining agreements; and

c.

terms are clearly set out and agreed to by employees in their contracts; and

d.

appropriate safeguards are put in place to protect the employee’s health and safety.

Indicator applicability: any person aged 18 and above.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • The normal workday is a maximum of 8 hours, excluding breaks, and the normal work week is a maximum of 48 hours.

  • Where collective bargaining agreements, industry standards or national law require a shorter day or week, this applies.

  • The ILO defines shift work as: ‘a method of organisation of working time in which workers succeed one another at the workplace so that the establishment can operate longer than the hours of work of individual workers at different daily and night hours’4848ILO (2004) What is shiftwork? Geneva, ILO, Information Sheet No. WT-8. https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/—ed_protect/—protrav/—travail/documents/publication/wcms_170713.pdf.

  • Where collective bargaining and national law allows, the UoC can employ people to work in shifts:

    • They may choose to work more than eight hours per day and more than 48 hours in one week, if the number of hours averaged over a period of 17 weeks does not exceed a normal workday and normal work week.

  • Long working hours can mean that employees can get fatigued, which can result in accidents or mistakes.

  • The UoC should recognise that employees could be working two jobs which, whilst outside the scope of the ASC Farm Standard, is still a risk to their health and safety, and consideration should be given to fatigue caused by excessive working hours.

  • Appropriate safeguards in place to protect employees’ health and safety can include:

    • a risk assessment looking specifically at the risk of fatigue

    • adequate or extra rest breaks and places for employees to rest during long shifts

    • enough food and drink available for employees to ensure that they are not hungry

    • avoiding employees who have worked long hours of overtime conducting hazardous work (for example, operating heavy machinery)

    • ensuring that dark areas are well lit

    • ensuring that, where possible, employees are not working alone for long hours.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • employee contracts

  • payslips

  • working hours records

  • health and safety risk assessment.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • any different shift patterns have been entered into voluntarily by employees;

  • the UoC understands the risk inherent in long working hours and fatigue and appropriate mitigations are being implemented.

Useful Resources 

N/A

3.9.4 The UoC shall ensure that overtime hours are;

a.

are voluntary; and

b.

are not requested regularly; and

c.

have appropriate safeguards in place to protect the employee’s health and safety.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Overtime should not occur regularly but under exceptional circumstances, for example, overtime can be requested:

    • for unexpected peak production times

    • if staff are absent and others must cover their work.

  • The UoC should plan work in such a way to minimise the risk of regularly requesting overtime.

  • If the UoC continues to need the same jobs done in overtime repeatedly, this is an indication that the UoC may need to:

    • review resources

    • plan work differently

    • hire additional employees.

  • Any overtime is voluntary, meaning it can only take place if the employee:

    • consents to work extra hours

    • is not discriminated against or penalised for refusing overtime.

  • Health and safety hazards related to excessive overtime can be avoided by implementing a clear overtime policy that:

    • limits excessive overtime

    • ensures that overtime requirements are announced in advance when possible

    • ensures that overtime is voluntary

    • rotates schedules so that overtime is not always assigned to the same employees

    • ensures that health and safety training shows how to recognise and manage signs of fatigue and stress.

  • The UoC should allow regular rest breaks during overtime shifts.

  • The UoC can maintain open and transparent communication channels with employees to encourage them to provide feedback about their work conditions and overtime hours, and use this input to adjust schedules.

  • Appropriate safeguards in place to protect employees’ health and safety can include:

    • a risk assessment looking specifically at the risk of fatigue

    • adequate or extra rest breaks and places for employees to rest during long shifts

    • enough food and drink available for employees to ensure that they are not hungry

    • avoiding employees who have worked long hours of overtime conducting hazardous work (for example, operating heavy machinery)

    • ensuring that dark areas are well lit

    • ensuring that, where possible, employees are not working alone for long hours.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • health and safety risk assessment

  • contracts

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand that overtime hours are voluntary;

  • management understand the risks in working long hours and are well prepared to mitigate those risks;

  • regular activities are carried out in regular working hours and that overtime is used for exceptional circumstances.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.9.5 The UoC shall ensure that employees do not work more than 12 hours of overtime per week.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • Overtime is any additional hours spent working beyond normal working hours

  • This requirement does not allow these overtime hours to exceed more than 12 per week.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • contracts

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • employees understand how much overtime they are allowed to
    work.

Useful Resources 

N/A

3.9.6 The UoC shall ensure that overtime hours are paid at a premium rate of at least 125% of the agreed wages, or as defined by applicable legal requirements or any collective bargaining agreements in place, whichever is higher.

How do I interpret this requirement?  

  • For overtime hours 125% of the basic wage is paid to employees.
  • Overtime work often involves sacrifices from employees, such as time away from family and personal life, and this additional effort needs to be rewarded.

  • Where collective bargaining agreements or applicable law include a premium rate that is below 125%, the ASC minimum of 125% applies.

  • The premium rate should be:

    • documented in payslips

    • documented in the employee contract

    • clearly understood by all employees.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:  

  • contracts

  • working hours records

  • payslips.

Auditors should confirm: 

  • employees understand that overtime hours are paid at a premium rate;

  • employees understand the difference between regular hours and overtime hours;

  • if the bar of ‘exceptional circumstances’ is being used to determine overtime requirements.

Useful Resources 

N/A

3.9.7 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are granted breaks during work shifts. Where this is defined by applicable legal requirements or any collective bargaining agreements in place, these shall be followed.

Indicator applicability: any person aged 18 and above.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The amount, length and frequency of rest breaks that employees are entitled to can be specified by:
    • collective bargaining agreements in place
    • national laws.
  • The UoC should ensure that rest breaks are clearly agreed upon and set out for employees.
  • Rest breaks:
    • provide employees with essential rest during the workday
    • help reduce fatigue, which can also reduce the risks of accidents or errors
    • may also accommodate personal needs, like restroom or prayer breaks.
  • Ensuring clean and hygienic facilities for breaks is vital in workplaces with potential hygiene risks due to factors like chemicals, noise, or pollutants, where employees cannot leave the premises during breaks. 
  • Management should consider climate conditions when they plan breaks and rest times. In very hot temperatures, employees will need:
    • more frequent access to breaks,
    • breaks taken in the shade where possible
    • access to drinking water.
  • This requirement refers to rest time when an employee can be asked to work, only if:
    • they agree to work during their rest time
    • the rest time is made up at a different time.
  • There can be situations where an employee is on standby, which is when:
    • the employee is required to be on-site, even if they are not required to be working for that period of time
    • the hours that they are required to be on-site are counted as working hours
    • they must be fully compensated.
  • Examples of when employees may be on standby includes any time spent at the UoC where they could be at the direction of the company to perform a work-related task. For example:
    • an employee waiting for the arrival of a delivery of feed, which they will help to unload
    • an employee who is responsible for feeding the fish and in between feeds, they are waiting at the site for the next feeding time.
  • There can also be situations when an employee is on-call, which is when:
    • the employee is not required to be on site
    • the employee is required to be reachable and available during a defined period of time
    • this time of being available is not counted as normal working hours
    • this time should be compensated in some way.
  • Examples of when employees may be on-call can include:
    • an employee who is at home overnight, but is available to be called in case there is an emergency on the site and they are called into the site.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts

  • any collective bargaining agreements that are in place.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the pattern of rest breaks that they are entitled to;

  • rest breaks are adequate for the needs of the employees in their context.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.9.8 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are granted at least 11 consecutive hours of rest within a 24-hour period.

Indicator applicability: any person aged 18 and above.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Rest for a period of 11 consecutive hours within a 24-hour period ensures that employees have an adequate amount of time for both sleep and personal free time.

  • All employees, regardless of their shift pattern, require this rest.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts

  • any collective bargaining agreements that are in place

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the rest time that they are entitled to.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.9.9 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are granted at least 24 consecutive hours of rest within a 7-day period, or at least 48 consecutive hours of rest within a 14-day period if allowed by applicable law.

Indicator applicability: any person aged 18 and above.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The ILO’s 1921 Weekly Rest Convention (No. 14) mandates a 24-hour weekly rest period (within a 7-day period).

  • Where the UoC may be located more remotely or where shift patterns may require a longer number of consecutive days of work, 48-hours rest can be taken within a 14-day period, if allowed by applicable law and collective bargaining agreements.

  • Where there is a longer number of consecutive days working, the UoC should ensure that there are adequate safeguards for employees’ health and safety, as per Indicator 3.9.3.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts

  • any collective bargaining agreements that are in place

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand the rest time that they are entitled to.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.9.10 The UoC shall ensure that additional breaks are granted for pregnant women and breastfeeding women. These breaks shall be counted as working time and appropriate facilities shall be provided.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • According to ILO, the lack of support at the workplace is one of the main reasons that women stop breastfeeding before the recommended time4949https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/newsroom/comment-analysis/WCMS_218710/lang–en/index.htm.

  • Employers can support breastfeeding women by providing:

    • ample time away from work activities

    • a comfortable, private location to express breast milk

    • access to a fridge to store it

    • a clean and safe environment (other than a bathroom).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • policy, for example addressing new and expectant mothers

  • health and safety risk assessment

  • contracts

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • entitlement to paid nursing breaks in the country/region where the UoC is located;

  • confirm that a location for breastfeeding mothers is suitable;

  • confirm that the relevant employees understand these requirements.

Useful Resources

  • https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/newsroom/comment-analysis/WCMS_218710/lang–en/index.htm
  • Ontario, Canada Public Health Association recommendations for creating a breastfeeding friendly workplace: https://www.opha.on.ca/OPHA/media/Resources/Resource%20Documents/BreastfeedingFriendlyWorkplace-Sep08.pdf
  • Region of Waterloo, Canada recommendations for creating a breastfeeding friendly workplace: https://www.regionofwaterloo.ca/en/doing-business/resources/Documents/Breastfeeding_Friendly_Workplace_Toolkit.PDF

3.9.11 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are granted paid leave as defined by applicable legal requirements or any collective bargaining agreements in place.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Paid leave can include:

    • public holidays

    • annual leave

    • maternity/paternity leave

    • sick leave.

  • Types of leave can be defined by national law and collective bargaining agreements.

  • Annual leave:

    • is the longest period of rest available to employees

    • allows physical and mental recuperation and a break from the workplace

    • is paid with normal wages or with additional holiday pay on top of the normal wage (e.g. 13th month)

    • can be taken in days or weeks, with employees being allowed at least a 2-week block, as suggested by ILO standards.

  • Laws in many nations set fixed monthly and yearly minimum leave days.
  • ILO Convention No. 132 (Holidays with Pay Convention, 1970) specifies that annual leave is:

    • 3 weeks of leave for 1 year of service,

    • typically accrued monthly, and

    • calculated pro-rata to their contracted working hours.

  • ILO Convention No. 146 (Seafarers’ Annual Leave with Pay Convention, 1976) can apply in aquaculture when vessels used by the site and subcontractors travel between sites in open water. This convention specifies:
    • 30 days of annual leave for 1 year of service.
  • Annual leave days are not the same as public holidays, which are:

    • set by governments for cultural or historical reasons

    • not counted as part of annual leave days.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • contracts

  • collective bargaining agreements

  • working hours records.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand their entitlement to paid leave;

  • employees do not feel discriminated against when they take annual leave.

N/A

Workplace Conduct Response 3.10

3.10.1 The UoC shall have a written workplace conduct response policy with the intent of setting out the process to respond to breaches of company rules.

The policy shall define clear levels of escalation and shall ensure that the employee’s dignity is upheld at all times.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The written policy should:

    • outline the process for when employees break any rules of the UoC, detailing:

      • what behaviour may trigger disciplinary action

      • the corresponding action to be taken

    • adhere to local legislation and any collective bargaining agreements in place, particularly regarding cases of potential dismissal

    • list who is responsible for decision-making at different levels

    • outline how employees are rewarded for good work and encouraged to improve

    • be accessible and understandable to all employees

    • be integrated in company processes through training for supervisors and managers, including:

      • how to communicate effectively

      • carry out any responses in a fair and respectful manner.

  • Suspension can sometimes be used as a disciplinary action. This period of suspension should always be paid unless:

    • suspension for a time is offered to the employee as an alternative to dismissal, this period could be unpaid as long as:

      • the employee has agreed accept this

      • it is not enacted after the event as deduction from wages.

Table 5. Examples of levels of escalation in disciplinary procedures (adapted from SA8000):

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • written workplace conduct response policy

  • training records

  • records of any disciplinary process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the workplace conduct response policy complies with the ASC Farm Standard’s intention;

  • employees are aware of the workplace conduct response policy;

  • employees confirm that the company adheres to their policy and actions are fair;

  • there are no monetary deductions imposed during the process.

Useful Resources

  • ACAS statutory Code of Practice on discipline and grievance procedures: https://www.acas.org.uk/acas-code-of-practice-for-disciplinary-and-grievance-procedures/html

  • Auditors can consult with and seek information from competent authorities and interested parties. For example, local worker welfare organisations, NGOs, labour lawyers and civil society.

3.10.2 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are aware of, and understand, the workplace conduct response policy.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC can inform employees about the workplace conduct response policy by:

    • including it in the employee contract or staff handbook

    • distributing the written policy to employees in languages they understand

    • including the workplace conduct response policy in orientation or ongoing training.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • written workplace conduct response policy
  • training records
  • employee handbook.

Auditors should confirm:

  • training records and employee handbook;

  • employees understand workplace response procedures

  • how employees were trained on workplace response procedures.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.10.3 The UoC shall maintain records of responses to breaches of company rules.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • These records should include:
    • the observed misconduct by the employee
    • the actions taken by the employer, including:
      • copies of written notices
      • withholding of bonuses, suspensions, demotions or dismissals, if applicable
    • the investigation carried out
    • the appeals process by the employee, if applicable
    • who was involved in or witnessed each of these steps.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • written workplace conduct response policy

  • records of any workplace response procedures.

Auditors should confirm:

  • records of any investigations, actions and responses.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.10.4 The UoC shall not deduct from wages or benefits as part of any response to breaches of company rules.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A person’s livelihood and ability to feed and provide for themselves and their families should not be impacted by a disciplinary action at work.

  • Wages cannot be withheld for disciplinary action from any:

    • regular wages

    • payments for overtime

    • other benefits such as fixed year-end bonuses.

  • Non-fixed bonuses that are determined based on performance are not considered a benefit.

  • This indicator applies even if local laws or regulations allow monetary fines to be imposed as part of disciplinary procedures.

  • Suspension can sometimes be used as a disciplinary action. This period of suspension should always be paid unless:

    • suspension for a time is offered to the employee as an alternative to dismissal, this period could be unpaid as long as:

      • the employee has agreed to accept this

      • it is not enacted after the event as deduction from wages.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • written workplace conduct response policy

  • payroll documentation to verify if they are deductions other than legally mandated deductions (for example, taxes and employees’ contributions towards social security or health insurance).

Auditors should confirm:

  • if there have been any fines, as they are not always reflected on pay records;

  • if there are any specific methods of discipline for production targets not being met or for quality issues;

  • any fines that employees have had to pay (for example, for coming late to work, excessive use of toilets, being absent or sick etc.).

Employee Accommodation 3.11

3.11.1 The UoC shall ensure that any accommodation provided for employees or their family:

a)

is according to applicable legal requirements; and

b)

has adequate safety provisions; and

c)

is regularly maintained and kept in good working order; and

d)

is clean and hygienic; and

e)

allows for adequate privacy, including separation by gender if required; and

f)

meets the basic needs of the employees and their families; and

g)

is sufficient for the number of people using them.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • On-site accommodation is typically offered by workplaces:
    • in remote locations
    • when local housing supplies are otherwise very limited.
  • On-site accommodation can mean that there is a higher risk of forced and child labour because:
    • employees and their families living in on-site accommodation can be less integrated into a local community
    • their presence on site can mean they are asked to work more hours than their contracts specify
    • high rental costs relative to employee income mean that employees can incur debt.
  • The UoC is not required to provide accommodation for its employees.
  • Employees are not required to reside in employer-provided accommodation.
  • The UoC monitors and ensures the quality, safety and maintenance of housing that is provided, regardless of whether it owns, leases or contracts the facility.
  • Facilities should:
    • be built to withstand recurring extreme weather conditions
    • be located in a non-hazardous location, with adequate drainage, pest control and hygiene procedures in place
    • have fire safety and other emergency response measures in place, for example:
      • marked safety exits
      • emergency escape routes
      • assembly points
      • firefighting equipment, which is maintained annually or when required
    • include separate accommodations by gender that ensure adequate privacy, for example:
      • locking doors when both genders are present
      • an individual bed for each employee in shared dormitories
      • an individual storage space for each employee in shared dormitories, including lockable storage space for personal or valuable items
    • ensure that families with children have separate rooms from employees who are not members of that family
    • ensure that children live with their parents
    • provide separate spaces for sleeping and social life
    • provide a separate, well-ventilated canteen or space for cooking and eating.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of scheduled housekeeping such as cleaning of common areas like toilets, shower stalls, corridors and garbage disposal

  • records of maintenance, for example, fire alarm service, extinguisher service, emergency lighting service, gas, electrical, etc.

Auditors should confirm:

  • by conducting a walkthrough of the accommodation, that all provisions of this Indicator are being met;

  • what employees report about the living conditions in the accommodation.

Useful Resources

  • ILO guidance on worker’s housing: wcms_116344.pdf (ilo.org)

3.12.2 The UoC shall have an employee grievance mechanism which is accessible, fair and applicable to all employees.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Rates are ‘reasonable’ when:

    • below or comparable to similar accommodation available on the market

    • not more than a reasonable proportion of the employee’s income.

  • Where an employee or employee and their family plans to live in employer-provided accommodation:

    • the level of rent is a part of the contracting agreement

    • the site is able to provide a calculation and rationale for the level of rent.

  • If an employee lives in employer-provided accommodation and has an early termination of their contract (for example, due to gross misconduct), they should be entitled to a reasonable period of time to vacate the premises.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of rental agreements and payments

  • employee contracts

  • payslips.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the costs of any accommodation;

  • average local rental rates;

  • any additional charges for the provision of water and
    electricity, which should not be more than what employees would have to
    pay if they stayed outside the employer-provided accommodation.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.11.3 The UoC shall provide access to appropriate sanitary facilities that:

a)

are clean and hygienic; and

b)

include adequate privacy measures; and

c)

include separation by gender if required; and

d)

are sufficient for the number of people using them.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Appropriate sanitary facilities:

    • are located within or in close proximity (i.e. less than 60 metres) to the dormitory or housing facilities

    • are dry and warm

    • have a source of ventilation (e.g. window or fan)

    • have adequate lighting

    • have doors that close and lock for privacy

    • are separated for men and women except in family accommodation

    • are constructed of hard materials that are easy to clean

    • include at least one of the following:

      • pit latrines

      • flush toilets

      • urinals

    • have taps and running water

    • have facilities for the safe disposal of sanitary products.

  • Waste and wastewater are disposed of in accordance with Criterion 2.12.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of scheduled housekeeping such as cleaning of common areas like toilets, shower stalls, corridors and garbage disposal.

Auditors should confirm:

  • through a walkthrough of the sanitary facilities that all provisions of this Indicator are met;

  • what employees report on the quality of drinking water, maintenance of sanitary equipment like taps and toilet flushing systems.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.11.4 The UoC shall arrange for an annual meeting with employees or their representatives to discuss any reasonable improvements required to accommodation. The UoC shall maintain records of these meetings and shall take actions where necessary.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Employees can use this meeting to:

    • make suggestions on improvements to ensure accommodation meets requirements related to:

      • safety

      • hygiene

      • privacy

      • sanitary facilities

      • rates

    • highlight any maintenance issues that need to be addressed.

  • Any agreed improvements are acted upon by the UoC.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of meetings held between the UoC management employee representatives.

Auditors should confirm:

  • if any issues have been brought to the notice of management and how they have been resolved;

  • the process of raising grievances about living conditions.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.11.5 The UoC shall ensure that all employees working in remote locations have access to a free, private, real-time communication link to communicate externally.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Having access to outside communication is important for employees to:

    • protect their mental wellbeing

    • have an opportunity to raise any issues that occur on site.

  • Employees can use this communication link to communicate with:

    • family and friends

    • any independent organisation that they may be aware of (either through information from the UoC or other sources) who can support them.

  • This communication can happen through:

    • an employee’s own mobile phone

    • a telephone provided by the UoC

    • WiFi provided by the UoC for employees.

  • This line of communication is available 24 hours a day.
  • Outside an employee’s working hours there are no restrictions on when employees are able to connect with people outside the UoC.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • information about the availability of an outside communication link

  • evidence that the communication link is working.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that lines of communication are actually working;
  • the availability of these lines of communication for employees.

Grievance Mechanisms

3.12.1 The UoC shall, when concerns arise, engage in dialogue with employees or their representatives, with the intent of avoiding an escalation to a grievance. The UoC shall ensure that employees understand how to engage in this dialogue.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC proactively implements a dialogue system that:

    • allows for open participation of all employees

    • is easily accessible to employees on a regular basis

    • provides options for anonymous feedback.

  • Mechanisms for employees to provide feedback and engagement with management could include:

    • dialogue between management and employees

    • engagement with elected employee or union representatives

    • employee meetings or assemblies to solicit feedback

    • employee committees

    • suggestion box that is safely accessible for employees

    • access to an online feedback form or dedicated email address or phone number

    • employee surveys.

  • Issues raised during this process may include suggestions for improvement or highlight negative impacts on employees from the UoC’s activities. Examples can include:

    • operational inefficiencies such as inadequately maintained machinery that may impact efficiency and could cause health risks

    • employee rights such as female employees are paid less than male employees with similar jobs

    • harassment, such as an employee is pressured to begin a romantic
      or sexual relationship with a supervisor (whether this occurs during or
      outside work hours and work location)

    • working conditions, such as:

      • employees are frequently asked to work excessive overtime hours

      • employees are not properly compensated for their work.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • documentation on the mechanisms available

  • meeting minutes

  • records of actions taken to address issues.

Auditors should confirm:

  • how the mechanisms for reporting any issues are communicated to the employees;

  • what the procedures are to facilitate dialogue;

  • employees’ awareness of any processes to raise or discuss concerns with managers;

  • how and how often issues can be communicated to the management;

  • the system for reviewing and addressing any issues.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.2 The UoC shall have an employee grievance mechanism which is accessible, fair and applicable to all employees.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A grievance mechanism is a formal complaint process that can be used by employees to resolve a grievance.
  • Based on UN Guiding Principle No. 31, and effective a grievance mechanism must:
    • engender trust among participants
    • be transparent: ensure that users are given clear information about what is happening
    • be fair: ensure that users have access to sources of information and expertise necessary to engage in a grievance process

    • be predictable: ensure that users understand the process, how long it takes and what the outcomes can be

    • be accessible: ensure that users have been informed about it and can use it

    • be rights-based: ensure that outcomes and remedies are compatible with international human rights

    • be based on dialogue and engagement, ensuring that stakeholders are consulted and included in the process

    • be a source for continuous learning, analysing individual complaints to help prevent other grievances.

  • Mechanisms for submitting grievances are best determined together with employee representatives and can include:

    • in-person meetings

    • dedicated telephone numbers

    • email addresses

    • instant messaging or other online submission mechanisms

    • letters or written notes

    • a suggestion box

    • via employee representatives, trade unions, and worker associations

    • worker voice tools to conduct anonymous worker surveys.

  • For a grievance mechanism to be accessible for employees they must understand:

    • their labour rights (Criterion 3.1)

    • rights related to other workplace issues, such as health and safety regulations (Criterion 3.5)

    • how the grievance mechanism functions and what kinds of issues may be brought to the grievance mechanism (see also 3.12.3).

  • Foreign migrant workers may be given the option to raise issues:

    • internally with the UoC using the same channels open to other employees

    • with the local Consular Office of the Labour Attaché for their country in the country where the UoC is located

    • websites or Facebook pages of the Consulate or Embassy where migrant workers can raise grievances.

  • An effective grievance process will incorporate elements of the following steps at a minimum (adapted from Rainforest Alliance’s Grievance Guidance):

    • Step 1: Receive and acknowledge grievance complaint

    • Step 2: Take immediate action on human rights or hazardous issues (see Appendix 10 for the Remediation Procedure)

    • Step 3: Review the grievance complaint to check if it is admissible.

      • if it is inadmissible, this is communicated along with the reason, to the person who brought the grievance.
      • an inadmissible complaint is one that is unrelated to the activities or location of the UoC.
    • Step 4: Investigate the grievance complaint to establish what happened, maintaining confidentiality.

      • for complex issues or where there are conflicts of interest, external experts may be brought in to support.

    • Step 5: Communicate findings to the person who brought the grievance.

    • Step 6: Agree on a remediation plan with the person who brought the grievance.

      • for complex issues, external arbitration and external remediation support including NGOs or rights experts may be brought in.

    • Step 7: Provide an opportunity for an appeals process, if agreement cannot be reached.

    • Step 8: Implement and monitor the remediation plan.

    • Step 9: Communicate the progress of the remediation to the person who brought the grievance and to any relevant stakeholders when confidentiality is not a concern.

    • Step 10: Engage in continuous improvement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • grievance policy or procedure

  • employee survey results

  • employee notices and notice boards

  • employee handbook

  • records from grievance procedures and their outcomes

  • meeting minutes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • if the grievance procedure provides employees with clearly written and understandable instructions on how to report grievances using different methods that involve formal, informal and anonymous reporting;
  • if the grievance procedure applies to and is accessible to all employees, including full-time, permanent, contract, seasonal, migrant (domestic and foreign) and temporary employees.

Useful Resources

  • Rainforest Alliance’s Grievance Guidance: https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/business/resource-item/guidance-e-grievance-mechanism/

  • SHIFT Project is a non-profit consultancy focused on human rights Due Diligence based on the UN Guiding Principles for Business and Human rights. They have published two guidance documents on grievance mechanisms with clear definitions, both for community and employee-focused grievance. https://shiftproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/191210_publication_grievance-mechanism.pdf

  • https://shiftproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/Shift_remediationUNGPs_2014.pdf

  • The Global Compact Network Netherlands, Oxfam and Shift also developed a ‘Doing Business With Respect for Human Rights’ guide for companies to translate expectations in the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights into concrete action, with a chapter on Remediation and Grievance: https://www.businessrespecthumanrights.org/en/page/349/remediation-and-grievance-mechanisms

  • https://www.ihrb.org/uploads/reports/EC-Guide_OG-12_Part-3_Section-VI.pdf

3.12.3 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are trained on the employee grievance mechanism.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Training on the grievance mechanism is provided to all employees. This can take place:
    • as part of the induction process
    • at the start of each production cycle.
  • Awareness of this mechanism is:
    • essential for all employees
    • important for a positive environment in the workplace.
  • The UoC can communicate the grievance mechanism to employees through a variety of ways, including:
    • induction training and other ongoing training
    • information posted in public areas of the UoC
    • distributing it to employees in flyers, via text messages, instant messaging, emails or other private forms of communication
    • discussing it in employee meetings and assemblies
    • including it in employment contracts or the employee handbook.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • grievance policy or procedure

  • employee handbook

  • training materials or distributed materials

  • meeting minutes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees’ understanding of how to raise issues and how they were made aware of the grievance mechanisms.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.4 The UoC shall ensure that all employees are trained on the employee grievance mechanism.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For the grievance mechanism for communities, the guidance under Indicator 3.12.2 for employees also applies.

  • Mechanisms for submitting grievances are best determined together with community representatives. Examples of channels for submitting grievances include:

    • in-person meetings

    • dedicated telephone numbers

    • email addresses

    • instant messaging or other online submission mechanisms

    • letters or written notes

    • via community leaders and representatives, or community
      organisations.

  • Different communities may prefer different channels for submitting grievances.

  • Vulnerable populations may need special consideration in terms of how the grievance is submitted to enable their participation. For example:

    • when persons of the same gender, or ethnic group are available to receive a complaint, that may increase the likelihood of participation.

  • The following steps can be taken to inform potential users about the grievance mechanism:

    • conduct a stakeholder mapping and engagement process to identify communities and Indigenous and tribal peoples who may use the grievance mechanism.

    • make them aware of their rights under the law and under the ASC Farm Standard, including the grievance mechanism.

    • share information about the grievance mechanism, for example through:

      • local community representatives, community leaders and relevant community organisations

      • local publications

      • printed materials such as company newsletters, flyers, posters

      • digital means such as company website, online newsletter or social media.

    • give special consideration to reaching vulnerable groups within the population, as they are:

      • most likely to be impacted

      • unlikely to be comfortable with raising issues to the company.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • materials used to inform communities of the grievance mechanisms

  • minutes of meetings where grievance mechanisms are discussed.

Auditors should confirm:

  • community representatives (including Indigenous people’s representatives where applicable) understand:

  • how they can raise concerns and grievances with the UoC;

  • who their point of contact at the UoC is;

    • how the grievance mechanism was communicated to communities;

    • when discussions were had between UoC management and communities;

    • when grievances were raised in the past and how they were resolved.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.5 The UoC shall ensure the grievance mechanisms in Indicators 3.12.2 and 3.12.4 include provisions for non-retaliation.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Non-retaliation means that no action can be taken by the UoC against a person or an entity bringing a grievance that has been raise in good faith.
  • If retaliation occurs, this means that the grievance mechanism is inadequate.
  • This protection against retaliation applies to those bringing grievances and to whistleblowers.
  • ILO defines whistleblowing as: ‘the reporting by employees or former employees of illegal, irregular, dangerous or unethical practices by employers’5050https://www.ilo.org/media/406736/download.
  • Examples of retaliation in the workplace can include:
    • direct consequences, such as:
      • firing
      • demotion
      • salary reduction
      • reduced hours
    • more subtle consequences, such as:
      • reassignment to work that causes personal hardship
      • exclusion from key meetings and group events
      • threats
      • harassment
      • bullying
    • indirect consequences, such as:
      • encouraging shunning, harassment or bullying by other staff members.
  • Examples of retaliation for a community member or Indigenous or tribal person can include:
    • direct actions
    • indirect actions through others
    • threats
    • harassment
    • damage to a person or property.
  • Ways to protect employees and communities from retaliation can include:
    • having clear grievance processes and policies that include accountability (see 3.12.2)
    • raising a confidential grievance (see also 3.12.9)
    • raising an anonymous grievance through a hotline or similar, where the identity of the person bringing the grievance is never known:
      • in this case, remediation is likely to affect a wider population and is not tied to a specific individual

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • grievance policy or procedure, including provision for confidentiality

  • records of grievance processes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • policies and provisions for non-retaliation with employee and community representatives.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.6 The UoC shall ensure that:

a)

grievances are acknowledged within 10 days from submission; and

b)

grievances are resolved within 90 days from submission.

Where resolution is not possible within 90 days, justification and an alternative timeline shall be provided to relevant parties.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC follows the procedure to address grievances, beginning with acknowledging the receipt of the grievance within 10 days from submission.

  • The UoC develops a clear action plan to resolve the grievance within 90 days from submission.

  • Urgent concerns should be addressed sooner. For example:

    • If the grievance relates to a workplace hazard related to equipment that could harm an employee, that equipment must be removed from operation and repaired immediately.

    • If the UoC suspects that the person making the claim or other people may be at risk, and if the case involves human rights, including potential cases of child labour or forced labour, the UoC follows Appendix 16 (Remediation Protocol).

  • Full remediation of the issue may take place over a longer timeframe when required by the circumstance. For example:

    • until the child has reached school-leaving and working age.

  • Simple grievances may not require a 90-day timeframe.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of grievance processes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the timeframe in which grievances are resolved.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.7 The UoC shall maintain written records of all grievances, responses and resolutions.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The system used to track grievances, responses, communication and remedy should include:

    • the name of the person who brought the grievance

    • the date it was submitted

    • the person or department against whom the grievance was made

    • the category of the grievance

    • dates and the results of internal investigations carried out

    • the outcome of the investigation

    • dates when a response was provided to the person who brought the grievance.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • records of grievance processes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • records of grievance processes are complete.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.8 The UoC shall facilitate the establishment of employee representation to support the implementation and maintenance of the grievance mechanism.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Employee representation is freely chosen or elected by their peers without interference from management.
  • The UoC staff may wish to have employee representation in the form of a committee to support the grievance mechanism. In this case, the committee:
    • can vary in size depending on the size of the UoC
    • should include representation for diverse groups and consider the needs of vulnerable groups. For example:
      • ensuring a representative number of men and women
      • ensuring that migrant employees are included
    • if the UoC is unionised, a member of the Trade Union should be included.
  • The UoC staff may wish to have employee representation in the form of a committee to support the grievance mechanism. In this case, the committee:
  • Employee representatives:
    • have been trained and are knowledgeable about the business and common grievances that occur
    • understand human rights issues including labour rights, community rights, and Indigenous peoples’ rights, as applicable
    • are seen as accessible and impartial
    • have appropriate skills and authority level to investigate and resolve grievances, and where appropriate, facilitate dialogue, remedy and identify areas of improvement
    • are protected from any reprisals, particularly where they are involved in sensitive issues.
    • The same employee representation may also take on the role of supporting the implementation of the human rights policy (see indicator 3.1.3).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • evidence of training for employee representatives on the relevant topics

  • clearly documented roles and authority levels needed for employee representatives

  • job descriptions for employee representatives

  • records of employee representative selection process

  • minutes of any committee meetings.

Auditors should confirm:

  • that employees feel represented by the employee representatives;

  • how employee representatives feel the system is working in practice.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.12.9 The UoC shall ensure that grievance mechanisms are confidential, and information is only shared where necessary to investigate the grievance.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • If a confidential grievance process has been requested, anyone managing the grievance process receives, processes, files and monitors records with particular attention to ensuring that the identity of the person raising the claim is:

    • kept confidential

    • not in any public documentation.

  • Sometimes there may be a situation where in order to properly investigate and understand the grievance, the UoC has to share some information about the grievance. If this is the case:

    • the person bringing the grievance should be informed,

    • the information should be shared sensitively and only to those who need to know it.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • grievance policy with provisions for confidential procedures

  • records of grievance processes.

Auditors should confirm:

  • employees understand that the grievance processes are confidential;

  • those processing grievances understand how to keep the process confidential.
