Footnotes

Criterion 3.12 – Grievance Mechanisms

Community Engagement 3.13

3.13.1 The UoC shall not restrict or negatively affect the legal or customary rights of Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities to sites that are of special cultural, ecological, economic, religious or spiritual significance.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The aim of this criterion is that the UoC:
    • commits to responsible and ethical land and resource management
    • respects the rights and wellbeing of Indigenous and tribal peoples, and local communities.
  • Communities may have lived in the area for centuries, and the natural resources may:
    • hold cultural or religious significance
    • provide them with food security
    • provide them with economic benefits.
  • These areas can include:
    • land
    • lakes 
    • rivers 
    • streams 
    • mangroves
    • marine areas.
  • Communities’ use of these areas and natural resources can be assessed in consultation with communities. 
  • It is the responsibility of the UoC to:
    • assess which communities could potentially be affected by its operations;
    • understand and document which resources are vital to the communities;
    • seek and obtain community approval before undertaking changes that have the risk of restricting access to resources;
    • involve local communities in a consultative process to discuss the proposed changes;
    • document any community approvals;
    • engage with communities in a continuous process with annual reviews;
    • set up a permanently accessible mechanism for communities to raise any issues.
  • The UoC can take several steps to engage in these responsibilities:
    • Step 1: The UoC engages in regular consultation and collaboration:
      • identifies the communities, and Indigenous and tribal peoples who may be significantly impacted by the site’s activities
      • initiates a genuine and ongoing engagement and dialogue process with these stakeholders, which includes establishing and maintaining open lines of communication to understand their needs, concerns, and aspirations
      • commits to continually improving practices by being open to feedback and adapting to changing circumstances (see also Indicator 3.13.5).
    • Step 2: The UoC conducts social impact assessments:
      • assesses which communities may be affected by their operations:
        • the physical proximity of a community is less important than the extent of the impact experienced by them
      • engages these communities to conduct thorough impact assessments to understand the potential cultural, and socio-economic consequences of site operations on significant sites (also 3.13.2)
      • If an adequate and up-to-date social impact assessment has already been carried out for another purpose, there is no need to carry out another one. In some cases, the assessment will need to be complemented. The UoC will also need to show it has followed up on its findings.
    • Step 3: The UoC develops a mitigation plan:
      • that is based on the social impact assessments, to eliminate adverse effects on significant sites, in consultation with affected communities
      • implements this plan
      • monitors this plan.
    • Step 4: The UoC educates and trains employees about:
      • the cultural, historical, and ecological significance of the land and water resources in the area to foster a deeper understanding and respect for these resources
      • the mitigation plan
      • ensures that there are employees with the required competencies to conduct community engagement.
    • Step 5: The UoC integrates community engagement into management systems (see also Criterion 1.2):
      • integrates the mitigation plan in company policies
      • ensures there is a member of senior management who is responsible for implementation of these company policies and the mitigation plan
    • Step 6: The UoC establishes conflict resolution mechanisms, which are:
      • clear and fair
      • for resolving disputes or conflicts that may arise between the UoC and Indigenous or local communities
      • agreed upon in advance and involve impartial third parties if necessary (see also Indicators 3.12.4 – 3.12.9).
    • Step 7: The UoC ensures transparency, reporting and communication, internally, to the communities and to other interested stakeholders. This can include:
      • maintaining transparency in operations
      • reporting on community engagement efforts accessible to communities.
      • communicating clearly and well in advance about any activities that have the potential to affect communities.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • reports from environmental and social impact assessments

  • impact mitigation plan

  • reports or meeting minutes from community meetings and other engagement

  • documentation from grievance procedures

  • brochures, posters and other materials used for communication with communities.

Auditors should confirm:

  • which communities may be impacted by the operations of the UoC and if they are Indigenous communities or not;

  • whether the methodology for stakeholder mapping was robust enough to identify the key rightsholders and stakeholders.

  • if the stakeholders identified include diverse groups representing different segments of the community.

  • where possible with communities, that the assessments were conducted in good faith and include all significant sites that the UoC may have an impact on, or where this is not possible seek input from local NGOs or other organisations.

    • the mitigation plan is being implemented;

    • communities understand how to access the UoC’s community grievance mechanism;

    • documentation from grievance processes, the nature of the grievances and how they have been resolved;

    • how communities engage with the UoC;

  • whether there are any conflicts about the use of resources by the UoC or if the UoC has restricted access to sites of religious or spiritual significance for Indigenous people;

  • whether there are any other negative impacts they experience from the UoC.

Useful Resources

  • IFC stakeholder engagement handbook: https://www.ifc.org/en/insights-reports/2000/publications-handbook-stakeholderengagement–wci–1319577185063

  • Guide to social impact assessment: https://www.eianz.org/document/item/5876

  • World Resources Institute “Breaking Ground: Engaging communities in extractive and infrastructure projects”: https://www.wri.org/research/breaking-ground

  • Guidance for Free Prior and Informed Consent (but also useful for community engagement more generally):

    • Accountability framework guidance on FPIC: https://accountability-framework.org/fileadmin/uploads/afi/Documents/Operational_Guidance/OG_FPIC-2020-5.pdf

    • FPIC-360°: https://fpic360.org/

    • World Resources Institute “Development without conflict: The business case for community consent”: https://www.wri.org/research/development-without-conflict

    • Oxfam “Guide to Free Prior and Informed Consent”: https://www.culturalsurvival.org/sites/default/files/guidetofreepriorinformedconsent_0.pdf

3.13.2 The UoC shall identify, avoid and mitigate potential negative impacts on the surrounding communities resulting from its activities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC can be a busy environment, and operations can have an impact on surrounding communities, who may experience increased:

    • noise

    • light

    • pollution

    • dirt and dust

    • traffic and damage to roads

    • restrictions on where people can move around the
      community.

  • Sometimes the UoC can cause disruption to communities who are further away, for example through increased traffic on the roads by trucks delivering feed early in the morning.

  • In consultation with the community the UoC should:

    • identify if any negative impacts are taking place

    • decide on ways to mitigate these impacts

    • inform the community of the contents of any mitigation plan.

  • See also the guidance for Indicator 3.13.1.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • an analysis of any negative impacts caused by the UoC
    • records or minutes of meetings or other engagement with the community
    • a mitigation plan for any negative impacts.

Auditors should confirm:

  • the UoC understands who the communities are who are potentially impacted by its operations;

  • the UoC has carried out a process of understanding what, if any, the impacts from its operations are for the local communities;

  • where possible, if communities have been engaged in a process of understanding the impacts of the operations of the UoC;

  • communities are aware of the mitigation plan.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.13.3 The UoC shall, where possible, source goods and services, including employment, from Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Ensuring that the community benefits economically from the UoC can:
    • improve wellbeing
    • foster positive relationships between the UoC and the communities.
  • The UoC can develop partnerships and agreements that ensure that nearby communities benefit economically from site operations. This may include: 
    • job opportunities
    • sourcing goods from the community, for example:
      • food for the canteen
      • machinery needed for running the site
      • feed.
    • sourcing services from the community, for example:
      • cleaning company
      • diving company
      • security guard provider.
    • revenue-sharing
    • infrastructure development, for example:
      • the improvement of roads
      • connections to other services for the community, such as internet access. 
  • Actions that the site can take include:
    • local posting of jobs and active recruitment in neighbouring communities,
    • partnerships with local businesses for the delivery of goods and/or services, such as catering.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • sourcing policy

  • recruitment processes and advertisements for jobseekers

  • employee records

  • agreements with local businesses.

Auditors should confirm:

  • how jobs are advertised and goods are sourced;

  • the degree of locally recruited employees and locally sourced goods and services;

  • the reasoning for recruiting employees or sourcing goods and services from elsewhere.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.13.4 The UoC shall demonstrate its right to use the land and water including, where applicable, transfer of ownership or usage of land from Indigenous and tribal peoples, local communities or other stakeholders to the UoC.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC:
    • recognises and respects the legal and customary rights of Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities over land and resources
    • ensures land titles and deeds are in place and that it follows national laws
    • can demonstrate this right by showing:
      • legal ownership documentation
      • leaseholds
      • any other use right documentation
      • there are/were no land conflicts when starting the site operations, and/or
      • any land conflicts have been resolved.
  • Where required (and this can be applied anywhere as a good practice) the UoC obtains Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) from Indigenous and tribal communities before undertaking any activities that may impact significant sites or resources.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • review local legislation related to legal or customary rights of Indigenous and tribal people to water

  • land titles, deeds, licences

  • evidence of agreements with communities

  • evidence of FPIC agreements with Indigenous communities.

Auditors should confirm:

  • how community members engage with the UoC;

  • the UoC has all appropriate land titles, deeds and licences in place;

  • whether there are any past or ongoing conflicts between the community and the UoC about the UoC’s use of resources.

Useful Resources

N/A

3.13.5 The UoC shall proactively engage with Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities to identify, avoid, and mitigate significant negative impacts resulting from the activities of the UoC.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Proactive engagement means that the UoC should:
    • make contact with Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities to establish and maintain a relationship with them
    • make efforts to involve Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities in decisions that may impact them
    • keep Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities informed about the activities of the UoC, particularly any changes that may take place
    • ensure that Indigenous and tribal peoples and local communities are aware of and understand how to use the community grievance mechanism (3.12.4).
  • Guidance for Indicator 3.13.1 offers information about how to:
    • engage with communities
    • assess and mitigate any negative impacts.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • evidence of engagement with local communities

  • minutes from any meetings with community members

  • documented grievances and their resolutions.

Auditors should confirm:

  • confirm that the UoC is aware of which communities may be impacted by their activities;

  • confirm that the UoC understands some of the possible negative impacts that their activities may have on communities;

  • confirm that the UoC has engaged in some way with local communities.

Fish (Including Cleaner Fish) 4.1

Training

Training Content

Our training content is designed to help you better understand key requirements of the ASC Farm Standard.

Videos are publicly accessible, and most offer subtitles in multiple languages.

Our online courses and learning pathways require you to log in to the ASC Training Centre. They are currently available in English, with additional languages coming soon.

Video Fish Slaughter

Fish Slaughter Under the ASC Farm Standard

4.1.1.1 The UoC shall ensure that all relevant employees are trained on general animal health and welfare awareness, including biosecurity, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.1.1.2 The UoC shall ensure that any person involved in animal husbandry and handling activities is trained on animal health and welfare, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.1.1.3 The UoC shall ensure that the content of the training in Indicators 4.1.1.1 and 4.1.1.2 is updated as necessary and is approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For each employee:

    • The level of training should be appropriate to their role:

      • For all relevant employees: a basic level of awareness of bio security, fish health and welfare is required.

      • For any person involved in husbandry, handling, and slaughter operations: a more advanced level of training on fish health and welfare, handling and slaughter practices is required on an annual basis.

    • Evidence of training participation must be maintained:

      • Certificates of attendance.

      • Certificates of competency.

  • The trainer should be competent in the topic of animal health and welfare and the competence should be demonstrable, e.g.:

    • Curriculum Vitae.

    • Records of qualifications.

    • Work experience.

  • Best practices on the implementation of the training content should be visible during the audit.
    • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of that content at interviews.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A list of employees and subcontracted personnel involved in animal husbandry and handling operations.

  • Records:

    • Training.

    • Trainer’s competence.

    • Certificates of competency.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Employees received the required level of training for their roles by cross-checking employees and subcontracted personnel lists with:

    • Training records.

    • Certificates of competency.

    • Trainer’s competence.

    • Revision of training resources/contents.

  • Adequate level of personnel knowledge of the training content should be verified by:

    • Interviews.

    • Observation of real operations during handling and slaughter of fish.

Useful Resources

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) – Competency and Curriculum Guidelines for Community Animal Health Workers. Paris, 39 pp. (https://doi.org/10.20506/woah.3535).

4.1.1.4 The UoC shall implement a vaccination plan that:

a)

considers the relevant diseases and vaccine availability; and

b)

includes justification for vaccine selection; and

c)

is approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The vaccination plan should consider:
    • Local regulations.
    • Relevant diseases for the species in the country, based on scientific literature and publicly available information.
    • Commercially licensed vaccines registered for the species being farmed and autogenous vaccines produced by a licensed producer.
      • Commercially licensed vaccines are recognised by the relevant country authorities to ensure quality control, safety and efficacy.
      • Autogenous vaccines are custom vaccines produced from pathogens isolated directly from affected sites on which the vaccines are subsequently deployed under a minor use or restricted permit by a licenced producer.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Local regulations.
  • List of relevant diseases for the species in the country and
    available vaccines.

  • Vaccine permits.

  • Vaccine purchase invoices.

  • Records:

    • Vaccination.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The vaccination plan in place is overseen and signed off by a veterinarian and includes a list of relevant diseases for the country and the vaccines available.
    • The information should be cross-checked with local regulations and records.

Useful Resources

  • Domínguez-Odio, A; Rodríguez Martínez, E; Leonardo Cala Delgado, D. (2024) Commercial vaccines used in poultry, cattle, and aquaculture: a multidirectional comparison. Frontiers In Veterinary Science.

  • Yang, Du; Xioman, Hu; Liang, Miao; Jiong, Chen (2022) “Current status and development prospects of aquatic vaccines” Frontiers in Immunology.
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2021) Tackling Disease Outbreaks. WOAH Article.
  • Mondal H, Thomas J. (2022) “A review on the recent advances and application of vaccines against fish pathogens in aquaculture”. Aquaculture International.

4.1.1.5 The UoC shall only stock a single cohort of fish per site.

Indicator applicability: marine salmonids in cages

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Gaps of up to six months between stocking inputs are acceptable as long as:

    • The smolts are derived from the same stripping.

    • There is a period when the site is fully fallow after harvest, in accordance with regulatory requirements.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:
  • Purchase.
  • Transportation.
  • Delivery.
  • Stocking.
  • Fallowing.
  • Production (fish size).

Auditors should confirm:

  • The size of the fish matches that of a single year class by observing the stock.
    • The observation should be cross-checked with records.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.1.6 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific mortality limits, according to Appendix 2 (2.3).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.1.7 The UoC shall only stock batches of fish that have been tested prior to stocking and are free from diseases of regional concern.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Testing should be relevant to:
    • The species.
    • The production system.
    • The scale of production.
    • The local regulations.
      • For example:
        • Gyrodactlylus salaris for Atlantic salmon in Norway.
        • Tilapia lake virus (TiLV) for tilapia in Asia. 
        • Viral hemorrhagic septicemia (VHS) in freshwater fish.
  • Testing might consist of:
    • Clinical examination of the fish.
    • Laboratory tests:
      • Bacteriology.
      • Molecular biology (e.g. PCR).
      • Histopathology.
      • Virology (e.g. cell culture).
  • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should determine:
    • The diseases to include in the testing, based on local regulations, scientific literature and/or publicly available information (see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.1.4). 
    • The sample size, based on local regulations and/or technical judgement.
  • Compulsory governmental testing programme results are acceptable for demonstrating conformance with this requirement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • List of relevant diseases for the species in the country (see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.1.4).

  • Testing results written report or document that includes as a minimum:

    • The batch of fish tested.

    • The site of the test

    • The pathogen tested

    • The results of the test

  • Records

    • Purchase.

    • Transportation.

    • Delivery.

    • Stocking.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Every batch of fish has been tested by cross-checking the list of relevant diseases for the species in the country with the testing result’s written report or document and records.

Useful Resources

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.3. Diseases listed by WOAH.

  • Council Regulation (2016) Transmissible animal diseases and amending and repealing certain acts in the area of animal health (‘Animal Health Law’). Official Journal

4.1.1.8 The UoC shall ensure that a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional periodically visits the site to perform routine checks. Checks shall be carried out at least annually for all fish species and quarterly for salmon, as well as reactively in cases of fish health or welfare concerns.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Regular veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visits may fall into two categories:
    • Routine: Performed on a regular basis to monitor the health and welfare of the farmed fish.

    • Reactive: Performed in response to deterioration of, or concerns about, the health or welfare status of the farmed fish.

      • Sites should be prepared to provide the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional with detailed information about the observed symptoms, recent changes in behaviour, morphology, water quality or mortality and any relevant history of disease or treatments.

      • The site should use reactive health visits to address immediate health or welfare concerns, diagnose underlying causes of problems, and implement targeted interventions to mitigate risks and prevent further spread of disease.

  • For routine visits, preparation is recommended to ensure a meaningful outcome from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional. Below are some practical considerations:
    • Visit scheduling: Ensure key employees are available during the visit to provide relevant required information and to facilitate adequate follow-up.

      • Designate a senior member of the employees to serve as the primary point of contact for the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional during the visit.

      • This individual can help coordinate the activity, ensure relevant information is available, assist during the visit and ensure follow-up.

    • Gather and organise relevant information:

      • Compile relevant information about the operations, including:

        • Species being cultured,

        • Production systems,

        • Stocking densities,

        • Recent health history, including treatments, water quality monitoring results,

        • Behaviour data,

        • Morphology and mortalities data,

        • Feeding plan,

        • Any previous veterinary reports,

        • Details of any ongoing issue.

      • Having this information readily accessible will facilitate discussion and decision-making during the visit.

    • Prepare the UoC for the visit: Ensure the UoC is prepared for the visit and for providing full access to all relevant areas to the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

      • Address any maintenance issues, clean tanks or ponds as needed and ensure clear access to all relevant areas of the facility.

      • Ensure handling and other equipment that might be needed during the visit, such as nets, containers and sampling equipment is available and in good working condition.

      • Make sure employees are aware of the visit and its objectives and encourage them to proactively participate in it.

    • During the visit: Ensure relevant information is discussed with the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and that the visit includes all relevant areas within the UoC.

    • After the visit: Follow up on any recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.

      • Implement any necessary revisions or changes to management practices, treatment protocols, or facility conditions based on the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional’s feedback and any sample or testing results.

    • Continuous improvement: Use the insights gained from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit to identify opportunities for continuous improvement in health and welfare management.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Health reports.

  • Testing results.

  • Records:

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional qualifications.

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit.

    • Recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The qualifications of the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and cross-check the frequency of visits with records.

  • Existence of health reports and testing results.

Useful Resources

  • FAO eLearning Academy (2024) Emergency preparedness for aquatic disease outbreaks. Online course

4.1.1.9 The UoC shall develop and implement a feeding plan that includes at least the following:

a)

time and frequency of feeding; and

b)

feed rations; and

c)

feeding methods; and

d)

different environmental conditions; and

e)

prevention of the use of feed which has expired, spoiled or shows signs of excessive leakage; and

f)

feed types for the nutritional needs and life stages of the species.

An exception applies to (f) when such feeds are not available, in which case the UoC shall use feed suitable for animals with similar nutritional needs.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The feeding plan:

    • Outlines the site’s feeding strategy.

    • As a minimum, it must include the following parameters:

      • Time and frequency, e.g. at daybreak and early afternoon (08:30 am and 02:00 pm).

      • Feed rations, e.g. feed type and daily amount.

      • Feeding adaptation to fit different life stages, e.g. transfer diets for Atlantic salmon smolts recently transferred to saltwater.

      • Feeding adaptation to fit different ambient conditions, e.g. stop feeding during algae blooms or use functional feeds when facing specific health issues.

    • Should include considerations to guarantee the good working order of mechanical equipment used to deliver feed, e.g. scheduled maintenance checks of automatic feeders

  • The UoC should document the rationale for changes in the feeding plan to better inform management decisions.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • Purchase.

    • Transportation.

    • Delivery.

    • Stocking.

    • Maintenance which affected feeding.

    • Any environmental or health issues which affected feeding.

    • Feeding periods (time and frequency).

    • Feeding rations.

  • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of the feeding plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Feeding plan includes the minimum required parameters and is implemented:

    • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the plan with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • The International Aquaculture Feed Formulation Database.

  • Hasan, M.R, New, M.B. eds. (2013) On-farm feeding and feed management In aquaculture. FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper No. 583. Rome, FAO. 67pp.

  • Alevra, A., Llorente Manzanares, M., Mente, E., Xandri Royo, P.M., (2024) Good husbandry practices for aquaculture, Publications Office of the European Union.

4.1.1.10 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP), approved by a registered veterinarian, with the intent of preventing disease outbreaks, and ensuring the good health and welfare of farmed fish.

The HWMP shall include all of the following:

a)

disease monitoring; and

b)

response, including quarantine, treatment, and humane culling; and

c)

reporting mechanisms, including reporting WOAH-notifiable disease to authorities; and

d)

biosecurity risks; and

e)

predation risks.

The HWMP shall be reviewed and revised as necessary:

f)

at least annually for sites with cycles under one year or using continuous production methods; or

g)

after each cycle for sites with longer cycles or all-in-all-out production methods.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP): 
    • Aims to support the development and implementation of preventive, rather than remedial, actions that ensure good fish health and welfare.
    • Must be developed by the UoC in collaboration with a veterinarian who approves it. In countries where other professions have comparable rights and duties and are subject to the same authorization and regulatory requirements as veterinarians, they may also approve the HWMP (e.g., aqua medicine biologists in Norway).
  • For developing and establishing a site-specific disease monitoring, response and reporting mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Developing standardised health and welfare monitoring protocol
      • This may involve conducting visual inspections, monitoring Operational Welfare Indicators (OWIs) and performing diagnostic tests for pathogens.
    • Producing and maintaining detailed records.
      • Including records of health observations, diagnostic test results, treatments administered, mortalities, and other relevant data.
      • It is recommended to use a centralised database or electronic system for efficient data management and retrieval.
    • Implementing an early detection system. 
      • To detect signs of disease outbreaks or abnormal health conditions promptly. 
        • This could include environmental monitoring tools.
    • Establishing response protocols for responding to disease outbreaks or health emergencies.
      • Outlining procedures for:
        • Isolating affected individuals or populations.
        • Implementing strategies for treatments or others (e.g. culling affected batches of fish [see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.1.10.4]).
        • Notifying relevant stakeholders, including other sites in the vicinity and the authorities.
    • Establishing communication channels.
      • Effective communication channels should be implemented for reporting health-related issues both internally within the facility and externally to relevant authorities (e.g., WOAH-notifiable diseases) or stakeholders. 
        • Employees should understand their roles and responsibilities in reporting and responding to disease events.
    • Maintaining a readily accessible notification list.
      • Including contact names numbers and emails for key employees and other relevant stakeholders. 
      • The list should be kept up-to-date to ensure quick and efficient communication during emergencies (see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.2.3).
  • For developing a site-specific biosecurity mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Determining the objectives and scope of the biosecurity mechanism.
    • Identifying relevant regulatory requirements.  
    • Gathering information about the site, including an up-to-date layout of buildings and production units identifying the possible movements of animals, animal products, animal waste, water, feed and fomites/vectors. 
    • Identifying potential transmission pathways into, within and from the site. 
    • Carrying out a risk analysis to identify and evaluate disease threats and ensure that the plan addresses them. 
      • A risk analysis can be carried out either on the whole operation or only partially, e.g. disease transmission during transportation. 
        • This will depend on the objectives of the biosecurity mechanism. 
    • Identifying mitigation measures and assessing their effectiveness and their management requirements.  
    • Establishing emergency procedures in the event of a biosecurity failure.  
    • Defining internal and external communication procedures, roles, and responsibilities. 
    • Creating a monitoring and internal audit schedule.  
    • Carrying out performance evaluations. 
    • Creating the necessary Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to support the implementation of the mitigation measures and the biosecurity mechanism.  
    • Training employees in the different elements of the biosecurity mechanism. 
    • Maintaining a record-keeping system that provides evidence of compliance with the biosecurity mechanism.  
  • For developing predator control measures within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Identifying potential predators.
      • Create a list of the predators that are present in the area and that might interact with the UoC.
        • Predators may include birds, mammals, reptiles, and other aquatic species known to prey on fish.
    • Assessing the risk of predation. 
      • Evaluate the risk posed by each predator species identified based on factors such as proximity to the site, population size, means of accessing the site, likelihood of predation, etc.
    • Implementing predator control measures. 
      • Develop and implement predator control measures tailored to the specific risks identified. This may include:
        • Physical barriers such as nets, fences, or screens to prevent access to fish tanks or ponds.
        • Scare tactics such as visual deterrents to discourage predators from approaching the facility.
    • Implementing ongoing monitoring and surveillance. 
      • To detect predator activity and intervene as needed.
    • Regular reviewing and revision. 
      • Based on the outcome of the ongoing monitoring and surveillance. 
      • Adjustments to the measures should be made when the results of monitoring indicate the need to optimise protection for fish and the containment system.
    • Collaborating with local authorities or local wildlife agencies to address predator issues in the surrounding area.
  • A periodic review and, if necessary, a revision of the HWMP must be conducted in response to changes in farming activities or external factors or as directed by the veterinarian. 
    • As a minimum, the review should occur annually in cases of production cycles shorter than one year or using continuous stocking/cropping methods, or following each production cycle, in the case of UoCs with production cycles longer than one year or using all-in-all-out stocking/cropping methods.  
    • The UoC should develop feedback mechanisms to inform the review, e.g. proactively seeking feedback from employees and subcontracted personnel, such as the vaccination team, on the operationalisation of the site-specific biosecurity mechanism. 
    • For a single producer overseeing multiple UoCs in a shared waterbody, a unified HWMP that incorporates site-specific details is acceptable; however, for larger companies managing multiple UoCs in one country, while common plans may apply, it is crucial to ensure HWMP adaptation to individual site circumstances, particularly in aspects like biosecurity measures, disease surveillance programs, and monitoring systems.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The HWMP includes considerations for:
    • Site-specific disease monitoring, responses and reporting requirements.

      • Specific considerations should be given to reporting WOAH-notifiable diseases (see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.1.11).

    • Site-specific biosecurity mechanism.

    • Predators control measures.

    • Veterinarian sign-off.

    • Reviews and revisions.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HWMP includes the required five minimum considerations above and all relevant records associated with the HWMP implementation.

  • Employees are:

    • Familiarised with the HWMP and the feedback mechanisms for its review by conducting employee interviews and observations.

    • Trained on the site-specific biosecurity mechanism by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code – World Organisation for Animal Health.

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2023) Assessment and listing of emerging diseases – WOAH Bulletin

  • Scottish Finfish Aquaculture (2023) Code of Good Practice for Scottish Finfish Aquaculture.

  • The Fish Site (2005) The benefits of a veterinary health plan.

  • Alevra, A., Llorente Manzanares, M., Mente, E., Xandri Royo, P.M., (2024) Good husbandry practices for aquaculture. Publications Office of the European Union.

  • APROMAR (2022) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture – Volume 1: Concepts and generalities. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 36 pp.

  • APROMAR (2024) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture- Volume 2: Welfare of European sea bass. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 49 pp.

  • APROMAR (2024) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture – Volume 3: Welfare of gilthead sea bream. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 49 pp.PerfromFISH (2021) Best therapeutics practices for Mediterranean farmed fish. Report 151pp.

4.1.1.10.1 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a water quality monitoring process according to Appendix 12 (12.3, Table 2).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Maintaining good water quality is a critical factor when culturing any aquatic organism.
    • Concentrations of substances within the water system that rise above or fall below specific levels can be harmful to fish populations.

  • Concerning health and welfare, water quality has a dual role as a cause or a consequence of poor health and welfare:

    • Poor water quality can cause health and welfare hazards in an aquaculture facility, e.g. heavy metals derived from forest runoff in a flow-through system or leaking from equipment in a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS).
    • Poor water quality can also result from poor husbandry practices resulting in a risk to health and welfare, e.g. if stocking density is too high the water quality is likely to deteriorate, especially in closed and semi-closed systems.

  • While Table 2 of Appendix 12 of the standard specifies water quality parameters that must be included in the monitoring process, other parameters may be considered based on the site-specific requirements of the UoC.

  • Conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds for the required parameters, customised to suit the species and environmental conditions, should be incorporated as part of the water quality monitoring process. Water quality parameters that are described as risk assessed will be determined by:

    • Site history of water quality parameters (detailed records),

    • Previous results,

    • The sensitivity of the species.
  • Tables 6 and 7 below give examples for the majority of the required water quality indicators that may be considered acceptable as a reference to develop and implement a water quality monitoring process.

Table 6: Water Quality Monitoring for Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) based on Pedrazzani, A.S., Quintiliano, M.H., Bolfe, F., Sans de Oliveira, E.C. & Molento, C.F.M. (2020) Tilapia On-Farm Welfare Assessment Protocol for Semi-intensive Production Systems Frontiers in Veterinary Science and Bregnballe, J. 2022. and A guide to recirculation aquaculture – An introduction to the new environmentally friendly and highly productive closed fish farming systems. Rome. FAO and Eurofish International Organisation.

Table 7: Water Quality Monitoring for yellowtail kingfish (Seriola lalandi) In a marine recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) with artificial seawater based on J. Orellana, U. Waller, B. Wecker, (2014) Culture of yellowtail kingfish (Seriola lalandi) in a marine recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) with artificial seawater. Aquacultural Engineering and FAO (2022) A guide to recirculation aquaculture – An introduction to the new environmentally friendly and highly productive closed fish farming systems. Rome. FAO and Eurofish International Organisation.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The water quality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.
  • Records confirming the monitoring of the required parameters and their conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds.
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established water quality monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The water quality monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and is implemented. 
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • The Fish Site (2015) How to achieve good water quality management in aquaculture. 
  • Prema D, Jenni B, Reena V Joseph, Vysakhan P, Prajitha K and Kripa V (2020) Water Quality Management In Aquaculture. CMFRI
  • EU Platform on Animal Welfare Own Initiative Group on Fish (2020) Guidelines on Water Quality and Handling for the Welfare of Farmed Vertebrate Fish.
  • FAO (2022) A guide to recirculation aquaculture – An introduction to the new environmentally friendly and highly productive closed fish farming systems. Rome. FAO and Eurofish International Organisation.

4.1.1.10.2 The UoC shall ensure5151An exemption applies for Seabass due to its high sensitivity to handling practices. the HWMP includes a morphological scoring monitoring process for live fish. Monitoring shall be conducted at least once a month, and shall include at least the following scoring parameters:

a)

eye damage

b)

operculum damage

c)

skin damage

d)

fin damage

e)

deformities

f)

change of colouration

g)

emaciation

An exception applies where deviation from monitoring frequency is justified by any of the following reasons:

h)

immediately after smolting and stocking; or

i)

under environmental conditions that affect the welfare of the fish or the health and safety of employees; or

j)

fish are undergoing a disease event and/or being treated, in which case the maximum deviation shall be two weeks.

The reason for any deviation must be recorded.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Morphological scoring is frequently used as an immediate indicator of welfare.
    • However, changes in morphology may have a variety of causes and therefore must be further analysed before drawing conclusions.
  • Examples that may be considered as references to develop a morphological scoring are provided in Table 8.
  • The K factor is based primarily on the degree of nourishment and sexual maturity. The K factor does not include all the requested parameters and cannot be used to show compliance to this Indicator.

Table 8: Morphological scoring for European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) based on Pavlidis, M., Samaras, A., Papaharisis, L., (2024). Welfare assessment study for European sea bass. University of Crete.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The morphological scoring monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.
  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the morphological scoring.
  • Monitoring can be carried out using camera technology, as long as this method is validated against traditional assessments.
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established morphological scoring monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The morphological monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and it is implemented.
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.
  • If using camera technology, the assessment has been validated against traditional assessments.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Behavioural scoring is frequently used as an immediate indicator of welfare.
    • However, changes in behaviour may have a variety of causes and therefore must be further analysed before drawing conclusions.
    • The daily monitoring should consider feeding behaviour and other behaviours relevant to the species being farmed.

  • The behavioural scoring monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.
  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the behavioural scoring.
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established behavioural scoring monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The feeding behavioural scoring monitoring process is implemented.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

4.1.1.10.4 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality monitoring process which includes at least the following:

a)

daily monitoring and recording of mortalities; and

b)

removal of mortalities at least every two days; and

c)

classification of all recovered mortalities and a post-mortem analysis for each mortality event; and

d)

investigation of mortality events which remain unexplained or unattributed to fish health reasons; and

e)

daily collection of moribund fish and culling according to Criterion 4.1.3.

Where any of the listed items above are not possible, the UoC shall record the reason.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Monitoring for mortality is understood as visual observation of whether there is mortality at the site, e.g. observations of the bottom of the pens with cameras; observations by divers or from the surface.  
  • Possible causes that would justify no daily monitoring or every second day removal of mortality are severe bad weather, or a major equipment failure not related to poor maintenance.
  • Mortality stems from diverse factors that appear linked to suffering, particularly during disease outbreaks and critical development or production phases. 
  • Scrutiny of mortality records and cause determination is essential for preventing further avoidable deaths and improving overall fish health and welfare in aquaculture. 
  • Mortality monitoring thresholds should be established as these will identify when the level of mortalities can be classified as a mortality event. 
  • If on-site diagnosis is inconclusive, off-site laboratory diagnosis is required.
  • When designing the mortality monitoring process, the UoC should consider carrying out a post-mortem analysis for each mortality event, not necessarily every fish.
    • A statistically relevant number of fish from the mortality event shall be analysed.
      • A statistically relevant number of fish refers to a sample size that is large enough to yield meaningful and reliable results when conducting statistical analysis.
        • In other words, the sample size should be sufficient to accurately represent the population being studied and to draw valid conclusions from the data.
      • The specific size needed for statistical relevance depends on various factors such as the variability within the population, the desired level of confidence, and the statistical methods being used.
        • Typically, larger sample sizes provide more reliable estimates and stronger evidence for drawing conclusions.
      • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should assist the site in determining the appropriate sample size required for statistical analysis and must conduct all diagnosis.
  • The UoC should develop a procedure (e.g. SOP) to describe moribund collection and culling operations.
    • Employees should be trained on this procedure.
  • Moribund fish should be collected using appropriate equipment to prevent further injuries and stress, e.g. hand net according to fish size. 
  • Collected moribund fish should be humanely slaughtered as per Criterion 4.1.3.
  • Possible causes that would justify no collection of moribund fish include severe bad weather or a major equipment failure not related to poor maintenance.
  • Possible causes of several moribund fish must be investigated.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Mortality monitoring.

  • Mortality removal.

  • The mortality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum
    elements required, as well as what they consider a mortality event,
    included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the mortality including
    the results of post-mortem analysis and the rationale for determining
    the sample size required for statistical analysis.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established
    mortality removal and monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The mortality monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements, is implemented and threshold levels to determine mortality events.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

  • Moribunds are collected daily and culled following responsible stunning and killing according to Criterion 4.1.3.

    • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the frequency of collection and culling methods with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

4.1.1.10.5 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a traffic light system for water quality (Indicator 4.1.1.10.1), morphological scoring (Indicator 4.1.1.10.2), behavioural scoring (Indicator 4.1.1.10.3), and mortality (Indicator 4.1.1.10.4). The system shall identify ranges of acceptable levels (green), warning levels (amber), and unacceptable levels (red) of health or welfare.

Where levels are identified as amber or red, the UoC shall increase monitoring and implement appropriate corrective actions to restore the levels back to green.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The traffic light system should be tailored to accommodate the species being farmed, their life stage and the UoC’s monitoring procedures.

  • General guidelines on how to develop the traffic light system for each OWI are presented as follows:

Water Quality Indicators:

Step 1. Identify the parameters to be monitored based on Table 2, Appendix 12.

Step 2. Establish species and life stage-specific thresholds for the parameters identified:

  • Base these values on either published scientific literature, the recommendation of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional, or ASC reference table for water quality.

    • If the farm is growing more than one life stage or species, then the creation of specific values for each life stage will be expected.

Example 1, for Atlantic salmon farmed in a seawater net pen, the traffic light system could be:

Example 2, Tilapia farmed in a pond, the traffic light system could be (based on Pedrazzani, A.S., Quintiliano, M.H., Bolfe, F., Sans de Oliveira, E.C. & Molento, C.F.M. (2020) Tilapia On-Farm Welfare Assessment Protocol for Semi-intensive Production Systems. Frontiers in Veterinary Science):

Morphological Indicators:

Step 1. Develop a scoring system for each of the morphological parameters required by Indicator 4.1.1.10.2.

  • It is recommended to score morphological parameters based on their severity, location and timing when applicable.

Step 2. Once a scoring system has been developed, simulate different scenarios to develop a traffic light system. These scenarios should include at least:  

  • The best case, e.g.; where fish have no morphologic issues.  
  • The second-best scenario, e.g. where fish have mild morphologic issues.  
  • The third-best scenario, e.g. where fish have moderate morphologic issues.  
  • The worst case, e.g. where fish have the highest score possible.  

Each scenario will have a corresponding score:

Best case scenario

Worst case scenario

Second best case scenario

Third best case scenario

Step 3. Create a traffic light system, for example:  

With time, and as more information is gathered, these thresholds might require re adjustments.

Behavioural Indicators:  

Step 1. Identify behaviours that are relevant for the species and the life stage being farmed.  

Step 2. Grade the identified behaviours based on the scientific literature available or the opinion of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional. A few possible behaviours to monitor are listed below.

  • How to interpret these behaviours will vary depending on the species of fish, the life stage and the farming system.
    • It is important to understand that, apart from the species and life stage variability, there will also be an individual component that will vary from one fish to the other.

Step 3. Simulate scenarios.

Step 4. Create a traffic light system, for example:

Mortality Indicators: 

Step 1. Develop a mortality classification system that adjusts to the species, the life stage and the farming context (e.g. the geography or farming system where fish are reared). Staff must be trained in the mortalities classification. Broadly, the following groupings can be made: 

  • Infectious:  

    • Bacterial. 

    • Viral.

    • Parasitic. 

    • Fungal. 

    • Amoebic.

  • Non-infectious:   

    • Husbandry related (e.g. transportation, treatment, vaccination, grading, etc.) 

    • Environmental (e.g. algal bloom, currents, etc.) 

    • Predation (e.g. birds, seals, others). 

    • Poor doers or runts. 

    • Physical lesions. 

    • Nephrocalcinosis. 

    • Moribund. 

    • Deformities. 

    • Undiagnosed/unknown. 

    • Decomposed. 

    • Sampled.

    • Failed smolts (only for salmon). 

Step 2. Based on the site’s historic mortality trends and those of the industry, establish mortality thresholds with the support of a veterinarian or health manager.

  • Mortality thresholds should be based on fish numbers, and it is recommended that they are also expressed as biomass thresholds.

    • The use of both metrics is considered complementary.

    • Using biomass on its own is discouraged, as small biomasses might lead to inaccurate assessments when fish are small.   

Step 3. Create a traffic light system, for example for:  

Mortality ranges for production period of tilapia grown in a pond based on the FAI Tilapia Welfare Course: 

Another example, mortality ranges for the production period of sea bass on-growing in an open water net system based on: Pavlidis, M., Samaras, A., Papaharisis, L., (2024). Welfare
assessment study for European sea bass. University of Crete.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The traffic light system for the required OWIs identifies ranges of acceptable (green), warning (amber), and unacceptable (red) levels of health or welfare, included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm the increased monitoring and associated short-term corrective measures in case of amber or red traffic light results as soon as reasonably possible.

  • Rationale for the grading of the OWIs (e.g. based on scientific literature available or the recommendation of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional).

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established traffic light system.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The traffic light system included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and it is implemented.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the system with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

  • Pedrazzani, A.S., Quintiliano, M.H., Bolfe, F., Sans de Oliveira, E.C. & Molento, C.F.M. (2020) Tilapia On-Farm Welfare Assessment Protocol for Semi-intensive Production Systems Frontiers in Veterinary Science

4.1.1.10.6 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes trend analysis to determine changes in health and welfare over time. This analysis shall consider drivers of the trends and shall be based on the data analysed in indicator 4.1.1.10.5 and feedback from the processing plant where relevant. 

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The analysis of OWIs data over time, as well as information gathered from the mortality classification and post-mortem analysis and the feedback from the processing plant:

    • Allows for the identification of trends that provide insights into factors influencing health, welfare and mortality events.

      • Regular reviews of trends, such as monthly and at least annually or at the end of the production cycle, are recommended.

    • Inform decision-making to improve overall production.

      • The veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should assist the UoC with the trends analysis and drawing conclusions to build effective corrective measures for improving health or welfare over time.

  • Feedback from the processing plant can, for example, disclose the presence of recurring trends like skin wounds or deformities.

    • Sharing observations and feedback with the UoC enables prompt and thorough investigations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The mechanism or trend analysis included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm trend analysis has been conducted include as a minimum:

    • Mortality classification.

    • Post-mortem analysis.

    • Feedback from the processing plant.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The trend analysis mechanism included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and its outcome is implemented:

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the mechanism with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Aunsmo, A., Persson, D., Stormoen, M., Romstad, S., Jamtøy, O., & Johan Midtlyng, P. (2023) Real-time monitoring of cause-specific mortality- and losses in industrial salmon farming. Aquaculture

4.1.1.10.7 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality reduction plan which defines annual targets for both total and unexplained mortalities by considering the results of the trend analysis in Indicator 4.1.1.10.6 and shall implement appropriate actions to meet the annual targets.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The mortality reduction programme should address the various factors contributing to fish mortality. 
  • When building the programme, the UoC should consider:
    • Current mortality rates and causes, including unexplained mortality.
    • Set achievable goals and objectives.
    • Identify priority areas for intervention according to the goals and objectives.
    • Develop strategies addressing priority areas for intervention.
    • Monitor and evaluate progress regularly.
    • Provide employees with training.
    • Foster a culture of continuous improvement.
    • Collaborate with industry experts for knowledge sharing.
    • Seek health professionals’ involvement in developing the reduction plan.
    • When building the programme, the UoC should consider:
  • Special attention should be given to unexplained mortalities which may indicate underlying health issues or poor management practices
    • Identifying and addressing the root causes of unexplained mortalities is essential for improving overall management practices and reducing mortality rates.
  • In addition, consistent, clear downward trends in OWIs indicate declining health or welfare.
    • Examples of such trends include a consistent increase in overall morphological scoring, repeated observations of abnormal behaviour, deteriorating water quality with one or more parameters that are outside of the acceptable ranges, or increasing mortality.
  • If a declining trend is observed, then the UoC should assess the situation and investigate the causes behind the trends.
    • One or multiple issues may be causing the decline, including those of infectious or non-infectious origin. 
    • In many cases, poor or inadequate husbandry practices can predispose animals to succumb to infectious diseases.  
    • Also, when declining trends are observed, the UoC is expected to review at least the following husbandry practices if appropriate:
      • Stocking densities.
      • The feeding plan.
      • Water quality.
      • Handling practices.
      • Enclosure characteristics.
      • Environmental enrichment.
      • The rearing environment, for example:
        • Additional aeration.
        • Deployment of environmental enrichment5252Development of EE targets is an ambition but is not currently a requirement within ASC Farm Standard. The application of EE in commercial fish farming setups is still very limited, due to various reasons. Some of them include contradicting scientific studies, hygiene and biosecurity concerns, inappropriate materials, a sound knowledge of the species ethology to avoid distress, lack of commercial-scale studies among others. ASC encourages both industry and academia to work together to enhance EE knowledge. While recognising EE benefits, ASC acknowledges the need for further research to ensure safe and visible implementation, while committing to adapting requirements as new knowledge emerges.View More (EE), (e.g. bubble curtains, change of tank colouration, adjustments in the light system), amongst others.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Mortality reduction programme.

  • Long-term animal health and welfare improvement measures as well as short-term mitigation measures to react to situations of declining health or welfare, included in the HWMP.

  • Mortality records that allow for trend analysis for the development of a mortality reduction programme.

  • Records of long-term animal health and welfare improvement measures and short-term mitigation measures to react to situations of declining health or welfare.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The mortality reduction programme and the improvement and mitigation measures included in the HWMP incorporate the minimum required elements and that its outcome is implemented:
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the programme and measures with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Mellor, D.J. (2016) Moving beyond the “Five Freedoms” by Updating the “Five Provisions” and Introducing Aligned “Animal Welfare Aims”. Animals.
  • Lawrence, A.B., Vigors, B., & Sandøe, P. (2019) What Is so Positive about Positive Animal Welfare?—A Critical Review of the Literature. Animals.
  • Wang, B., Thompson, K.D.,  Wangkahart, E., Yamkasem, J., Bondad-Reantaso, M.G., Tattiyapong, P., Jian, J., & Surachetpong, W. (2023) Strategies to enhance tilapia immunity to improve their health in aquaculture. Reviews in Aquaculture.

4.1.1.10.8 The UoC shall report the following to a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional:

a)

all mortality events; and

b)

fish health and welfare concerns identified during mortality classification.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.1.11 The UoC shall report to the relevant authorities if a WOAH-notifiable disease is confirmed at a site, and shall:

a)

apply the measures according to applicable legal requirements; and

b)

increase disease-monitoring in other batches of fish; and

c)

coordinate oversight by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Upon a WOAH-notifiable disease being confirmed, the UoC should consider within its response mechanism included in the HWMP (see Indicator 4.1.1.10) an emergency response procedure for culling the affected batches of fish (see also Criterion 4.1.3).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HWMP includes site-specific disease monitoring, responses and reporting requirements.
    • Specific considerations should be given to WOAH-notifiable diseases, including an emergency response procedure for culling the affected batches of fish.

  • National regulations. In some countries where WOAH-notifiable diseases are considered endemic, the UoC should follow the legal reporting requirements.

  • Records:

    • Reporting to authorities.

    • Measures applied.

    • Notification to other sites in the vicinity or the ABM.

    • Disease monitoring.

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional
      coordination.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HWMP includes considerations for WOAH-notifiable diseases (see interpretation for Indicator 4.1.1.10).
  • In case a WOAH-notifiable disease has been confirmed:

    • Reporting to authorities and implementation of regulatory measures.

    • Notification to other sites in the vicinity or the ABM.

    • Increased monitoring to other batches of fish.

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional coordination

1).

1).

4.1.1.17 The UoC shall only use native cleaner fish species.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.1.18 The UoC shall carry out a risk assessment prior to stocking cleaner fish, considering at least the following:

a)

the suitability of use of cleaner fish for parasite control (see Indicator 4.5.17); and

b)

the disease history of the cleaner fish to avoid cross contamination (only where using farmed cleaner fish); and

c)

site-specific environmental conditions considering the species-specific needs of cleaner fish; and

d)

net mesh size; and

e)

salmon size in relation to cleaner fish.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • A risk assessment regarding the use of cleaner fish should be developed.

  • As part of the risk assessment the site should, along with the designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional, review previous information:

    • Parasite infection history at the site.

    • Disease history at the site.

    • Disease history of available farmed cleaner fish.

    • Water quality history at the site.

    • Site specific environmental conditions.

    • Net mesh size.

    • Salmon size.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A completed risk assessment

    • This is to be reviewed at the start of each cycle.
    • Developed in accordance with the designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

Auditors should confirm:

  • That at the start of each cycle, a risk assessment is carried out to ensure that cleaner fish are a viable option for the site.

Useful Resources

  • Norwegian Seafood Research Fund (2018) Best Practice Guidelines from the Norwegian Seafood Research Fund. Technical Report 62 pp.

4.1.1.19 The UoC shall only stock batches of cleaner fish that have been tested prior to stocking and are free from diseases of regional concern5353An exemption applies to wild caught species sourced from zones or compartments declared disease free. See COUNCIL DIRECTIVE 2006/88/EC of 24 October 2006 on animal health requirements for aquaculture animals and products thereof, and on the prevention and control of certain diseases in aquatic animals and {European Union Reference Laboratory for Fish Diseases: Cleaner fish in aquaculture: Health management and legislative issues.} and European Union Reference Laboratory for Fish Diseases: Cleaner fish in aquaculture: Health management and legislative issues.View More. 

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The testing will be determined on where fish are sourced from:

Wild caught:

  • Should be held in a quarantine facility to observe for disease symptoms before stocking.
    • There should be enhanced biosecurity employed during capture and holding phases to minimise pathogen exposure.
  • Are to be caught from aquatic disease-free zones.
    • Note: Since lumpfish and wrasse species are not listed as susceptible species or vector species in accordance with Part II of Annex IV of the Council Directive 2006/88/EC, these species can be traded between aquaculture sites in Europe, including those in Member states, zones or compartments declared disease-free, and are only subject to notification under the Traces system. Therefore, these species can be freely traded between intra-community and third country without any certification declaring VHS freedom5454European Union Reference Laboratory for Fish Diseases: Cleaner fish in aquaculture: Health management and legislative issues..

Farmed:

  • Testing will be relevant to:
    • The species.
    • The production system.
    • The scale of production.
    • The local regulations.
      • For example- viral haemorrhagic septicaemia in lumpfish and wrasse.
    • Testing might consist of:
      • Clinical examination of the fish.
      • Laboratory tests:
        • Bacteriology.
        • Molecular biology (e.g. PCR).
        • Histopathology.
        • Virology (e.g. cell culture).
  • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should determine:
    • The diseases to include in the testing, based on local regulations, scientific literature and/or publicly available. 
    • The sample size, based on local regulations and/or technical judgement.
  • Compulsory governmental testing programme results are acceptable for demonstrating conformance with this requirement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • List of relevant diseases for the species in the country.
  • For wild caught cleaner fish, quarantine information and report from designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

  • For farmed cleaner fish, testing results written report or document that includes as a minimum:

    • The batch of fish being tested.

    • The date of the test.

    • The pathogen tested.

    • The results of the test.

  • Records:

    • Purchase.

    • Transportation.

    • Delivery.

    • Stocking.

Auditors should confirm:

  • That every batch of wild caught cleaner fish has a record of quarantine and assessment.

  • The record of capture of the wild caught cleaner fish including disease free status.

  • That every batch of farmed cleaner fish has been tested by cross-checking the list of relevant diseases for the species in the country with the testing result’s written report or document and records.

4.1.1.26 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP), approved by a registered veterinarian, with the intent to prevent disease outbreaks and ensure good health and welfare of cleaner fish.

a)

disease monitoring; and

b)

response, including quarantine, treatment, and humane culling; and

c)

reporting mechanisms, including reporting WOAH-notifiable disease to authorities; and

d)

biosecurity risks; and

e)

predation risks.

4.1.1.26.2 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a morphological scoring monitoring process for live cleaner fish. Monitoring shall be conducted at least once every three months, and shall include at least the following scoring parameters:

  • eye damage
  • operculum damage
  • skin damage
  • fin damage
  • deformities
  • change of colouration
  • emaciation

An exception applies where deviation from monitoring frequency is justified by any of the following reasons:

  • immediately after stocking; or
  • under environmental conditions that affect the welfare of the cleaner fish or the health and safety of employees; or
  • cleaner fish are undergoing a disease event and/or being treated.

The reason for any deviation shall be recorded.

How do I interpret this requirement?
