4.1.1.26.3 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a feeding behaviour scoring monitoring process for live cleaner fish. Monitoring shall be conducted weekly.

An exception applies where deviation from weekly monitoring is justified under environmental conditions that affect the welfare of the cleaner fish or the health and safety of employees. The reason for any deviation shall be recorded.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.1.1.10.3 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.1.1.10.3 for a detailed description.

4.1.1.26.4 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality monitoring process which includes at least the following:

a)

daily monitoring and recording of mortalities; and

b)

removal of mortalities at least every second day; and,

c)

classification of all recovered mortalities and conducting a post-mortem analysis for each mortality event; and

d)

investigation of mortality events which remain unexplained or unattributed to fish health reasons; and

e)

daily collection of moribund fish and culling according to Criterion 4.1.3.

Where any of the listed items above are not possible, the UoC shall record the reason.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.1.1.10.4 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.1.1.10.4 for a detailed description.

4.1.1.26.5 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality reduction plan which defines annual targets for both total and unexplained mortalities and shall implement appropriate actions to meet the annual targets.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.1.1.10.7 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.1.1.10.7 for a detailed description.

4.1.1.26.6 The UoC shall report the following to a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional:

a)

all mortality events; and

b)

cleaner fish health and welfare concerns identified during mortality classification.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.1.27 The UoC shall calculate cleaner fish stocking densities in relation to salmon stocking, following the method outlined In Appendix 12 (12.5.4).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.1.28 The UoC shall report to ASC mortality data of cleaner fish, according to ASC data submission procedures, and following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.1).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

Comment box

In this first version of Principle 4 in the ASC Farm Standard, there is no requirement to develop a traffic light system (see indicator 4.1.1.10.5) or analyse trends to determine changes in health and welfare (see indicator 4.1.1.10.6) for cleaner fish.

However, it is expected that going forward, all these requirements will also be included for cleaner fish.

4.1.2 – Fish (including Cleaner Fish) – Handling

4.1.2.1 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Handling Management Plan (HMP), with the intent of ensuring the good health and welfare of farmed fish.

The HMP shall be periodically reviewed and revised as necessary.

4.1.2.2 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes all handling activities carried out on site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Handling Management Plan (HMP):
    • Aims to support the development and implementation of preventive, rather than remedial, actions that prevent poor fish health and welfare at handling.
      • Examples of handling:
        • Crowding.
        • Grading (active or passive).
        • Sampling.
        • Transportation (including loading, transfer and unloading).
        • Vaccination (by immersion or injection).
        • Application of treatments (therapeutants or physical).
    • Should consider a description of:
      • Processes.
        • A separate process description may be required for outsourced events e.g. transportation up to the point of harvest.
      • Equipment.
        • A description of equipment, and verification if applicable may be required for both UoC, and outsourced events e.g. vaccination equipment.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Confirmation that the HMP includes considerations that allow for performing standardised handling operations, e.g.:
    • Site-specific description of processes and equipment.
    • Documents:
      • Planning of handling events, e.g.:
        • Emails, reports and site ‘whiteboard’ communications.
      • Handling procedures.
    • Monitoring the effectiveness of the HMP.
      • Documents:
      • Handling logs, e.g.:
        • Reports detailing regular observation of fish behaviour, environmental parameters and fish conditions during and after handling procedures, including injuries, mortalities, or deviations from procedures.
        • Records documenting fitness assessment before handling, incidences of disease, and mortalities, with details on potential correlations with handling activities.
      • Handling incidents reports, e.g.:
        • Emails, reports detailing any incidents during handling procedures, including injuries, mortalities, or deviations from procedures.
      • Feedback from staff, e.g.:
        • Emails, anonymous box asking feedback from staff involved in handling procedures regarding their observations and any difficulties encountered.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes a description of the handling processes and equipment and considerations for planning handling events.

  • Employees are familiarised with the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations.

  • Handling logs are available documenting handling processes, environment, and fish conditions.

  • Existence of handling incidents reports, including feedback from staff and discussions regarding any handling procedure changes.

  • Open communication is encouraged via formal documents and employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  1. Alevra, A., Llorente Manzanares, M., Mente, E., Xandri Royo, P.M., (2024) Good husbandry practices for aquaculture. Publications Office of the European Union.  
  2. APROMAR (2022) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture – Volume 1: Concepts and generalities. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 36 pp.
  3. APROMAR (2024) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture- Volume 2: Welfare of European sea bass. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 49 pp.
  4. APROMAR (2024) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture – Volume 3: Welfare of gilthead sea bream. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 49 pp.
  5. Zaman Sajid,  A., Gamperl, K., Parrish, C.C., et AL., (2024) An aquaculture risk model to understand the causes and consequences of Atlantic Salmon mass mortality events: A review. Reviews In Aquaculture.

4.1.2.3 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes contingency plans for handling activities, including at least the following:

a)

immediate response measures in the case of system failure; and

b)

humane culling response measures (see Indicator 4.1.3.2); and

c)

mass mortality event response measures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The contingency plans should consider:
    • Identification of potential failures.
    • Effective corrective measures, e.g.:
      • Backup power generators.
      • Oxygen support.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes processes’ contingency plans.

  • Records:

    • Backup system testing.
  • Additional oxygen source available.

Auditors should confirm:

  • HMP includes considerations on fish health and welfare before handling events, including considerations for the existence of a backup system.

    • Backup system testing records.

  • Presence of backup system.

  • Employees are familiarised with the contingency plans by conducting employee interviews and observations.

  • Records:

    • Backup system testing.

Useful Resources

  • Singh, G.G.,  Sajid, Z., &  Mather, C. (2024) Quantitative analysis of mass mortality events in salmon aquaculture shows increasing scale of fish loss events around the world. Nature; Scientific Reports

  • Barathan, B., Wang, Y., Su, Y., Hamilton, D., et al., (2022). Methods to control harmful algal blooms: a review. Environmental Chemistry Letters.

  • FAO eLearning Academy (2024) Emergency preparedness for aquatic disease outbreaks. Online course

4.1.2.4 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes consideration of the environmental conditions associated with handling activities, with the intent of preventing handling under adverse conditions that could affect the health and welfare of the fish.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Examples of considerations of external conditions:
    • Avoid mechanical treatments in the event of storms.
    • Avoid crowding fish for treatment without using a shade net on a sunny day.
    • Avoid transferring juveniles during period where there are less than favourable conditions:
      • Spring tides can result in stronger currents and rapid changes in water levels, juveniles may become disoriented or stressed potentially leading to injuries or escape.
        • Risk of entrapment and loss of equipment can be associated with spring tides.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes consideration for external conditions necessary to perform handling.

  • Records:

    • Weather forecast verification.
  • Employees should demonstrate knowledge of the considerations and the verification of external conditions before handling.

Auditors should confirm:

  • HMP includes considerations for external conditions for handling and are implemented.
    • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the HMP with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.2.5 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP, following consultation with a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional, considers the use of anaesthesia during handling activities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The use of anaesthesia is not required in every handling operation, but it should be considered in operations that can inflict pain, e.g.:

    • Inter-peritoneal vaccinations.

    • Stripping.

    • Handling operations that require fish immobilisation.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes consideration for the use of anaesthesia during handling.
  • List of handling operations requiring the use of anaesthesia.
  • List of licenced anaesthetics available on site.
  • Records:
    • Anaesthetic prescriptions.
    • Anaesthetic usage.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes consideration of the use of anaesthetics during handling.

  • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the HMP with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Readman, G.D., Owen, S.F., Knowles, T.G. et al. (2017) Species specific anaesthetics for fish anaesthesia and euthanasia. Scientific Reports.

  • Brønstad A. (2022) Good Anesthesia Practice for Fish and Other Aquatics. Biology.

  • European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) (2009) General approach to fish welfare and to the concept of sentience in fish. EFSA Journal.

  • Pathinathan, P., & Roshan, H. (2024). Exploring Anesthetic Strategies in Aquaculture: Enhancing Welfare and Management Practices. The Science World.

  • Husen, Md & Sharma, S. (2014). Efficacy of Anesthetics for Reducing Stress in Fish During Aquaculture Practices – A Review. Kathmandu University Journal of Science, Engineering and Technology.

4.1.2.6 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a fitness assessment of the fish prior to handling activities5555An exemption applies to handling activities related to health examinations (e.g. health assessment, parasite counting) and in the case of emergencies (e.g. containment of an escape)., approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

For the specific handling activities listed below, the fitness assessment shall be carried out:

  • within a two-week period prior to transport or treatment that requires handling of the fish, except when the same type of treatment is repeated, in which case the assessment shall be carried out at least once a month after the initial treatment;  
  • within a two-week period prior to net change and passive grading.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Fitness assessment may fall into two categories:

    • Single assessment: Performed within a two-week period prior to the handling.

    • Recurring assessment: Performed at least once a month in the case of serial, repeated treatments, e.g.:

      • Handling for administering multiple rounds of treatment to fish populations over a period of time, e.g.:

        • Bacterial infections, such as bacterial gill disease, furunculosis, or red spot diseases.
        • Fungal diseases, such as saprolegniasis.
        • Treatments for parasites control such as formalin treatments, hydrolysers or thermal delousing.

  • A successful fitness for handling record should demonstrate:

    • Fish free of diseases.

    • Minimal morphologic damage.

    • Normal behaviour.

    • Low mortality rate.

    • Usual feeding rates.

  • An example of a fitness for handling assessment record is provided in the Table 9 below.

Table 9: An example of a fitness for handling assessment record with information collated from assessments and routine data collected on the site.

  • Handling in case of emergencies are exempt from requiring fish fitness assessments e.g.:

    • Containment of an escape.

    • Imminent risk of predation.

      • It is recommended to have a health representative verify the emergency operations together with written advice to support decision-making when handling is required in an emergency.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes consideration for fitness assessment prior to handling.

  • Fitness assessment report.

  • Records:

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional handling approval.

    • Documented reasons for exemptions with written advice.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Fitness assessments status before handling.
  • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the frequency of fitness assessment and handling records, information from employee interviews and observations.
  • The rationale for any deviation from the frequency of fitness assessment before handling is in accordance with those highlighted by the indicator and respective footnotes.

Useful Resources

  • EFSA (2008) Animal welfare aspects of husbandry systems for farmed Atlantic salmon ‐ Scientific Opinion of the Panel on Animal Health and Welfare.

  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Molento, C., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Tilapia welfare indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.1.2.7 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers crowding activities with the intent of preventing stress, injury and mortality. Crowding activities shall be carried out:

a)

under supervision; and

b)

gradually; and

c)

partially; and

d)

for a maximum of two hours.

An exception applies where a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional demonstrates that exceeding two hours of crowding does not negatively impact fish welfare, in which case the maximum time period shall be defined by the registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Appropriate crowding intensity is achieved when there is a balance between fish welfare, minimising abnormal behaviour and having sufficient fish in the crowd area for an effective handling.

  • Abnormal behaviour may be defined as fish behaviour commonly found or seen when fish are stressed.

  • During crowding operations consider an appropriate fish density avoiding:

    • Vigorous escape behaviour.

    • Violent splashing.

    • Escape attempts (jumping).

    • Burrowing into the crowding net.

    • Air gasping.

    • Excessive gill movement.

    • Inability to fish maintain body position (white sides constantly on surface).

    • Skin colour changes.

    • Presence of fish scales in the water.

  • Narrow deep nets are recommended over wide shallow nets for fish crowding.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Considerations, plans and actions taken pre- and during crowding for achieving an appropriate crowding intensity.

  • Records:

    • That confirms the monitoring of the crowding, e.g. time and intensity.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established crowding operation.

  • Rationale for exceeding the crowding time as directed by the veterinarian or aquatic health professional.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The crowding operation incorporates considerations for an appropriate crowding, and it is implemented.
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the crowding operations with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Stien, L., Nilsson, K., Noble, C., Izquierdo-Gomez, D., Ytteborg, E., Timmerhaus, G., & Madaro, A. (2024) Evaluating a crowding intensity scale and welfare indicators for Atlantic salmon in sea cag es. Aquaculture Reports.

4.1.2.8 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers biosecurity risks specific to the types of handling activities and shall include appropriate biosecurity measures to prevent the transfer of disease.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For developing a site-specific biosecurity mechanism within the HMP, the UoC should consider:

    • Indicator 4.1.1.10 d)

    • Biosecurity measures related to the type of handling, e.g.:

      • Equipment segregation.

      • Equipment disinfection.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes the considerations for:

    • Site-specific biosecurity mechanism.

    • Biosecurity specifications related to the type of handling operations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes the required minimum considerations above.

  • Employees are:

    • Familiarised with the biosecurity considerations in the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations.

    • Trained on biosecurity specifications related to the type of handling operations by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Subasinghe, R.,   Alday-Sanz, V., Bondad-Reantaso, M.G., Jie H., Shinn, A.P., & Sorgeloos P. (2024) Biosecurity: Reducing the burden of disease. World Aquaculture Society.

  • Australian Government (unknown) Biosecurity plan and translocation policy guidelines – DAFF

  • Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (2023) Guidebook on Biosecurity and Good Aquaculture Policies and Practices for small-scale farmers of tilapia (Oreochromis sp.) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) . Manual 45pp.

4.1.2.9 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers predation risks specific to the types of handling activities and shall include appropriate predator control measures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For developing a site-specific predator control within the HMP, the UoC should consider:

    • The site-specific characteristics required to be assessed by Indicator 4.1.1.10 e) predator control measures specific to the type of handling, e.g.:

      • Birds scaring devices.

      • Use of anti-predator nets while moving fish from one cage/unit/pond to another.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Predator control measures specific to the type of handling operations.

  • Verification of mortalities associated with predators during handling operations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes the required considerations above.

  • Employees are:

    • Familiarised with the predator control considerations in the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations.

    • Trained on predator control verifications, e.g.:

      • Verification of mortality events specific to the type of handling operations by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.2.10 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a water quality monitoring process according to Appendix 12 (12.3, Table 2).

In the case of live transport5656An exemption applies where live transport after harvest is conducted by a third party outside of the scope of the UoC’s certification. Once the product leaves the certified supply chain it can no longer be sold as ASC certified., monitoring shall be conducted at the point of departure, during transport and on arrival. An exception applies where monitoring during transport negatively affects fish health and welfare, in which case monitoring is not required.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Maintaining good water quality is a critical factor during fish handling.
    • Concentrations of substances within the water system that rise above or fall below specific levels can be harmful to fish populations and should be monitored.  
  • For developing an adequate environment for fish during handling the UoC should consider:
    • Water quality monitoring equipment e.g.
      • Constant monitoring. 
      • Every 15 minutes (by hand, automatic).
    • Water quality monitoring frequency.
      • Prior to, during, and post handling. 
    • Water quality monitoring for live transport.
      • Departure/arrival and during live transport unless this could cause detrimental impact.
  • While Table 2 of Appendix 12 of the ASC Farm Standard specifies water quality parameters that must be included in the monitoring process, other parameters may be considered based on the specific requirements of the UoC.
  • Conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds for the required parameters, customised to suit the species and environmental conditions, should be incorporated as part of the HMP water quality monitoring process.
  • Corrective actions must be provided according to the HWMP that may be considered acceptable as a reference to develop and implement a water quality monitoring process (Indicator 4.1.1.10.1).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The water quality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.

  • Records confirming the monitoring of the required parameters and their conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established water quality monitoring process during handling.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The water quality monitoring, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP. and cross-checking with the handling operations present in the HMP.
  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • The Fish Site (2012) Monitoring Pond Water Quality to Improve Production.

  • Lindholm-Lehto, P. (2023) Water quality monitoring in recirculating aquaculture systems. Aquaculture Fish and Fisheries

  • Fahad, A., N’Doye, I., & Taous-Meriem, L.K. (2023). Feeding control and water quality monitoring in aquaculture systems: Opportunities and challenges. arXiv

  • Erikson, U., Rosten, C., Klebert, P., Aspaas, S., & Rosten, T. (2022) Live transport of Atlantic salmon in open and closed systems: Water quality, stress and recovery. Aquaculture Research

4.1.2.11 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a visual inspection process to identify abnormal behaviour in relation to the handling activity and defines mitigation measures when identified.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Visual inspection during handling should be included in the HMP.

    • When direct visual inspections are not possible (e.g. pangasius transportation) or considered invasive (e.g. during live fish transport inside a well), cameras can be used. Alternatively, fish behaviour can be assessed when loading and discharging the fish as a minimum requirement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The monitoring process, that incorporates the corrective actions required, included in the HMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the behaviour.

    • A checked box on the monitoring records indicating whether monitoring behavioural took place or not is accepted.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established behavioural monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The monitoring process included in the HMP that incorporates the corrective actions and is implemented.
  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Bhadmus, Z. T. (2022) Effect of crowding on behaviour of Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in aquaculture. Thesis; The Artic University of Norway.

  • Stien, L., Nilsson, K., Noble, C., Izquierdo-Gomez, D., Ytteborg, E., Timmerhaus, G., & Madaro, A. (2024) Evaluating a crowding intensity scale and welfare indicators for Atlantic salmon in sea cag es. Aquaculture Reports.

4.1.2.12 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a post-handling evaluation process that considers at least the following:

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Abnormal behaviour related to the handling should be recorded.

  • During and post-handling moribund fish and mortalities related to the handling should be recorded and removed.

  • Moribund fish should be collected and culled following responsible stunning and killing according to Criterion 4.1.3.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Behavioural monitoring.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the behaviour, moribund and mortalities during and post-handling.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established behavioural and mortality monitoring process above.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The behavioural monitoring process included in the HMP incorporates the minimum required elements and it is implemented.
  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Pavlidis, M., Samaras, A., Papaharisis, L., (2024). Welfare assessment study for European sea bass. University of Crete.

4.1.2.13 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes acclimatisation measures to prevent sudden changes in water conditions affecting the health and welfare status of the fish.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Standardised acclimatisation measures should be designed and maintained, e.g.:

    • Water temperature during transportation must be as close as possible to that which the fish came from.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Standard acclimatisation measures and monitoring of the water quality according to the HMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of acclimatisation parameters before stocking.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the acclimatisation measures and monitoring process above.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The acclimatisation measures included in the HMP incorporate the minimum required elements and are implemented.
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • APROMAR (2024) A guide on fish welfare in Spanish aquaculture – Volume 3: Welfare of gilthead sea bream. Spanish Aquaculture Business Association. 49 pp.

4.1.2.14 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes consideration of the use of appropriate equipment during handling activities to avoid affecting the health and welfare status of the fish.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.2.15 The UoC shall adhere to a limit of 15 seconds maximum time out of water5757An exemption applies to anaesthetised fish and pangasius (due to its ability to breathe air facultatively)..

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • When fish are out of water:
    • Their gills collapse, preventing oxygen exchange.
    • They show violent escape behaviour accompanied by a stress response.
  • Time out of water should be minimised to avoid unnecessary stress to the fish during handling.
  • Conformance with maximum required time out of water, customised to suit the species, should be part of the HMP and associated with good handling practices.

  • Time out of water should be minimised considering the biological needs of the fish e.g. oxygen exchange, gills collapse and stress response.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records confirming the required parameter and their conformance with maximum value.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established maximum time out of water.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The maximum time of water is included in the HMP, and it is implemented.

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.2.16 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific limits on maximum fasting duration5858An exemption applies in exceptional situations of severe weather, adverse environmental conditions (e.g. jellyfish, algal bloom) or during disease events., according to Appendix 2 (2.4).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Fasting duration:
    • Calculation in degree days provides a more precise indication of fish metabolic activity because it incorporates time and temperature, which better reflect the biological processes, and provides a standardised metric across different locations and time periods.
      • The concept of degree days involves accumulating the average daily temperature over a period of time, i.e. 3 days at an average daily temperature of 19 °C, are 57-degree days.
  • In the case of exceptional situations (see requirement footnote) the length of fasting would be linked to the duration of the event rather than a pre-set timing or veterinarian or aquatic health professional rationale.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records confirming the required parameter and their conformance with minimum/maximum value.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established minimum/maximum fasting time.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The minimum/maximum time fasting time is included in the HMP and incorporates considerations related to intrinsic factors and is implemented.

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.2.22 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a fitness assessment of the cleaner fish prior to handling activities5959An exemption applies to handling activities related to health examinations (e.g. health assessment, parasite counting) and in the case of emergencies (e.g. containment of an escape)., approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

For the specific handling activities listed below, the fitness assessment shall be carried out:

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.4 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.4 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.23 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers crowding activities with the intent to prevent stress, injury and mortality. Crowding activities shall be carried out:

  • under supervision; and
  • gradually; and
  • partially; and
  • for a maximum of two hours.

An exception applies where a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional demonstrates that exceeding two hours of crowding does not negatively impact cleaner fish welfare, in which case the maximum time period shall be defined by the registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Prior to the crowding activity, the impacts of the cleaner fish should be discussed and an action plan developed to ensure the cleaner fish are handled appropriately.

    • This may include moving the hides or refuges to one side of the net prior to the crowding.

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.7 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.7 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.24 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a water quality monitoring process according to Appendix 12 (12.3, Table 2).

In the case of live transport6060An exemption applies where live transport after harvest is conducted by a third party outside of the scope of the UoC’s certification, monitoring shall be conducted at the point of departure, during transport and on arrival. An exception applies where monitoring during transport negatively affects cleaner fish health and welfare, in which case monitoring is not required.

How do I interpret this requirement?

This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.10 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.10 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.25 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a visual inspection process to identify abnormal behaviour in relation to the handling activity and defines mitigation measures when identified.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.11 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.11 for a detailed description.

Useful Resources

  • Gutierrez Rabadan, C., Spreadbury, C., Consuegra, S. & Garcia de Leaniz, C. (2021) Development, validation and testing of an Operational Welfare Score Index for farmed lumpfish Cyclopterus lumpus L. Aquaculture

RENSVEL OWI FACT SHEET SERIES: An introduction to Operational and Laboratory-based Welfare Indicators for ballan wrasse (Labrus bergylta). 43 pp.

4.1.2.26 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a post-handling evaluation process that considers at least the following:

a)

abnormal behaviour; and

b)

morphological scores; and

c)

moribund animals and mortalities.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.12 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.12 for a detailed description.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.1.2.27 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes acclimatisation measures to prevent sudden changes in water conditions affecting the health and welfare status of the cleaner fish.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.13 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.13 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.28 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes consideration of the use of appropriate equipment during handling activities to avoid affecting the health and welfare status of the cleaner fish.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.2.29 The UoC shall demonstrate that the fishing gear used avoids injuries and unnecessary stress, and that it is suitable for the size and species of cleaner fish being captured.

Indicator applicability: cleaner fish from wild caught origin

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The fishing vessel sourcing the cleaner fish must be registered in the region and adhere to the local regulations.

  • Cleaner fish must be visually assessed for injuries in their holding facility.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Fishermen must be registered and aware of the transport regulations in their area.

  • Records:

    • Fishing vessel.

    • Date of capture.

    • Number of cleaner fish.

    • Assessment of cleaner fish.

Auditors should confirm:

  • There are records of the source of the cleaner fish.

  • The assessment of the cleaner fish and any communication regarding sourcing of cleaner fish.

  • Norwegian Seafood Research Fund (2018)Best Practice Guidelines from the Norwegian Seafood Research Fund. Technical Report 62 pp.

4.1.2.30 The UoC shall adhere to a limit of 15 seconds maximum time out of water6161An exemption applies to anaesthetised fish..

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.15 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.15 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.31 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific limits on maximum fasting duration6262An exemption applies in exceptional situations of severe weather, adverse environmental conditions (e.g. jellyfish, algal bloom) or during disease events., according to Appendix 2 (2.4).

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicator 4.2.1.16 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicator 4.2.1.16 for a detailed description.

4.1.2.32 The UoC shall segregate cleaner fish in advance of any salmonid-specific treatments and ensure they are retained under appropriate conditions.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Prior to any salmonid-specific treatments, the cleaner fish should be segregated.

    • The hides/refuges should be checked and then moved away from the crowding area.
    • Ensure the dragnet does not include the hides/refuges.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The procedure of salmonid-specific treatments should include how to handle the cleaner fish prior to the start of the treatment.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of how the cleaner fish are segregated prior to salmonid-specific treatments.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the procedure and with employee interviews.

Useful Resources

  • Norwegian Seafood Research Fund (2018) Best Practice Guidelines from the Norwegian Seafood Research Fund. Technical Report 62 pp.

4.1.3 – Fish (including Cleaner Fish) – Slaughter and Killing

Indicators 4.1.3.1-4.1.3.7:

Scope: all fish species except cleaner fish (see Indicators 4.1.3.8-4.1.3.16)

4.1.3.1 The UoC shall appoint a staff member responsible for overseeing the implementation of fish health and welfare requirements during slaughter.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.3.2 The UoC shall ensure all fish, including fish not destined for human consumption, are stunned prior to killing according to the methods and transition periods outlined in Appendix 12 (12.4, Table 5).

4.1.3.3 The UoC shall ensure that at least 95% of the fish lose consciousness immediately after stunning, and any remaining conscious fish are re-stunned. Unconsciousness shall persist until the fish are killed

4.1.3.4 The UoC shall ensure that stunning and killing are effective by verifying the absence of all of the following:

a)

opercular movements; and

b)

eye movements; and

c)

body movements (except for involuntary muscular spasms); and

d)

reaction to a painful stimulus.

4.1.3.5 The UoC shall have measures in place to immediately respond to ineffective stunning or killing, including the presence of a back-up system, and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Slaughter is generally a two-stage process:

    • The animal is first stunned to make it insensible to pain.
    • Killing is then carried out.

  • Stunning methods are required to induce immediate or rapid (less than one second) unconsciousness.

    • Ice-slurry is not an approved stunning method but can be used as a killing method after immediate or rapid (less than one second) unconsciousness.

    • Brain perforation techniques such as ‘spiking’ or ‘ikijime’, involve instruments that physically perforate the brain, causing severe and irreversible damage and leading to almost immediate stunning and death.

  • An effective stun is determined by the loss of consciousness using an electroencephalogram (EEG) measured in a laboratory, which is not practicable at a site level.

  • To ensure that at least 95% of the fish are stunned before killing, the sample size should accurately reflect the scale of the harvest operations. Variable sample sizes per harvest day may be accepted, provided that justification is given based on the specific scenarios. Stunning effectiveness should be assessed by confirming signs of unconsciousness:

    • Loss of balance or coordination.

    • Reduced or absent reflex responses.

    • Cessation of opercular movements (in succession and with rhythm).

    • Absence of eye roll.

  • The use of body movement as an indicator for the effectiveness of stunning or killing can be misleading as muscular spasms often occur in unconscious or dead fish.
    • Body movements indicating struggling, a swimming activity or efforts to remain upright or regain equilibrium are relevant movements to watch out for and that indicate consciousness. Visual assessment comparing stunned and non-stunned fish:
  • Body movements indicating struggling, a swimming activity or efforts to remain upright or regain equilibrium are relevant movements to watch out for and that indicate consciousness.
  • A back up stunning system e.g. a priest, must be available.

  • The requirement to stun the fish before the killing also applies to fish not destined for human consumption e.g. wild species, cleaner fish.

  • Ensure there is no chance of recovery of consciousness before fish death:

    • Minimise the stun to kill time to less than one second.

    • Consider that stun and kill can occur together, for example, pneumatic stunning with automatic gill cutting, but they are distinct operations.

  • If there is uncertainty about whether a fish is unconscious, the stunning should be repeated or the harvest shall stop to verify stun parameters before proceeding, e.g. more than 5 fish in 10 seconds requiring backup stun.

    • Or use an alternative backup method, e.g. a priest or secondary stunner.

  • For electrical stunning, machines must adhere to manufacturers recommendations for that species, or if not available, to documented electric stunning parameters from research.

Table 10: Electrical stunning methods which have been validated in the laboratory by EEG to prove that unconsciousness was reached within 1 second.

* Adapted killing method from reference article.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Employees should demonstrate knowledge confirming the stun and kill monitoring.

  • Records:

    • Employee training (see Appendix 12)

    • Slaughter monitoring, e.g.:

      • Verification and registration of stunning and killing.

      • Observation of signs of unconsciousness.

      • Records of the use of a backup method.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Monitoring of stunning and slaughter in conformance to the requirements.
  • Records, employee interviews and observations of stunning and slaughter operations during the audit should demonstrate the implementation of the requirements.

Useful Resources

  • Farm Animal Welfare Committee- UK Government (2014) Opinion on the Welfare of Farmed Fish at the Time of Killing. Technical report 36pp.
  • Humane Slaughter Association. (2016) Signs of Recovery. Blog.
  • The  EFSA  Journal (2009) Scientific  Opinion  of  the  Panel  on  Animal  Health  and  Welfare  on  a  request  from  the  European  Commission  on  Species-specific  welfare  aspects  of  the  main  systems  of  stunning  and  killing  of  farmed  carp. Scientific Opinion 37pp.
  • Humane Slaughter Association. (2018) Humane Harvesting of Halibut. Technical Report 5 pp.
  • Aquatic Life Institute (2023) Stunning and Slaughter: Best Practices for Animal Welfare in Aquaculture. Report 4pp.
  • De La Rosa, I., Castro, P. & Ginés, R. (2021). Twenty Years of Research in Seabass and Seabream Welfare during Slaughter. Animals. 11. 2164. 
  • Kestin, S., Devis, J. & Robb, D. (2002). Protocol for assessing brain function in fish and the effectiveness of methods used to stun and kill them. The Veterinary record. 150. 302-7.
  • Jung-Schroers, V., Hildebrandt, U., Retter, K. et al. (2020) Is humane slaughtering of rainbow trout achieved in conventional production chains in Germany? Results of a pilot field and laboratory study. BMC Veterinary Research 16, 197.
  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Molento, C., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Tilapia behaviour & welfare indicators: from foraging to humane slaughter [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.1.3.6 The UoC shall not use any of the following methods to kill fish:

a)

asphyxiation in air; or

b)

carbon dioxide (CO2) bath; or

c)

salt bath; or

d)

ammonia bath; or

e)

evisceration.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The methods outlined above do not induce immediate or rapid loss of consciousness and therefore do not meet the requirements of Indicator 4.1.3.2.

  • Approved methods for each species are outlined in Appendix 12 (Table 5).

Useful Resources

  • Welfarm (2023) Farmed Fish Slaughter Methods Report. Recommendations for Rainbow trout, Atlantic salmon, European sea bass and Gilthead sea bream. Technical report 132pp.

  • French Reference Centre for Animal Welfare (2024) Opinion of the FRCAW on slaughter conditions for farmed fish. Technical report. 109pp.

4.1.3.7 The UoC shall maintain records of the activities carried out under Indicators 4.1.3.3 and 4.1.3.4.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

Indicators 4.1.3.8-4.1.3.16:

Scope: Cleaner fish

4.1.3.8 The UoC shall appoint a staff member responsible for overseeing the implementation of cleaner fish health and welfare requirements during slaughter.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.3.9 The UoC shall ensure all cleaner fish are stunned prior to killing according to the methods and transition periods outlined in Appendix 12 (12.4, Table 5).

4.1.3.10 The UoC shall ensure that at least 95% of the cleaner fish lose consciousness immediately after stunning, and any remaining conscious fish are re-stunned. Unconsciousness shall persist until the cleaner fish are killed.

4.1.3.11 The UoC shall ensure that stunning and killing are effective by verifying the absence of all of the following:

a.

opercular movements; and

b.

eye movements; and

c.

body movements (except for involuntary muscular spasms); and

d.

reaction to a painful stimulus.

4.1.3.12 The UoC shall have measures in place to immediately respond to ineffective stunning or killing, including the presence of a back-up system, and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicators 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicators 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5 for a detailed description of slaughter.

  • In addition to the interpretation supplied in Indicator 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5, there are additional requirements for cleaner fish. These include:

    • The cleaner fish should be removed prior to the salmonid stunner system.

    • The cleaner fish should undergo a specific stunning and killing process.

4.1.3.13 The UoC shall not use any of the following methods to kill cleaner fish:

a.

asphyxiation in air; or

b.

carbon dioxide (CO2) bath; or

c.

salt bath; or

d.

ammonia bath; or

e.

evisceration.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Examples of current humane methods:
    • An overdose of anaesthetic.
    • Electrical stunning in combination with immersion in a chilled water bath. 
    • Electrical stunning followed by immediate grinding.

Useful Resources

  • van de Vis, H; Reimert, H; Grimsbø, E; Gerritzen, M; Foss, A; Roth, B. (2024) NOFIMA Electrical stunning and killing of lumpfish with commercial waterbath and dry stunners. Nofima Technical Report.

4.1.3.14 The UoC shall maintain records of the activities carried out under Indicators 4.1.3.10 and 4.1.3.11.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.1.3.15 The UoC shall re-use cleaner fish where possible and under the following conditions:

a)

re-use shall only occur once; and

b)

re-use shall only occur within the site or the ABM (see Indicator 4.5.1); and

c)

re-use shall only occur if the outcome of a health assessment indicates low risk of disease transfer. The health assessment shall:

consider the health status of the salmon and the cleaner fish at the origin and destination sites; and

be conducted no longer than two weeks before re-use; and

d)

be approved by a registered veterinarian or an aquatic animal health professional; and cleaner fish are segregated from the salmon before transfer to the destination site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Prior to the end of the salmon production cycle, discuss with the veterinarian or animal health professional to decide if the cleaner fish are to be re-used or killed.
    • This will depend on:
      • If there are suitable sites for re-use within the same site or ABM (see Indicator 4.5.1).
      • The disease history of the cleaner fish.
      • The disease history of the salmon.
      • Whether the cleaner fish can be re-used within two weeks from being separated from the original salmon companions. 
      • The approval by the registered veterinarian or animal health professional.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:
    • The original source of cleaner fish.
    • The date of the addition of the cleaner fish.
    • The date of the end of the salmon production cycle.
    • The approval by the registered veterinarian or animal health professional.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The approval process by reviewing records and cross-checking dates or stocking, disease history, end of salmon production as well as approval records for re-use.

Useful Resources

  • Norwegian Seafood Research Fund (2018) Best Practice Guidelines from the Norwegian Seafood Research Fund. Technical Report 62 pp.

4.1.3.16 The UoC shall ensure that cleaner fish are humanely slaughtered where re-use is not possible. The UoC shall not release cleaner fish into the wild.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • This clause overlaps with Indicators 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5 regarding fish. Please refer to Indicators 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5 for a detailed description of slaughter.
  • In addition to the interpretation supplied in Indicators 4.1.3.2 to 4.1.3.5, there are additional requirements for cleaner fish. These include:
    • The cleaner fish should be removed prior to the salmonid stunner system.
    • The cleaner fish should undergo a specific stunning and killing process.
    • The dead cleaner fish should be disposed of appropriately.
