ASC Farm Standard: Crustaceans Slaughter Under the ASC Farm Standard

4.2.1 – Crustaceans – Health and Welfare

4.2.1.1 The UoC shall ensure that all relevant employees are trained on general animal health and welfare awareness, including biosecurity, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.2.1.2 The UoC shall ensure that any person involved in animal husbandry and handling activities is trained on animal health and welfare, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.2.1.3 The UoC shall ensure that the content of the training in Indicators 4.2.1.1 and 4.2.1.2 is updated as necessary and is approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For each employee:
    • The level of training should be appropriate to their role:
      • For all relevant employees: a basic level of awareness of crustacean health and welfare, including biosecurity, is required.
      • For any person involved in animal husbandry and handling activities: a more advanced level of training on crustacean health and welfare, handling and slaughter practices is required on an annual basis.
    • Evidence of training participation must be maintained:
      • Certificates of attendance.
      • Certificates of competency.
  • The trainer should be competent in the topic of animal health and welfare and the competence should be demonstrable, e.g.:
    • Curriculum Vitae.
    • Records of qualifications.
    • Work experience.
  • Best practices on the implementation of the training content should be visible during the audit.
    • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of that content at interviews.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A list of employees and subcontracted personnel involved in animal husbandry and handling operations.
  • Records:
    • Training.
    • Trainer’s competence.
    • Certificates of competency.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Employees received the required level of training for their roles by cross-checking employees and subcontracted personnel lists with: 
    • Training records.
    • Certificates of competency. 
    • Trainer’s competence.
    • Revision of training resources/contents.
  • Adequate level of personnel knowledge of the training content should be verified by:
    • Interviews. 
    • Observation of real operations during handling and slaughter of crustaceans.

Useful Resources

  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Ostrensky, A., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Shrimp Welfare Indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) – Competency and Curriculum Guidelines for Community Animal Health Workers. WOAH Report, Paris, 39 pp.

4.2.1.4 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific mortality limits, according to Appendix 2 (2.3).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

Useful resources (if applicable)

  • https://tomota.vn/en/shrimp-survival-rate-calculator

  • McKay, H., & McAuliffe, W. (2024) Methods for Pre-slaughter mortality of farmed shrimp. ReThink Priorities: Technical report. 24pp.

  • Šimčikas, S., & Waldhorn, D.R. (2020) Farmed shrimp and prawn numbers | Guesstimate

4.2.1.5 The UoC shall only stock batches of crustaceans, including nauplii, larvae, post-larvae and broodstock, that have been tested prior to stocking and are free from diseases of regional concern, and met importation guidelines when applicable.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Testing should be relevant to:
    • The species.
    • The production system.
    • The scale of production.
    • The local regulations.
      • For example:
        • Early mortality syndrome (EMS), which is also known as acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND).
        • Enterocytozoon hepatopenaei (EHP).
        • White spot syndrome (WSS).
  • Testing might consist of:
    • Clinical examination of the crustaceans.
    • Laboratory tests:
      • Bacteriology.
      • Molecular biology (e.g. PCR).
      • Histopathology.
      • Virology (e.g. cell culture).
  • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should determine:
    • The diseases to include in the testing, based on local regulations, scientific literature and/or publicly available information (see interpretation for Indicator 4.2.1.8). 
    • The sample size, based on local regulations and/or technical judgement.
  • Compulsory governmental testing programme results are acceptable for demonstrating conformance with this requirement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • List of relevant diseases for the species in the country (see interpretation for Indicator 4.2.1.8).
  • Testing results written report or document that includes as a minimum:
    • The batch of crustaceans being tested.
    • The date of the test.
    • The pathogen tested.
    • The results of the test.
  • Records:
    • Purchase.
    • Transportation.
    • Delivery.
    • Stocking.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Every batch of crustaceans has been tested by cross-checking the list of relevant diseases for the species in the country with the testing result’s written report or document and records.

Useful Resources

  • Lee D, Yu YB, Choi JH, Jo AH, Hong SM, Kang JC, Kim JH. (2022) Viral Shrimp Diseases Listed by the OIE: A Review. Viruses.

  • The Fish Site (2020) Everything you need to know about EMS in shrimp farming.

4.2.1.6 The UoC shall ensure that a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional periodically visits the site to perform routine checks. Checks shall be carried out at least annually, as well as reactively in cases of crustacean health or welfare concerns.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Regular veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visits may fall into two categories:
    • Routine: Performed on a regular basis to monitor the health and welfare of the farmed crustaceans.

    • Reactive: Performed in response to deterioration or concerns for the health or welfare status of the farmed crustaceans.

      • Sites should be prepared to provide the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional with detailed information about the observed symptoms, recent changes in behaviour, morphology, water quality or mortality and any relevant history of disease or treatments.

      • The site should use reactive health visits to address immediate health or welfare concerns, diagnose underlying causes of problems, and implement targeted interventions to mitigate risks and prevent further spread of disease.

  • For routine visits, preparation is recommended to ensure a meaningful outcome from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional. Below are some practical considerations:

    • Visit scheduling: Ensure key employees are available during the visit to provide relevant required information and to facilitate adequate follow-up.

      • Designate a senior employee to serve as the primary point of contact for the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional during the visit.

        • This individual can help coordinate the activity, ensure relevant information is available, assist during the visit and ensure follow-up.
    • Gather and organise relevant information: Compile relevant information about the operations including, for example, species being cultured, production systems, stocking densities, recent health history including treatments, water quality monitoring results, behaviour, morphology and mortalities data, feeding plan, any previous health report and of any ongoing issue.
      • Having this information readily accessible will facilitate discussion and decision-making during the visit.
    • Prepare the UoC for the visit: Ensure the UoC is prepared for the visit and for providing full access to all relevant areas to the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

      • Address any maintenance issues, clean tanks or ponds as needed and ensure clear access to all relevant areas of the facility.

      • Ensure handling and other equipment that might be needed during the visit, such as nets, containers and sampling equipment, is available and in good working condition.

      • Make sure employees are aware of the visit and its objectives and encourage them to proactively participate in it.

    • During the visit: Ensure relevant information is discussed with the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and that the visit includes all relevant areas within the UoC.

    • After the visit: Follow up on any recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.

      • Implement any necessary revisions or changes to management practices, treatment protocols, or facility conditions based on the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional’s feedback and any sample or testing results
    • Continuous improvement: Use the insights gained from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit to identify opportunities for continuous improvement in health and welfare management.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Health reports.

  • Testing results.

  • Records:

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional qualifications.

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit.

    • Recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The qualifications of the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and cross-check the frequency of visits with records.
  • Existence of health reports and testing results.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.1.7 The UoC shall develop and implement a feeding plan which includes at least the following:

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

a)

time and frequency of feeding; and

b)

feed rations; and

c)

feeding methods; and

d)

different environmental conditions; and

e)

prevention of use of feed which has expired, spoiled or shows signs of excessive leakage; and

f)

feed types for the nutritional needs and life stages of the species.

An exception applies to (f) when such feeds are not available, in which case the UoC shall use feed suitable for animals with similar nutritional needs.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The feeding plan:
    • Outlines the site’s feeding strategy.
    • As a minimum, it must include the following parameters:
      • Time and frequency, e.g. at daybreak and early afternoon (06:00 am and 01:00 pm).
      • Feed rations, e.g. feed type and daily amount.
      • Feeding adaptation to fit different life stages, e.g. maturation diets for black tiger with excellent digestible protein, essential fatty acids, cholesterol and chemo-attractant properties similar to which are found in natural food sources in the crustacean habitat.
      • Feeding adaptation to fit different ambient conditions, e.g. at times of crustacean stress due to water quality issues, it is accepted to reduce feeding by 50% or completely stop feeding for 2 to 4 days.
    • Should include considerations to guarantee the good working order of mechanical equipment used to deliver feed, e.g. scheduled maintenance checks of automatic feeders.
  • The UoC should document the rationale for changes in the feeding plan to better inform management decisions.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records:

    • Purchase.

    • Transportation.

    • Delivery.

    • Stocking.

    • Maintenance.

    • Environmental and health.

    • Feeding periods (time and frequency).

    • Feeding rations.

  • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of the feeding plan.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Feeding plan includes the minimum required parameters and its implemented:

    • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the plan with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Tacon, A.G.J., Jory, D. and Nunes, A. (2013) Shrimp feed management: issues and pe rspectives. In M.R. Hasan and M.B. New, eds. On-farm feeding and feed management in aquaculture. FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper No. 583. Rome, FAO. pp. 481–488.

  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Ostrensky, A., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Shrimp Welfare Indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.2.1.8 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP), approved by a registered veterinarian, with the intent to prevent disease outbreaks and ensure good health and welfare of farmed crustaceans.

The HWMP shall include all of the following:

a)

disease monitoring; and

b)

response, including quarantine, treatment, and humane culling; and

c)

reporting mechanisms, including reporting WOAH-notifiable disease to authorities; and

d)

biosecurity risks; and

e)

predation risks.

The HWMP shall be reviewed and revised at least annually.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP): 
    • Aims to support the development and implementation of preventive, rather than remedial, actions that ensure good crustacean health and welfare.
    • Must be developed by the UoC in collaboration with a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional who approves it.
  • For developing and establishing a site-specific disease monitoring, response and reporting mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Developing standardised health and welfare monitoring protocols.
      • This may involve conducting visual inspections, monitoring OWIs and performing diagnostic tests for pathogens.
    • Producing and maintaining detailed records.
      • Including records of health observations, diagnostic test results, treatments administered, mortalities, and other relevant data.
        • It is recommended to use a centralised database or electronic system for efficient data management and retrieval.
    • Implementing an early detection system.
      • To detect signs of disease outbreaks or abnormal health conditions promptly.
        • This could include environmental monitoring tools.
    • Establishing response protocols for responding to disease outbreaks or health emergencies.
      • Outlining procedures for:
        • Isolating affected individuals or populations.
        • Implementing strategies for treatments or others (e.g. culling affected batches of crustaceans, see interpretation for Indicator 4.2.3.2)
        • Notifying relevant stakeholders, including other sites in the vicinity and the authorities.
    • Establishing communication channels.
      • Effective communication channels should be implemented for reporting health-related issues both internally within the facility and externally to relevant authorities (e.g. WOAH-notifiable diseases) or stakeholders.
        • Employees should understand their roles and responsibilities in reporting and responding to disease events.
    • Maintaining a readily accessible notification list.
      • Including contact names numbers and emails for key employees and other relevant stakeholders.
        • The list should be kept up-to-date to ensure quick and efficient communication during emergencies.
  • For developing a site-specific biosecurity mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Determining the objectives and scope of the biosecurity mechanism.
    • Identifying relevant regulatory requirements.  
    • Gathering information about the site, including an up-to-date layout of buildings and production units identifying the possible movements of animals, animal products, animal waste, water, feed and fomites/vectors. 
    • Identifying potential transmission pathways into, within and from the site. 
    • Carrying out a risk analysis to identify and evaluate disease threats and ensure that the plan addresses them.
      • A risk analysis can be carried out wholly or only partially, e.g. disease transmission during transportation. 
        • This will depend on the objectives of the biosecurity mechanism.
    • Identifying mitigation measures and assessing their effectiveness and their management requirements.  
    • Establishing emergency procedures in the event of a biosecurity failure.  
    • Defining internal and external communication procedures, roles and responsibilities. 
    • Creating a monitoring and internal audit schedule.  
    • Carrying out performance evaluations. 
    • Developing procedures (e.g. Standard Operating Procedures, ‘SOPs’) to support the implementation of the mitigation measures and the biosecurity mechanism.  
    • Training employees in the different elements of the biosecurity mechanism. 
    • Maintaining a record-keeping system that provides evidence of compliance with the biosecurity mechanism.
  • For developing predator control measures within the plan, the UoC should consider:
    • Identifying potential predators.
      • Create a list of the predators that are present in the area and that might interact with the UoC.
        • Predators may include birds, mammals, reptiles, and other aquatic species known to prey on crustaceans.
    • Assessing the risk of predation.
      • Evaluate the risk posed by each predator species identified based on factors such as proximity to the site, population size, means of accessing the site, likelihood of predation, etc.
    • Implementing predator control measures.
      • Develop and implement predator control measures tailored to the specific risks identified. This may include:
        • Physical barriers such as nets, fences or screens to prevent access to crustacean tanks or ponds.
        • Scare tactics such as visual deterrents to discourage predators from approaching the facility.
    • Implementing ongoing monitoring and surveillance.
      • To detect predator activity and intervene as needed.
    • Regular reviewing and revision.
      • Based on the outcome of the ongoing monitoring and surveillance. 
      • Adjustments to the measures should be made when the results of monitoring indicate the need to optimise protection for crustaceans and the containment system.
    • Collaborating with local authorities or local wildlife agencies to address predator issues in the surrounding area.
  • A periodic review and, if necessary, a revision of the HWMP must be conducted in response to changes in farming activities or external factors or as directed by the veterinarian. 
    • As a minimum, the review should occur annually.
  • The UoC should develop feedback mechanisms to inform the review, e.g. proactively seeking feedback from employees and subcontracted personnel, such as the harvest team, on the operationalisation of the site-specific biosecurity mechanism. 
  • For a single producer overseeing multiple UoCs in a shared waterbody, a unified HWMP that incorporates site-specific details is acceptable; however, for larger companies managing multiple UoCs in one country, while common plans may apply, it is crucial to ensure HWMP adaptation to individual site circumstances, particularly in aspects like biosecurity measures, disease surveillance programmes and monitoring systems.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The HWMP includes the required five minimum considerations above and all relevant records associated with the HWMP implementation.

  • Employees are:

    • Familiarised with the HWMP and the feedback mechanisms for its review by conducting employee interviews and observations.

    • Trained on the site-specific biosecurity mechanism by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HWMP includes the required five minimum considerations above and all relevant records associated with the HWMP implementation.

  • Employees are:

    • Familiarised with the HWMP and the feedback mechanisms for its review by conducting employee interviews and observations.

    • Trained on the site-specific biosecurity mechanism by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2022) Collection and Evaluation of Existing Guidelines and Awareness Materials on Aquaculture Biosecurity for Smallscale Farms in the Asia-Pacific Region. Report 36pp.

  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.1. Notification of diseases, and provision of epidemiological information.

4.2.1.8.1 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a water quality monitoring process according to Appendix 12 (12.3, Table 3).

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Maintaining good water quality is a critical factor when culturing any aquatic organism.
    • Concentrations of substances within the water system that rise above or fall below specific levels can be harmful to crustacean populations.
  • Concerning health and welfare, water quality has a dual role as a cause or a consequence of poor health and welfare:

    • Poor water quality can cause health and welfare hazards in an aquaculture facility, e.g. heavy rain promoting quick pH changes in a flow-through system or leaking from equipment in a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS).

    • Poor water quality can also result from poor husbandry practices resulting in a risk to health and welfare, e.g. if stocking density is too high the water quality is likely to deteriorate, especially in closed and semi-closed systems.

  • While Table 3 of Appendix 12 of the ASC Farm Standard specifies water quality parameters that must be included in the monitoring process, other parameters may be considered based on the site-specific requirements of the UoC.

  • Conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds for the required parameters, customised to suit the species and environmental conditions, should be incorporated as part of the water quality monitoring process.

  • Table 11 below gives examples that may be considered acceptable as a reference to develop and implement a water quality monitoring process.

Table 11: Water quality parameters for shrimp in ponds based on information from the FAI shrimp course.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The water quality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.
  • Records confirming the monitoring of the required parameters and their conformance with maximum and minimum thresholds.
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established water quality monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The water quality monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and is implemented.
    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Srinivas, Durbha & Venkatrayulu, Ch. (2023). Water quality management in shrimp aquaculture. Book.

  • Cuéllar-Anjel, J., Lara, C., Morales, V., De Gracia, A., & Gracía-Suárez, O. (2010) Manual of Best Management Practices for white shrimp Penaeus vannamei farming. OIESA_OSPESCA, C.A. pp. 132.

4.2.1.8.2 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a morphological scoring monitoring process for live crustaceans. Monitoring shall be conducted at least once a week, and shall include at least the following scoring parameters:

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

  • exoskeleton damage, including at least eyes, antennas, appendages and rostrum;
  • hepatopancreas colouration and size; 
  • gill colouration;
  • size dispersion/variation;
  • shell blisters and necrosis;
  • full/empty digestive tube and colouration;
  • loss of appendages, categorised according to causes.

An exception applies where deviation from monitoring frequency is justified by any of the following reasons:

  • immediately after stocking; or 
  • under environmental conditions that affect the welfare of the crustaceans or the health and safety of employees; or 
  • crustaceans are undergoing a disease event and/or being treated.

The reason for any deviation shall be recorded.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Morphological scoring is frequently used as an immediate indicator of welfare.
    • However, changes in morphology may have a variety of causes and therefore must be further analysed before drawing conclusions.
    • Loss of appendages shall be segregated according to potential causes e.g. bacterial infection or cannibalism.
    • Table 12 below gives examples that may be considered acceptable as a reference to develop and implement morphological scoring.

Table 12: Morphological parameters showing acceptable, warning level and unacceptable levels for shrimp based on Pedrazzani, Ana Silvia, Nathieli Cozer, Murilo Henrique Quintiliano, Camila Prestes dos Santos Tavares, Ubiratã de Assis Teixeira da Silva, and Antonio Ostrensky. 2023. “Non-Invasive Methods for Assessing the Welfare of Farmed White-Leg Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei)” and the FAI course.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The morphological scoring monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the morphological scoring.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established morphological scoring monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The morphological monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and is implemented.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Pedrazzani, A.S., Cozer, N., Quintiliano, M.H., dos Santos Tavares, C.P., da Silva, U.A.T & Ostrensky, A. (2023) “Non-Invasive Methods for Assessing the Welfare of Farmed White-Leg Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei)” Animals.

  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Ostrensky, A., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Shrimp Welfare Indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.2.1.8.3 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a monitoring process for behavioural scoring on live crustaceans from feeding trays or similar structures.  Monitoring shall be conducted daily.

An exception applies where deviation from monitoring frequency is justified by any of the following reasons:

  • immediately after stocking; or 
  • under environmental conditions that affect the welfare of the crustaceans or the health and safety of employees; or 
  • crustaceans are undergoing a disease event and/or being treated.

The reason for any deviation shall be recorded.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • To meet the ASC methodology for behaviour, only feeding behaviour needs to be monitored (see example in Table 13). However, other behaviours may also be considered. Further time is needed to develop quality behavioural analyses, which, while valuable for welfare and system management, must be tailored to the species, farming systems and available resources.
    • Additionally, changes in behaviour may have a variety of causes and, therefore, must be further analysed before drawing conclusions.  
  • Table 13 below gives examples that may be considered acceptable as a reference to develop and implement feeding behaviour scoring.

Table 13: Description of acceptable, warning levels and unacceptable behaviour of shrimp during feeding adapted from Pedrazzani, et al (2023). “Non-Invasive Methods for Assessing the Welfare of Farmed White-Leg Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei)”

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The feeding behaviour scoring monitoring process which incorporates the minimum elements required is included in the HWMP.
  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the feeding behaviour scoring.
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established behavioural scoring monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The behavioural scoring monitoring process is included in the HWMP.
  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Darodes de Tailly, J.B., Keitel, J., Owen, M.A.G., Alcaraz-Calero, J.M., Alexander, M.E. & Sloman, K.A. (2021) Monitoring methods of feeding behaviour to answer key questions in penaeid shrimp feeding. Reviews In Aquaculture.

  • Li D, Liu C, Song Z, Wang G. (2021) Automatic Monitoring of Relevant Behaviors for Crustacean Production in Aquaculture: A Review. Animals (Basel).

  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Ostrensky, A., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Shrimp Welfare Indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.2.1.8.4 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality monitoring process which includes at least the following:

a)

monitoring and recording of mortalities when spotted; and

b)

removal of mortalities when spotted; and

c)

conduct a post-mortem analysis for each mortality event; and

d)

investigation of mortality events which remain unexplained or unattributed to crustacean health reasons; and

e)

collection of moribund crustaceans when spotted and cull them according to Criterion 4.2.3.

Where any of the listed items above are not possible, the UoC shall record the reason.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The UoC should develop a procedure (e.g. SOP) to describe moribund collection and culling operations. 
    • Employees should be trained on this procedure. 
  • Moribund crustaceans should be collected using appropriate equipment to prevent further injuries and stress, e.g. hand net according to crustacean size. 
  • Slaughtered moribund crustaceans should be considered for the calculations needed to demonstrate compliance with Indicator 4.2.1.4. 
  • Whole pond/tank health issues should be addressed under a contingency plan for emergency culling.
  • Possible causes of several moribund crustaceans should be investigated.
    • A contingency plan for emergency culling should be in place.
  • Monitoring for mortality is understood as visual observation of whether there is mortality at the site, e.g. observations of the crustaceans in feeding trays, observations of mortalities at the tank/pond discharge.  
  • Possible causes that would justify no monitoring or removal of moribunds and mortality when spotted are severe bad weather, or a major equipment failure not related to poor maintenance.
  • Scrutiny of mortality records and cause determination is essential for preventing further avoidable deaths and improving overall crustacean health and welfare in aquaculture. 
  • If on-site diagnosis is inconclusive, off-site laboratory diagnosis is required.
  • When designing the mortality monitoring process, the UoC should consider carrying out a post-mortem analysis for each mortality event, not necessarily every crustacean. 
  • A statistically relevant number of crustaceans from the mortality event shall be analysed. 
    • A statistically relevant number of crustaceans refers to a sample size that is large enough to yield meaningful and reliable results when conducting statistical analysis.
      • In other words, the sample size should be sufficient to accurately represent the population being studied and to draw valid conclusions from the data.
  • The specific size needed for statistical relevance depends on various factors such as the variability within the population, the desired level of confidence and the statistical methods being used. 
    • Typically, larger sample sizes provide more reliable estimates and stronger evidence for drawing conclusions. 
  • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should assist the site in determining the appropriate sample size required for statistical analysis and must conduct all diagnosis.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records: 
    • Mortality monitoring.
    • Mortality removal, including the results of post-mortem analysis and the rationale for determining the sample size required for statistical analysis. 
    • Culling.
  • The mortality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the HWMP. 
  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established mortality monitoring, removal process and culling method.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The mortality monitoring process included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and is implemented.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.
  • Moribunds are collected when spotted and culled following responsible stunning and killing according to Criterion 4.2.3.
    • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the frequency of collection and culling methods with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

  • Contingency plan for ‘treatment’ culling

  • Monitoring and removal of mortality in conformance with the frequency required.

    • Records, employee interviews and observations should demonstrate acceptable frequency.

Useful Resources

  • McKay, H., & McAuliffe, W. (2024) Pre-slaughter mortality of farmed shrimp. ReThink Priorities: Technical report. 24pp.

4.2.1.8.5 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a traffic light system for water quality (Indicator 4.2.1.8.1), morphological scoring (Indicator 4.2.1.8.2), behavioural scoring (Indicator 4.2.1.8.3), and mortality (Indicator 4.2.1.8.4). The system shall identify ranges of acceptable levels (green), warning levels (amber), and unacceptable levels (red) of health or welfare.

Where levels are identified as amber or red, the UoC shall increase monitoring and implement appropriate corrective actions to restore the levels back to green.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The traffic light system should be tailored to accommodate the species being farmed, their life stage and the UoC’s monitoring procedures.
  • General guidelines on how to develop the traffic light system for each OWI are presented as follows:

Water Quality Indicators:

Step 1. Identify the parameters to be monitored according to Appendix 12 (Table 3).

Step 2. Establish species and life stage-specific thresholds for the parameters identified:

  • Base these values on either published scientific literature, the recommendation of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional, or ASC reference table for water quality.
    • If the site is growing more than one life stage or species, then the creation of specific values for each stage and species will be expected.

For example, based on the FAI shrimp score card for shrimp, the traffic light system for three of the indicators could be:

Morphological Indicators:

Step 1. Develop a scoring system for each of the morphological parameters required by Indicator 4.2.1.8.2.

  • It is recommended to score morphological parameters based on their severity, location and timing, when applicable.

Step 2. Once a scoring system has been developed, simulate different scenarios to develop a traffic light system. These scenarios should include at least:

  • The best case, e.g. where shrimp have no morphologic issues.

  • The second-best scenario, e.g. where shrimp have mild morphologic issues.

  • The third-best scenario, e.g. where shrimp have moderate morphologic issues.

  • The worst case, e.g. where shrimp have the highest score possible.

Each scenario will have a corresponding score:

Best case scenario

Worst case scenario

Third best case scenario

Second best case scenario

Step 3. Create a traffic light system, for example:

With time, and as more information is gathered, these thresholds might require re-adjustments.

Behavioural Indicators:

Step 1. Identify feeding behaviours that are relevant for the species of shrimp and the life stage being farmed (see example in Indicator 4.2.1.8.3 Table 13).

Step 2. Grade the identified feeding behaviours based on the scientific literature available or the opinion of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional. A few possible feeding behaviours to monitor are listed below.

  • How to interpret these behaviours will vary depending on the species of shrimp, the life stage and the farming system.

  • It is important to understand that, apart from the species and life stage variability, there will also be an individual component that will vary from one shrimp to the other.

Step 3. Simulate scenarios.

Step 4. Create a traffic light system, for example:

Mortality Indicators:

Step 1. Develop a mortality classification system that adjusts to the species, the life stage and the farming context (e.g. the geography or farming system where shrimp are reared). Staff must be trained in the mortality classification. Broadly, the following groupings can be made:

  • Infectious:
    • Bacterial. 
    • Viral. 
    • Parasitic. 
    • Fungal.
    • Amoebic.
  • Non-infectious: 
    • Husbandry related (e.g. acclimatisation, etc.) 
    • Environmental (e.g. extreme temperatures, etc.) 
    • Predation (e.g. birds, others). 
    • Physical lesions. 
    • Moribund. 
    • Deformities. 
    • Undiagnosed/unknown. 
    • Decomposed. 
    • Sampled.

Step 2. Based on the site’s historic mortality trends and those of the industry, establish mortality thresholds with the support of a veterinarian or health manager.

  • Mortality thresholds should be based on shrimp numbers, and it is recommended that they are also expressed as biomass thresholds.

    • The use of both metrics is considered complementary.

    • Using biomass on its own is discouraged, as small biomasses might lead to inaccurate assessments when shrimp are small.

Step 3: Create a traffic light system, for example for shrimp mortality based on the FAI Course:

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The traffic light system for the required OWIs that identify ranges of acceptable (green), warning (amber) and unacceptable (red) levels of health or welfare, included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm the increased monitoring and associated short-term corrective measures in case of amber or red traffic light results.

  • Rationale for the grading of the OWIs (e.g.: based on scientific literature available or the recommendation of a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional).

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established traffic light system.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The traffic light system included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and is implemented.

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the system with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.1.8.6 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes trend analysis to determine changes in health and welfare over time. This analysis shall consider drivers of the trends and shall be based on the data analysed in Indicator 4.2.1.8.5 and feedback from the processing plant where relevant.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The analysis of OWIs data over time, as well as information gathered from post-mortem analysis and the feedback from the processing plant:
    • Allows for the identification of trends that provide insights into factors influencing health, welfare and mortality events.
      • Regular reviews of trends, such as monthly and at least annually or at the end of the production cycle, are recommended.
    • Inform decision-making to improve overall production.
      • The veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should assist the UoC with the trends analysis and drawing conclusions to build effective corrective measures for improving health or welfare over time.
        • Feedback from the processing plant can, for example, disclose the presence of recurring trends like shell or antenna damage.
        • Sharing observations and feedback with the UoC enables prompt and thorough investigations.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The mechanism or trend analysis included in the HWMP.

  • Records that confirm trend analysis has been conducted include as a minimum:

    • Post-mortem analysis.

    • Feedback from the processing plant.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The trend analysis mechanism included in the HWMP incorporates the minimum required elements and its outcome is implemented:

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the mechanism with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.1.8.7 The UoC shall ensure the HWMP includes a mortality reduction plan which defines annual targets for both total and unexplained mortalities by considering the results of the trend analysis in Indicator 4.2.1.8.6 and shall implement appropriate actions to meet the annual targets.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The mortality reduction programme should address the various factors contributing to crustacean mortality. 
  • When building the program, the UoC should consider:
    • Current mortality rates and causes, including unexplained mortality.
    • Set achievable goals and objectives.
    • Identify priority areas for intervention according to the goals and objectives.
    • Develop strategies addressing priority areas for intervention.
    • Monitor and evaluate progress regularly.
    • Provide employees with training.
    • Foster a culture of continuous improvement.
    • Collaborate with industry experts for knowledge sharing.
    • Seek health professionals’ involvement in developing the reduction plan.
  • Special attention should be given to unexplained mortalities which may indicate underlying health issues or poor management practices.
    • Identifying and addressing the root causes of unexplained mortalities is essential for improving overall management practices and reducing mortality rates.
  • In addition, consistent, clear downward trends in OWIs indicate declining health or welfare.  
    • Examples of such trends include a consistent increase in overall morphological scoring, repeated observations of abnormal behaviour, deteriorating water quality with one or more parameters that are outside of the acceptable ranges or increasing mortality.  
  • If a declining trend is observed, then the UoC should assess the situation and investigate the causes behind those trends. 
    • One or multiple issues may be causing the decline, including those of infectious or non-infectious origin. 
    • In many cases, poor or inadequate husbandry practices can predispose animals to succumb to infectious diseases.  
    • Also, when declining trends are observed, the UoC is expected to review at least the following husbandry practices if appropriate:
      • Stocking densities.
      • The feeding plan.
      • Water quality.
      • Handling practices.
      • Enclosure characteristics.
      • Environmental enrichment.
      • The rearing environment, for example:
        • Additional aeration.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Mortality reduction programme.

  • Long-term animal health and welfare improvement measures as well as short-term mitigation measures to react to situations of declining health or welfare, included in the HWMP.

  • Mortality records that allow for trend analysis for the development of a mortality reduction programme.

  • Records of long-term animal health and welfare improvement measures and short-term mitigation measures to react to situations of declining health or welfare.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The mortality reduction programme and the improvement and mitigation measures included in the HWMP incorporate the minimum required elements and that its outcome is implemented:

    • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the programme and measures with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.1.9 The UoC shall report the following to a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional:

a)

all mortality events; and

b)

crustacean health and welfare concerns identified during mortality classification.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.2.1.1.0 The UoC shall report to the relevant authorities if a WOAH-notifiable disease is confirmed at a site, and shall:

a)

apply the measures according to applicable legal requirements; and

b)

increase disease-monitoring in other batches of crustaceans; and coordinate oversight by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Upon a WOAH-notifiable disease being confirmed, the UoC should consider within its response mechanism included in the HWMP (see Indicator 4.2.1.8) an emergency response procedure for culling the affected batches of crustaceans (see also Indicator 4.2.1.8.4).

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HWMP includes site-specific disease monitoring, responses and reporting requirements.
    • Specific considerations should be given to WOAH-notifiable diseases, including an emergency response procedure for culling the affected batches of crustaceans.
  • National regulations.
  • Records:
    • Reporting to the authorities.
    • Measures applied.
    • Notification to other sites in the vicinity or the ABM.
    • Disease monitoring.
    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional coordination.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HWMP includes considerations for WOAH-notifiable diseases (see interpretation for Indicator 4.2.1.8.4).

  • In case a WOAH-notifiable disease has been confirmed:

    • Reporting to authorities and implementation of regulatory measures.

    • Increased monitoring of other batches of crustaceans.

    • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional coordination

Useful Resources

  • Asia Farming (2022) Common shrimp/prawn diseases, symptoms, treatment. Article.
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.3. Diseases listed by WOAH. 
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.1. Notification of diseases, and provision of epidemiological information.

4.2.1.11 The UoC shall calculate stocking densities, following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.4).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.2.1.12 The UoC shall report to ASC survival rate, according to ASC data submission procedures, following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.1).

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.2.1.13 The UoC shall demonstrate that received nauplii, larvae or post-larvae (PL) originates from ablation free (AF) female broodstock according to the transition periods outlined in Appendix 12 (12.4, Table 4). This includes an agreement with the hatchery that allows ASC or its designated agents to conduct oversight activities to verify the AF sources within the facility.

Indicator applicability: Penaeus vannamei and Penaeus monodon

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Scope applicable to Penaeus vannamei and Penaeus monodon species.
  • Transition periods span from May 2025 to May 2031, with staged percentages for AF broodstock compliance (see Appendix 12 table 4).
  • The objective is to ensure a gradual shift toward using only ablation-free female broodstock, aligning with improved welfare practices.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The monitoring process involves developing and implementing a tracking system to monitor the origin of stock (nauplii, larvae or PL).
  • Where feasible, conduct physical audits or site visits of hatcheries to verify by visual inspection compliance with AF broodstock sourcing.
  • Hatcheries supplying the stock should provide clear documentation of the broodstock’s status (AF or non-AF).
    • Maintain records of sourcing, including certificates or declarations from hatcheries confirming broodstock compliance with AF requirements.
    • Maintain detailed production logs showing the percentage of stock derived from AF broodstock at each transition phase.
  • Employees involved in sourcing should demonstrate understanding to comply with the requirement to ensure they can explain the sourcing process to verify compliance during audits.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The monitoring process to confirm that the UoC has a documented system to track and verify the origin of nauplii, larvae, or PL.
  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Zacarias, S PowerPoint Presentation

4.2.2 – Crustaceans – Handling

4.2.2.1 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Handling Management Plan (HMP), with the intent of ensuring good health and welfare of farmed crustaceans.

The HMP shall be periodically reviewed and revised as necessary.

4.2.2.2 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes all handling activities carried out on site.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The Handling Management Plan (HMP):

    • Aims to support the development and implementation of preventive, rather than remedial, actions that prevent poor crustacean health and welfare at handling.

      • Examples of handling:

        • Crowding.

        • Sampling.

        • Transportation (including loading, transfer and unloading).

    • Should consider a description of:

      • Processes.

        • A separate process description may be required for outsourced events e.g. live transportation of PL to the site.
      • Equipment.
        • A description of equipment, and verification if applicable may be required for both UoC and outsourced events e.g. harvest equipment.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes standardised handling operations, e.g.:
    • Site-specific description of processes and equipment.
    • Documents:
      • Planning of handling events, e.g.:
        • Emails, reports and site ‘whiteboard’ communications.
      • Handling procedures.

  • Monitoring the effectiveness of the HMP.

    • Documents:
      • Handling logs, e.g.:
      • Reports detailing regular observation of crustacean behaviour, environmental parameters and crustacean conditions during and post-handling procedures, including injuries, mortalities or deviations from procedures.
      • Handling incidents reports, e.g.:
        • Emails, reports detailing any incidents during handling procedures, including injuries, mortalities or deviations from procedures.
    • Feedback from staff, e.g.:

      • Emails, anonymous box asking feedback from staff involved in handling procedures regarding their observations and any difficulties encountered.

        • Encourage open communication.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes a description of the handling processes and equipment and considerations for planning handling events.  
  • Employees are familiarised with the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations. 
  • Handling logs are available documenting handling processes, environment and crustacean conditions. 
  • Existence of handling incident reports, including feedback from staff and discussions regarding handling procedure changes. 
  • Open communication is encouraged via formal documents and employee interviews and observations. 

Useful Resources

  • Amatul-Samahah, Md.A., Omar, W.H.H.W., Ikhsan, N.F.M., et al (2020) Vaccination trials against vibriosis in shrimp: A review. Aquaculture Reports.

4.2.2.3 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes contingency plans for handling activities, including at least the following:

a)

immediate response measures in the case of system failure; and

b)

culling response measures (see Indicators 4.2.3.2 and 4.2.3.7); and

c)

mass mortality event response measures.

Exception applicability: every UoC using feed

An exception to (b) applies in the extreme circumstances of culling whole ponds for disease control, in which case a solution of chlorine is allowed in a concentration that ensures that death occurs rapidly.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The contingency plans should consider:
    • Identification of potential failures.
    • Effective corrective measures, e.g.:
      • Backup power generators.

      • Oxygen support.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes processes’ contingency plans.
  • Records:
    • Backup system testing.
  • Additional oxygen source available.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes considerations on crustacean health and welfare
    before handling events, including considerations for the existence of a
    backup system.
  • Presence of a backup system.
  • Employees are:
    • Familiarised with the contingency plans by conducting employee
      interviews and observations.
  • Records:
    • Backup system testing.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.2.4 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes consideration of the environmental conditions associated with handling activities, with the intent of preventing handling under adverse conditions that could affect the health and welfare of the crustaceans.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Examples of considerations of external conditions:
    • Avoid handling in the event of storms.
    • Avoid handling crustacean without using a shade net on a sunny day.
    • Avoid transferring post-larvae during periods where there are less than favourable conditions:
      • Rainfall can quickly alter pond conditions and trigger a chain of events resulting in sub-optimal conditions for crustaceans.
        • Potential for Vibrio spp. to flourish, increasing the risks of bacterial infection to the shrimp.

        • Trigger the production of hydrogen sulphide. This is a toxic gas produced by sulphate reducing bacteria and is highly toxic to shrimp.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • HMP includes consideration for external conditions necessary to perform handling.

  • Records:

    • Weather forecast verification.
  • Employees should demonstrate knowledge of the considerations and the verification of external conditions before handling.

Auditors should confirm:

  • HMP includes considerations for external conditions for handling and are implemented.

  • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the HMP with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.2.5 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a pond preparation process including at least the following:

a)

drying of the pond. An exception applies where areas cannot be dried, in which case they shall be disinfected; and

b)

removal of any dead or live animals from the pond; and

c)

removal of excess organic material; and

d)

adjustment of acidic pH; and

e)

preparation of the surface of earthen ponds to facilitate oxygenation and UV exposure.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Draining the pond completely helps in eliminating unwanted organisms and disease.

  • Areas that cannot be completely drained should be treated with disinfectants to kill any pathogens, e.g.:

    • If a few wet patches are observed after draining the pond, spray these patches with a bleach solution for disinfection, ensuring no harmful bacteria or parasites survive.

  • Removing any dead or living animals helps in preventing disease spread and decay, which can affect the water quality and the health of future pond crops, e.g.:

    • If a few dead crustaceans and some frogs are found, remove all these animals and dispose of them properly, ensuring the pond is free of any potential contaminants.

  • Remove any organic debris such as leaves, branches and sludge. If the pond water is too acidic, agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) may be added to neutralise the pH, making the environment more suitable for crustacean e.g.:

    • After removing leaves and decaying plant matter from the pond bed, the pH level was 5.5. After applying agricultural lime, the pH level rose to approximately 7, a neutral level.

  • Tilling the surface of earthen ponds (those with natural soil bottoms) helps to aerate the soil, promoting better oxygenation. It also exposes the soil to sunlight, which helps in killing pathogens and breaking down organic matter through UV radiation.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Records confirming the monitoring of the required parameters for pond preparation and their conformance with acceptable quality levels included in the HMP prior to stocking.

  • Record of drying period.

  • Record of addition of lime if applied.

  • The water quality monitoring process, that incorporates the minimum elements required for pond preparation.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established water quality monitoring process during handling.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Pond preparation process, that incorporates the minimum elements required, included in the indicator and cross-checking with the handling operations present in the HMP.

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • The Fish Site (2016) Management of intensive Vannamei shrimp ponds. Article.

4.2.2.6 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes acclimatisation measures to prevent sudden changes in water conditions affecting the health and welfare status of the crustaceans.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Acclimatisation measures should be designed and maintained, e.g.:
    • Water temperature during transportation must be as close as possible to that which the crustaceans came from.
    • Crustaceans shall be released into a small area of the pond ‘hapa’ or net enclosures in the grow-out pond itself for a risk-assessed period to evaluate the capacity of the PL to adjust to the pond conditions.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • acclimatisation measures and monitoring of the water quality according to HMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of acclimatisation parameters before stocking.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the acclimatisation measures and monitoring process above.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The acclimatisation measures included in the HMP incorporate the minimum required elements and are implemented.

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.2.7 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes a visual inspection process to identify abnormal behaviour in relation to the handling activity and defines mitigation measures when identified.

Indicator applicability: every UoC using feed

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Visual inspection after handling should be included in the HMP.

    • Crustacean morphology and behaviour can be assessed when verifying the crustacean feeding trays as a minimum requirement.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • The monitoring process, that incorporates the corrective actions required, included in the HMP.

  • Records that confirm the monitoring of the morphology and behaviour at the feeding trays. A checked box on the monitoring records indicating whether monitoring morphology and behaviour took place or not is accepted.

  • Employees should demonstrate awareness of the established behavioural monitoring process.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The monitoring process included in the HMP that incorporates corrective actions and is implemented.

  • Implementation can be verified by cross-checking the process with relevant records, information from employee interviews and observations.

N/A

4.2.2.8 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers biosecurity risks specific to the types of handling activities and shall include appropriate biosecurity measures to prevent the transfer of disease.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For developing a site-specific biosecurity mechanism within the HMP, the UoC should consider:
    • Indicator 4.2.1.8.d)
    • Biosecurity measures related to the type of handling, e.g.:
      • Equipment segregation.
      • Equipment disinfection.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • For developing a site-specific biosecurity during handling the HMP includes the considerations for:
    • Site-specific biosecurity mechanism.
    • Biosecurity specifications related to the type of handling operations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes the required minimum considerations above.
  • Employees are:
    • Familiarised with the biosecurity considerations in the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations.
    • Trained on biosecurity specifications related to the type of handling operations by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

  • Lightner, D.V. (2007), Biosecurity in Shrimp Farming: Pathogen Exclusion through Use of SPF Stock and Routine Surveillance. Journal of the World Aquaculture Society.

4.2.2.9 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP considers predation risks specific to the types of handling activities and shall include appropriate predator control measures.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For developing a site-specific predator control within the HMP, the UoC should consider:
    • The site-specific characteristics required to be assessed by Indicator 4.2.1.8.e) predator control measures specific to the type of handling, e.g.:
      • Birds scaring devices.
      • Use of appropriate nets sizes while moving crustaceans from one unit/pond to another.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Predator control measures specific to the type of handling operations.

  • Verification of mortalities associated with predators during handling operations.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The HMP includes the required considerations above.
  • Employees are:
    • Familiarised with the predator control considerations in the HMP by conducting employee interviews and observations.
    • Trained on predator control verifications, e.g.:
      • Verification of mortality events specific to the type of handling operations by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.
