4.2.2.10 The UoC shall ensure that the HMP includes consideration of the use of appropriate equipment during handling activities to avoid affecting the health and welfare status of the crustaceans

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.2.3 – Crustaceans – Slaughter and Killing

4.2.3.1 The UoC shall appoint a staff member responsible for overseeing the implementation of crustacean health and welfare requirements during slaughter.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

4.2.3.2 The UoC shall ensure crustaceans are killed immediately after harvest:

a)

by immersion in an ice slurry bath; or

b)

through an electrical device followed by immersion in an ice slurry bath.

4.2.3.3 The UoC shall not process crustaceans alive.

4.2.3.4 The UoC shall ensure ice slurry baths are maintained at ≤4°C at all times and crustaceans are immersed for an appropriate amount of time to be killed effectively.

4.2.3.5 The UoC shall ensure that if electrical devices are used for stunning the manufacturer’s instructions are followed.

4.2.3.8 The UoC shall ensure that killing has been effective by verifying the absence of coordinated leg and body movements.

4.2.3.9 The UoC shall have measures in place to immediately respond to ineffective stunning or killing, including the presence of a back-up system, and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • Slaughter is generally a two-stage process: 
    • The crustacean is first stunned to make it insensible to pain.
    • Killing is then carried out (see interpretation in Indicator 4.2.3.10).
  • An effective stun is determined by the loss of consciousness using an electroencephalogram (EEG) measured in a laboratory, which is not practicable at a site level.
  • Current stunning methods for crustaceans include a controlled ice slurry bath at ≤4 °C or electric stunning followed by an ice bath.
    • To ensure a controlled ice slurry bath at ≤4 °C, the ice slurry bath should be adjusted in relation to the amount and crustacean size. Below is an example for a batch of crustaceans using an ice slurry bath maintained at ≤4 °C.
    • Preparation: determine the approximate amount and size of crustacean by considering the amount planned for slaughter and taking a sample of the pond.
    • Results of amount and size: e.g. 5kg of medium-sized crustaceans (approximately 15cm each).
    • Ice slurry preparation: create an ice slurry bath in a large, insulated container. For 5kg of crustaceans, prepare an ice slurry mixture with approximately 10 Liters of water and a sufficient amount of ice to maintain the temperature at ≤4 °C. 
    • Add ice gradually to the water, continuously stirring to create an even slurry.
    • Monitor the temperature using a thermometer, ensuring it reaches and stays at ≤4 °C.
    • Adjust according to crustacean size and amount: since the crustaceans are medium-sized and weigh a total of 5kg, ensure that the ice slurry bath can accommodate the entire batch without overcrowding. Overcrowding can reduce the effectiveness of the ice slurry by raising the temperature.
    • Immersion: gently place the 5kg of crustaceans into the ice slurry bath, ensuring they are fully submerged.
    • Stir the ice-slurry occasionally to maintain uniform temperature distribution.
    • Define the timing for effective Killing: for medium-sized shrimp, a typical immersion time in an ice slurry bath at ≤4 °C is around 2-7 minutes.

Table 14: Suggested time In Ice bath for killing of Penaeus vannamei shrimp

  • Immersion time: set a timer to ensure all shrimp are effectively killed using the timings worked out.
  • Monitoring and verification: periodically check the temperature of the slurry bath to ensure it remains at ≤4°C. Add more ice if necessary to maintain the temperature. Check for indicators of death according to Indicator 4.4.5.
  • In extreme hot conditions, and the impossibility to stabilise the temperature of the slurry bath, a range of temperatures may be accepted.
  • After the set time, remove a few shrimp and check for the absence of movements; the shrimp should also exhibit body rigidity, indicative of effective killing.

Table 15: Determination of the effectiveness of stunning and / or killing based on behaviour

  • The use of body movement as an indicator for the effectiveness of stunning or killing can be misleading as muscular spasms regularly occur in unconscious or dead shrimp. Studies on crustaceans, including shrimp, indicate that they can exhibit reflex actions and movements even when they are unconscious or brain dead. This is because such movements are often dominated by nerve circuits in the peripheral nervous system rather than the brain. Body movements indicating walking leg movements and coordinated swimming movements are relevant movements to watch out for, and that may indicate consciousness
  • Killing effectiveness in the UoC should be assessed by confirming signs of unconsciousness:
    • Immediate loss of balance.
    • Absence of voluntary movements.
    • Absence of coordinated swimming movements.
    • Limited pleopods and pereipod movements.
    • Laying on side with no activity.
  • The requirement for killing also applies to animals not destined for human consumption, e.g. bycatch, wild species.
  • If there is uncertainty about whether a crustacean is unconscious:
    • When using an electrical stunning, the stunning should be repeated or the harvest shall stop to verify stun parameters before proceeding, e.g. more than 5 crustaceans in 10 seconds requiring backup stun.
    • Or use an alternative backup method, e.g. ice slurry bath or a secondary electric stunner.
      • When using the ice slurry bath method, the temperature of the bath should be checked, and the length of time in the bath extended.
  • Electric stunning should be performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Employees should demonstrate knowledge of the approved slaughter methods and monitoring.

  • Records:

    • Employee training (see Appendix 12).

    • Slaughter monitoring, e.g.:

      • Verification and registration of stunning and killing of 100 individual crustaceans per harvest.

      • Observation of signs of unconsciousness.

      • Records of the use of backup.

      • Records of stunning and killing of crustaceans not destined for human consumption if applicable.

Auditors should confirm:

  • Monitoring of stunning and slaughter in conformance to the requirements.
    • Records, employee interviews and observations of stunning and slaughter operations during the audit should demonstrate the implementation of the requirements, and that there is an available backup method or knowledge of corrective measures to be carried out.

Useful Resources

  • Weineck, K., Ray, A.J., Fleckenstein, L.J., Medley, M., Dzubuk, N., Piana, E., & Cooper, R.L. (2018) Physiological Changes as a Measure of Crustacean Welfare under Different Standardized Stunning Techniques: Cooling and Electroshock Animals. 
  • CIWF (2020) Tesco and Hilton Seafood – Improving the welfare of whiteleg shrimp (Pennaus vannamei) at harvest. CIWF Report 7pp. 
  • Conte, F.; Voslarova, E.; Vecerek, V.; Elwood, R.W.; Coluccio, P.; Pugliese, M.; Passantino, A. (2021) Humane Slaughter of Edible Decapod Crustaceans. Animals.
  • Barrento, S., Pedrazzani, A., Ostrensky, A., & Quintiliano, M. (2023). Shrimp Welfare Indicators [Online course]. In S. Barrento, M. Quintiliano, & J. Muirhead (Eds.), FAI Academy. https://fai.academy/

4.2.3.6 The UoC shall not use any of the following methods to kill crustaceans:

  • asphyxiation in air; or
  • carbon dioxide (CO2) bath; or
  • salt baths; or
  • ammonia baths; or
  • evisceration.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The only killing method allowed for crustaceans is a controlled ice slurry:
    • This involves immersing crustaceans in a slurry of ice and water, causing rapid cooling.
    • To clarify, electrical stunning is a stunning method and not a killing method. Stunning methods are designed to render animals insensible to pain before they are killed, whereas killing methods result in the animal’s death. Stunning is a preliminary step followed by a killing method to ensure that the animal does not regain consciousness.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Employees should demonstrate knowledge confirming the approved killing methods.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The use of approved methods for killing and awareness of non-approved methods.

Useful Resources

  • Neil, D. M., Putyora E. & Albalat, A. (2024) Towards the humane slaughter of decapod crustaceans: identifying the most effective indicators of insensibility following electrical stunning. Frontiers in Animal Science

4.2.3.7 The UoC shall ensure that an overdose of anaesthetic is only used to kill crustaceans not destined for human consumption.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • The use of anaesthesia should be considered as a humane method for crustaceans not destined to human consumption.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • Consideration for the use of anaesthesia for killing.
  • Culling procedure.
  • Records:
    • Anaesthetic usage amount and number of culled crustaceans.

Auditors should confirm:

  • The UoCs consideration of the use of anaesthetics for killing.

  • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the culling procedure with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

Useful Resources

N/A

4.2.3.10 The UoC shall maintain records of the activities carried out under indicators 4.2.3.4 and 4.2.3.8.

No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

Bivalves and Abalone 4.3

4.3.1 The UoC shall ensure that all relevant employees are trained on general animal health and welfare awareness, including biosecurity, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.3.2 The UoC shall ensure that any person involved in animal husbandry and handling activities is trained on animal health and welfare, according to Appendix 12 (12.2, Table 1).

4.3.3 The UoC shall ensure that the content of the training in Indicators 4.3.1 and 4.3.2 is updated as necessary and is approved by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

How do I interpret this requirement?

  • For each employee:
    • The level of training should be appropriate to their role:
      • For all relevant employees: a basic level of awareness of biosecurity, animal health and welfare is required.
      • For any person involved in husbandry, handling and harvest operations: a more advanced level of training on animal health and welfare, handling and harvest practices is required on an annual basis.
    • Evidence of training participation must be maintained:
      • Certificates of attendance.
      • Certificates of competency.
  • The trainer should be competent in the topic of animal health and welfare and the competence should be demonstrable, e.g.:
    • Curriculum Vitae.
    • Records of qualifications.
    • Work experience.
  • Best practices on the implementation of the training content should be visible during the audit.
    • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of that content at interviews.

Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

  • A list of employees and subcontracted personnel involved in animal husbandry and handling operations.
  • Records:
    • Training.
    • Trainer’s competence.
    • Certificates of competency.

    Auditors should confirm:

    • Employees received the required level of training for their roles by cross-checking employees and subcontracted personnel lists with:
      • Training records.
      • Certificates of competency.
      • Trainer’s competence.
      • Revision of training resources/contents.
    • Adequate level of personnel knowledge of the training content should be verified by:
      • Interviews.
      • Observation of operations during handling and harvest of animals.

    Useful Resources

    • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) – Competency and Curriculum Guidelines for Community Animal Health Workers. Paris, 39 pp. (https://doi.org/10.20506/woah.3535).

    4.3.4 The UoC shall only stock batches of animals that have been tested prior to stocking and are free from diseases of regional concern

    How do I interpret this requirement?

    • Testing should be relevant to:
      • The species.
      • The production system.
      • The scale of production.
      • The local regulations.
      • For example:
        • Infection with Perkinsus marinus.
        • Infection with Bonamia exitiosa.
        • Infection with Abalone herpesvirus.
    • Testing might consist of:
      • Clinical examination of the animals.
      • Laboratory tests:
        • Bacteriology.
        • Molecular biology (e.g.: PCR).
        • Histopathology.
        • Virology (e.g.: cell culture).
    • The designated veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional should determine:
      • The diseases to include in the testing, based on local regulations, scientific literature and/or publicly available information (see interpretation for Indicator 4.3.6).
      • The sample size, based on local regulations and/or technical judgement.
    • Compulsory governmental testing programme results are acceptable for demonstrating conformance with this requirement.

    Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

    • List of relevant diseases for the species in the country (see interpretation for Indicator 4.3.6).
    • Testing results written report or document that includes, as a minimum:
      • The batch of animals being tested.
      • The date of the test.
      • The pathogen tested.
      • The results of the test.
    • Records:
      • Purchase.
      • Transportation.
      • Delivery.
      • Stocking.

    Auditors should confirm:

    • Every batch of animals has been tested by cross-checking the list of relevant diseases for the species in the country with the testing result’s written report or document and records.

    Useful Resources

    • Victoria Agriculture (2023) Abalone disease; Biosecurity. Webpage. 
    • Victoria Fisheries Authority (2024) Abalone diseases. Webpage.
    • Alevra, A., Llorente Manzanares, M., Mente, E., Xandri Royo, P.M. (2024) Good husbandry practices for  aquaculture. Publications Office of the European Union. Report 89pp.

    4.3.5 The UoC shall ensure that a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional periodically visits the site to perform routine checks. Checks shall be carried out at least annually, as well as reactively in cases of animal health or welfare concerns.

    How do I interpret this requirement?

    • Regular veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visits may fall into two categories:
      • Routine: Performed on a regular basis to monitor the health and welfare of the farmed animal.
      • Reactive: Performed in response to deterioration or concerns of the health or welfare status of the farmed animals.
      • Sites should be prepared to provide the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional with detailed information about the observed symptoms, recent changes in behaviour, morphology, water quality or mortality and any relevant history of disease or treatments.
      • The site should use reactive health visits to address immediate health or welfare concerns, diagnose underlying causes of problems, and implement targeted interventions to mitigate risks and prevent further spread of disease.
    • For routine visits, preparation is recommended to ensure a meaningful outcome from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional. Below are some practical considerations:
      • Visit scheduling: Ensure key employees are available during the visit to provide relevant required information and to facilitate adequate follow-up.
        • Designate a senior employee to serve as the primary point of contact for the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional during the visit.
        • This individual can help coordinate the activity, ensure relevant information is available, assist during the visit and ensure follow-up.
      • Gather and organise relevant information:
        • Compile relevant information about the operations, including:
          • Species being cultured,
          • Production systems,
          • Stocking densities,
          • Recent health history, water quality monitoring results,
          • Morphology and mortalities data,
          • Feeding plan,
          • Any previous veterinary reports,
          • Details of any ongoing issue.
          • Having this information readily accessible will facilitate discussion and decision-making during the visit.
      • Prepare the UoC for the visit: Ensure the UoC is prepared for the visit and for providing full access to all relevant areas to the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.
        • Address any maintenance issues, clean structures as needed and ensure clear access to all relevant areas of the facility.
        • Ensure handling and other equipment that might be needed during the visit, such as nets, containers and sampling equipment, is available and in good working condition.
        • Make sure employees are aware of the visit and its objectives and encourage them to proactively participate in it.
      • During the visit: Ensure relevant information is discussed with the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and that the visit includes all relevant areas within the UoC.
      • After the visit: Follow up on any recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.
        • Implement any necessary revisions or changes to management practices, treatment protocols or facility conditions based on the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional’s feedback and any sample or testing results.
      • Continuous improvement: Use the insights gained from the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit to identify opportunities for continuous improvement in health and welfare management.

    Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

    • Health reports.

    • Testing results.

    • Records:

      • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional qualifications.

      • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional visit.

      • Recommendations or actions discussed during the visit.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • The qualifications of the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and cross-check the frequency of visits with records.

      • Existence of health reports and testing results.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.3.6 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP), approved by a registered veterinarian, with the intent to prevent disease outbreaks and ensure good health and welfare of farmed animals.

      The HWMP shall include all of the following:

      a)

      disease monitoring; and

      b)

      response, including quarantine, treatment, and humane culling; and

      c)

      reporting mechanisms, including reporting WOAH-notifiable disease to authorities; and

      d)

      biosecurity risks; and

      e)

      predation risks.

      The HWMP shall be reviewed and revised at least annually

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • The Health and Welfare Management Plan (HWMP): 
        • Aims to support the development and implementation of preventive, rather than remedial, actions that ensure good animal health and welfare.
        • Must be developed by the UoC in collaboration with a registered veterinarian who approves it.
      • For developing and establishing a site-specific disease monitoring, response and reporting mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
        • Developing standardised health and welfare monitoring protocols.
          • This may involve conducting visual inspections, monitoring OWIs and performing diagnostic tests for pathogens.
        • Producing and maintaining detailed records.
          • Including records of health observations, diagnostic test results, treatments administered, mortalities and other relevant data.
          • It is recommended to use a centralised database or electronic system for efficient data management and retrieval.
        • Implementing an early detection system.
          • To detect signs of disease outbreaks or abnormal health conditions promptly.
            • This could include environmental monitoring tools.
        • Establishing response protocols for responding to disease outbreaks or health emergencies.
          • Outlining procedures for:
            • Isolating affected individuals or populations.
            • Implementing strategies, for example, for treatments or others (e.g. culling affected batches of animals)
            • Notifying relevant stakeholders, including other sites in the vicinity and the authorities.
        • Establishing communication channels.
          • Effective communication channels should be implemented for reporting health-related issues both internally within the facility and externally to relevant authorities (e.g. WOAH-notifiable diseases) or stakeholders.
            • Employees should understand their roles and responsibilities in reporting and responding to disease events.
        • Maintaining a readily accessible notification list.
          • Including contact names, numbers and emails for key employees and other relevant stakeholders. 
          • The list should be kept up-to-date to ensure quick and efficient communication during emergencies.
      • For developing a site-specific biosecurity mechanism within the plan, the UoC should consider:
        • Determining the objectives and scope of the biosecurity mechanism.
        • Identifying relevant regulatory requirements.  
        • Gathering information about the site, including an up-to-date layout of production units identifying the possible movements of animals, animal products, animal waste, water and fomites/vectors. 
        • Identifying potential transmission pathways into, within and from the site. 
        • Carrying out a risk analysis to identify and evaluate disease threats and ensure that the plan addresses them.
          • A risk analysis can be carried out either on their whole or only partially, e.g. disease transmission during transportation. 
          • This will depend on the objectives of the biosecurity mechanism.
        • Identifying mitigation measures and assessing their effectiveness and their management requirements.  
        • Establishing emergency procedures in the event of a biosecurity failure.  
        • Defining internal and external communication procedures, roles and responsibilities. 
        • Creating a monitoring and internal audit schedule.  
        • Carrying out performance evaluations. 
        • Training employees in the different elements of the biosecurity mechanism. 
        • Creating the necessary SOPs to support the implementation of the mitigation measures and the biosecurity mechanism.   
        • Maintaining a record-keeping system, that provides evidence of compliance with the biosecurity mechanism. 
      • For developing predator control measures within the plan, the UoC should consider:
        • Identifying potential predators.
          • Create a list of the predators that are present in the area and that might interact with the UoC.
            • Predators may include birds, mammals, reptiles, and other aquatic species known to prey on bivalves and abalone.
        • Assessing the risk of predation.
          • Evaluate the risk posed by each predator species identified based on factors such as proximity to the site, population size, means of accessing the site, likelihood of predation, etc.
        • Implementing predator control measures.
          • Develop and implement predator control measures tailored to the specific risks identified. This may include:
            • Physical barriers such as nets, or screens to prevent access to animals.
            • Scare tactics such as visual deterrents to discourage predators from approaching the facility.
        • Implementing ongoing monitoring and surveillance.
          • To detect predator activity and intervene as needed.
        • Regular reviewing and revision.
          • Based on the outcome of the ongoing monitoring and surveillance. Adjustments to the measures should be made when the results of monitoring indicate the need to optimise protection for animals and the containment system.
        • Collaborating with local authorities or local wildlife agencies to address predator issues in the surrounding area.
        • A periodic review and, if necessary, a revision of the HWMP must be conducted in response to changes in farming activities or external factors or as directed by the veterinarian.
          • As a minimum, the review should occur annually.
        • The UoC should develop feedback mechanisms to inform the review, e.g. proactively seeking feedback from employees on the operationalisation of the site-specific biosecurity mechanism. 
        • For a single producer overseeing multiple UoCs in a shared waterbody, a unified HWMP that incorporates site-specific details is acceptable; however, for larger companies managing multiple UoCs in one country, while common plans may apply, it is crucial to ensure HWMP adaptation to individual site circumstances, particularly in aspects like biosecurity measures, disease surveillance programmes and monitoring systems.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • The HWMP includes the considerations for:
        • Site-specific disease monitoring, responses and reporting requirements.
          • Specific considerations should be given to WOAH-notifiable diseases (see interpretation for Indicator 4.3.7).
        • Site-specific biosecurity mechanism.
        • Predators control measures.
        • Veterinarian sign-off.
        • Reviews and revisions.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • The HWMP includes the required five minimum considerations above and all relevant records associated with the HWMP implementation
      • Employees are:
        • Familiarised with the HWMP and the feedback mechanisms for its review by conducting employee interviews and observations.
        • Trained on the site-specific biosecurity mechanism by reviewing employees’ training records, conducting employees’ interviews and observations.

      Useful Resources

      • Alevra, A., Llorente Manzanares, M., Mente, E., Xandri Royo, P.M. (2024) Good husbandry practices for aquaculture. Publications Office of the European Union. Report 89pp.
      • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.3. Diseases listed by WOAH.

      4.3.7 The UoC shall report to the authorities if a WOAH-notifiable disease is confirmed at a site, and shall:

      a)

      apply the measures according to applicable legal requirements; and

      b)

      increase disease-monitoring in other batches of animals; and

      c)

      coordinate oversight by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Upon a WOAH-notifiable disease is confirmed, the UoC should consider within its response mechanism included in the HWMP (see Indicator 4.3.6) an emergency response procedure for dealing with the affected batches of animals.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • HWMP includes site-specific disease monitoring, responses and reporting requirements.

        • Specific considerations should be given to WOAH-notifiable diseases, including an emergency response procedure for dealing with the affected batches of animals.

      • National regulations / legal requirements.

      • Records:

        • Reporting to authorities.

        • Measures applied.

        • Notification to other sites in the vicinity.

        • Disease monitoring.

        • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional coordination.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • The HWMP includes considerations for WOAH-notifiable diseases (see interpretation for Indicator 4.3.7).

      • In case a WOAH-notifiable disease has been confirmed:

        • Reporting to authorities and implementation of regulatory measures.

        • Notification to other sites in the vicinity or the ABM.

        • Increased monitoring to other batches of animals.

        • Veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional coordination

      Useful Resources

      • World Organisation for Animal Health (2024) Aquatic Animal Health Code. Chapter 1.3. Diseases listed by WOAH.

      • Arzul I, et al (2021) Manual for bivalve disease management and biosec urity – H2020 VIVALDI Project – 44p.

      4.3.8 The UoC shall calculate stocking densities, following the method outlined In Appendix 12 (12.5.4).

      Indicator applicability: abalone only

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.3.9 The UoC shall report to ASC mortality data, according to ASC data submission procedures, and following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.1).

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      Veterinary therapeutants 4.4

      Intent: The aquaculture industry uses therapeutants responsibly and reduces reliance upon therapeutants over time.

      4.4.1 The UoC shall only use therapeutants as prescribed by a registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Therapeutant prescriptions should be accordance with regulatory requirements.

        • Prescribed by a registered veterinarian or a qualified aquatic animal health professional.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • If prescriptions are made by health professionals who are not veterinarians, obtain evidence of competency (e.g. accreditation) in diagnosing, for the purposes of the WOAH Aquatic Animal Health Code.
      • Records:
        • Prescriptions and therapeutants use (for details, refer to Indicator 4.4.2).

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Prescriptions and therapeutants use.

      • The observation should be cross-checked with records.

      • If a non-veterinarian wrote prescriptions, confirm that the individual is qualified as an aquatic animal health professional.

      Useful Resources

      • Desbois., A et al (2025) Aquaculture requires special consideration in National Action Plans for Antimicrobial Resistance. Science of the Total Environment. 958
      • Responsible Use of Medicines In Agriculture Alliance (2004) Responsible use of antimicrobials in fish production. Report 21pp.
      • Ibrahim, M., Ahmad, F., Yaqub, B., Ramzan, A., et al. (2020) Chapter 4 – Current trends of antimicrobials used in food animals and aquaculture. Book: Editor(s): Hashmi, M.Z. Antibiotics and Antimicrobial Resistance Genes in the Environment

      4.4.2 The UoC shall ensure that prescriptions for each application of therapeutants include at least the following:

      a)

      the name, address, telephone number and signature of the registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional; and

      b)

      the date of the prescription; and

      c)

      the name and address of the site; and

      d)

      the identification, including the species, of the batches of animals to be treated; and

      e)

      the name and quantity of the therapeutant prescribed; and

      f)

      the dosage and administration instructions; and

      g)

      the withdrawal period.

      The UoC shall maintain records of each therapeutant prescription.

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.3 The UoC shall not use hormones or antibiotics to stimulate growth.

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.4 The UoC shall only use hormones for the following purposes:

      a)

      sex-reversal; or

      b)

      to induce and coordinate spawning; or

      c)

      to produce single-sex stock.

      The UoC shall maintain records of each hormonal treatment.

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.5 The UoC shall not use antibiotics prophylactically.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • A registered veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional must confirm possible causes for antibiotic treatment procedures, e.g. a diagnosed bacterial infection.
      • Metaphylactic use of antibiotics is allowed if a veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional diagnoses a bacterial infection in the stock and prescribes treatment for the animals in contact with sick animals.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Health report.

      • Testing results that prove the diagnosis of a bacterial infection.

      • Records:

        • Mortality.

        • Treatments and veterinary prescriptions.

        • Recommendations or actions discussed.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • The qualifications of the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional and cross-check the records.

      • Recommendations or actions discussed.

      • Existence of health reports and testing results.

      • Log of medication events.

      Useful Resources

      • Bondad-Reantaso, M.G., MacKinnon, B., Karunasagar, I., et al (2023) Review of alternatives to antibiotic use in aquaculture. Reviews In Aquaculture.

      4.4.6 The UoC shall only use non-therapeutants registered or approved by applicable legal requirements and shall apply them according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • When using non-therapeutants:
        • Verify product registration or approval (e.g. identify regulatory authorities, check official database, contact regulatory authorities in case of uncertainties, consult association, verify through manufacturers or suppliers, check for local regulations).
        • Review product labels and documentation. Approved products usually have specific registration numbers or approval statements that indicate their status.
        • Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure their effectiveness and safety.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Verification of product registration or approval.

      • Records:

        • The name and amount of the product;

        • The reason to use;

        • The dosage and administration instructions.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Adequate level of knowledge related to product registration or approval and cross-checking with use records.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.4.7 The UoC shall monitor all probiotics produced in-house for build-up of bacteria antimicrobial resistance.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Probiotics are living microbial cells that help improve the natural immunity level and positively impact animal growth and reproduction.
      • Probiotics are often used in aquaculture, agriculture or food products. If they harbour antimicrobial-resistant genes, these could transfer to harmful bacteria in humans, animals, or the environment, posing public health risks.
      • Bacteria in probiotics can share resistance genes with pathogenic bacteria through horizontal gene transfer, worsening the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) problem.
      • Registration and maintenance of detailed records of the source and strain of probiotics used are relevant to:
        • Safety assurance- preventing adverse effects that might arise from compromised or contaminated batches.
        • Resistance monitoring-probiotics can potentially develop resistance to antimicrobials, which could undermine their therapeutic benefits and lead to the emergence of resistant strains.
        • Public health protection- preventing the spread of antimicrobial-resistant strains is essential for safeguarding public health.
        • Regulatory compliance – maintaining the integrity and the quality of probiotic products.
        • Traceability – maintaining records ensures the ability to trace the origin of probiotic strains, which is essential for quality control and accountability. In addition, confirm that the strain being used matches the intended species or subspecies, preventing the use of unverified or potentially harmful strains.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records:

        • Source and strain of all probiotic batches;

        • The name and amount of the product;

        • The reason to use;

        • The dosage and administration instructions.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Adequate probiotic source and strain knowledge and cross-checking with use records.

      Useful Resources

      • Okeke, E.S., Chukwudozie, K.I., Nyaruaba, R., et al (2022) Antibiotic resistance in aquaculture and aquatic organisms: a review of current nanotechnology applications for sustainable management. Environmental Science and Pollution Research.

      4.4.8 The UoC shall monitor for antibiotic resistance by carrying out antibiotic sensitivity testing either:

      a)

      before or during each antibiotic treatment; or

      b)

      at regular intervals.

      Indicator applicability: every UoC using antibiotic treatments.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Awareness of the epidemiological situation at a regional level may be relevant.

      • It is recommended that antibiotic sensitivity testing is carried out prior to the start of any antibiotic treatment:

        • Test results should be used to assist the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional in selecting the most adequate antibiotic.

        • Test results should be combined with clinical and postmortem examinations of the animals.

        • Other laboratory tests should be considered if deemed appropriate. In acute cases, treatment might need to be initiated immediately to avoid animal suffering or the spread of infection. It is still advisable to collect samples immediately prior to the start of treatment:

        • The results can be used to validate the choice of antibiotic, epidemiological follow-up and future treatments.

      • In some cases, the relative lack of standardised and validated methods for culture and antimicrobial sensitivity testing for a significant number of bacterial species of aquatic importance might mean this is not possible.

        • In such cases, efforts should be placed towards developing alternative monitoring processes.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Health reports.

      • Testing results.

      • Revision and discussion of disease surveillance and monitoring programmes.

        • Especially for those bacterial infections where limited laboratory tests are available or where bacteria are fastidious and difficult to grow.
      • For recurring bacterial infections, the site should demonstrate efforts to isolate and characterise the problematic strains and test them periodically (at least on a cyclical basis) for antibiotic resistance.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Existence of health reports and testing results.
      • Disease surveillance and monitoring programmes.
      • Especially for those bacterial infectious where limited laboratory tests are available or where bacteria are fastidious and difficult to grow.
      • For recurring bacterial infections, the site should demonstrate efforts to isolate and characterise the problematic strains and test them periodically (at least on a cyclical basis) for antibiotic resistance.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.4.9 The UoC shall investigate the root cause when an antibiotic treatment does not produce the expected efficacy and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to improve the efficacy of subsequent treatments.

      Indicator applicability: every UoC using antibiotic treatments.

      4.4.11 The UoC shall investigate the root cause when an antiparasitic treatment does not produce the expected efficacy and shall implement appropriate corrective actions to improve the efficacy of subsequent treatments.

      Indicator applicability: every UoC using antiparasitic treatments except for marine salmonids in cages treated for sea lice.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Treatment failure:

        • Persistent symptoms or signs of diseases, or continued detection of the infectious agent causing the diseases being treated.

        • In many cases, is detected in the form of sustained mortality that does not decrease in response to treatment.

          • Possible causes are multiple and varied e.g.:

            • The development of resistance.

            • Low appetite in the case of in-feed medication.

            • Inadequate dosage.

            • Inaccurate diagnosis.

            • Inaccurate treatment selection

            • Inadequate distribution of medicated feed

      • The UoC should document treatment efficacy and changes to inform disease management, leading to better future treatments and early resistance detection.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Treatment efficacy records:
        • Plotting received actual dose versus effect (for example, in terms of parasite clearance).
        • Plotting mortality trends.
        • Taking samples and testing them for the pathogen of interest.
      • Employees should demonstrate adequate knowledge of the treatment plan.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Treatment plan and efficacy checks implemented:

      • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the plan with records, information from employee interviews and observations.

      Useful Resources

      • St-Hilaire, S., Price, D., Chalmers, W. H., & McClure, J. (2020) Understanding Antibiotic Treatment Failures in Salmon Aquaculture. Asian Fisheries Society.  
      • Responsible Use of Medicines In Agriculture Alliance (2010) Responsible Use of Anti-Parasitics In Aquaculture. RUMA Guidelines 30pp.

      4.4.10 The UoC shall monitor for antiparasitic resistance by carrying out bioassays6969An exemption applies where no methods exist to determine resistance using bioassays. either:

      a)

      before or during each antiparasitic treatment; or

      b)

      at regular intervals.

      Indicator scope: every UoC using antiparasitic treatments except for marine salmonids in grow-out cages.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • It is recommended that bioassays are carried out prior to the start of any antiparasitic treatment:

        • Test results should be used to assist the veterinarian or aquatic animal health professional in selecting the most adequate antiparasitic.

        • Test results should be combined with clinical and postmortem examinations of the animals.

      • Other laboratory tests should be considered if deemed appropriate.

        • Awareness of the epidemiological situation at a regional level may be relevant.

      • In acute cases, treatment might need to be started immediately to avoid animal suffering or the spread of infection. It is still advisable to collect samples immediately prior to the start of treatment:

        • The results can be used to validate the choice of antiparasitic, treatment, epidemiological follow-up and future treatments.

      • In some cases, the relative lack of standardised and validated methods for culture and testing for a significant number of parasite species of aquatic importance might mean this is not possible.

        • In such cases, efforts should be placed towards developing alternative monitoring processes.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Health reports.

      • Testing results.

      • Revision and discussion of disease surveillance and monitoring programmes.

        • Especially for those parasitic infectious where limited laboratory tests are available or where parasites are fastidious and difficult to grow.
      • For recurring parasitic infections, the site should demonstrate efforts to characterise and test them periodically (at least on a cyclical basis) for antiparasitic resistance.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Existence of health reports and testing results.

      • Disease surveillance and monitoring programmes.

        • Especially for those parasites where limited laboratory tests are available or where parasites are fastidious and difficult to grow.

        • For recurring parasitic infections, the site should demonstrate efforts to characterise and test them periodically (at least on a cyclical basis) for antibiotic resistance.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.4.12 The UoC shall not use7070Batches treated with antimicrobials listed as Critically Important Antimicrobials for Human Medicine are not eligible for ASC certification. antimicrobials listed as Critically Important Antimicrobials (CIA) for Human Medicine by the World Health Organisation (WHO)7171https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515528.

      An exception applies where the following can be demonstrated:

      a)

      all other available antimicrobials are not effective, or there is no availability of antimicrobials other than the CIA; and

      b)

      previous monitoring has not determined build-up of antimicrobial resistance.

      A registered veterinarian shall provide a written justification for the use of any CIA under the exceptional circumstances listed above.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • The use of CIA is not allowed unless they are the only possible treatment option and there is no indication of resistance.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • If CIA are used, the decision should be documented.

      • Specific registered veterinarian justification should be in place, including evidence that there is no resistance towards the selected CIA.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Veterinary considerations for the use of CIA and resistance testing.

      Useful Resources

      • Luthman, O., Robb, D.H.F., Henriksson, P.J.G., J∅rgensen, P.S. & Troell, M. (2024) Global overview of national regulations for antibiotic use in aquaculture production. Aquaculture International. 
      • Responsible Use of Medicines In Agriculture Alliance (2004) Responsible use of antimicrobials in fish production. RUMA Alliance Guidelines 21pp.

      4.4.13 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific limits on antibiotic7272Crustaceans treated with antibiotics are not eligible for ASC certification. treatments, according to Appendix 2 (2.5).

      4.4.14 The UoC shall adhere to species-specific limits on parasiticide treatments, according to Appendix 2 (2.5).

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.15 The UoC shall calculate the antibiotic load, following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.2).

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.16 The UoC shall reduce the antibiotic load over time and shall demonstrate measures being taken to achieve this reduction.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • When the UoC has a history of using antibiotics, they shall reduce the antibiotic load over time and shall demonstrate measures being taken to achieve this reduction.
      • Antibiotic load reduction is evaluated by comparing the last 6 years or cycles prior to the audit. For the first 6 audits, comparisons can be made with 1 to 5 years or cycles before the audit.
      • The target would be to decrease antibiotic use until a situation is reached where treatments are only sporadic. Sporadic means that treatments are not required every year or every production cycle. ASC emphasises the importance of improved prevention strategies and reduced dependency on antibiotics.
      • This approach reduces the risk of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a major concern and aligns with the ‘One Health’ framework, which recognises the interconnected health of humans, animals and the environment.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Prescriptions.

      • Antibiotic treatment records.

      • Antibiotic load calculations.

      • Actions or measures aimed to reduce antibiotic use.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Antibiotic treatments and accuracy of antibiotic load calculation:

        • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the treatment records and information from employee interviews and observations.

      Useful Resources

      • Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquauclure Science (2020) One Health Aquaculture – Marine Science. Blog 
      • Milijasevic M, Veskovic-Moracanin S, Babic Milijasevic J, Petrovic J, Nastasijevic I. (2024) Antimicrobial Resistance in Aquaculture: Risk Mitigation within the One Health Context. Foods.

      4.4.17 The UoC shall adhere to the withdrawal period defined by the country where the product is sold. An exception applies where a withdrawal period is not defined, in which case the UoC shall adhere to a minimum of 500 degree days.

      4.4.18 The UoC shall adhere to the Maximum Residue Limits (MRL) defined by the country where the product is sold. An exception applies where an MRL is not defined, in which case the UoC shall adhere to the limits set by the European Union.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • To make sure that products sold are below the indicated MRLs, the UoC should comply with the relevant withdrawal periods.

      • If there is no specific withdrawal period provided for therapeutants used, a minimum withdrawal period of 500 degree-days must be observed.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Prescriptions.

      • Treatment records.

      • Degree day of treated products at the time of harvest.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Treatments and withdrawal checks implemented:

      • Implementation can be confirmed by cross-checking the treatment records and information from employee interviews and observations.

      Useful Resources

      • Ranjan, A., Sahu, N.P., Gupta, S., & Aklakur, Md. (2017) Prospects of Medicated Feed in Aquaculture. Nutrition & Food Science.

      4.4.19 The UoC shall annually, or within a month of concluding a production cycle, publicly disclose per site:

      a)

      the use of any CIA, including the written justification for use under the exceptional circumstances listed in Indicator 4.4.12; and

      b)

      the antibiotic load calculated in Indicator 4.4.15.

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.4.20 The UoC shall report to ASC the antimicrobial related data, according to ASC data submission procedures.

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      Parasite Management (Sea Lice) 4.5

      Scope: Cage-culture marine Salmonids

      4.5.1 The UoC shall participate in an Area-Based Management (ABM) scheme following the method outlined in Appendix 13 (13.2).

      4.5.2 The UoC shall establish, review annually, and revise where needed, a maximum sea lice load for the entire ABM and for the individual site, following the method outlined in Appendix 13 (13.2).

      Scope: areas with native salmonids7373Within 75 kilometres of a wild salmonid migration route or habitat. This definition is expected to encompass all, or nearly all, of salmon-growing areas in the northern hemisphere.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Appendix 13 (13.2.1), states that if an ABM is a regulatory requirement in a jurisdiction and its definition of ‘area’ aligns with the considerations outlined in this section, sites may use that definition for the requirements in Criterion 4.5.
        • The Marine Scotland Management Areas7474Fish disease management areas: maps, Scottish Government. https://www.gov.scot/publications/fish-diseasemanagement-areas/. and the Agrupación de Concesiones de Salmónidos7575Servicio Nacional de Pesca y Acuicultura, SERNAPESCA. https://www.sernapesca.cl/normativas/agrupacion-deconcesiones-de-salmonidos/., set by SERNAPESCA in Chile, are examples of regulatory requirements where the definition of ‘area’ aligns with the considerations of Appendix 13 (13.2.1).
      • The shared ABM objectives for disease management, required by Appendix 13 (13.2.1), should be drafted and agreed upon by all participants within the ABM.
        • It is advisable to assign a focal point who will coordinate information, data sharing and the coordination required by this section.
          • The focal point should ideally be a rotating position, though determination is left to the discretion of the ABM.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records relating to the establishment of the ABM, including:
        • Definition of the area.
        • Participation in the ABM.
        • Required documentation.
        • Information and data sharing.
        • Coordination.
        • The definition of area by ABM regulatory requirements (if applicable).
      • Records relating to the establishment, review and revision of ABM sea lice load and on-site sea lice levels, including:
        • Documentation showing how the ABM protects native salmonids by interpreting sea lice data from native salmonids monitoring.
        • Final documented recommendation and justification for maintaining or revising maximum sea lice loads in the ABM and the on-site sea lice thresholds.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • ABM includes the required attributes of Appendix 13 (13.2.1).
        • The establishment, review and revision (if applicable) of an ABM sea lice load and on-site sea lice levels.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.3 The UoC shall demonstrate commitment to collaborating with NGOs, academics and regulators on areas of mutually agreed research to measure possible impacts of sea lice on native fish species, including native salmonids. The collaboration shall include as a minimum:

      a)

      provisions for sharing site-level data; and

      b)

      granting access to sites; and

      c)

      provision of other non-financial support.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • If a site does not receive any requests to collaborate on research, the site may demonstrate compliance by showing evidence of commitment through other proactive means.

        • Examples may include published policy statements or directed outreach to relevant organisations or stakeholders.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that demonstrate verification of how the site or Certificate Holder has communicated with external groups (NGOs, academics, regulators) to agree on and collaborate towards areas of research to measure the impacts of sea lice on native fish.

        • Records should include requests for research support and collaboration, and responses to those requests.

      • Records that demonstrate collaboration with NGOs, academics and regulators.

        • When a site or Certificate Holder denies a request to collaborate on research, there should be a written justification for rejecting the request.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Evidence that the site or Certificate Holder has communicated with external groups to agree on areas of research and is tracking and responding to research requests.

        • As applicable, a written justification rejecting proposals to confirm that denials were justified and there is no consistent pattern that indicates a lack of demonstrated commitment to collaborate on research.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.4 The UoC shall collect sea lice data on native salmonids, following the method outlined in Appendix 13 (13.3).

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • The collected sea lice data on native salmonids will inform the review and potential revision of the maximum sea lice load for the ABM and the corresponding sea lice levels at individual sites (see Indicator 4.5.2 and Appendix 13 (13.2.2).

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that verify:

        • The methodology used for collecting sea lice data on native salmonids complies with the requirements in Appendix 13 (13.3).

        • The site’s participation in collecting sea lice data on native salmonids.

        • The application of an exception as per Appendix 13 (13.3).

      Auditors should confirm:

      • The site’s participation in collecting sea lice data on native salmonids.

      • The rationale for any exception.

      • That the methodology used for collecting sea lice data on native salmonids complies with the requirements in Appendix 13 (13.3).

      • The information should be cross-checked with local regulations and records.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.5 The UoC shall publicly disclose sea lice data on native salmonids within 30 days of finalising the collection of the data.

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      No additional guidance is provided for this Indicator.

      4.5.6 The UoC shall conduct on-site sea lice sampling, following the method outlined Appendix 13 (13.4).

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • The following are examples of exceptions to the sampling frequency required by Appendix 13 (13.4) regarding environmental conditions that may affect fish welfare:

        • Water temperature (i.e. below 4oC).

        • Low oxygen.

        • Algal bloom.

        • Jellyfish event.

      • The person conducting on-site sea lice sampling should demonstrate competence and training.

        • Including competence and training in identifying sea lice species and stages.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that demonstrate:
        • On-site sea lice sampling complies with the requirements in Appendix 13 (13.4).

        • The application of an exception as per Appendix 13 (13.4).

        • The competence and training of the person conducting on-site sea lice sampling.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • On-site sea lice sampling complies with the requirements in Appendix 13 (13.4).

      • If practicable, auditors should observe sampling while on-site.

      • The rationale for any exception.

      • Competence and training of the person conducting on-site sea lice sampling.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.7 The UoC shall publicly disclose on-site sea lice levels per site. The disclosure shall:

      include data for L. salmonis for at least the stages required in Appendix 13 (13.4); and,

      include data for adult Caligus spp. for sites located on the west coast of Canada; and,

      a.

      be made publicly available within seven days after the last day of sampling; and,

      b.

      remain publicly available for the duration that the site is ASC certified.

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      4.5.8 The UoC shall report to ASC the on-site sea lice level, according to ASC data submission procedures.

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      No additional guidance is provided for these Indicators.

      4.5.9 The UoC shall, during sensitive periods, maintain on-site sea lice levels below the threshold outlined in Appendix 13 (13.5).

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      4.5.10 The UoC shall notify the CAB if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded (see Indicator 4.5.9). The notification shall be made by the next working day following the last day of sampling, according to ASC data submission procedures.

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      4.5.11 The UoC shall, if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded, (see Indicator 4.5.10) reduce on-site levels below the threshold within 21 days following the last day of sampling.

      If the reduction is not achieved within 21 days, the UoC shall submit a formal notification to the CAB for cancellation of certification by the next working day.

      Scope: areas with native salmonids

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • The following are examples of allowed reasons for delaying fish from being treated, thus affecting the site’s ability to reduce sea lice levels within the timeframe required by Indicator 4.5.11 (see exceptions to the timeframe for reducing sea lice levels in Appendix 13 (13.5):

        • Adverse environmental conditions:

          • Water temperature (i.e. below 4oC).

          • Low oxygen.

          • Algal bloom.

          • Jellyfish event.

        • Logistical considerations:

          • Strikes (trucks, cargo, freight, vessels, customs, etc.).

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that demonstrate:

        • On-site sea lice levels are below the threshold outlined in Appendix 13 (13.5) during sensitive periods (Indicator 4.5.9).

        • The site notified the CAB within the next working following the last day of sampling if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded (Indicator 4.5.10).

        • The application of an exception to the timeframe for reducing sea lice levels as per Appendix 13 (13.5) (Indicator 4.5.11).

        • The site’s process for notifying the CAB if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded (Indicator 4.5.10).

      Auditors should confirm:

      • On-site sea lice levels are below the threshold outlined in Appendix 13 (13.5) during sensitive periods (Indicator 4.5.9).

      • The site’s process for notifying the CAB if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded (Indicator 4.5.10).

      • That the site notified the CAB within the next working day following the last day of sampling if sea lice thresholds have been reached or exceeded (Indicator 4.5.10).

      • The rationale for any exception to the timeframe for reducing sea lice levels (Indicator 4.5.11).

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.12 The UoC shall demonstrate that the Weighted Number of Medicinal Treatments (WNMT) for sea lice is at or below the Entry Level (EL) per site, following the method outlined in Appendix 13 (13.6).

      4.5.13 The UoC shall reduce the WNMT for sea lice by 25% every production cycle until the WNMT is at or below the Global Level (GL) per site, following the method outlined in Appendix 13 (13.6).

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • By requiring sites to continuously reduce the number of medicinal treatments applied in treating sea lice, the indicators aim to incentivise the development and implementation of non-medicinal treatments (e.g. biological and mechanical control).
        • The ultimate vision is to no longer have to treat sea lice with medicinal treatments.
      • The calculation of the WNMT should be made and updated on an ongoing basis throughout the production cycle.
      • Some examples of how to count the WNMT are given below:
        • Treating an entire site (all cages) once, counts as WNMT = 1.
        • Treating 1 cage, out of 10, once, count as WNMT = 0.1.
        • Treating 1 cage, out of 10, twice (i.e. two unique treatments), count as WNMT = 0.2.
        • Treating 1 cage, out of 10, once as a ‘coupled treatment7676A ‘coupled treatment’ is defined as a bath treatment applied in two treatment events (i.e. one treatment at t1 and a follow-up treatment at t2). Each treatment (t1 and t2) shall be included in the calculation of the WNMT.‘, count as WNMT = 0.2.
        • Treating 5 cages, out of 20, once, count as WNMT = 0.25.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that demonstrate:

        • Medicinal parasiticide treatments, including the number of cages
          treated from the total number of cages in use.

        • The WNMT calculation.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • WNMT calculation is conducted as per the requirements in Appendix 13 (13.6).

        • WNMT results should be cross-checked with medicinal parasiticide treatment records.

      • WNMT conform with the Entry Level (EL), the 25% reduction or the Global Level (GL), as applicable.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.14 The UoC shall, when two consecutive applications of a sea lice treatment per site have not produced the expected efficacy, carry out a bioassay to determine resistance.

      4.5.15 The UoC shall, when bioassays determine resistance, apply an alternative sea lice treatment or immediately harvest all fish at the site.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Expected efficacy will vary depending on the health condition of the fish and type of medicinal treatment.
        • Therefore, the site will need to review the pre- and post-treatment sea lice levels to understand and evaluate the efficacy of treatment.
          • Example: sea lice treatment with emamectin benzoate.
            • A typical baseline for the effectiveness of emamectin benzoate is a minimum of 90% reduction in the abundance of sea lice on the farmed fish.
            • To determine whether an emamectin benzoate treatment has produced the expected efficacy, the percent reduction between pre-and post-treatment sea lice levels should be calculated.
            • If the calculated percent reduction in sea lice is <90%, then the treatment did not produce the expected efficacy, and a bioassay shall be carried out to determine whether sea lice have developed resistance.
      • The person conducting bioassays should demonstrate competence, experience and training.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Records that demonstrate:

        • for cases where the site uses two consecutive applications of a sea lice treatment.

          • The observed efficacy of treatment against the expected efficacy of treatment.

        • Calculated percent reduction in sea lice levels between pre- and -post treatment.

        • The bioassay results for every case where two consecutive applications of a sea lice treatment have not produced the expected efficacy.

        • Alternative sea lice treatment or records to confirm harvest of all fish at the site when bioassays determine resistance.

        • Competence, experience and training of the person conducting the bioassay.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Medicinal parasiticide treatments.

        • With a focus on cases where the site uses two consecutive applications of a sea lice treatment.

      • Pre-and post-treatment calculated percent reduction in sea lice levels.

      • Bioassay result for every case where two consecutive applications of a sea lice treatment have not produced the expected efficacy.

      • Alternative sea lice treatment or harvest of all fish at the site when bioassays determine resistance.

      • Competence, experience and training of the person conducting the bioassay.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.16 The UoC shall apply treatment rotation where more than one effective sea lice treatment is available. Every third treatment shall belong to a different family of drugs.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • A single treatment is considered to have taken place when the majority of a site (i.e. more than half of all cages) is treated.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • List of effective sea lice medicinal treatments available.

        • Including rationale for the non-inclusion of other available sea lice medicinal treatments.

      • Records that demonstrate medicinal parasiticide treatments.

      • If applicable, records shall demonstrate that every third treatment belongs to a different family of drugs.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Effective sea lice medicinal treatments available.

      • Medicinal parasiticide treatments.

      • If applicable, whether every third treatment belongs to a different family of drugs.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.17 The UoC shall develop, implement and maintain a site-specific Integrated Parasite Management Plan (IPMP) with the intent of controlling sea lice using multiple prevention and control strategies. The IPMP shall:

      a)

      consider non-therapeutic treatments; and,

      b)

      be approved by a registered veterinarian; and,

      be periodically reviewed and revised as necessary.

      How do I interpret this requirement?

      • Effective integrated parasite management:

        • Is essential for robust sea lice control.

        • Involves:

          • The use of various techniques and strategies primarily aimed at slowing the development of resistance.

          • The coordinated application and integration of all available management practices to control sea lice.

      • The Integrated Parasite Management Plan (IPMP) should:

        • Emphasise the importance of surveillance, communication, and cooperation among sites within a defined area (see Indicators 4.5.1 and 4.5.2).

        • Be reviewed and updated, if necessary, on a production cycle basis.

      Evidence of implementation should be maintained, e.g.:

      • Documented IPMP, which conforms with Indicator 4.5.17.

      • Rationale for setting the frequency of revisions of the IPMP.

      Auditors should confirm:

      • Documented IPMP, which conforms with Indicator 4.5.17.

      • The revision process of the IPMP.

        • Including the rationale for the frequency of its revisions.

      Useful Resources

      N/A

      4.5.18 The UoC shall calculate and report to ASC parasiticide load for each agent over the production cycle, according to ASC data submission procedures, and following the method outlined in Appendix 12 (12.5.3).

      4.5.19 The UoC shall publicly disclose:

      a.

      the Weighted Number of Medicinal Treatments (WNMT) for each production cycle per site; and

      b.

      parasiticide load for each agent over the production cycle per site.

      4.5.20 The UoC shall publicly disclose the Integrated Parasite Management Plan (IPMP) per site.

      No additional guidance is provided for these Indicators.
